explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of intense ear pain, otorrhea unresponsive to antibiotics, granulation tissue in the ear canal, and facial nerve paralysis strongly suggests malignant otitis externa (MOE). MOE is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external ear and skull base, primarily caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It is most commonly seen in elderly patients, diabetics, or immunocompromised individuals. Facial nerve paralysis indicates advanced disease with cranial nerve involvement.

Malignant (Necrotizing) Otitis Externa (MOE)

  • Inflammatory condition caused by Pseudomonas infection.
  • Commonly affects elderly diabetic patients or those on immunosuppressive therapy.
  • Severe ear pain, granulations in the ear canal, and facial paralysis are common symptoms.
  • Infection can spread to the skull base, jugular foramen, and cause multiple cranial nerve palsies.

[[figure-1]]

Etiopathogenesis:

  • Early presentation mimics diffuse otitis externa but with intense pain.
  • Granulations in the ear canal indicate disease progression.
  • Infection can extend:
    • Anteriorly to the temporomandibular fossa.
    • Posteriorly to the mastoid.
    • Medially into the middle ear and petrous bone.

Investigations:

  • Clinical suspicion based on severe otalgia and granulation tissue in elderly diabetics.
  • Imaging:
    • CT scan/MRI: Shows bone destruction and soft tissue involvement.
    • Gallium-67 scan: Indicates soft tissue infection; useful for diagnosis and follow-up.
    • Technetium-99 bone scan: Detects bone infection but not useful for disease monitoring due to prolonged positivity.

Treatment:

  • Control of diabetes: Essential for management.
  • Ear canal toilet: Clean the ear, remove discharge, debris, and granulations.
  • Antibiotics:
    • IV Gentamicin with Ticarcillin (both ototoxic/nephrotoxic).
    • Third-generation cephalosporins (e.g., Ceftriaxone or Ceftazidime), combined with an aminoglycoside.
    • Quinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin 750 mg orally) can be combined with Rifampin.
    • Antibiotic therapy typically lasts 6-8 weeks or longer.
  • Culture and sensitivity of ear discharge to adjust antibiotics if non-responsive to treatment.
  • Prolonged antibiotic treatment has largely replaced the need for radical surgery.

Incorrect Options:

Otomycosis (Option A): Otomycosis is a fungal infection of the external ear, typically presenting with itching, mild discomfort, and discharge. It does not cause severe pain, granulation tissue, or cranial nerve involvement, as seen in this case.

Serous otitis media (Option B): Serous otitis media involves non-infectious fluid accumulation in the middle ear, often following an upper respiratory infection or eustachian tube dysfunction. It does not present with otorrhea, granulation tissue, or facial nerve paralysis.

Eczematous otitis externa (Option D): Eczematous otitis externa is an inflammatory condition of the external ear, associated with itching, scaling, and mild discomfort. It does not cause granulation tissue, severe pain, or cranial nerve paralysis.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery 8th edition, Page 61

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • For a child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) who has not experienced improvement with hearing aids, a cochlear implant is the next appropriate step. A cochlear implant bypasses the damaged parts of the cochlea and directly stimulates the auditory nerve, enabling hearing in individuals with severe-to-profound SNHL who derive limited or no benefit from conventional hearing aids.
  • Cochlear implantation is recommended in cases where:
    • Hearing aids provide insufficient benefit.
    • The patient has severe-to-profound SNHL as confirmed by audiological assessments.
    • Speech and language development is at risk due to hearing impairment (especially in children).

Indications:

  • B/L severe (70-90 dB) to profound (>90 dB) SNHL
  • Prelingual deafness: A child who is born deaf and has not yet developed speech.
  • Post lingual deafness: Child/adult who has become deaf but has already developed speech.

Contraindications:

  • Cochlear aplasia
  • 8th nerve abnormality (like aplasia or retrocochlear pathology, conduction via the auditory nerve is dysfunctional)
  • Central auditory lesions
  • Michel aplasia: Complete absence of the bony and membranous labyrinth, including the petrous apex, while the external and middle ears remain unaffected.

Prerequisites:

  • Age in prelingual deafness: Minimum age as early as possible, maximum age 7 years
  • There is no age limit for post-lingual deafness
  • Failed trial of hearing aid
  • Intact acoustic nerve and central hearing tract

Incorrect Options:

Bone-anchored hearing aid (Option A): This is suitable for patients with conductive or mixed hearing loss, or those with anatomical issues preventing the use of regular hearing aids (e.g., chronic otitis media, atresia). It is not appropriate for severe-to-profound SNHL.

Tympanoplasty (Option B): Tympanoplasty is a surgical procedure to repair the tympanic membrane or middle ear structures and is used in conductive hearing loss, not in sensorineural hearing loss.

Normal hearing aid (Option C): The child has already tried hearing aids without improvement. Recommending a different hearing aid would not be beneficial in cases of severe-to-profound SNHL.



Reference:
  1. Cochlear Implants - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
  2. Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery 8th edition, Page 135, 146

This flat-shaped tympanogram suggests that the middle ear is filled with fluid, preventing the eardrum from moving normally in response to changes in air pressure. It is one of the most common findings in middle ear effusion.

Otosclerosis (Option B): Otosclerosis is associated with stapes fixation and reduced middle ear compliance. It results in an As tympanogram (shallow curve) due to reduced mobility of the ossicular chain, not a flat B curve.

Normal ear (Option D): A normal ear produces a type A tympanogram, indicating normal compliance and middle ear pressure.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely explanation for this scenario is that, after initial inner ear involvement (possible labyrinthine fistula or perilymphatic fistula), progressive damage (possibly sensorineural deafness due to labyrinthitis or complete loss of function) has occurred.
  • Rinne’s test would likely show a "false negative" result
  • The Rinne test compares bone conduction (BC) to air conduction (AC) of sound. In conductive hearing loss, BC > AC (i.e., the sound is heard better through bone conduction). In sensorineural hearing loss, AC > BC (i.e., the sound is heard better through air conduction).

  • In severe sensorineural hearing loss, the patient cannot hear either air or bone conduction. So Rinne’s test appears negative (bone > air), mimicking a conductive loss, even though it’s actually profound sensorineural loss.

  • The fistula test, now negative, suggests no more labyrinthine response; severe sensorineural loss is present.

True Positive (Option A): A true positive result would suggest that air conduction is better than bone conduction in the ear with hearing loss, which is inconsistent with the clinical picture of worsening hearing loss and a likely sensorineural component.

True Negative (Option B): A true negative would indicate that the patient has normal hearing, which does not match the patient's reported symptoms of hearing loss and worsening condition.

False Positive (Option C): A false positive Rinne is not typically described; if used, it would imply that the test appears positive (AC > BC) despite the presence of a conductive component — which does not apply here.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page 26

Periorbital hematoma (Option B) is incorrect because periorbital hematoma, also known as "raccoon eyes," refers to bruising around the eyes, which is a sign of trauma to the face or base of the skull, but it is not Battle's sign.

Bezold abscess (Option C) is incorrect because a Bezold abscess is a collection of pus in the neck, often caused by a middle ear infection, and does not relate to the bruising over the mastoid.

Perichondritis (Option D) is incorrect because perichondritis refers to inflammation of the cartilage of the ear, typically caused by infection, but it does not involve bruising behind the ear.

explanationHtml:
• A perilymphatic fistula (PLF) refers to an abnormal communication between the middle ear and the fluid-filled spaces of the inner ear, known as the cochlea and vestibular system.
  • It can occur as a result of trauma, such as barotrauma or previous ear surgery.
  • The main symptoms associated with a PLF include vertigo (dizziness), tinnitus (ringing in the ears), and sensorineural hearing loss.

Features of Perilymph Fistula:

Feature

Description

Etiology

Can occur after head trauma, barotrauma (e.g., diving), temporal bone anomalies, or ear surgery (e.g., stapedectomy).

Symptoms

Fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus, and sometimes a sense of fullness in the ear.

Complications

Recurrent meningitis (especially in children with temporal bone defects), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak.

Diagnosis

Often clinical, based on history and symptoms; confirmed through surgical exploration if suspected.

Temporal bone CT: Shows pneumolabyrinth, accumulation of fluid in the middle ear, and/or ossicular chain disruption, but also can often be normal.

Treatment

Surgical closure of the fistula to prevent further complications, such as meningitis; limited improvement in hearing.

Prognosis

Hearing improvement post-surgery is usually limited; however, vertigo symptoms often improve or resolve.

Labyrinthitis (Option B): Labyrinthitis is an inflammation of the labyrinth. It is often caused by a viral or bacterial. infection. The main symptoms of labyrinthitis include vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss, and ear fullness. However, in this case, the patient's history of surgery and the absence of infection-related symptoms make labyrinthitis less likely.

Paget disease (Option C): Paget's disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by abnormal bone remodeling. It typically affects older individuals and can involve various bones, including the skull. While Paget's disease can cause hearing loss and other symptoms, the presence of vertigo, tinnitus, and head tilt, in this case, make it an unlikely diagnosis.

Vestibular schwannoma (Option D): Vestibular schwannoma, also known as acoustic neuroma, is a benign tumor that arises from the Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve in the inner ear. It typically presents with symptoms such as unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance. However, the absence of significant hearing loss and the recent surgery suggest that vestibular schwannoma is less likely in this case.

  2. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery 8th Edition, Chapter 20: Balance Disorders In Children, Pg 225

question: What would be your diagnosis for a patient who has presented with symptoms of vertigo, tinnitus, and fullness of ears. The symptoms improve on keeping the right ear up. He had previously been operated on for a safe type of right side chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) six months ago?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Schwannoma, also known as neurilemmomas, are benign nerve sheath tumors that arise from Schwann cells, which are the cells responsible for producing the myelin sheath that covers peripheral nerves. Histologically, the following findings are characteristic of Schwannoma.

Vestibular Schwannoma:

Description
  • Origin: Schwann cells; Site: CP angle

Pathology
  • Antoni A areas: These areas are composed of tightly packed spindle-shaped cells with elongated nuclei. The cells are arranged in palisades or whorls, forming Verocay bodies. The cells in Antoni A areas exhibit nuclear hyperchromasia (increased staining intensity) and cellular cohesion.
  • Antoni B areas: These areas are less cellular and show a looser arrangement of cells with a myxoid or microcystic appearance. The cells in Antoni B areas may have more irregular nuclei and a less distinct cytoplasmic organization compared to Antoni A areas.

Clinical presentation
  • 40-60 years, Males = Females
  • Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss associated with tinnitus

Radiology
  • Investigation of choice/Gold standard: MRI with Gadolinium contrast - ice cream cone appearance seen on CP angle.

[[figure-1]]
  • Other investigations:
    • CT (with/without contrast): done when MRI is not feasible
    • Vertebral Angiography: though helps in localizing the tumor, it is not the investigation of choice.

Association
  • Neurofibromatosis type-2 (NF-2): Presents with bilateral Schwannomas and other tumors like Meningioma, ependymoma may also be associated.

Differential diagnoses

CP angle meningioma:

  • MRI: Dural tail sign seen

[[figure-2]]

Glomus tumor: (Glomus jugulare)

  • Arises from the dome of Jugular bulb within the jugular fossa.
  • CT: Phelp sign (Bony erosion seen between carotid canal and jugular fossa)

[[figure-3]]

Incorrect Options:

Neurofibromas (Option A): These are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors that arise from Schwann cells, fibroblasts, and other supporting cells. Histologically, neurofibromas typically show a mixture of cellular and myxoid areas. They are composed of a combination of Schwann cells, fibroblasts, and perineurial-like cells.

Leiomyoma (Option C): Leiomyomas are benign tumors that arise from smooth muscle cells. Histologically, leiomyomas exhibit bundles of spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells with elongated nuclei arranged in a swirling pattern. Immunohistochemical staining for smooth muscle actin and desmin is positive in leiomyomas.

Rhabdomyoma (Option D): Rhabdomyomas are rare benign tumors that arise from skeletal muscle cells. They are most commonly seen in the heart (cardiac rhabdomyomas) and are often associated with tuberous sclerosis. Histologically, rhabdomyomas show sheets or clusters of polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. The cells may have cross-striations, which are characteristic of skeletal muscle differentiation. Immunohistochemical staining for desmin and myogenin is positive in rhabdomyomas.



Reference:
  1. Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology 7th edition pages- 1607-1609.
  2. Diseases of ENT and Head & Neck surgery by PL Dhingra pages- 128,132-134

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In a patient with bilateral external auditory atresia we use hearing devices. The first image shows such device known as BAHA. BAHA stands for Bone Anchored Hearing Aid.
  • Bone-anchored hearing aid (BAHA) captures the sound and transmits vibrations to the skull, stimulating the cochlea directly and bypassing the external auditory canal and middle ear. It is used when the air conduction method of rehabilitation cannot be used.

Components:

  • Titanium Fixture: Surgically embedded in the skull. It bonds with the surrounding skin (osseointegration)
  • Titanium Abutment: Connects the sound processor.
  • Sound Processor: Attached after osseointegration (2 to 6 months after implantation).

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Indication:

  • Chronic ear discharge.
  • Single-sided hearing loss.
  • Children with microtia, anotia, canal atresia.
  • Conductive or mixed hearing loss (e.g., otosclerosis, tympanosclerosis) with contraindications for surgery.
  • Following MRM (large mastoid cavity).
  • Excessive feedback or discomfort from AC hearing aids.
  • Age of implantation: >5yrs

Surgical Procedure:

  • Adults typically have a single-stage surgery with a 3-month osseointegration wait.
  • Children usually undergo a two-stage procedure, with the fixture placed first and the abutment connected after 6 months.

Incorrect Options:

The second image shows a cochlear implant (Option B): A cochlear implant is a medical device that is used to restore hearing in individuals with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss. Unlike traditional hearing aids, which amplify sound, cochlear implants bypass the damaged parts of the inner ear (cochlea) and directly stimulate the auditory nerve to provide a sense of sound.

The Platinum K piston is a type of middle ear prosthesis (Option C): The Platinum K piston is designed to replace or bypass the damaged or malfunctioning ossicles in the middle ear, specifically the incus. The piston is attached to the incus on one end and to the tympanic membrane on the other end.

Ossicular prosthesis (Option D): Also known as middle ear prosthesis or ossicular replacement prosthesis, is a device used in otologic surgery to restore or improve hearing in patients with middle ear conditions that affect the function of the ossicles. The ossicles are the three small bones in the middle ear: the malleus, incus, and stapes.

Explanation:

  • Dix-Hallpike maneuver: The Dix-Hallpike maneuver is used to diagnose benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), a common cause of vertigo.
  • It involves rapidly moving the patient from a sitting position to a supine position with their head turned to one side, and then observing for signs of nystagmus (involuntary eye movement).
  • BPPV typically presents with vertigo triggered by head movement but no hearing loss, making this maneuver the correct diagnostic tool for such cases.

Dix-Hallpike Maneuver:

  • The Dix-Hallpike maneuver is specifically used to diagnose BPPV, where tiny calcium crystals (canaliths) become dislodged and move into the semicircular canals of the inner ear. This leads to episodes of vertigo.
  • The maneuver helps to provoke the vertigo and nystagmus by positioning the patient's head in a way that stimulates the affected semicircular canal, aiding in diagnosis.

Incorrect Options:

Yacovino maneuver (Option A): is incorrect because it is not a standard diagnostic maneuver for vertigo. The Yacovino maneuver is typically used to test for peripheral vestibular dysfunction.

Epley’s maneuver (Option C): is incorrect because while Epley’s maneuver is used for treating BPPV, it is not used for diagnosis. It helps reposition the canaliths to alleviate the vertigo.

Simon's maneuver (Option D): is incorrect as it is not commonly used for vertigo diagnosis. It is a historical maneuver that was more relevant in older diagnostic practices.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The accurate order for the auditory pathway is as follows:

  1. Cochlear Nucleus (B): The first structure where auditory information from the cochlea synapses. It is located in the brainstem.
  2. Superior Olivary Nucleus (A): After the cochlear nucleus, the auditory information is relayed to the superior olivary nucleus, which is involved in sound localization and the processing of binaural auditory signals.
  3. Lateral Lemniscus (D): The lateral lemniscus transmits auditory signals from both the superior olivary nucleus and the cochlear nucleus to higher brainstem centers.
  4. Inferior Colliculi (C): Located in the midbrain, the inferior colliculi are involved in auditory processing and reflexes.
  5. Medial Geniculate Ganglion (E): The final relay station in the thalamus before auditory signals reach the auditory cortex for perception.

Auditory Pathway:

  • The auditory system processes sound information starting from the cochlea.
  • The cochlear nucleus receives the initial signal, which is then sent to the superior olivary nucleus for sound localization.
  • The signal then travels via the lateral lemniscus to the inferior colliculi for further processing, followed by the medial geniculate ganglion in the thalamus before reaching the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

ABCDE (Option A): This order is incorrect because lateral lemniscus comes after the superior olivary nucleus and should not be placed before it.

BACDE (Option C): Incorrect because the inferior colliculi should come before the medial geniculate ganglion, not after it.

BAEDC (Option D): Incorrect as the medial geniculate ganglion should not come before the inferior colliculi.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat - PL Dhingra - 8th Edition • Page no: 17

Objective Hearing Tests

  • BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) : An objective neurological test measuring the brainstem's response to sound. It does not require patient participation and is valuable for infants and uncooperative adults.
  • OAE (Otoacoustic Emission) : An objective test that evaluates cochlear (specifically outer hair cell) function. Used widely in newborn and infant screening, as it does not need active patient response.
  • Tympanometry : Also an objective test, tympanometry measures eardrum movement in response to pressure changes and helps assess middle ear function.

Subjective Hearing Test

  • PTA (Pure Tone Audiometry): This is a subjective test requiring the patient to respond when they hear tones. It is the gold standard for assessing hearing thresholds, but it depends on patient cooperation.

Meniere’s Disease

Feature

Description

Cause

Excess endolymph accumulation (endolymphatic hydrops)

Triad of Symptoms

1. Vertigo (episodic, lasts minutes to hours)

Dietary modifications (low sodium), diuretics, vestibular suppressants, intratympanic steroids, and surgery in refractory cases

Acute mastoiditis is characterized by:

  • Reservoir sign: It refers to the collection of fluid or pus in the mastoid air cells, which can be visualized during otoscopy or imaging.
  • Mastoid tenderness: This is a key clinical sign of acute mastoiditis, where the patient experiences pain and tenderness over the mastoid process due to inflammation.

Acute Mastoiditis:

  • Acute mastoiditis is an infection of the mastoid bone, typically following an untreated or inadequately treated middle ear infection (acute otitis media).
  • It involves the inflammation of the mastoid air cells, which can lead to symptoms like:
    • Pain and tenderness over the mastoid process
    • Swelling behind the ear
    • Fever and irritability in children
  • It can be diagnosed through clinical examination (looking for the reservoir sign and mastoid tenderness) and imaging like CT scans.
  • If left untreated, it can lead to severe complications like hearing loss, intracranial infections, and abscess formation.

Incorrect Options:

Otosclerotic lesion (Option A): is incorrect because otosclerosis is a bone condition affecting the stapes in the middle ear, and it does not cause mastoid tenderness or a reservoir sign.

Intratympanic glomus tumor (Option C): is incorrect because glomus tumors, though they can cause ear symptoms, do not cause mastoid tenderness or reservoir sign. These tumors are typically vascular and are located in the middle ear or jugular bulb.

Chronic suppurative otitis media (Option D): is incorrect because while chronic otitis media may have purulent discharge, it does not typically present with mastoid tenderness or the reservoir sign unless there's a complication such as cholesteatoma or a coexisting acute mastoiditis.

Lateral Sinus Thrombosis:
Lateral sinus thrombosis is a rare but serious condition that can result from the spread of infection from the middle ear or mastoid to the lateral sinus. It is characterized by:

Brain Abscess (Option C) is incorrect because a brain abscess would present with neurological symptoms, such as focal deficits or altered consciousness, and would not typically show the empty delta sign on CT.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) is a non-invasive diagnostic test that measures the auditory pathways' response to sound stimulation.

  • It is primarily used to assess the sensorineural hearing loss, as it evaluates the function of the auditory nerve and brainstem.

  • BERA is particularly helpful in diagnosing hearing loss in infants, young children, and patients who are unable to cooperate with standard hearing tests.

BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry):

  • Procedure: During BERA, electrodes are placed on the scalp, and sound stimuli are presented through headphones. The electrical response generated by the brainstem in reaction to the sound is recorded and analyzed.

  • Uses: It is primarily used to assess the function of the auditory pathway up to the brainstem, particularly to detect sensorineural hearing loss, and can help in identifying conditions like auditory neuropathy or brainstem lesions.

Incorrect Options:

It is an invasive procedure (Option B): is incorrect because BERA is non-invasive. It does not require any surgical intervention or insertion of instruments inside the body.

It can be used for screening for hearing loss (Option A): While BERA can aid in diagnosing hearing loss, it is not commonly used for general screening in routine practice. It is more useful for confirming and assessing hearing loss, particularly sensorineural types, in specific cases (e.g., infants, patients who cannot cooperate with standard tests).

It is a subjective investigation (Option D): is incorrect because BERA is objective, as it records the brainstem's electrical response to sound stimuli, which is an automated and measurable process, not dependent on patient feedback or subjective interpretation.

Correct Option: B) Serous otitis media

  • Based on the otoscopy finding of a retracted and opaque tympanic membrane with fluid visible behind it, the foremost likely diagnosis is serous otitis media.

Serous Otitis Media (SOM):

Category

Details

Symptoms
  • Hearing Loss: Conductive, mild to moderate (20-40 dB), gradual onset, may fluctuate; children may not complain, but parents may notice difficulties in hearing.
  • Delayed/Defective Speech
  • Mild Earaches
  • Fullness in Ear.

Signs

  • Tympanic Membrane Appearance: Dull, opaque, possibly yellow, grey, or bluish; absence of the usual light reflex.
  • Visible Fluid/Bubbles: Air-fluid levels or bubbles visible behind the eardrum.
  • Retracted Tympanic Membrane: Negative middle ear pressure causing eardrum retraction, with the malleus handle appearing shortened or horizontal.
  • Reduced Tympanic Membrane Mobility.

Diagnostic Tests for SOM:

Test

Description

Rinne Test
  • In conductive hearing loss (SOM), bone conduction is better than air conduction (negative Rinne test).

Weber Test
  • In conductive hearing loss (SOM), the sound is louder in the affected ear when the tuning fork is placed on the forehead.

Absolute Bone Conduction (ABC) Test
  • Both patient and examiner hear the tuning fork for a similar duration when placed on the mastoid bone (ear canals plugged) in conductive hearing loss (SOM). (Bone conduction not impaired)

Schwabach's Test
  • In conductive hearing loss (SOM), the patient hears the tuning fork for a longer duration than the examiner when placed on the mastoid bone (ear canals not plugged).

Pneumatic Otoscopy
  • Visualizes eardrum movement with air pressure changes; reduced/absent movement indicates fluid presence.

Impedance audiometry
  • Measures eardrum movement; typically shows a flat/dome-shaped curve with negative pressure, indicating reduced compliance.

Audiometry
  • Conductive hearing loss (20-40 dB).
  • Sometimes, associated sensorineural hearing loss (d/t fluid on the round window membrane.

X-ray/CT Scan of Temporal Bone
  • May show mastoid air cell clouding due to fluid

Myringitis bullosa (Option A):

  • In any case, the otoscopy finding within the given scenario does not describe to have any blisters or erythema.

Acute otitis media (Option C):

Pneumo tympanum (Option D):

  • The otoscopy finding within the given scenario does not describe any bulging or increased air space within the middle ear.

question: Which nerve is most likely to be affected in a patient who complains of an inability to close the eye, drooling of saliva, and deviation of the angle of the mouth?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: B) Stria vascularis

The basilar membrane lies inside the cochlea and plays a crucial role in detecting sound frequency. In a 70-year-old patient with high-frequency hearing loss, the basal turn of the cochlea (closest to the oval window) is typically affected. The stria vascularis, located on the lateral wall of the cochlear duct, is closely associated with the basilar membrane, both anatomically and functionally.

  • The basilar membrane is responsible for tonotopic mapping of sound frequencies in the cochlea.

  • The stria vascularis lies directly adjacent to the basilar membrane, on the lateral wall of the scala media.

  • It produces endolymph and maintains the ionic composition required for hair cell function.

  • Hearing loss in higher frequencies is typically due to damage near the base of the cochlea, where the stria vascularis and basilar membrane are closely related.

Modiolus (Option A): The central bony core of the cochlea; provides structural support but is not adjacent to the basilar membrane.

Oval window (Option C): Located at the base of the cochlea, where the stapes footplate transmits vibrations to the scala vestibuli. While functionally related, it is not close or parallel to the basilar membrane.

Helicotrema (Option D): A small opening at the apex of the cochlea that connects the scala vestibuli and scala tympani; far from the basilar membrane’s primary region of involvement in high-frequency hearing loss.



Reference:

Diseases of the Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page no: 98

Correct Option A. - Schwannoma:

Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical features and the histopathological findings, the most likely diagnosis is Schwannoma (also known as vestibular schwannoma/ acoustic neuroma).
  • The patient presents with progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and unsteadiness, which strongly suggest involvement of vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). MRI shows a CPA (cerebellopontine angle) mass, which is the most common location for vestibular schwannomas.

Histopathology typically shows:

  • Antoni A areas: densely packed spindle cells arranged in palisades (Verocay bodies).
  • Antoni B areas: loosely arranged cells in a myxoid background.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Ependymomas are tumors arising from the ependymal lining of the ventricles or central canal of the spinal cord. They do not present in the CPA and are more commonly intraventricular or intraspinal. Histology shows perivascular pseudorosettes, not Antoni patterns.

Option C - Meningiomas can occur in the CPA but are extra-axial, dural-based tumors. On histology, they show whorled patterns, psammoma bodies, and syncytial cells, not Antoni A/B areas.

Option D - Neurofibromas also arise from Schwann cells but are non-encapsulated, infiltrative tumors involving multiple nerve fascicles. Histology lacks Verocay bodies and the distinct Antoni A/B areas. They are more diffuse than the well-circumscribed schwannoma.
question:
A 45-year-old female presents with a 2-year history of progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and unsteadiness. An MRI scan reveals a well-defined tumor located in the cerebellopontine angle (CPA). A surgical resection is performed, and subsequent histopathological examination of the tumor tissue is given below.

Based on these histopathological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Inner hair cells of the basal turn
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical picture describes age-related, symmetric, slowly progressive sensorineural hearing loss, which is characteristic of presbycusis.

The basal turn of the cochlea is responsible for detecting high-frequency sounds.
In presbycusis, there is degeneration of inner hair cells—primarily at the basal (proximal) turn of the cochlea—resulting in:

  • Loss of high-frequency hearing (first and most prominent)
  • Difficulty understanding consonants (e.g., “s”, “t”, “k”, “f”)
  • Poor speech discrimination, especially in noisy environments

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Striae vascularis (Option A): Atrophy of the striae vascularis causes strial/metabolic presbycusis, which mainly affects endolymph production and overall cochlear metabolism, resulting in flat hearing loss across all frequencies.

[[figure-2]]

Major stria vascularis cell types (marginal (MC), intermediate (IC) and basal (BC) cells) are colored as red, green and blue, respectively.

Tectorial membrane (Option B): Damage to the tectorial membrane may affect mechanical transduction between stereocilia and the organ of Corti, but it is not the characteristic pathology of age-related high-frequency hearing loss; it more commonly affects sound amplification and tuning.

Outer hair cells of the apical turn (Option D): The apical turn detects low-frequency sounds, and its outer hair cells contribute to sound amplification. Damage here would cause low-frequency hearing loss.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 19.

question: A 60-year-old man presents with gradual, progressive hearing loss. On examination, he has difficulty perceiving high-frequency sounds, but the other findings are normal. Which structure is primarily affected in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) requires the patient to actively respond (e.g., by raising a finger or pressing a button) when they hear a sound. Infants cannot give reliable behavioral responses, so PTA cannot be used in hearing assessment until about 5–6 years of age when the child can understand and follow instructions.

Incorrect Options:

OAE (Option A): Measures echoes generated by outer hair cells of the cochlea when a sound stimulus is given. It is for detecting cochlear (outer hair cell) dysfunction.

BERA (Option B): An electrophysiological test that records electrical activity along the auditory pathway up to the brainstem, which can be performed in newborns, infants, and even during natural sleep. It can determine the hearing threshold, site of lesion (cochlear vs. retrocochlear), and the degree of hearing loss. It is often done when OAE fails or when neurogenic hearing loss is suspected.

Free field audiometry (Option D): A behavioural audiometry technique, done in older infants (~6 months-2 years). The infant is placed in a sound-treated room and sounds of different frequencies and intensities are delivered through loudspeakers. Infant’s responses include head turn, eye widening and cessation of activity.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 138.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The tensor veli palatini muscle originates from the scaphoid fossa, the spine of the sphenoid bone, and the lateral cartilaginous lamina of the Eustachian tube.
  • It inserts into the palatine aponeurosis of the soft palate.
  • Its primary physiological function is to open the Eustachian tube during swallowing or yawning by pulling its lateral wall, which equilibrates middle ear pressure.
  • It is innervated by the mandibular nerve (V3).
  • Dysfunction may contribute to:
    • Eustachian tube dysfunction
    • Middle ear ventilation problems.

[[figure-1]]

Muscles Related to the Eustachian Tube:

Muscle

Main Action

Nerve Supply

Tensor veli palatini

Opens the auditory tube

CN V3

Levator veli palatini

Elevates the soft palate

CN X

Stylopharyngeus

Elevates pharynx

CN IX

Superior constrictor

Constricts pharynx

CN X

Stylopharyngeus (Option A): This muscle arises from the styloid process and inserts into the thyroid cartilage and pharyngeal wall. It acts to elevate the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

Levator veli palatini (Option B): This muscle originates from the petrous apex and the medial cartilaginous part of the Eustachian tube. It acts to elevate the soft palate to close the nasopharyngeal isthmus. While it is anatomically close, the primary dilator/tensor that matches this classic anatomical description of pulling open the lumen is the tensor veli palatini.

Superior constrictor (Option D): This is a quadrilateral muscle forming the upper part of the pharyngeal wall, originating from the pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, and alveolar border of the mandible, rather than directly controlling the Eustachian tube lumen.

  • While they are benign and typically don't cause bone destruction, long-standing, massive polyps can cause pressure necrosis/erosion of the nasal turbinates or sinus walls, and they occur frequently in females.

Antrochoanal Polyp:

  • An antrochoanal polyp is a benign solitary polyp arising from the maxillary sinus mucosa that extends through the sinus ostium into the choana and nasopharynx.

Etiology

  • Chronic rhinosinusitis

  • More common in children and young adults

Part

  • CT PNS show

  • Complete removal of:

    • Nasal component

Condition

Key Difference

Ethmoidal polyp

Usually bilateral and multiple

JNA

Inverted papilloma with malignant transformation (Option B): This is a neoplastic growth of the nasal cavity that carries a 5% to 15% risk of transforming into squamous cell carcinoma. It is locally destructive, produces recurrent epistaxis, causes significant bony erosion, and can readily affect female patients.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (Option C): This is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumour. While it classically causes recurrent, profuse epistaxis, a nasal/nasopharyngeal mass, and localised bony erosion (characteristically causing anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, known as the Holman-Miller sign), it exclusively occurs in adolescent males.

Olfactory esthesioneuroblastoma (Option D): Also known as olfactory neuroblastoma, this is a malignant neuroectodermal tumour arising from the olfactory epithelium at the roof of the nasal cavity. It presents with epistaxis, a nasal mass, and explicit localised bone erosion on CT scans, affecting both genders equally.

question: A female patient presents with a history of recurrent epistaxis and a nasal mass. CT scan shows localised bony erosion. Which of the following is the least likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. A- Unilateral cleft lip, B - Bilateral cleft lip, C - Cleft palate, D - Oblique facial cleft
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Unilateral Cleft Lip (Image A): Occurs due to the failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the intermaxillary segment (derived from the merged medial nasal prominences) on one side. This is an anterior cleft anomaly located anterior to the incisive foramen.

Bilateral Cleft Lip (Image B): Occurs when both the right and left maxillary prominences fail to fuse with the central intermaxillary segment, resulting in a prominent, isolated premaxillary tissue block.

Cleft Palate (Image C): Represents a failure of the secondary palate to close properly. It results from the incomplete fusion or failure of the palatine shelves (medial extensions of the maxillary processes) to meet with each other in the midline or with the nasal septum/primary palate posterior to the incisive foramen.

Oblique Facial Cleft (Image D): A rare craniofacial defect caused by the complete failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the lateral nasal prominence along the line of the nasolacrimal groove. Consequently, the nasolacrimal duct remains exposed as an open furrow on the face.

[[figure-1]]

Types of cleft lip:

Midline cleft lower lip

Due to the non-fusion of the mandibular process

[[figure-2]]

Midline cleft upper lip (rare)

Due to the non-fusion of the medial nasal processes

[[figure-3]]

Unilateral cleft upper lip

Due to the non-fusion of the maxillary process with the medial nasal process on one side

[[figure-4]]

Bilateral cleft upper lip/hare lip

Due to the non-fusion of both maxillary processes with both medial nasal processes on either side

[[figure-5]]

Oblique facial cleft

Due to the non-fusion of the lateral nasal process and the maxillary prominence along the line of the nasolacrimal groove

[[figure-6]]


Reference:

Logan Turner's Diseases of the Nose, Throat and Ear, Head and Neck Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 268, 269.

question: Identify the congenital craniofacial anomalies given below:

correctAnswer: D. Sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Rinne test: AC > BC in both ears

  • Indicates either normal hearing or sensorineural hearing loss
  • Rules out conductive hearing loss (which would show BC > AC).

Weber test: Sound lateralizes to the left ear

  • Weber lateralizes:
    • To the bad ear in conductive loss
    • To the good ear in sensorineural loss

Interpretation: Since Rinne excludes conductive loss, Weber lateralizing to the left indicates the left ear is better (with sensorineural loss in the right ear).

Final diagnosis: Sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear.

Conductive hearing loss in the left ear (Option A) would make Weber go to the left ear, but Rinne would be BC > AC.

Conductive hearing loss in the right ear (Option B) would make Weber go to the right ear, not the left.

Sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear (Option C): Weber would go to the right ear, not the left.



Reference:

Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 8th Edition, Page 26-27.

question: A 35-year-old patient presents with hearing loss. Clinical examination reveals a Rinne test where Air Conduction is greater than Bone Conduction in both ears. The Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in stria vascularis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Furosemide is a loop diuretic that temporarily affects the stria vascularis, a structure responsible for maintaining the endolymph ionic composition in the cochlea.

  • Inhibit the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the stria vascularis.
  • This disrupts endolymph production and endocochlear potential, leading to hearing loss.
  • The effect is usually reversible, but high doses can cause permanent damage.

Drugs Causing Ototoxicity (Cochleotoxicity)
  • Aminoglycosides (kanamycin, neomycin, amikacin) → damage Organ of Corti hair cells & cochlear VIII nerve (Option A ruled out)
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid, bumetanide) → affect stria vascularis
  • Antineoplastics (cisplatin, carboplatin) → damage outer hair cells & spiral ganglion
  • Salicylates (aspirin) → reversible high-frequency SNHL, tinnitus.

Drugs Causing Vestibulotoxicity (Balance dysfunction)
  • Streptomycin → vestibular hair cell damage → vertigo, ataxia
  • Gentamicin → predominantly vestibulotoxic; used for labyrinth ablation in Ménière’s disease.

Vestibulocochlear nerve (Option C): Nerve damage causes retrocochlear hearing loss, seen with conditions like vestibular schwannoma, not loop diuretics.

Cochlear duct basement membrane (Option D): Not affected in furosemide ototoxicity, no role in transporter disruption.



Reference:

Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 8th Edition, Page 39, 41.

question: Furosemide-induced hearing loss occurs primarily by damaging which structure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This audiogram shows a characteristic 4 kHz notch, which is strongly associated with noise-induced hearing loss.

  • Occupational noise damages outer hair cells in the basal turn of the cochlea, causing bilateral high-frequency hearing loss with a characteristic 4 kHz notch and partial recovery at 8 kHz, typically after long-term exposure.
  • Management:
    • Noise protection (earplugs/earmuffs)
    • Periodic audiometric screening for exposed workers
    • Reducing exposure levels at the workplace
    • No medical reversal; focus on prevention and rehabilitation.

Presbycusis (Option A): Age-related sensorineural hearing loss showing progressive high-frequency decline, not a 4 kHz notch. More common in the elderly, not specific to factory workers.

[[figure-1]]

Meniere’s disease (Option C): Typically shows low-frequency SNHL, episodic vertigo, and tinnitus. The pattern does not show a 4 kHz dip.

[[figure-2]]

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (Option D): Acute onset unilateral hearing loss; does not show a chronic 4 kHz notch pattern.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 8th Edition, Page 40-41.
question: A 50-year-old construction worker presents with gradual bilateral hearing loss for several years. He has history of chronic exposure to loud noise at work. Audiogram (shown) reveals characteristic dip at 4000 Hz with relative preservation of lower frequencies. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Bilateral Conductive Hearing Loss, more severe on the right side.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The audiogram shows a Bilateral Conductive Hearing Loss.

  • Bone Conduction (BC) is Normal: The BC thresholds (brackets/carets) are ≤25 dB across all frequencies in both ears, indicating a normal cochlear/inner ear function.
  • Air-Bone Gap (ABG) is Present: A significant gap exists between the AC and BC thresholds in both ears, which is the definition of a conductive component.
  • Conductive Hearing Loss Classification: A hearing loss with an ABG >10 dB and normal BC is classified as a Conductive Hearing Loss.
  • Severity: The AC thresholds are much poorer (gap is wider, reaching 60-70 dB) in the right ear than in the left ear (AC around 35-45 dB), indicating a conductive loss that is more severe on the right side.

Bilateral Sensorineural Hearing Loss (Option A) requires BC to be abnormal (>25 dB) and an ABG to be absent (≤10).

Bilateral Mixed Hearing Loss (Option B) requires the BC to be abnormal (>25 dB), which is not the case here.

Conductive Hearing Loss on the right side only (Option D): Conductive loss, though milder, is also present and evident in the left ear.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose, and Throat, 8th Edition, Pages 25, 27, 28.

Conductive Hearing Loss on the right side only.

question: The audiogram below demonstrates a hearing loss. Based on the Air-Conduction (AC) and Bone-Conduction (BC) thresholds, what is the most specific type of hearing loss shown?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) is the gold standard subjective test used to quantify hearing loss and its characteristics.
  • The results of PTA are graphically plotted on a chart called an audiogram, which uses the X-axis for frequency (Hz) and the Y-axis for intensity (dB).
  • PTA specifically measures both the Air-Conduction (AC) and Bone-Conduction (BC) thresholds, which allows for the accurate classification and degree of hearing loss.

Tympanometry (Option A): An objective test of middle ear function (compliance vs. pressure).

Brainstem evoked response audiometry (Option B): An objective test measuring electrical activity of the auditory pathway (waveform plot of latency vs. amplitude).

Otoacoustic emissions (Option C): An objective test measuring sounds generated by the outer hair cells in the cochlea, mainly for screening.



Reference:

question: A 45-year-old patient complains of difficulty breathing through their nose. He also reports complaints of smell perception. The otolaryngologist decides to perform both the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) and rhinomanometry. correctAnswer: C. Maximum airflow during quiet respiration occurs through inferior turbinate
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The maximum airflow during quiet respiration occurs through middle turbinate, not inferior turbinate.

  • The nose is the natural and instinctive pathway for breathing, especially crucial for newborns. Mouth breathing is learned with age. (Option A ruled out)
  • Inspiratory and expiratory airflows follow different patterns, with expiration being more complex and involving eddy current formation causing ventilation of sinuses. (Option D ruled out)
  • The turbinates play a significant role in regulating airflow through swelling and shrinkage.
  • The nasal cycle involves alternating congestion and decongestion of nasal chambers, regulating airflow. Each cycle lasts between 1.5-4 hours.
  • The nose is multifunctional, allowing for simultaneous breathing and eating, as well as playing a crucial role in olfaction and air conditioning.
  • Very little air passes through the inferior meatus or olfactory region of the nose. (Option B ruled out)
  • The maximum airflow during quiet respiration occurs through middle turbinate in a parabolic pattern.


Reference:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Conchal Pneumatization involves minimal air space and dense trabecular bone, making surgical access to the sella tursica extremely difficult.
  • The pneumatization of the sphenoid sinus refers to the extent to which air cells develop within the sphenoid bone, creating the hollow spaces of the sinus;Greater pneumatization makes the pituitary gland easier to access, while lesser pneumatization makes access more difficult.

This pattern can vary significantly among individuals, and it is categorized into three main types:

  • Sellar Pneumatization - air cells extend posteriorly beyond the sella turcica.
    • This type results in a well-developed sphenoid sinus.
    • Most common(82%)
    • It is ideal for this surgery because the sinus is well pneumatized
  • Presellar Pneumatization - reaches up to the anterior wall of the sella but does not extend beyond it.
    • This creates a smaller sinus compared to the sellar type.
    • Sellar and Presellar Pneumatization provide adequate access for surgery. (Option A and B)
  • Conchal Pneumatization - shallow bowl with minimal sphenoid pneumatization and trabecular bone between the sinus and sella.
  • Lateral Pneumatization - extending into the pterygoid processes, resulting in the formation of a lateral sphenoid recess.
    • While complex, is not a contraindication but may require additional surgical expertise.
  • Post-sellar Pneumatization is a variant with pneumatization extending beyond the sella, which is generally acceptable for surgery, though it may carry additional risks depending on surrounding anatomy.

correctAnswer: B. Regulating airflow resistance and airflow dynamics
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The nasal valve is the narrowest area in the nose and plays an important part in regulating the flow of air into the nose. Physiologically, it provides resistance to the flow of air and thus helps in filtration, warming, and humidification of air.

  • It has 2 valves.
  • Its upper limit on the lateral wall is marked by limen nasi (also called nasal valve).

Nasal valve:

  • Boundaries: Medially by the septum, superiorly by the lower border of the upper lateral cartilage, and inferiorly by the head of the inferior turbinate.
  • The upper lateral cartilage meets the nasal septum in the midline forming an angle of 10-15°.
  • During hump removal and medialization of the nasal dorsum in rhinoplasty, the function of this valve may get disturbed leading to nasal obstruction.

Nasal valve area:

  • It is the cross-sectional area at the level of the lower border of upper lateral cartilage, the corresponding part of the caudal septum, and the head of the inferior turbinate and measures nearly 55-73 mm.

External nasal valve:

  • Is the cross-sectional area of the nasal vestibule, i.e. the opening of the nasal vestibule.
  • It is made of alar cartilage and fibro-fatty tissue and is controlled by nasal muscles.
  • Boundaries: Medially by columella, laterally by ala of nose, and inferiorly by the skin of the floor

To provide resonance to the voice is the functions of paranasal sinuses(Option A)

Modulating the temperature and humidity of inspired air is a function that occurs in the nasal cavity, but it's not the primary function of the nasal valve specifically. (Option C)


Sensing and processing olfactory stimuli are sensed and processed by the olfactory receptors located in the upper part of the nasal cavity, not by the nasal valve(Option D)

      • Frontal sinus (Option A)
      • Maxillary sinus (Option D)

lessonTitle: Anatomy of Nose and Paranasal Sinuses II
question: Which of the following anatomical structures is not classified as a paranasal sinus?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The maxillary sinus, also called the Antrum of Highmore, is the largest paranasal sinus.

  • It is a pyramidal-shaped cavity situated within the body of the maxilla and begins to develop during intrauterine life, making it the first paranasal sinus to appear.
  • Its roof is formed by the floor of the orbit, and its floor is related to the roots of the premolar and molar teeth, which explains why dental infections can spread to the maxillary sinus.
  • The sinus drains through its natural ostium into the middle meatus via the hiatus semilunaris.
  • Because this ostium is located high on the medial wall, drainage is relatively poor, and the sinus is therefore particularly prone to stasis and maxillary sinusitis.


Pyriform sinus (Option B) is a clinical subsite of the hypopharynx located on either side of the laryngeal inlet, common for foreign body entrapment.

Sinus of Morgagni (Option C) is a space between the base of the skull and the superior constrictor muscle, through which the eustachian tube and levator veli palatini pass.

Fossa of Rosenmüller (Option D): is a deep mucosal recess in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, situated posterior to the torus tubarius, representing the most common site of origin for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 218.
lessonTitle: Anatomy of Nose and Paranasal Sinuses II
question: The maxillary sinus is also known as:

correctAnswer: A. Pyramidal in shape, with base towards the lateral wall of the nose and apex towards the zygomatic process
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The maxillary sinus is a pyramidal-shaped cavity.

  • Its base is directed medially and forms part of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, where the natural ostium is located.
  • Its apex is directed laterally toward the zygomatic process of the maxilla, and it may sometimes extend into the zygomatic bone.
  • The roof of the sinus is formed by the floor of the orbit, while the floor is related to the roots of the premolar and molar teeth, which explains the close relationship between maxillary sinusitis and dental infections.
  • Antigravity drainage leads to fluid or blood sequestration (haemosinusitis) after trauma and frequent bacterial stasis.

Caldwell-Luc Operation

  • Surgical approach to maxillary sinus via canine fossa (above canine tooth)
  • Indications:
    • Chronic maxillary sinusitis (refractory)
    • Removal of cysts, polyps, tumors
    • Removal of foreign bodies
  • Key anatomical relations:
    • Close to infraorbital nerve → risk of paresthesia of upper lip, cheek
    • Thin anterior wall → easy surgical access

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 218.

question: Regarding the morphological orientation of the maxillary sinus, which of the following statements is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The maxillary sinus, like the other paranasal sinuses, is lined by respiratory epithelium, that is, pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.

  • This specialised mucosa, also called the Schneiderian membrane, contains ciliated cells and goblet cells that help in mucociliary clearance.
  • The coordinated beating of cilia transports mucus, along with trapped dust, debris, and microorganisms, toward the natural ostium, helping maintain normal sinus drainage and preventing infection.

Keratinising stratified squamous epithelium (Option A) is characteristic of the skin and the nasal vestibule.

Non-keratinising stratified squamous epithelium (Option B) is found in the oropharynx and esophagus, providing protection against mechanical stress.

Simple columnar epithelium (Option D): While the cells are columnar, the respiratory lining is pseudostratified and ciliated to perform its clearing function.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 160.

  • The lower two-thirds are cartilaginous and are formed by the upper lateral cartilages, lower lateral (major alar) cartilages, and septal cartilage, which provide flexibility and shape to the nasal dorsum, tip, and ala.
  • This distinction is clinically important in nasal trauma and rhinoplasty.

question: Which of the following descriptions correctly defines the structural composition of the external nose?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The nasal septum is a median osteocartilaginous partition separating the two nasal cavities. Its main anterior cartilaginous component is the septal cartilage, also called the quadrangular cartilage.

  • It is described as a quadrilateral because of its four-sided shape.
  • The septal cartilage forms the major anterior support of the nasal septum and contributes significantly to the support of the nasal dorsum and tip.
  • It is related superiorly to the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and nasal bones, posteriorly to the vomer, and inferiorly to the maxillary and palatine crests.
  • Preservation of this cartilage is important in septal surgery and rhinoplasty because loss of septal support can lead to saddle nose deformity and tip collapse.

question: The primary cartilaginous component of the nasal septum, which provides major support to the nasal dorsum and tip, is characteristically described as having which geometric shape?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The external nasal framework consists of bones that form the visible bridge and root of the nose.

  • These include:
    • The paired nasal bones (Option A ruled out) form the bridge of the external nose
    • The frontal process of the maxilla (Option D ruled out) contributes to the lateral support of the external nose
    • The nasal spine of the frontal bone (Option B ruled out) contributes to the root of the nose
  • These bones are superficial and, therefore, commonly involved in external nasal fractures following direct trauma.

The sphenoid bone is located deep within the skull, forming the posterior part of the nasal cavity and the skull base.

  • While severe pan-facial or skull base fractures (like Le Fort III) can involve the sphenoid, it does not contribute to the external nasal framework and is therefore not involved in simple external nasal fractures. (Option C)

question: Which of the following anatomical structures does not contribute to the formation of the nasal septum?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The posterior apertures of the nasal cavity are called the choanae, also known as the posterior nares.

  • These are two oval openings that establish communication between the nasal cavity and the nasopharynx and therefore form the posterior boundary of the nasal cavity.
  • Each choana is bounded medially by the posterior edge of the vomer, laterally by the medial pterygoid plate region, superiorly by the body of the sphenoid, and inferiorly by the posterior border of the hard palate.
  • The choanae are clinically important because choanal atresia, a congenital failure of posterior nasal aperture formation, presents in neonates with cyclical cyanosis that worsens during feeding and improves on crying, as newborns are obligate nasal breathers.

Features

External nasal valve

Internal nasal valve

Location

Opening of the nasal vestibule.

Junction of Upper Lateral Cartilage (ULC) and Septum.

Boundaries

  • Medial Boundary: Columella and caudal border of septal cartilage.
  • Lateral Boundary: Caudal border of alar cartilage (lateral crus) and fibro-fatty tissue.
  • Inferior: Nasal sill (floor of vestibule).
  • Medial Boundary: Nasal Septum.
  • Lateral Boundary: Caudal margin of ULC and head of inferior turbinate.
  • Superior: Apex (Upper Lateral Cartilage meets septum)
  • Inferior: Nasal floor.

Clinical significance

First point of resistance; affected by alar collapse.

Narrowest part of upper airway; primary "flow limiter.”

Other

Controlled by nasalis muscle

10° to 15° normal (angle reduction causes severe obstruction).

Anterior nares (Option A) are the external openings of the nose onto the face

Limen nasi (Option C) is a mucosal ridge that marks the boundary between the nasal vestibule and the nasal cavity proper.

Agger nasi (Option D) is the most anterior ethmoid air cell, located just in front of the attachment of the middle turbinate, and is a landmark in endoscopic sinus surgery.



Reference:
  1. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK544232/
  2. PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 155.

question: The posterior apertures of the nasal cavity, which provide communication between the nose and the nasopharynx, are termed as?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image depicts Cottle’s test, which is used to identify collapse or stenosis of the internal nasal valve, the narrowest part of the nasal airway.

  • The internal nasal valve is a triangular space that provides the highest resistance to airflow.
  • Its boundaries are:
    • Medially by the nasal septum. (Statement 1)
    • Superiorly and laterally by the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage. (Statement 2)
    • Inferiorly by the floor of the nose and the anterior head of the inferior turbinate. (Statement 3)
  • The angle between the septum and upper lateral cartilage normally measures about 10-15°, and narrowing of this angle can produce significant nasal obstruction.
  • A positive Cottle’s test is suggested when airflow improves with lateral traction on the cheek, indicating possible nasal valve dysfunction.
  • The middle turbinate does not form part of the internal nasal valve. (Statement 4)


Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 155, 172, 173.

question:
A patient presents with nasal obstruction, and the clinical test shown in the image is performed.

Which of the following anatomical structures contribute to the boundaries of the internal nasal valve area being evaluated?

  1. Nasal Septum
  2. Upper lateral cartilage
  3. Head of inferior turbinate
  4. Middle turbinate

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image provides a direct endoscopic view of the right nasal cavity, with the septum marked S on the right side of the frame. The arrow indicates the inferior turbinate

  • The inferior turbinate is the largest turbinate and is an independent bone of the skull.
  • It is the most prominent landmark encountered during anterior rhinoscopy and the start of nasal endoscopy.
  • This structure is highly vascular and contains cavernous venous plexuses, allowing it to swell and shrink as part of the physiological nasal cycle.
  • This helps regulate airflow, humidification, warming, and filtration of inspired air.

[[figure-1]]


Middle turbinate (Option B): Situated superior to the inferior turbinate; it is a part of the ethmoid bone and acts as a primary landmark for the middle meatus.

Superior Turbinate (Option C): A significantly smaller structure located in the posterosuperior aspect of the nasal cavity, usually hidden from direct anterior view unless the middle turbinate is medialized.

Uncinate process (Option D) is a thin, hook-shaped process of the ethmoid bone located in the lateral wall of the middle meatus



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 156-159.
lessonTitle: Anatomy of Nose and Paranasal Sinuses II
question: Identify the structure marked by the arrow in this endoscopic view of the nasal cavity.

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Inferior turbinate

Explanation:

The inferior turbinate is the only independent bone among the nasal conchae.

  • In contrast, the superior, middle, and supreme turbinates are processes of the ethmoid bone.
  • The inferior turbinate articulates with the conchal crest of the maxilla and the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone, and also has attachments to the lacrimal bone and ethmoid.
  • It has three important processes: the lacrimal process, ethmoidal process, and maxillary process.
  • Clinically, the inferior turbinate is important because the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus beneath it.

Superior turbinate (Option A) is a projection of the ethmoid bone, not an independent bone.

Middle turbinate (Option B) is also a part of the ethmoid bone and forms an important landmark for the middle meatus and osteomeatal complex.

Supreme turbinate (Option D), when present, is an additional ethmoidal projection and not an independent bone.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 156.

question: The lateral wall of the nasal cavity is a complex structure formed by several bones. Which of the following nasal turbinates is an independent bone of the skull that directly articulates with the maxilla?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical features point to a Septal Abscess.
  • When left untreated, septal abscesses can lead to serious complications like necrosis of the septal cartilage, septal perforation, and even life-threatening conditions such as meningitis or cavernous sinus thrombosis.
  • Immediate surgical drainage of the abscess is necessary to remove the pus collection and prevent these severe outcomes. Antibiotic therapy should also be started after drainage.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Septal Abscess

  • Observation and follow-up in a week (Option B): This would be inappropriate for managing a septal abscess, as delaying treatment worsens infection, leading to significant complications.

    Nasal decongestants (Option C): Although decongestants might provide temporary relief from nasal obstruction, they do not treat the underlying infection or address the collection of pus within the septum.

    Corticosteroid therapy (Option D): Corticosteroids are used to reduce inflammation in many conditions, but in the case of a septal abscess, the issue is infection. Corticosteroids would not resolve the abscess and could worsen it by suppressing the immune response.




Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg.174

question: A 45-year-old man with a history of trauma 1 week back, presents with fever, frontal headache, nasal bridge redness, and septal tenderness. O/E there smooth bilateral swelling of the nasal septum. What should be the initial approach to managing this patient's condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Trauma is the most common etiology of nasal septal perforation. This primarily includes iatrogenic trauma occurring during nasal surgeries like submucous resection (SMR) or septoplasty, where opposing mucosal tears are made. It also includes "habitual" trauma from nose picking (epistaxis digitorum).

Etiology of Septal Perforation

Traumatic

  • Iatrogenic (post Submucous Resection or Septoplasty)
  • Habitual nose picking → Hajek’s ulcer
  • Bilateral cauterization for epistaxis

Pathological

  • Septal Abscess causing cartilage necrosis (Option A ruled out)
  • Syphilis, Tuberculosis, Leprosy (Option C and D ruled out)

Inflammatory or Vasculitis
  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).
  • Sarcoidosis.

Chemical/Irritants

Wood dust, chrome salts, and cocaine use

Idiopathic

-



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 174-175.

question: Which of the following is recognized as the most common cause of nasal septal perforation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presentation suggests a Nasal Septal Hematoma, commonly occurring after trauma. Blood collects between the septal cartilage and mucoperichondrium, compromising cartilage nutrition and risking necrosis. If untreated, secondary infection may lead to a Septal Abscess. The resulting deformity is typically saddle nose, not hump nose.

Etiology

Most commonly due to trauma (falls, sports injury, nasal surgery). (Statement 1)

Pathophysiology

Blood collects in the subperichondrial space; septal cartilage fracture often makes it bilateral (Statement 2)

Clinical complications

If the hematoma is not drained, the resulting necrosis of the septal cartilage leads to a loss of dorsal support. This manifests as a saddle nose deformity (supratip depression), not a hump nose deformity (which is a convex excess of the bridge) (Statement 3 ruled out)

Infection

Stagnant blood may get infected. Secondary infection, most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus, can rapidly convert the hematoma into a septal abscess. (Statement 4)



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 173-174.

question:
A 7-year-old child presents with total nasal obstruction and a tender, bilateral, fluctuant septal swelling 24 hours after a nasal injury. Which of the following statements regarding this condition are correct?

  1. Trauma is the most frequent cause.
  2. Blood accumulates under the perichondrium.
  3. It can result in a hump-nose deformity.
  4. Secondary infection can lead to a septal abscess.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Septoplasty is a conservative procedure that preserves most of the septal framework. It typically involves limited, selective dissection with unilateral mucoperichondrial flap elevation, maintaining blood supply from the opposite side and reducing complications like Septal perforation.

Hence, bilateral mucoperichondrial flap elevation is not a characteristic feature of septoplasty.

Feature

Submucous Resection (SMR)

Septoplasty

Dissection

Extensive; removes most deformed parts except caudal/dorsal struts.

Limited, selective correction. (Option B ruled out)

Age Limit

Avoided before 17 yrs

Can be done in children (Option A ruled out)

Flaps

Bilateral mucoperichondrial flaps

Usually unilateral flap (Option C)

Management

Bony and cartilaginous parts are excised.

Deformed cartilage is corrected by scoring, cross-hatching, or wedge excision (Option D ruled out)

Complications

Higher risk of supratip depression and columellar recession.

Significantly lower risk of complications.

Reoperation

Technically difficult due to fibrosis.

Technically easier.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 490.

question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic feature of septoplasty?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Incision for a submucous resection (SMR) is Killian’s incision.

It is an oblique or curvilinear incision made on the side of the septal convexity, approximately 5 to 8 mm behind the caudal border of the septal cartilage. This allows for the easy elevation of mucoperichondrial and mucoperiosteal flaps on both sides of the septum before the deviated parts of the bone and cartilage are resected.

This differs from septoplasty, where a more anterior incision is used to preserve more of the septal framework.

[[figure-1]]

Transfixion incision (Option B) is a surgical technique used in endonasal rhinoplasty and septoplasty, involving a vertical cut through the membranous septum just in front of the caudal edge of the septal cartilage.

Freer’s incision (Option C) is a septocolumellar incision between caudal end of septal cartilage and columella (hemitransfixion incision). This approach is used in septoplasty when the dislocation is at the caudal end.

Weber-Ferguson incision (Option D) is a surgical approach used for a maxillectomy to provide exposure to the maxillary bone and is not used for internal septal surgery.



Reference:
  1. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Volume 1, Page 1137.
  2. PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 491.

question: A patient with a markedly deviated nasal septum is planned for submucous resection (SMR). Which of the following incisions is classically used to perform this procedure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Septoplasty is a functional surgical procedure indicated for correcting mechanical impairments and specific clinical complications caused by a structural deformity of the nasal septum.

Indications:

  • Symptomatic nasal obstruction (unilateral/bilateral). (Statement 1)
  • Part of septorhinoplasty for cosmetic correction.
  • Recurrent epistaxis from a septal spur. (Statement 2)
  • Recurrent/chronic sinusitis due to septal deviation.
  • Contact point headache (Sluder’s neuralgia) from septum touching lateral nasal wall.
  • To improve surgical access in Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (ESS).
  • Access for Endoscopic Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).
  • Trans-septal trans-sphenoidal approach to pituitary fossa. (Statement 3)
  • Septal deviation contributing to **Obstructive Sleep Apnea.

Chronic allergic watery discharge (Statement 4) is a mucosal symptom associated with hypersensitivity and hyper-responsiveness, not an indication for septoplasty.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 489.

Which of the following are recognized clinical indications for performing a septoplasty?

  1. Nasal obstruction on one or both sides
  2. Recurrent epistaxis usually from a septal spur
  3. Trans-sphenoidal approach to the pituitary fossa
  4. Chronic allergic watery discharge

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cottle's test is a diagnostic maneuver used to evaluate nasal valve patency. In this test, the cheek is pulled laterally while the patient inspires; if this action relieves the sensation of nasal obstruction, the test is considered positive.

A positive result indicates that the site of obstruction is the nasal valve. This helps the surgeon decide if a simple septoplasty is sufficient or if the nasal valve needs to be addressed surgically.

Rinne's test (Option B) is a tuning fork test used in audiology to compare air conduction with bone conduction.

Cold spatula test (Option C) involves placing a cold metal spatula under the nostrils to observe the misting pattern, used to subjectively assess the patency of each nasal airway.

Posterior rhinoscopy (Option D) is a clinical procedure using a mirror or endoscope to visualize the nasopharynx and the posterior ends of the turbinates.

question: This clinical maneuver seen in the image is known as:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated inflammatory disease of the nasal mucosa and does not cause mechanical changes to the osseocartilaginous framework of the septum.

Primary Etiological Factors for DNS

Trauma

Most common cause; includes birth trauma (septal molding, forceps delivery) and later nasal injuries. (Option A ruled out)

Developmental Error

Disproportionate growth between the septum and facial skeleton (e.g., high-arched palate pushing the vomer upward). (Option B ruled out)

Hereditary

Genetic influence on the size and shape of the septum; familial tendency.

Racial Factors

Higher incidence reported in Caucasians. (Option C ruled out)

Masses

Long-standing nasal polyps or tumors may push the septum to one side

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 171.

question: Which of the following conditions is not recognized as a primary etiological factor for deviated nasal septum?

correctAnswer: D. Application of saline nasal washes and insertion of septal button
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The initial management of a large nasal septal perforation focuses on alleviating symptoms, such as crusting, obstruction, and irritation, while preventing further damage.

  • Saline nasal washes help keep the nasal cavity clean and free from crusting.
  • A silastic sheet or septal button is a prosthetic device inserted into the perforation to physically seal it.
    • This improves airflow, reduces crusting, and minimizes irritation, significantly enhancing the patient's comfort.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Septal Perforation

Etiology:

  • Bony perforations: Caused by syphilis or other conditions affecting the bony septum.
  • Cartilaginous perforations: Commonly result from trauma, tuberculosis, or septal abscess.
  • Total perforations: Can occur in systemic diseases like Wegener’s granulomatosis.


Surgical closure with plastic flaps (Option A): This is reserved for small, inactive perforations where the hole in the septum can be closed surgically using plastic flaps. However, for larger perforations, closure can be challenging and is not the first-line treatment.


Cauterization of the perforation (Option B): Cauterization involves burning tissue and is used to stop nosebleeds or other issues, but it is not a recommended treatment for septal perforations.


Use of steroid nasal sprays (Option C): While nasal sprays are commonly used to treat allergies and reduce inflammation, they can also contribute to septal perforations, especially when used long-term. Therefore, this is not an appropriate treatment and may exacerbate the issue rather than help manage it.



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pages 174,175
  2. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology, 8th Edition, Volume 1, Page 1152
  3. emedicine.medscape.com/article/863325-clinical?form=fpf

question: A 35-year-old man presents with nasal obstruction and frequent crusting. Examination reveals a large perforation in the nasal septum. What is the most appropriate initial management?

correctAnswer: B. Cancellous bone graft from the iliac crest
explanationHtml:
Correct answer: B) Cancellous bone graft from the iliac crest

Explanation:

This presentation suggests saddle nose deformity, characterized by a depressed nasal bridge, often following trauma or previous nasal surgery. The goal of treatment is to restore the nasal structure and improve both the aesthetic appearance and airway function.

When both the bony and cartilaginous structures of the nose are depressed, the best treatment involves using cancellous bone. This graft, often harvested from the iliac crest, provides structural support to restore the shape of the nose.

  • If depression involves:
    • Only cartilage: Cartilage is taken from the nasal septum or the auricle.
    • Both Bone and Cartilage: Cancellous bone from the iliac crest is the best.

Causes of Saddle Nose Deformity:

  • Nasal trauma
  • Excessive septum removal
  • Septal damage due to septal hematoma or abscess.
  • Conditions like leprosy, tuberculosis, or syphilis.

A cartilage graft from the nasal septum (Option A) is used when only the cartilage of the nose is affected by the deformity.

Silicone implant (Option C): Although synthetic materials like silicone can be used to fill the nasal dorsum, autologous grafts like bone are generally preferred due to lower risks of complications such as extrusion or rejection by the body.

Observation without intervention (Option D): Leaving the deformity untreated, especially when it is causing functional issues like difficulty breathing, is not advisable.



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg.165
  2. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology, 8th Edition, Volume 1, Pg.435
