options.text: Perform a non-contrast CT scan and plan for FESS
Plain X-ray and perform a biopsy.

question: A 10-year-old child presents with a history of nasal obstruction predominantly on the right side, mouth breathing, and occasional snoring for the past year. He also has intermittent right-sided nasal discharge and postnasal drip. There is no history of allergies or asthma. A smooth, grayish mass is seen in the right nasal cavity extending into the nasopharynx on rhinoscopic examination. Which among the following is the most appropriate next step in managing his condition?

correctAnswer: B. A globular mass behind the soft palate in the nasopharynx
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Antrochoanal Polyp often presents with a globular mass visible in the nasopharynx on posterior rhinoscopy due to its growth pattern.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Antrochoanal Polyp

Examination

Findings

Anterior Rhinoscopy
  • May miss the polyp if posterior; visible as a smooth, greyish mass with nasal discharge.
  • Can be soft and movable, or protrude pink and congested from the nostril.

Posterior Rhinoscopy
  • Reveals a globular mass in the nasopharynx, behind the soft palate.
  • Anterior nasal cavity, nasal dorsum, maxillary antrum are not visible on posterior rhinoscopy

Nasal Endoscopy

Provides detailed view of the polyp’s origin in the maxillary antrum, its three parts, and its extent within the nasal cavity and nasopharynx.


Pink and congested mass (Option A) would more likely be seen with a nasal dermoid cyst or other conditions.

Firm, non-movable mass in the maxillary antrum (Option C) might be seen on imaging but not on posterior rhinoscopy.

Midline pit with protruding hair (Option D) is characteristic of nasal dermoid cysts, not antrochoanal polyps.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, Edition 8, Page 200

A globular mass behind the soft palate in the nasopharynx

question: A 9 y/o child presents with a unilateral nasal obstruction, hyponasality, and a mucoid nasal discharge. Anterior rhinoscopy shows a smooth, greyish mass, but the polyp is not fully visible. What is the most likely finding on posterior rhinoscopy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Stages of rhinoscleroma

Characteristic features

1. Atrophic stage

c. Foul smelling purulent nasal discharge and crusting.

2. Granulomatous stage

b. Painless and non-ulcerative nodules.

3. Cicatricial stage

a. Stenosis of nares and nasopharynx.

Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by the gram-negative bacillus, Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis or Frisch bacillus.

Atrophic stage:

  • Foul-smelling purulent nasal discharge and crusting.
  • Resembles atrophic rhinitis.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Rhinoscleroma Atrophic stage

Granulomatous stage:

  • Formation of granulomatous, painless, and non-ulcerative nodules in the nasal mucosa.
  • Subdermal infiltration of the lower part of the external nose and upper lip gives a “woody” feel- aka Hebra nose.

[[figure-2]]

Fig: Rhinoscleroma Granulomatous stage

Cicatricial stage:

  • Stenosis of nares, upper lip distortion, nose adhesions, nasopharynx, and oropharynx.
  • In the larynx, subglottic stenosis is the most common causing respiratory distress.

[[figure-3]]

Fig: Bilateral Nasal Vestibular Stenosis



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition- Page 181, 183

question:
Match the stages of rhinoscleroma with its characteristics features:

Stages of rhinoscleroma

Characteristic features

1. Atrophic stage

a. Stenosis of nares and nasopharynx.

2. Granulomatous stage

b. Painless and non-ulcerative nodules.

3. Cicatricial stage

c. Foul smelling purulent nasal discharge and crusting.

d. Black membrane in the nasal mucosa.

correctAnswer: C. Surgical excision of the cyst and sinus tract
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario is of a dermoid cyst (a benign cutaneous developmental anomaly that arises from the entrapment of ectodermal elements along the lines of embryonic closure).

Surgical excision is necessary to remove the cyst and sinus tract, particularly to prevent complications like infection or intracranial extension.

  • Simple Dermoids:
    • Surgical removal by splitting nasal bones if necessary.
  • Dermoids with Sinus or Intracranial Connection:
    • Requires combined neurosurgical and otolaryngological approach to remove the cyst and close the bony defect.

Observation and monitoring (Option A) would not address the risk of infection or intracranial involvement.

Topical antibiotics (Option B) may manage superficial infection but do not treat the underlying cyst or sinus tract.

Corticosteroid injection (Option D) is not appropriate for treating dermoid cysts and would not resolve the underlying structural issue.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, Edition 8, Page 165, 238

Corticosteroid injection to reduce the cyst

question: A 5 y/o child presents with a midline pit on the nasal dorsum, with hair protruding from the opening. Imaging reveals a sinus tract leading to a cyst under the nasal bone. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanationHtml:
• Gliomas are firm, subcutaneous swellings on the bridge of the nose that appear as independent masses not connected to the brain.
  • They represent congenital anomalies related to encephaloceles, formed from “nipped-off” portions during embryonic development.

Presentation Types

Extranasal (60%)

Firm, subcutaneous swellings. Common locations: bridge of the nose, side of the nose, near the inner canthus (corner of the eye).

Intranasal (30%)

Located entirely within the nasal cavity.

Combined (10%)

Have both intranasal and extranasal components.

Treatment:

  • Extranasal gliomas: Encapsulated and easier to remove surgically via an external nasal approach.
  • Intranasal glioma: Minimally Invasive Endoscopic Surgery is essential for intranasal glioma to confirm diagnosis, prevent complications, and address cosmetic concerns.

Nasal polyps (Option A) typically arise from the nasal mucosa and are not encapsulated.

Encephaloceles (Option B) maintain a connection to the brain, unlike gliomas.

Dermoid cysts (Option D) are also firm but often contain skin elements like hair or sebaceous glands, and they are not encapsulated masses.



Reference:
  1. Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 166
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3743595/
lessonTitle: Granulomatous Lesions, Congenital Anomalies, and Nasal Polyps
question: A 3 year old child presents with a firm swelling on the bridge of the nose. Imaging reveals that the mass is encapsulated and has no connection to the brain. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Meningoencephalocele is a congenital defect where brain tissue and meninges herniate through an opening in the skull, forming a pulsatile, subcutaneous swelling.

Characteristics:

  • Subcutaneous and pulsatile swelling
  • May be reducible (can be pushed back into the skull)
  • Cough impulse: Swelling size changes with coughing

Locations

Nasofrontal

At the root of the nose

Nasoethmoid

Side of the nose

Naso-orbital

Anteromedial aspect of the orbit (eye socket)

Dermoid cysts (Option A) are non-pulsatile and do not change with coughing. They might change depending on the intra cranial connections.

Nasal polyps (Option B) are not associated with a pulsatile mass.

Hemangiomas (Option D) are vascular lesions that may be compressible but are not associated with brain tissue herniation.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, Edition 8, Page 165, 166
lessonTitle: Granulomatous Lesions, Congenital Anomalies, and Nasal Polyps
question: A 2 month old infant presents with a pulsatile swelling at the root of the nose that changes size when the infant coughs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above scenario is suggestive of meningocele, and cross-sectional imaging is the initial step in management to identify the extent of the cranial defect and assess the presence of herniated meninges or brain tissue.

Meningocele

Definition

Herniation of the meninges with the CSF through a congenital defect in the skull base.

Clinical Features
  • Soft, cystic swelling
  • Positive compressibility, reducibility, transillumination and cough impulse.
  • Furstenberg test - positive(the size of a nasal or cranial mass increases upon applying pressure to the internal jugular veins or by valsalva)

Diagnosis
  • CT and MRI imaging are critical;
  • Biopsy is contraindicated.

Treatment

Surgical excision and skull base reconstruction.

Fine-needle aspiration (Option A) and biopsy (Option B) are contraindicated in meningocele due to the risk of causing a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak, leading to further complications such as infection.


Antibiotic treatment (Option D) is not indicated unless there are signs of infection, which is not present in this case.



Reference:

Greenberg Handbook of Neurosurgery, Edition10., Page 269
lessonTitle: Granulomatous Lesions, Congenital Anomalies, and Nasal Polyps
question: A 6-month-old infant presents with a soft, compressible mass at the root of the nose. The mass increases in size when the baby cries and shows a positive Furstenberg test. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this condition?

correctAnswer: A. Inserting a wide bore feeding nipple into the mouth of the infant
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Inserting a wide bore feeding nipple into the mouth of the infant, known as McGovern’s technique can be used to bypass nasal obstruction in choanal atresia. An oropharyngeal airway can also be used to provide immediate relief by maintaining an open airway.

Choanal Atresia

Etiology

Persistence of nasobuccal membrane of Hochstetter.

Management

Immediate:

  • Oral airway placement.
  • A wide bore feeding nipple is inserted into the mouth of the infant - Mc Govern’s technique. (Option A)

Definitive: Surgery (at 1.5 years of age)

  • Endoscopic transnasal approach (most common).
  • Transpalatal approach used in complex cases.

Bag-mask ventilation(Option B), Immediate tracheostomy(Option C), and Endotracheal intubation(Option D) are not the immediate line of management for choanal atresia, but are used if initial management with Mc Govern’s technique or an oral airway fails.



Reference:

Scott Brown’s otorhinolaryngology,(volume 2) Edition 8, Page 251 - 253.

Logan Turner’s Diseases of the Nose, Throat and Ear, Edition 11, Page 637.

question: A 2-day-old full-term male infant is brought to the emergency room with difficulty breathing, especially when feeding, and cyanosis. The cyanosis improves when the infant cries but worsens when feeding. The baby is in respiratory distress. What is the best initial emergency management for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The condition described above is choanal atresia, which occurs due to persistence of Nasobuccal membrane.

Choanal Atresia

Clinical Features

Bilateral choanal atresia (presents during neonatal period):

  • Acute respiratory distress (as neonates are obligate nasal breathers)
  • Cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying.
  • Cyanosis during feeding.

Unilateral choanal atresia (presents later in life):

  • Failure to pass nasogastric tube on that side

Associated Syndrome

CHARGE syndrome: (due to mutations in the CHD7 gene on chromosome 8)

  • Coloboma
  • Heart defects
  • Atresia choanae
  • Retardation of growth
  • Genital anomalies
  • Ear abnormalities

These abnormalities must be excluded in a child with choanal atresia and therefore the minimum investigations in addition to the nasal CT scan are cardiac echo, renal ultrasound scan, and an ophthalmology and audiology review.

Diagnosis

Clinical:

  • Misting test with a metal spatula below nasal aperture.
  • Inability to pass a nasogastric tube

Definitive investigations:

  • CT scan ( after suction and nasal decongestants)
  • Nasal endoscopy


Buccopharyngeal membrane (Option A) is involved in the separation of the primitive mouth from the foregut, not related to nasal structures.


Orobuccal membrane (Option B) is not a recognized anatomical term.


Oropharyngeal membrane (Option D) is involved in the formation of the mouth and throat, not the nasal passages.



Reference:

Scott Brown’s otorhinolaryngology,(volume 2) Edition 8, Page 251 - 253.

Logan Turner’s Diseases of the Nose, Throat and Ear, Edition 11, Page 637.
lessonTitle: Granulomatous Lesions, Congenital Anomalies, and Nasal Polyps
question: A newborn is brought to the clinic with respiratory distress, which worsens during feeding and improves with crying. The baby shows difficulty in passing a nasogastric tube through one nasal passage, and a CT scan reveals a mixed bony and membranous obstruction in the posterior nasal cavity. This condition is due to the persistence of which membrane during development?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario, with nasal endoscopy showing strawberry mucosa and biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas is suggestive of Sarcoidosis.
  • Systemic steroids are the mainstay of treatment for sarcoidosis.

Clinical features of Sarcoidosis

  • Nasal obstruction
  • Crusting
  • Purplish discoloration - lupus pernio (specific)
  • Nasal bleeding
  • Facial pain.
  • Nasal mucosa - characteristic ‘strawberry’ appearance of inflamed erythematous mucosa covered with pale granulomas.
  • Anterior septal perforation- usually only involves cartilagenous part.

Investigations
  • Non-specific: Elevated serum ACE, hypercalcemia.
  • Kveim test (outdated)
  • Imaging: CXR (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy), CT for sinus/nasal involvement.
  • Biopsy: Non-caseating granulomas. (Confirmatory)

Management
  • Systemic steroids (Option C) (mainstay), methotrexate (steroid-sparing).
  • Topical: Nasal steroids, douching, lubricants.

[[figure-1]]

Image showing Lupus pernio

[[figure-2]]

Image showing strawberry mucosa

Methotrexate (Option A) may be used in certain cases but is not the first-line treatment.

Inhaled corticosteroids (Option B) are less effective and are not the mainstay of treatment.

Antihistamines (Option D) are not effective for this condition.



Reference:
  1. Scott Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology, Volume 1, 8th Edition, Pages 1211 - 1213.
  2. Logan Turner’s Diseases of the Nose, Throat and Ear, 11th Edition, Pages 45, 46.
lessonTitle: Granulomatous Lesions, Congenital Anomalies, and Nasal Polyps
question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with symptoms of nasal obstruction, crusting, and facial pain that have been worsening over the past few months. She reports persistent nasal congestion and frequent nosebleeds. On physical examination, there is purplish discoloration of the nasal skin and a nasal endoscopy reveals erythematous mucosa covered with pale granulomas, as shown in the image. A biopsy of the nasal lesion reveals non-caseating granulomas. Which of the following is the mainstay of treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario and biopsy findings are suggestive of Lupus vulgaris, a low-grade cutaneous TB infection in the nasal vestibule characterized by caseating granulomas.
  • It is usually secondary to pulmonary TB.
  • The image shows apple jelly nodule- pale reddish nodules on the dorsum or tip of the nose, which blanch on pressure, revealing a translucent "apple jelly" appearance on diascopy
  • Antitubercular therapy (ATT) is the treatment of choice to address the underlying tuberculosis infection.

Methotrexate (Option A) and systemic steroids (Option B) are not appropriate may worsen the condition as primary treatments in lupus vulgaris, and surgical excision (Option C) is not the first-line approach.



Reference:

Logan Turner’s Diseases of the Nose, Throat and Ear, Edition 11, Page 47.
lessonTitle: Granulomatous Lesions, Congenital Anomalies, and Nasal Polyps
question: A 45-year-old man presents with a chronic, non-healing lesion on his nasal tip, accompanied by intermittent nasal obstruction. Over the past several months, the lesion has progressively worsened. On examination, the following lesion is seen as shown in the image. A biopsy of the lesion reveals caseating granulomas. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?

correctAnswer: D. Complete excision of the mass
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation and biopsy showing sporangia with spores is most consistent with rhinosporidiosis.
  • The primary treatment is the complete excision of the mass with a diathermy knife and cauterization of its base.

Diagnosis of rhinosporidiosis:

  • Biopsy shows several sporangia, oval or round in shape and with spores

[[figure-1]]

  • Diagnosis cannot be established on culture.

Treatment:

Surgery: (Option D)

  • It is the primary treatment option.
  • Complete excision of the mass with a diathermy knife and cauterization of its base.
  • Recurrence is very common.

Medical treatment:

  • Dapsone is partially effective; it is also used post op to prevent recurrence. (Option C)


Amphotericin B (Option A): It is an antifungal, used in the treatment of fungal infections, not used in the treatment of rhinoscleroma

Cyclophosphamide (Option B): It is a cytotoxic drug, not used in the treatment of rhinosporidiosis



Reference:
  1. Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition- Page 186, 184, 183, 187
lessonTitle: Granulomatous Lesions, Congenital Anomalies, and Nasal Polyps
question: A 35-year-old man presents with nasal obstruction, recurrent nasal bleeding, and a mass protruding from his nasal cavity. On examination, a polypoidal, pink-colored mass with white dots on the surface is noted. It bleeds easily on touch. A biopsy is shown below. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

correctAnswer: A. Polypoidal, pink-colored mass with white dots on the surface
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Rhinosporidiosis presents with a leafy, polypoidal, pink to purple in color mass. It is very vascular and bleeds easily to the touch. Its surface is studded with white dots representing the sporangia of protozoa- Mulberry/ Strawberry tumors.

Rhinosporidiosis:

  • It is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by an aquatic protozoan- Rhinosporidium seeberi.
  • It is a water-borne disease- contaminated water of pond usually with cow dung.

Clinical Features: (Option A)

  • Blood-tinged nasal discharge
  • Nasal block
  • Epistaxis
  • Leafy, polypoidal, pink to purple colored mass attached to the nasal septum or lateral wall.
  • Very vascular mass and bleeds easily on touch.
  • White dots are studded on its surface representing the sporangia.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Rhinosporidiosis


Soft, dark red, pedunculated, or sessile mass (Option B):

  • Capillary haemangioma presents as a soft, dark red, pedunculated, or sessile tumor arising from the anterior part of the nasal septum.
  • It is usually smooth but can ulcerate and present with recurrent epistaxis and nasal obstruction.

Pale polypoidal mass (Option C):

  • Inverted papilloma presents as a pale polypoidal mass resembling a simple nasal polyp or polypi.
  • It manifests almost always unilaterally with nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis.

Firm, rounded, yellowish mass with blood vessels on the surface (Option D):

  • Schwannoma is a benign tumor arising from the Schwann cells of the nerve sheath.
  • It presents a rounded, firm, yellowish-colored mass with blood vessels on its surface.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition- Page 185, 186, 236, 237
lessonTitle: Granulomatous Lesions, Congenital Anomalies, and Nasal Polyps

Soft, dark red, pedunculated or sessile mass

question: A 42-year-old man presents with a long-standing history of nasal obstruction, recurrent nasal bleeding, and mass protruding from his nasal cavity. He reports frequent swimming in freshwater ponds. Which of the following findings on clinical examination is most characteristic of rhinosporidiosis?

correctAnswer: A. Prolonged course of tetracycline and streptomycin
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation with histopathology showing Mikulicz cells and a positive test for Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis is consistent with rhinoscleroma.
  • The primary treatment is combined streptomycin and tetracycline for a minimum duration of 4-6 weeks.

Treatment of Rhinoscleroma:

Medical therapy:

  • Streptomycin + tetracycline for a minimum duration of 4-6 weeks. (Option A)
  • After 1 month it is repeated if necessary.
  • Treatment is stopped only if two consecutive cultures from the biopsy material are negative.
  • To reduce fibrosis steroids can be combined (Option C)

Surgery: (Option D)

  • Surgical debridement, laser ablation, and correction of sclerotic defects.
  • These are considered only secondary to antibiotic therapy.

Amphotericin B (Option B): This antifungal is used to treat fungal infections like aspergillosis and mucormycosis. It is not used to treat rhinoscleroma, a bacterial infection.



Reference:
  1. Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 181, 183, 184

question: A 45-year-old woman has a history of progressive nasal obstruction, recurrent nosebleeds, and crusting. On examination, she has a nasal deformity with a firm mass in the nasal cavity. A biopsy of the mass shows Mikulicz cells and is positive for Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. What is the most appropriate treatment strategy for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of nasal obstruction, crusting, and progressive nodular nasal swelling is most consistent with rhinoscleroma.
  • It is caused by the bacteria Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis.
  • Mikulicz cells are large, foamy histiocytes filled with bacteria, which are characteristic of Rhinoscleroma.

[[figure-1]]

Diagnosis of Rhinoscleroma:

  • Confirmatory diagnosis is done by biopsy
  • On biopsy/ HPE:
    • Infiltration of submucosa with plasma cells, lymphocytes, eosinophils, Mikulicz cells, and Russell bodies.
    • Mikulicz cells: Large foamy cells with a central nucleus and vacuolated cytoplasm containing bacilli.
    • Russell bodies: Eosinophilic inclusions in plasma cells. It forms due to the accumulation of immunoglobulins secreted by the plasma cells.

[[figure-2]]

  • Culture from the biopsy

Psammoma Bodies (Option A): These are concentric, laminated calcifications often seen in certain tumors, such as papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous papillary ovarian carcinoma, meningioma, and mesotheliomas. They are not characteristic of rhinoscleroma.

Aschoff Bodies (Option C): These are specific granulomatous lesions found in the myocardium in cases of acute rheumatic fever. They are not associated with nasal pathology or rhinoscleroma.

Verocay Bodies (Option D): These are palisading arrangements of Schwann cells and nuclei within Antoni A areas of schwannomas (neurilemomas), often appearing as alternating cellular and anuclear zones. They are a feature of neural sheath tumors, not infectious granulomas like rhinoscleroma.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 181

question: A 35-year-old woman from a rural area has nasal obstruction, crusting, and a history of progressive nasal swelling over the past several months. On examination, nodular masses in the nasal cavity are noted. A biopsy is done and shown below. Which of the following histopathological findings is characteristic of the condition in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D) Asch’s forceps

Explanation:

The instrument shown in the above image is Asch’s forceps, an angulated forceps that is used in the closed reduction of the nasal septum.

Tilley’s forceps (Option A), also known as Tilley’s dressing forceps, have a box joint. They are used for nasal packing, ear dressing, and removing foreign bodies from the nose.


Walsham’s forceps (Option B) are straight and covered by rubber tubing. They are used to disimpact and reduce nasal bone fractures.

Hartmann’s forceps (Option C) have a screw joint, and the jaw is serrated and grooved. It is used the same as Tilley’s forceps, i.e., for nasal packing, ear dressing, and removing foreign bodies from the nose.

question: During a closed reduction procedure for a nasal septum, the surgeon selected a forceps, as depicted in the image, and asked the intern to identify it. What is the name of these forceps?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Clinical triad of unilateral nasal obstruction, foul-smelling discharge, and blood staining in a young child is highly suggestive of a Nasal Foreign Body.

Children often insert small objects like beads, seeds, or foam into the nasal cavity, which triggers an intense mucosal inflammatory response and secondary bacterial infection. The resulting tissue necrosis and suppuration produce the characteristic fetid odor and occasionally lead to mucosal erosions that cause blood-tinged discharge.


Atrophic rhinitis (Option B) causes a characteristic foul smell (ozena) and greenish crusting, but it is a bilateral process and more frequently diagnosed in young adults.

Fungal sinusitis (Option C) can cause unilateral purulent discharge and sinus pressure, but it is a rare diagnosis in a healthy 4-year-old and presents with thicker, peanut-butter-like mucus.

Rhinolith (Option D) occurs when a long-standing, neglected foreign body becomes a nucleus for the deposition of calcium and magnesium salts, forming a hard, stony mass that is more common in older children and adults.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 189.
question: A 5-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a persistent, malodorous, blood-tinged discharge localized to the left nasal cavity. Physical examination is difficult due to the patient's irritability. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the elderly population, Hypertension is recognized as the most common systemic cause of epistaxis. Chronic high blood pressure leads to degenerative changes in the arterial walls, such as arteriosclerosis, which makes the vessels brittle and less capable of contracting.

While local factors like a dry mucosa or trauma are frequent, the presence of hypertension often makes the bleeding more profuse, posterior in location, and significantly harder to control, requiring intensive management of both the bleeding and the blood pressure.

Medication (Option A): Use of anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents (e.g., Aspirin, Warfarin) is common in the elderly and can exacerbate bleeding; they are considered a predisposing factor rather than the primary systemic cause.

Carcinoma (Option B): Malignancy of the nose or paranasal sinuses can cause blood-stained discharge or epistaxis, but it is a less common cause compared to cardiovascular associations.

Idiopathic (Option C): Although idiopathic remains a frequent classification when no clear cause is found in the general population, the elderly demographic has a much stronger and specific association with hypertensive vascular disease.



Reference:
  1. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25558573/
  2. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/270121675_Epistaxis_in_geriatric_patients

explanationHtml:

The internal carotid artery (ICA) contributes to the nasal vasculature via the ophthalmic artery, which enters the orbit and gives off the anterior ethmoidal (Marker 1) and posterior ethmoidal arteries (Marker 2).

Marker 1 and Marker 2 in the provided image correspond to the anterior ethmoidal and posterior ethmoidal arteries, which are the ICA-derived vessels supplying the superior nasal cavity. These arteries provide essential blood supply to the ethmoid air cells and the superior aspects of the nasal septum and lateral wall.


External carotid system: Majority of the blood supply to the respiratory portion of the nasal cavity.

  • Sphenopalatine (Marker 3 ruled out)

question: Which of the marked structures represent branches originating from the Internal Carotid Artery system?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The artery marked as 3 represents the Sphenopalatine artery, the terminal branch of the maxillary artery.

  • It enters the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen at the posterior end of the middle turbinate.
  • It is designated as the artery of epistaxis because it provides the majority of the blood supply to the nasal mucosa.
  • In cases of intractable posterior epistaxis, endoscopic ligation of this specific vessel (ESPAL) is the definitive surgical management to control the haemorrhage.

Other structures marked in the diagram are as follows:

  • 1 - Anterior ethmoidal artery
  • 2 - Posterior ethmoidal artery
  • 4 - Greater palatine artery

[[figure-1]]

question: Identify the artery that is clinically recognised as the artery of epistaxis.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The posterior ethmoidal artery does not contribute to Kiesselbach’s plexus

  • Instead, it supplies the superior and posterior parts of the nasal cavity.
  • Kiesselbach’s plexus is a rich arterial anastomosis located in Little’s area on the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum and is the most common site of anterior epistaxis.
  • It receives contributions from both the internal and external carotid systems.

The arterial components included are:

  • Internal Carotid artery:
    • Anterior ethmoidal artery (Option C ruled out)
  • External Carotid Artery
    • Septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery (Option A ruled out)
    • Greater palatine artery (Option B ruled out)
    • Septal branch of the superior labial artery

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 205.
question: Which of the following arteries does not contribute to the formation of Kiesselbach's plexus?

correctAnswer: B. Anteroinferior part of the septum
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Little’s area is the most common site of anterior epistaxis, especially in children and young adults. It is located in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum, just above the vestibule, near the mucocutaneous junction.

[[figure-1]]

  • This region overlies the anterior cartilaginous septum and contains Kiesselbach’s plexus, a rich vascular anastomosis formed by septal branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine, and superior labial arteries.
  • Because of its superficial vessels, Little’s area is particularly vulnerable to digital trauma, mucosal drying, upper respiratory infections, and local irritation, making it the usual source of recurrent mild anterior nosebleeds.
  • In contrast, posterior epistaxis is more often seen in older adults and is usually more severe.


Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 205.
question: A 25-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of mild, self-limiting anterior epistaxis. On anterior rhinoscopy, a highly vascular area is noted on the nasal septum. In which anatomical location is this region situated?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given scenario is a blowout fracture showing a teardrop sign in a CT scan.

Blowout Fracture (fracture of floor of orbit):

Cause

A large blunt object striking the eye globe.

Location

The floor of the orbit.

Clinical features

  • Ecchymosis of the lid, conjunctiva and sclera.
  • Enophthalmos with inferior displacement of the eyeball.
  • Diplopia (displacement of the eyeball or entrapment of inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles).
  • Hypoaesthesia or anaesthesia of the cheek and upper lip (infraorbital nerve involvement).
  • Presence of periorbital emphysema and oedema.
  • Restricted eye movement (entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle)

Forced duction test
  • To determine if the inferior rectus muscle is impinged at the fracture site.
  • A small forceps is used to release the muscle from the fracture site. Improvement in eye movement suggests muscle impingement.

Diagnosis

X-ray and CT scan shows the characteristic “teardrop” sign due to herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus.

Management

  • Reduction (Indicated if associated with zygomatic/maxillary fractures or significant functional impairment)
  • Surgery is required for persistent diplopia, enophthalmos, or muscle entrapment. It typically involves reconstructing the orbital floor to correct anatomical displacement and relieve symptoms.

Lateral rectus (Option B), Medial rectus (Option C) and Superior oblique (Option D) are not entrapped in blowout fracture.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 215
question: A 22-year-old woman reports experiencing pain, swelling, blurred vision, and double vision following a facial injury from a basketball. Based on the clinical presentation and radiograph findings, which extraocular muscle is most likely restricted, leading to impaired eye movement?

explanationHtml:

Explanation:

The most common site of mandibular fracture is the condylar region.

Fracture of Mandible

  • Fractures of the mandible have been classified according to the Dingman classification, as per their location as shown in the figure below,

Fig: Dingman classification

[[figure-1]]

  • The sequence of mandibular fracture sites, from most common to least common, is as follows:
    • Condylar region (weakest part of the mandible) (Option A)
    • Angle of mandible (Option B)
    • Body of mandible (Option D)
    • Symphysis menti. (Option C)
  • Clinical features:
    • Pain and trismus (most common)
    • Malocclusion of teeth and deviation of the jaw to the opposite side on opening the mouth (in case of displaced fragments)



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page 216, 217.
question: A 26-year-old male presents with jaw pain, swelling, difficulty opening his mouth, and trouble chewing after being struck in the face during a fight. What is the most common site for mandibular fractures?

correctAnswer: B. Le Fort type II fracture
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario is indicative of a Le Fort type II or pyramidal fracture, a type of maxillary fracture with the hallmark sign of a hanging maxilla.

Classification of Fractures of the maxilla:

Le Fort I

(Option A)

(Option B)

Le Fort III

(Option C)

Also known as

Note: can cause infraorbital nerve injury.

Management of maxillary fractures:

After diagnosing the fracture through clinical examination and x-ray, fixation of maxillary fractures can be achieved by:

  • Interdental wiring
  • Intermaxillary wiring using arch bars.
  • Open reduction and interosseous wiring as in zygomatic fractures.
  • Wire slings from the frontal bone, zygoma or infraorbital rim to the teeth or arch bars.


Tripod fracture (Option D), also known as a zygomatic fracture, involves three fracture lines: zygomaticofrontal, zygomaticotemporal, and zygomaticomaxillary. The characteristic features include depression of the zygomatic arch, localised pain aggravated by talking and chewing, and trismus (restricted jaw movement). It may cause infraorbital nerve injury.

[[figure-2]]

question: A 45-year-old male presents with severe facial pain, swelling, and trouble closing his mouth after a high-impact fall. Examination shows a hanging maxilla. What type of fracture does this indicate?

The clinical scenario is indicative of a Le Fort type I or Guerin’s fracture, characterised by the hallmark signs of a hanging palate and hanging teeth, with the absence of CSF rhinorrhea.

Features of Le Fort I Fracture:

  • A type of maxillary fracture, also known as Guerin’s fracture or Transverse maxillary fracture. (Option B)
  • The fracture line is horizontal and runs above and parallel to the palate, crossing the lower nasal septum, maxillary antra, and pterygoid plates. (Option D)

Fig: Le Fort I Fracture

[[figure-1]]

  • It is characterised by hanging palate and hanging teeth.
  • CSF rhinorrhea is absent.
  • Guerin’s sign is observed, which is characterised by bluish discolouration of the palate due to rupture of the Greater palatine artery. (Option A)

Fig: Guerin’s sign

question: A 32-year-old female involved in a car accident presents to the emergency department with a hanging palate and hanging teeth after her face collided with the dashboard. All of the following are true regarding this type of fracture, except:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The sphenopalatine artery, a terminal branch of the maxillary artery, is commonly involved in posterior nasal bleeding. It supplies the posterior part of the nasal cavity, including the posterior nasal septum and lateral walls.

Total Blood Supply to the Nasal Cavity:

  1. External Carotid Artery System:
    • Sphenopalatine Artery(AKA artery of Epistaxis): A terminal branch of the maxillary artery supplying the nasal septum and lateral nasal wall.
    • Greater Palatine Artery: A branch of the maxillary artery contributes to the supply of the hard palate and lower part of the nasal septum.
    • Superior Labial Artery: A branch of the facial artery supplies the anterior nasal septum, particularly Little’s area.
  2. Internal Carotid Artery System:
    • Anterior Ethmoidal Artery: A branch of the ophthalmic artery that supplies the anterior and superior nasal cavity.
    • Posterior Ethmoidal Artery is also a branch of the ophthalmic artery; it supplies the upper posterior portion of the nasal cavity.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

question: A 55-year-old patient presents with recurrent bleeding. Diagnostic imaging reveals that the bleeding is from the posterior nasal cavity. Which artery, derived from the maxillary artery, is most likely responsible for this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Closed reduction after oedema subsides
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Closed reduction after oedema subsides is the preferred approach as it is both effective and less invasive than open reduction.
  • Edema can interfere with accurate closed reduction (Option A ruled out). It is best to wait until swelling subsides, typically 5-7 days, before performing closed reduction.

Management of Nasal Fractures:

Diagnosis
  • Physical Examination is the best method for diagnosing nasal fractures. Look for signs such as swelling, periorbital ecchymosis, tenderness, nasal deformity, crepitus, epistaxis, and nasal obstruction.
  • X-rays: These may not always reveal fractures. Necessary views include Waters’ view, lateral views, and occlusal view.

Treatment
  • Simple Fractures: Generally, no treatment is required if there's no displacement. Monitor for natural healing.
  • Closed Reduction:
    • Timing: Ideally performed before significant edema develops or after it subsides (Option C) (usually 5-7 days).
    • Technique:
      • Use a straight blunt elevator guided by digital manipulation from outside for depressed fractures.
      • Reduce laterally displaced nasal bridge with firm digital pressure in the opposite direction.
      • Disimpaction of impacted fragments requires Walsham or Asch’s forceps.
      • Septal fractures and hematomas should be managed with Asch’s forceps.
    • Packing: Unstable fractures require intranasal packing and external splintage.
  • Open Reduction (Option B): Rarely required early & Considered if closed methods fail, for certain septal injuries & if a patient presents late.
  • Correction of Deformities: May need rhinoplasty or septorhinoplasty for healed deformities from trauma.

Nasal packing and observation (Option D) may help manage bleeding or minor fractures but does not address the alignment of the fractured bones.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page - 213
question: A 30-year-old patient presents with a nasal fracture from a frontal blow during a sports accident. The nasal bridge is deviated with swelling and bruising. The patient reports nasal obstruction, but no other facial fractures are noted. What is the most appropriate management approach?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Nasal fractures: Nasal fractures constitute about 40% of all facial fractures and are often accompanied by other facial injuries. Prompt management is crucial to prevent cosmetic and functional deformities.


Classification:

  • Nature of Injury: Most fractures result from lateral forces (>66%), with frontal impacts causing fewer injuries.
  • Extent of Deformity: A five-point grading system assesses lateral deviation
    • Grade 0: No deviation
    • Grade 1: Deviation <50% of nose width
    • Grade 2: Deviation 50%-100% of nose width
    • Grade 3: Deviation >100% of nose width
    • Grade 4: Bones almost touching the cheek
  • Pattern of Fracture: Fractures are categorised into three classes based on severity and treatment requirements:

Class I (Chevallet Fracture)

Class II (Jarjavay Fracture)

Class III (Naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture)

Cause

Blows from below

Impacts directed from the front

High-velocity trauma

Fracture Line

Vertical fracture from the anterior nasal spine upwards to the junction of the bony and cartilaginous dorsum of the nose.

Horizontal fracture starting just above the anterior nasal spine, running backwards just above the junction of septal cartilage and vomer.

Involves external buttresses of the nose and ethmoid labyrinth.

Pig-like appearance with foreshortened, saddled nose.

Clinical Relations
  • Assess for nasal obstruction and deformity.
  • Significant deformity might only develop later, especially in children.
  • Check for deviation greater than half the width of the nose, which may indicate a septal fracture.
  • Requires reduction of both nasal and septal fractures.
  • Look for signs of more severe injuries, such as CSF leaks, multiple dural tears, and potential cerebral herniation.
  • Evaluate for orbital and skull base involvement.


Reference:
  1. Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology and Head & Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 1184, 1185
  2. PL Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 171

Type of Fracture

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D) Young's Operation

Explanation:

Young's operation involves the permanent surgical closure of the nostrils and is considered a last-resort treatment for severe, persistent bleeding in patients with Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT) when other methods have failed.

Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT): (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease)

  • An autosomal dominant condition characterised by abnormal blood vessels in the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Common symptoms include telangiectasia, arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), and aneurysms.
    • Recurrent epistaxis (nosebleeds) occurs in 93% of cases.
  • Management:
    • Initial Treatments: Nasal packing (Option B), cautery, antifibrinolytics, systemic or topical estrogens.
    • Advanced Treatments: Coagulative lasers (Nd, Argon, KTP532) (Option C), septal dermoplasty (Option A), ligation, and embolization.
    • Last Resort: Young's operation, involving permanent surgical closure of the nostrils, is used for severe, persistent bleeding. Despite the significant disability it may cause, it often improves quality of life by reducing bleeding.


Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page - 210
  2. Scott Brown ENT, 8th Edition Page - 1180
question: A 45-year-old patient with Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia presents with recurrent epistaxis despite conservative measures. Which of the following treatments is considered the last resort for severe, persistent bleeding that has not responded?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Lynch-Howarth incision is the most appropriate for accessing the medial wall of the orbit to ligate the anterior ethmoidal artery.

  • The incision is made along the medial canthus of the eye, extending along the inner corner of the eyelid.
  • It allows direct access to this area where the artery can be effectively controlled.
  • Advantages: Direct Access & Minimally invasive.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Lynch-Howarth incision

Sublabial Incision (Option B) is typically used to access the maxillary sinus and palatal areas, but it is unsuitable for reaching the anterior ethmoidal artery.

Weber-Ferguson Incision (Option D) is a broader incision used for extensive access to the nasal cavity and maxilla, but not specifically for the anterior ethmoidal artery.

Gullwing Incision (Option C) is not commonly used in ENT procedures and is primarily used for cosmetic or reconstructive procedures involving the eyelids or facial skin.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page - 210
question: Which of the following incisions is most appropriate when ligating the anterior ethmoidal artery to control anterior epistaxis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

If a bleeding point is identified in the anterior epistaxis that persists despite initial first aid measures, cauterization with silver nitrate is the most appropriate next step.

Embolization and TESPAL (Temporal Endoscopic Surgery for Posterior Anterior Ligament) are reserved for more severe or posterior bleeding.

Management of Epistaxis:

First Line:

(Direct therapy)
  • First Aid:
    • Hippocrates method: Pinch the nose with the thumb and index finger for about 5 minutes to control bleeding, especially from Little’s area.
    • Trotter’s Method: Have the patient sit forward over a basin to spit blood and breathe through the mouth. Apply cold compresses to induce vasoconstriction.
  • Cauterization:
    • Indication: Effective for anterior epistaxis when the bleeding point is identified.
    • Apply topical anaesthesia and cauterize with silver nitrate or electrocautery.

Second Line: (Indirect therapy)
  • Anterior Nasal Packing: Clear the nasal cavity of blood clots, localise the bleeding site, and pack with ribbon gauze soaked in liquid paraffin. The packing may need to stay for 24-72 hours with systemic antibiotics to prevent infection.
  • Posterior Nasal Packing:
    • Use a cone-shaped gauze pack and a rubber catheter or nasal balloon. The pack is guided into the nasopharynx, with an anterior nasal pack to stabilize.
    • Patients need to be hospitalised & balloons with separate bulbs for the postnasal space and nasal cavity are used.

Third Line:

(Surgical Interventions)
  • Ligation of Vessels:
    • Maxillary Artery: Ligation via Caldwell-Luc operation for uncontrollable posterior epistaxis.
    • Ethmoidal Arteries: for bleeding from above the middle turbinate.
    • External Carotid: Ligate above the superior thyroid artery for persistent bleeding from the external carotid system.
  • Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation (TESPAL): Locate and ligate the Sphenopalatine artery (Artery of Epistaxis) to control refractory posterior bleeding. (Option D)

Fourth Line (Embolization)

(Option C)

Performed by an interventional radiologist through femoral artery catheterisation using absorbable gel foam or coils. It may require bilateral embolisation for unilateral bleeding.

Note: The order of ligation is 1. sphenopalatine 2. maxillary 3. ethmoid/ECA

Anterior nasal packing (Option A) is a first-line treatment for persistent anterior epistaxis. However, if a specific bleeding point is identified and persists, cauterisation is more effective than packing.



Reference:
  1. Scott Brown ENT, 8th Edition Page - 1180
  2. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page - 208,210
question: A 30-year-old patient presents with anterior epistaxis after sustaining a nose injury. Despite initial first aid measures, bleeding continues, and a bleeding point is identified. What is the most appropriate next step if the bleeding persists?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In children and young adults, the most common cause of epistaxis is nasal trauma, such as nose-picking or minor injuries.
  • The most common site for this is Kiesselbach's plexus (Little’s area), located in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum.

Causes and Common Sites of Epistaxis in Different Age Groups

Age Group

Most Common Cause

Most Common Site

Children/Young Adults

Nasal trauma (nose-picking)

Kiesselbach's plexus (anterior nasal septum)

Older Adults

Hypertension

Woodruff’s plexus (posterior nasal cavity)

All Ages

Infections or dryness

Kiesselbach's plexus (anterior nasal septum)

Hereditary Conditions

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia

Multiple sites in the nasal cavity

Hypertension (Option A) is a common cause of epistaxis; it is typically seen in older adults, not children.

Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Option C) is a genetic condition that causes recurrent epistaxis due to abnormal blood vessels but is a less common cause in children compared to trauma.

Coagulation Disorder (Option D) can lead to epistaxis, but they are not as common as local trauma in children and young adults.



Reference:

PL Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page 205, 206.
question: A 10-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of mild epistaxis. On examination, the bleeding site is found in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum. What could be the most common cause of epistaxis in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The sphenopalatine artery is the most common source of posterior epistaxis in hypertensive patients.
  • It supplies the lateral nasal wall and posterior nasal cavity.
  • Endoscopic ligation or cauterization of the sphenopalatine artery is the preferred treatment for severe, uncontrolled posterior nasal bleeding.

Posterior Epistaxis

Bleeding that flows backwards into the throat

Kiesselbach's plexus
(Anterior ethmoidal artery, Septal branch of Superior labial artery, Septal branch of Sphenopalatine artery, Greater palatine artery)
  • Sphenopalatine artery (Most common)
  • Posterior ethmoidal artery

Site

Little's area (anteroinferior nasal septum)

Posterior or superior parts of the nasal cavity (e.g.Woodruff's plexus)

Age Group

Mostly in children and young adults

More common in adults over 40 years old

Usual Cause

Trauma (e.g., nose picking, injury)

Spontaneous, often associated with hypertension and arteriosclerosis

Management

Local pressure and conservative measures

Postnasal pack, more aggressive treatment often required



Reference:

PL Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Pages 494, 207, 208
question: A 65-year-old male with hypertension presents with profuse nasal bleeding from the posterior part of the nasal cavity, unresponsive to pinching and anterior packing. Nasal endoscopy shows bleeding behind the middle turbinate. What is the likely source of bleeding and appropriate management?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Retrocolumellar vein

Explanation:

The Retrocolumellar vein is located in the anterior septum of the nasal cavity, specifically in the region just behind the columella. It is part of the venous drainage system of the anterior nasal septum, an area prone to anterior epistaxis in young people.

[[figure-1]]

Veinous drainage of Nasal cavity

The greater palatine vein (Option A) and sphenopalatine vein (Option B) are associated with posterior parts of the nasal cavity and palate and are less likely to be involved in anterior epistaxis.

The superior ophthalmic vein (Option D) is located in the orbit and drains structures of the eye, not typically involved in nasal bleeding.

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page 205
question: A 28-year-old patient presents with recurrent episodes of mild anterior epistaxis, mainly from the nasal septum. Upon examination, the source of the bleeding is traced to a venous structure near the anterior septum. Which of the following veins is most likely responsible for the bleeding?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A) Kiesselbach’s plexus


Explanation:

  • Kiesselbach’s plexus, also known as Little's area, is a highly vascularised region in the anteroinferior portion of the nasal septum, where multiple arteries converge.
  • It is the most common site of anterior epistaxis, especially in children and young adults.

[[figure-1]]


Vessels involved in forming the plexus:

Artery

Branch of

Sphenopalatine artery

Maxillary artery

Anterior ethmoidal artery

Ophthalmic artery (from internal carotid artery)

Greater palatine artery

Maxillary artery

Superior labial artery

Facial artery (from external carotid artery)

Note: The posterior ethmoidal artery is not part of this plexus


Clinical Significance:

  • Anterior epistaxis occurs most often in children and young adults, usually due to trauma (nose-picking), dry air, infections, or irritants.
  • Epistaxis in this area is typically mild and self-limiting and can be controlled with local pressure or simple cauterization.


Woodruff’s plexus (Option B) is a venous plexus located on the posterior lateral wall of the nasal cavity, particularly in the inferior nasal meatus. It is often involved in cases of posterior epistaxis. Its primary arterial contributors are the sphenopalatine artery, ascending pharyngeal artery, and posterior nasal branches of the sphenopalatine artery.


Pterygoid plexus (Option C) is a venous plexus located in the infratemporal fossa behind the maxilla. It is primarily involved in draining blood from the face and orbit.


Cavernous sinus (Option D) is a large venous sinus located at the base of the skull on either side of the pituitary gland. It is not involved in epistaxis but drains blood from the brain and orbits.



Reference:

PL Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 205
question: A 35-year-old patient presents with frequent episodes of anterior epistaxis, which are mild and self-limiting. Examination reveals the bleeding site to be in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum. Which vascular network is most likely involved in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In maxillofacial trauma, the first priority is ensuring an adequate airway to prevent obstruction, following the ABC protocol (Airway, Breathing, Circulation).

Facial Trauma - Management

ATLS (Advanced Trauma Life Support) protocol is followed, prioritizing Airway → Breathing → Circulation → Disability → Exposure (ABCDE)

Airway management (Option B)

Highest priority

  • Obstruction may occur from loss of skeletal support, swelling, or aspiration of blood/foreign bodies.
  • Secure airway via intubation or tracheostomy

Breathing
  • Assess respiratory rate, effort, oxygenation
  • Provide supplemental oxygen
  • Check for pneumothorax, hemothorax, chest injuries

Circulation (Option C ruled out)
  • Facial injuries may bleed profusely.
  • Check pulse, BP, skin perfusion
  • Control bleeding with pressure, ligation, or tourniquet
  • Give IV fluids or transfusion if needed

Disability

Assess consciousness (GCS), pupils, motor function (Option A ruled out)

Exposure

  • Fully expose patient to identify all injuries
  • Prevent hypothermia.


Fracture reduction (Option D) is a component of definitive surgical care and is never performed during the primary care or resuscitation phase of trauma management.



Reference:
  1. PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 211.
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547757/
question: A construction worker falls from a height, sustaining facial and jaw injuries. What is the first priority in his initial management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Nasal bone is the most frequently fractured bone of the facial skeleton. This high incidence is due to its prominent and central position on the face, which makes it the first point of contact in many injuries, combined with its relative structural fragility compared to the thicker bones like the mandible or the maxilla. Nasal fractures account for nearly 40% to 50% of all facial bone fractures.

Frequency of Facial Fractures:

  • Nasal Bone: Most common due to its projection and lack of support. (Option B)
  • Mandible: Condylar fractures are the most common in mandible fractures; followed by fractures of the angle, body, and symphysis. (Option D ruled out)
  • Zygoma fracture, aka tripod fracture, is the second most common fractured bone in maxillofacial injuries due to lateral impact trauma. (Option A ruled out)
  • Maxilla: These fractures (Le Fort I, II, III) are generally less frequent as they require a high-velocity impact to break the sturdy maxillary framework. (Option C ruled out)


Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 212.
question: Which bone of the face shows the greatest frequency of fractures?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The diagnosis is a Fracture of the zygoma, aka Tripod fracture. This injury typically occurs due to a high-impact blunt force to the malar eminence, resulting in fractures at the zygomaticofrontal suture, zygomaticomaxillary suture, and the zygomatic arch.

Tripod fracture:

  • Malar flattening: Sunken/flattened cheek due to zygomatic displacement
  • Step deformity: Palpable irregularity at infraorbital rim or zygomaticofrontal suture
  • Trismus: Limited mouth opening from zygomatic arch impinging on coronoid process
  • Infraorbital nerve anesthesia: Numbness of cheek, upper lip, side of nose
  • Diplopia: Due to inferior rectus muscle entrapment
  • Periorbital ecchymosis: Bruising and swelling around the eye (“black eye”).

Fracture of nasal bone (Option A) involves the central midface and presents with epistaxis and crepitus over the nasal bridge.

Fracture of maxilla (Option B): Le Fort fractures of the maxilla presents with dental malocclusion and a floating palate rather than the isolated lateral facial collapse seen in zygomatic injuries.

Isolated blow-out fracture (Option C) involves a fracture of the orbital floor with diplopia, enophthalmos, and orbital emphysema.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 214.
question: A professional boxer is brought to the emergency department after sustaining a heavy blow to the lateral aspect of his face. Clinical examination reveals a sunken appearance of the cheek, trismus, and a palpable step deformity along the infraorbital rim. The patient also reports double vision on upward gaze. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

CSF rhinorrhea is a hallmark of fractures involving the mid-facial region (Le Fort II and III) or the fronto-ethmoidal complex, where the dura mater is closely adherent to the bone.

Fracture of Zygoma (Tripod Fracture):

  • Malar flattening: Sunken or flat cheek
  • Step deformity: Palpable irregularity at infraorbital rim or zygomaticofrontal suture
  • Trismus: Limited mouth opening from zygomatic arch impinging on coronoid process (Option A ruled out)
  • Infraorbital nerve anesthesia: Numbness of cheek, upper lip, and side of nose
  • Diplopia: Inferior rectus muscle entrapment (Option B ruled out)
  • Periorbital ecchymosis: Bruising and swelling around the eye
  • Oblique palpebral fissure (anti-mongoloid slant): Lateral canthal displacement. (Option D ruled out)


Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 214.
question: Which of the following clinical features is not observed in a patient with a zygomatic complex fracture?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation described - loss of sensation over the lower eyelid, the lateral aspect of the nose, and the ipsilateral upper lip is the classic distribution of the infraorbital nerve, which is a branch of the Maxillary division of the Trigeminal nerve (V2)

Infraorbital nerve:

  • Branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2).
  • Courses through the infraorbital groove and canal in the floor of the orbit, which is almost always involved in zygomatic complex (tripod) fractures.
  • Compression or laceration of the nerve at this site results in anesthesia or paresthesia of the cheek triangle, which includes the lower eyelid, the side of the nose, and the skin and mucous membrane of the upper lip.

Injuries to the infraorbital nerve are characteristic of midface fractures where the fracture line intersects the orbital floor or the infraorbital foramen, leading to sensory loss in the "cheek triangle."

Fracture Type

Common Mechanism

Relation to Infraorbital Nerve

Classic Clinical Signs

Zygomatic Complex (Tripod)

Lateral impact to the cheekbone.

Fracture lines pass through the infraorbital rim/foramen and zygomaticofrontal suture.

Flattened cheek, subconjunctival hemorrhage, and mid-face numbness.

Orbital Floor (Blow-out)

Blunt trauma to the globe (e.g., a baseball or fist).

The nerve is compressed as the orbital floor collapses into the maxillary sinus.

Enophthalmos (sunken eye) and diplopia (double vision) on upward gaze.

Le Fort II (Pyramidal)

Central mid-face impact.

Fracture involves the infraorbital rims bilaterally as it crosses the maxilla.

"Step-off" deformity at the infraorbital rim; CSF rhinorrhea is possible.

Le Fort III (Dysjunction)

Massive high-velocity trauma.

The entire mid-face separates from the skull; the nerve is often damaged at the orbital floor level.

"Dish-face" deformity; massive edema and mobility of the entire middle third of the face.

Direct Maxillary Antrum

Direct strike to the "mustache" area.

The anterior wall of the maxilla is crushed, directly impacting the infraorbital foramen.

Localized swelling, crepitus over the sinus, and upper dental numbness.

Supraorbital nerve (Option A) is a branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1) that provides sensation to the forehead and upper eyelid; it is involved in frontal bone or superior orbital rim fractures.

Lingual nerve (Option C) provides sensory innervation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and is injured in mandibular fractures or third molar extractions.

Facial nerve (Option D) is the seventh cranial nerve responsible for the muscles of facial expression; injury results in motor paralysis (drooping of the face).



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 214.
question: Following a high-impact collision, a patient is diagnosed with a fracture of the zygomatic complex. On sensory testing, he exhibits a complete loss of sensation over the lower eyelid, the lateral aspect of the nose, and the ipsilateral upper lip. Injury to which nerve is responsible for this clinical finding?

correctAnswer: A. Fracture of the floor of the orbit
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Blowout fracture of the orbit occurs when a blunt object, larger than the orbital rim (such as a tennis ball or a fist), strikes the eye, and the force is transmitted to the orbital walls as a hydraulic surge.

Orbital floor is the most common site of fracture because it is extremely thin, particularly medial to the infraorbital groove. This leads to the herniation of orbital fat and the inferior rectus muscle into the maxillary sinus, causing enophthalmos and restricted upward gaze.

Fracture of lateral wall (Option B): Lateral wall is the thickest and strongest wall of the orbit, formulated by the greater wing of the sphenoid and the zygomatic bone rarely involved in blow-out injuries.

Fracture of medial wall (Option C): Medial wall (lamina papyracea) is the second most common site for blow-out fractures.

Fracture of roof of orbit (Option D) is usually associated with high-energy frontal bone trauma and is dangerous due to its proximity to the anterior cranial fossa.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 215.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Orbital cellulitis involves inflammation of the orbital tissues with pain on eye movement and restricted mobility, but without abscess formation. There is no proptosis or pus collection, which is consistent with Stage II of Chandler’s classification.

[[figure-1]]

Chandler’s Classification of Orbital Cellulitis

Stage

Description

Key Features

I - Preseptal cellulitis
(Option A)

Infection confined to the eyelid

Eyelid swelling, no ocular involvement

II - Orbital cellulitis

(Option B)

Infection spreads to the orbit

Pain with eye movement, restricted mobility, no abscess formation

III - Subperiosteal abscess (Option C)

Pus collection beneath periosteum

Localized pus, proptosis, pain on movement, swelling

IV - Orbital abscess (Option D)

Pus collection within the orbital tissues

Severe proptosis, potential vision loss, risk of optic nerve damage

V - Cavernous sinus thrombosis

Spread of infection to the cavernous sinus

Bilateral eye involvement, headache, cranial nerve palsies

question: A 12-year-old patient presents with a history of sinusitis and now has swollen, red eyelids, pain with eye movement,proptosis and restricted extraocular motion. There is no proptosis, and CT imaging shows diffuse inflammation of the orbital tissues without abscess formation. According to Chandler's classification, what is the most likely stage of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

During a total maxillectomy, the surgeon typically removes the hard palate and orbital floor and often involves areas around the ethmoid sinus. However, the zygomatic arch is not typically removed unless the tumor is specifically involved.

Maxillectomy:

Incision: A Weber-Fergusson incision or similar approach is often used to gain access.

Type of Maxillectomy

Structures Removed

Medial Maxillectomy
  • Middle turbinate
  • Inferior turbinate
  • Ethmoid sinus
  • Maxillary sinus.

Infrastructural Maxillectomy

Extends to include the upper alveolar ridge & adjoining hard palate.

Subtotal Maxillectomy

Removal of the entire Maxilla.

Total Maxillectomy

Removal of all the above structures along with the Orbital Floor.

Radical Maxillectomy

Total maxillectomy plus Orbital exenteration.

Bony box resection involves removing the maxilla as a unit containing the tumour to ensure complete excision of cancerous tissues. This approach maintains a clear boundary between the tumour and healthy tissues.



Reference:
  1. Cumming’s Review of Otorhinolaryngology, Page - 98
  2. Scott Brown ENT, 8th Edition, Pages 83, 85
question: During a total maxillectomy for an extensive malignant tumor, the surgeon is required to remove several structures to ensure complete resection. Which of the following structures is not typically removed during this procedure?

correctAnswer: B. Extension to the respiratory part of the nasal cavity.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Extension to the respiratory part of the nasal cavity is categorised as mesostructural in Lederman’s classification.

Lederman's classification divides sinonasal malignancies based on their anatomical location into three categories using two horizontal reference lines:

  • Horizontal Lines of Sebileau: These lines help delineate the categories by passing through the floors of the orbits and the antra.
  • Vertical Lines: Extend down the medial walls of the orbit, separating the ethmoid sinuses and nasal fossa from the maxillary sinuses.

  • [[figure-1]]


    Areas

    Structures Involved

    Prognosis

    Suprastructure
    • Ethmoid
    • Sphenoid (Option C)
    • Frontal sinuses
    • Olfactory area of the nose (Option A).

    Poor prognosis

    Mesostructure
    • Maxillary sinus
    • Respiratory part of the nasal cavity.

    Better prognosis than suprastructural category.

    Infrastructure

    Alveolar process (Option D) of maxilla

    Better Prognosis


Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pages 243,244

Extending to sphenoid sinus and the orbit.

question: A 65-year-old man presents with nasal obstruction, facial swelling, and proptosis. Imaging reveals a malignancy in the Sinonasal region. According to Lederman’s classification, which of the following tumor locations is categorized as mesostructural?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Tumours below Ohngren’s line generally have a better prognosis than those above the line.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Diagrammatic representation of Ohngren's line

Ohngren's Line is an imaginary anatomical plane used in the assessment of sinonasal malignancies (Maxillary).

  • It extends from the medial canthus of the eye to the angle of the mandible.
  • Helps in classifying the extent and prognosis of sinonasal tumors.

Ohngren’s Classification:

  • Suprastructural Tumors (Above Ohngren’s Line):
    • Tumors located above the line, which includes the ethmoid and frontal sinuses.
    • Generally have a poorer prognosis.
    • The involvement of the ethmoid and frontal sinuses often indicates a more advanced disease.
  • Intrastructural Tumors (Below Ohngren’s Line):
    • Tumors located below Ohngren's line, primarily involving the maxillary sinus and nasal cavity.
    • Tumors confined below this line tend to have a better prognosis.
    • They are usually less advanced and less likely to have spread extensively compared to those above the line.


Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 242
question: A 62-year-old man presents with nasal obstruction and facial swelling. Imaging shows a malignancy in the maxillary sinus. The oncologist uses Ohngren’s line to assess the prognosis. According to Ohngren’s line, which tumour location indicates a better prognosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Long-term exposure to hardwood dust has been linked to an increased risk of developing adenocarcinoma, particularly in the sinuses.
  • In contrast, exposure to softwood dust is more specifically associated with an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma.


Malignant Neoplasms of Paranasal Sinuses:

  • Common Sites: Maxillary (M/C), followed by ethmoid, frontal, and sphenoid sinuses.
  • Aetiology: Occupational Risks:
    • Wood dust impairs mucociliary clearance, increasing carcinogenic risk.
      • Hardwoods: Increase risk of adenocarcinoma.
      • Softwoods: Associated with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
    • Nickel Exposure: Increases the risk of sinonasal SCC by 250-fold.
    • Others: Chromium, Polycyclic Hydrocarbons, Aflatoxin, Mustard Gas


Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Option A): While SCC is the most common sinonasal malignancy overall, hardwood dust exposure specifically increases the risk for adenocarcinoma, not SCC.


Small Cell Carcinoma (Option C): Small cell carcinoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumor in this region and has no established occupational link to hardwood dust exposure.


Basal Cell Carcinoma (Option D): Basal cell carcinoma is primarily a skin cancer and is exceedingly rare in the sinonasal mucosa; it has no association with hardwood dust.



Reference:
  1. PL Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 240
  2. Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology and Head & Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 74
question: A 55-year-old male carpenter presents with symptoms of persistent nasal congestion, facial swelling, and occasional nasal bleeding. He has a long history of working in the hardwood furniture industry for 30 years. CT scan reveals findings, as shown in the image. Which type of carcinoma is he most at risk for?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Kadish Classification is the most widely used system for staging olfactory neuroblastoma.

Olfactory Neuroblastoma (Esthesioneuroblastoma):

  • Originates from the Olfactory Epithelium in the upper third of the nasal cavity which is characterised by neuroblastic differentiation and can be locally aggressive with a tendency to invade adjacent structures.
  • Bimodal peaks of incidence (10-20 years & 50-60 years)
  • Symptoms:
    • Early Symptoms: Unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis (nosebleeds).
    • Advanced Symptoms: Tumour invades the orbit or surrounding structures, causing proptosis, headache, epiphora, diplopia, and blurred vision.
    • Metastasis: Lymph node metastases in the neck can occur in 10-15% of cases.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Intranasal or Endoscopic Examination:
      • Reveals a friable, cherry-red, polypoidal mass
      • Highly vascular, so biopsy should be preceded by imaging studies.
    • Imaging Studies:
      • CT Scan: Shows tumour extent, and possible erosion of cribriform plate/orbital wall.
      • MRI: Detects orbital or intracranial extension.
    • Biopsy: Confirms the tumour type; it may be low-grade with pseudorosette formation or high-grade with nuclear pleomorphism but no rosette formation.
  • Treatment: Craniofacial resection, with or without preoperative radiation or chemotherapy, followed by adjuvant radiation for advanced cases.

Kadish Staging System (with Morita’s Modification)

Stage A

Tumour limited to the nasal cavity.

Stage B

Tumour involving the nasal cavity and sinuses.

Stage C

Tumour extending beyond the nasal and paranasal sinuses.

Stage D

Tumor with metastasis to cervical nodes or distant sites.

  • Other Staging Systems:
    • Morita’s Staging System
    • Dulguerov and Calcaterra Staging System

Breslow Classification (Option B) is used for staging melanoma based on the thickness of the tumor.

Ann Arbor Staging Classification (Option C) is used for staging lymphomas.

Gleason Classification (Option D) is used for grading prostate cancer based on the pattern of tumor cells.



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 239
  2. Scott Brown ENT, 8th Edition, Page - 80
question: A 45-year-old patient presents with nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and anosmia. A CT scan reveals an invasive mass in the nasal cavity, and a biopsy confirms the diagnosis of olfactory neuroblastoma. Which classification system is commonly used to stage olfactory neuroblastoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Patient's acute presentation, doughy swelling, and subperiosteal abscess with bone erosion are classic features of Pott's puffy tumor.

Pott's Puffy Tumour:

  • It refers to a subperiosteal abscess or cellulitis of the frontal bone, commonly associated with frontal osteomyelitis.
  • Typically presents with headache, swelling, and sometimes a discharging frontal fistula.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Pott's Puffy Tumour

  • Pus Formation: This can occur externally under the periosteum (resulting in a soft, doughy swelling) or internally as an extradural abscess.
  • Complications:
    • Intracranial Spread: The infection can spread posteriorly, potentially leading to intracranial complications, reported in 30% to 60% of cases.
    • This spread can occur via:
      • Erosion of the posterior table of the frontal bone
      • Septic thrombophlebitis through diploic veins

Frontal Sinus Mucocele (Option A) is a cystic lesion caused by obstructed sinus drainage, leading to mucus accumulation. It presents with gradual swelling, unlike the acute, doughy swelling seen in Pott's puffy tumour.

Frontal Sinus Abscess (Option C) involves localized pus formation and may cause swelling but lacks the diffuse, soft, subperiosteal characteristics of Pott's puffy tumour.

Frontal Sinus Osteoma (Option D) is a benign bone tumour that usually causes localized swelling or obstruction of the sinus and is more often asymptomatic or causes chronic symptoms rather than acute infection.



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pages 232,233
  2. Scott Brown ENT, 8th Edition, Page 1122
question: A 32-year-old patient presents with a history of frontal headache, noticeable swelling on the forehead, and a recent episode of sinusitis. Physical examination reveals a soft, doughy swelling over the frontal bone, and a CT scan shows a subperiosteal abscess with associated bone erosion. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Osteoma: Most common in the frontal sinus.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: X-ray showing Osteoma in frontal sinus

  • Fibrous Dysplasia: Most common in the maxillary sinus.

[[figure-2]]

  • Chronic Rhinosinusoitis with Polyps: Most common in the ethmoid sinuses.

[[figure-3]]

Condition

Definition

Most Common Site

Clinical Features

Management

Osteoma

Benign, slow-growing bony tumor affecting the paranasal sinuses.

Frontal sinus (most common), ethmoid, maxillary

Often asymptomatic; may cause sinus obstruction, mucocele formation, pressure symptoms (headache, orbital involvement).

Observation for asymptomatic cases; surgical excision for deformity, obstruction, or symptomatic cases.

Fibrous Dysplasia

Benign fibro-osseous condition where bone is replaced by fibrous tissue, causing structural weakness and deformity.

Maxillary sinus (most common), ethmoid, frontal

Facial disfigurement, nasal obstruction, eye displacement, facial pain, and swelling.

Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps

Chronic inflammatory condition with nasal polyps formation.

Ethmoid sinuses (most common)

Nasal obstruction, postnasal drip, anosmia/hyposmia, facial pressure, secondary infections, erosion into orbit or brain.

Medical management (corticosteroids, antihistamines, nasal irrigations); surgery (FESS) for obstructive polyps.


Reference:

PL DhingraDiseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page 201,240

question: A 55-year-old male presents with unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and a mass in the right nasal cavity. Nasal endoscopy reveals a mass arising from the lateral nasal wall with displacement of the middle turbinate. Biopsy confirms the diagnosis of inverted papilloma. All of the following are true regarding inverted papilloma except?

  • Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome (SOFS) occurs when the structures passing through the superior orbital fissure are compromised, typically due to infection, trauma, or tumors.
  • One of the most common sources of infection is the sphenoid sinus, which lies close to the fissure.

Fig: Superior Orbital Fissure Anatomy

[[figure-1]]

Feature

Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome (SOFS)

Superior orbital fissure (between lesser and greater wings of sphenoid bone)

Cranial Nerves (CN III, IV, VI,V1)
