explanationHtml:
The maxillary sinus drains into the middle meatus via the ostium located high on its medial wall. When a nasal polyp is present, it can obstruct this drainage pathway, leading to fluid accumulation in the maxillary sinus, as seen on CT.

The maxillary sinus or the Antrum of Highmore, is the largest of the paranasal sinuses, occupying the body of the maxilla.

  • Shape - Pyramidal
  • Size - 15mL
  • Base - toward the lateral wall of the nose
  • Apex - extends into the zygomatic process of the maxillary bone

Relations:

  • Anterior wall: Formed by the facial surface of the maxilla.
  • Posterior wall: Anterior surface of pterygopalatine fossa.
  • Medial wall: Thin and membranous in some areas, this wall borders the middle and inferior meatuses and separates the maxillary sinus from the nasal cavity.
  • Roof: Formed by the floor of the orbit
  • Floor: Located approximately 1 cm below the floor of the nasal cavity, it is formed by the alveolar and palatine processes of the maxilla. Closely related to the roots of the second premolar and first molar teeth. Cavities in these teeth are associated with oro antral fistula.

[[figure-1]]

Arterial supply: Branches of the maxillary artery, specifically the infraorbital artery, greater palatine artery, and the posterior superior alveolar artery.

[[figure-2]]

Venous drainage: Pterygoid venous plexus and the facial vein.

Lymphatic drainage: Submandibular lymph nodes.

Nerve supply: Infraorbital nerve, greater palatine nerve, and the posterior superior alveolar nerve, which are branches of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2).

Other Options:

Ethmoidal Sinus (Option A): Drains into the middle meatus (anterior ethmoids) or superior meatus (posterior ethmoids); obstruction causes ethmoid sinusitis.

Sphenoidal Sinus (Option B): Drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess; obstruction leads to sphenoid sinusitis, often with deep headaches.

Frontal Sinus (Option C): Drains into the middle meatus via the frontonasal duct; obstruction causes frontal sinusitis, often with forehead pain.

Atrophic Rhinitis is a chronic nasal condition characterized by the atrophy of the nasal mucosa, turbinates, and underlying bones, leading to the formation of foul-smelling nasal crusts. The patient presents with greenish-black nasal crusts and a merciful (foul) smell, which is characteristic of ozena (a term for atrophic rhinitis with a fetid odor).

Primary Atrophic Rhinitis:

Aspect

Details

Causes
  • Heredity
  • Endocrine disturbance
  • Racial factors
  • Nutritional deficiency
  • Infective: Klebsiella ozaenae
  • Autoimmune

Clinical Features

And Examination findings
  • Primarily affects females, starts around puberty
  • Foul-smelling nasal discharge; patients are usually unaware of it themselves and have anosmia (merciful anosmia).
  • Paradoxical nasal obstruction despite enlarged nasal chambers.
  • Epistaxis from crust removal.
  • Pale nasal mucosa, atrophied turbinates, potential septal perforation, nasal vestibule dermatitis, saddle nose deformity.
  • Possible extension to pharynx and larynx leading to atrophic pharyngitis and laryngitis.
  • Eustachian tube obstruction and middle ear effusion cause hearing impairment.


Other Options:

Allergic Rhinitis (Option A): Presents with watery rhinorrhea, sneezing, nasal congestion, and itching but not with foul-smelling crusts.

Rhinitis Caseosa (Option C): Characterized by caseous (cheese-like) nasal secretions, often seen in chronic fungal or bacterial infections, but not typically with greenish-black crusts.

Rhinitis Sicca (Option D): Involves dryness of the nasal mucosa due to environmental factors but lacks foul-smelling crust formation.

Explanation:

  • The anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus is called the Holman-Miller Sign
  • This is seen in Juvenile nasal angiofibroma
  • This tumor bleeds excessively because the tumor lacks smooth muscle that can contract.

Examination of Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA)

Anterior Rhinoscopy

Reveals a reddish-purple mass obstructing the nasal passages, often with blood-stained discharge.

Posterior Rhinoscopy

Visualizes a smooth or lobulated mass in the nasopharynx using a small mirror.

Oral Examination

Assesses for tumor extension into the oral cavity, possibly pushing the soft palate downwards.

Neck Palpation

Detects any enlarged lymph nodes, especially in the upper cervical region.

Neurological Examination

Assesses cranial nerve involvement, focusing on eye movements, facial sensation, and hearing.

Digital palpation

Caution, avoid digital palpation of the nasopharyngeal mass to prevent severe bleeding.

Investigations of Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA)

Contrast-Enhanced CT Scan
  • Investigation of choice; shows tumor size, location, and bony involvement.
  • Pathognomonic sign: Holman-Miller sign (bowing of maxillary wall).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)

Evaluates soft tissue and intracranial extension, differentiates between extradural and intradural spread. (Option A ruled out)

Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA)

Visualizes tumor vascularity, identifies feeding vessels and aids in preoperative embolization to reduce surgical blood loss.

Nasopharyngoscopy

Provides a direct view of the tumor, but biopsy is generally avoided due to high bleeding risk. (Option C ruled out)

Audiometry

Assesses hearing loss caused by Eustachian tube obstruction; establishes baseline and monitors post-treatment hearing.

Biopsy

Biopsy is contraindicated due to risk of profuse bleeding.

Incorrect Options:

Outgrown the blood supply (Option A): Outgrown the blood supply is a wrong statement because JNA is an extremely vascular tumor.

Bleeding is from the adjacent invading vessels (Option C): JNA has its blood supply which is most commonly by the internal maxillary artery.

It lacks capsule (Option D): Capsule is associated with the extension of the tumor and not bleeding.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page no: 250

Explanation:

  • The initial management for CSF Rhinorrhea is bed rest with head elevation and avoidance of straining activities.
  • It also includes administration of antibiotics and diuretics.

Treatment of CSF Rhinorrhea

  • Conservative Management:
    • Bed rest, head elevation
    • Stool softeners, avoidance of nose blowing, sneezing, and straining.
    • Prophylactic antibiotics to prevent meningitis
    • Acetazolamide to decrease CSF formation
    • Lumbar drain if indicated
  • Surgical Repair Approaches:
  1. Neurosurgical Intracranial Approach
  2. Extradural Approaches (rarely used):
  • External ethmoidectomy (cribriform plate/ethmoid area)
  • Transseptal sphenoidal approach
  • Osteoplastic flap (frontal sinus leaks)
  1. Transnasal Endoscopic Approach (preferred for anterior cranial fossa and sphenoid sinus):
  • Site identification (e.g., cribriform plate, sphenoid, ethmoid roof)
  • Grafting with fascia, and cartilage for large defects (>2 cm), followed by mucosa placement
  • Use of Surgicel and Gelfoam to further strengthen the area.
  • High-antibiotic nasal packing
  • Lumbar drain for high CSF pressure
  1. Frontal Sinus Leaks:
  • May require osteoplastic flap and sinus obliteration with fat.

Incorrect Options:

FESS (Option A): FESS is not used in the initial management for a patient with CSF Rhinorrhoea.

Administration of steroids (Option B): Administration of steroids is not preferred in the management of CSF Rhinorrhoea.

Immediate surgical repair without initial medical management (Option D): Immediate surgical repair without initial medical management is not preferred in management of CSF Rhinorrhea.

  • This condition is often referred to as anterior ethmoidal neuralgia or a form of contact-point headache.

Explanation:

  • The most common cause of CSF rhinorrhea is trauma, and the most common site of CSF leak (CSF Rhinorrhoea) is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, which is the weakest part of the bone.

Common Sites of CSF Rhinorrhea

Anterior cranial fossa

Middle cranial fossa

Temporal bone fracture
  • Cribriform plate(most common)
  • Roof of ethmoid air cells
  • Frontal sinus

Sphenoid sinus(following trauma)

CSF reaches the middle ear, escaping through the eustachian tube into the nose(CSF otorhinorrhea)

Aetiology

  • Trauma (Most common): Accidental or surgical (e.g., sinus surgery, nasal polypectomy, skull base surgery).
  • Inflammations: Mucocoeles, fungal infections, osteomyelitis, sinus polyposis.
  • Neoplasms: Benign and malignant tumours invading the skull base.
  • Congenital: Meningocele, meningoencephaloceles, gliomas with skull base defects.
  • Idiopathic: Spontaneous leaks with no known cause.

Investigations for CSF Rhinorrhea

  • Handkerchief test (Halo sign): Simple bedside test; CSF forms clear halo around blood spot.
  • Beta-2 transferrin: Gold standard biochemical test; highly specific for CSF.
  • High-Resolution CT (HRCT): Identifies bony defects in skull base.
  • CT Cisternography: Contrast-enhanced; precise localization of active CSF leaks.
  • MRI Cisternography: Non-invasive; useful for identifying meningoceles/encephaloceles.
  • Fluorescein Test: Intrathecal dye injection; helps in intraoperative leak localization.

Incorrect Options:

Options A, B & D: Hearing loss, visual loss, and diplopia are not the symptoms of trauma (fracture) to the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

Rhinosporidiosis:

  • It is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by an aquatic protistan protozoa- Rhinosporidium seeberi.

Trophic stage → Development of sporangium → Release of endospores

  • Leafy, polypoidal, pink to purple colored mass attached to the nasal septum or lateral wall.
  • Very vascular mass and bleeds easily on touch.
  • White dots are studded on its surface representing the sporangia.

Incorrect Options:

Rhinoscleroma (Option B): Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by the bacterium Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. It is characterized by the formation of fibrotic nodules in the nose and other respiratory passages as shown below. Histopathology shows Miculicz cells (large foam cells with central nucleus and cytoplasm with the bacilli) and Russell bodies (cells with eccentric nucleus and eosinophilic cytoplasm).

Rhinophyma (Option C): Rhinophyma is a condition characterized by progressive enlargement of the nose due to sebaceous gland hyperplasia as shown below. It is typically associated with acne rosacea.

Nasal polyp (Option D): Nasal polyps are non-cancerous growths that develop in the lining of the nose or sinuses. They are usually soft, painless, and non-inflammatory translucent tissue containing mucus unlike the fleshy polyps of rhinosporidiosis.



Reference:

Diseases of the Ear, Nose, and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page no: 236
question: A South Indian male farmer presents to the ENT OPD with complaints of reddish mass coming out from the nose and histopathology image as given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - Choanal atresia:

  • Choanal atresia is a congenital condition where there is a blockage or narrowing of the back of the nasal passage (choanae) that leads from the nasal cavity to the throat. This blockage can make it difficult for an infant to breathe through their nose. Interestingly, infants with choanal atresia often improve their breathing when they cry. When they cry, they open their mouths wider, allowing more air to flow into their lungs through their mouth, bypassing the blocked nasal passages. This temporary improvement in breathing during crying is a characteristic feature of choanal atresia.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Atrophic rhinitis: Atrophic rhinitis is a condition characterized by the thinning and inflammation of the nasal mucosa, leading to symptoms like nasal crusting, foul odor, and nasal congestion. Crying is unlikely to significantly improve symptoms in atrophic rhinitis.

Option B - Acute rhinosinusitis: Acute rhinosinusitis is an inflammation of the nasal and sinus passages, often caused by infections. While crying might lead to temporary relief of symptoms due to increased nasal secretions, it's not a defining characteristic of this condition.

Option C - Allergic rhinitis: Allergic rhinitis is an allergic reaction that leads to symptoms like sneezing, itching, runny or stuffy nose. Crying might temporarily relieve some symptoms, but it's not a specific feature of allergic rhinitis.
question: A infant developed difficulty in breathing. His symptoms improve with crying. In which disease, symptoms get improve with crying?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Wegener's granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis):

  • The combination of non-caseating granulomas and saddle nose perforation strongly points towards Wegener's granulomatosis (now often referred to as Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis), making option C the most likely diagnosis in this case.

  • Causes necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the upper airway.

  • Produces rapid septal destruction → septal perforation → saddle nose.

  • Occurs commonly in 30–50 years, matching the patient’s age.

  • TB, leprosy, and syphilis produce saddle nose, but only in late, long-standing disease and have other characteristic findings—none of which are mentioned here.

  • Therefore, GPA is the best single diagnosis for this combination of early aggressive cartilage destruction + granulomas.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - TB (Tuberculosis): While TB can also cause granulomas, the presentation of saddle nose perforation is not typically associated with TB. TB commonly affects the lungs and can cause symptoms like cough, fever, and weight loss.

Option B - Leprosy: Leprosy can cause granulomas as well, saddle nose only in advanced lepromatous leprosy. Leprosy usually affects the skin, nerves, and mucous membranes, leading to skin lesions and nerve damage.

Option D - Syphilis: Syphilis can cause granulomas as part of its secondary stage manifestations, Saddle nose occurs mainly in congenital syphilis or in tertiary gummatous syphilis.. Syphilis typically causes a variety of symptoms including skin rash, fever, and mucous membrane lesions.

question: A 40-year-old patient presenting with non-caseating granulomas and a saddle nose perforation, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Antro-choanal polyp: ]

An antro-choanal polyp is a benign growth that originates in the maxillary sinus (antrum) and extends into the nasal cavity, passing through the choanae (the openings at the back of the nasal cavity that lead to the throat). These polyps are typically unilateral and can cause nasal obstruction, especially if they protrude significantly into the nasal cavity.


Incorrect Options:

Option A - Thornwaldt Cyst: A Thornwaldt cyst (also known as nasopharyngeal cyst or pharyngeal bursitis) is a cyst that forms in the nasopharynx. However, it is usually not associated with an irregular mass protruding from the choanae. It might cause nasal symptoms, but it's less likely to present with the specific characteristics described in the scenario.

Option C - Hypertrophic Rhinitis: Hypertrophic rhinitis refers to the enlargement of the nasal turbinates due to chronic inflammation. While it can lead to nasal obstruction, it doesn't usually manifest as an irregular mass protruding from the choanae. It's more associated with internal nasal structures rather than external protrusions.

Option D - Adenoid Hypertrophy: Adenoid hypertrophy involves the enlargement of the adenoid tissue, which is in the back of the nasal cavity, near the choanae. However, adenoids don't typically present as an irregular mass protruding through the choanae. Instead, they might cause more generalized nasal obstruction and related symptoms.

question: A 7-year-old male presented with nasal obstruction. On examination there was an irregular mass protruding from the choanae. What is the possible diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: A) Orbital cellulitis

  • The given CT is confirmatory of orbital cellulitis as there is proptosis visible on the CT and the patient is also having orbital pain.

Orbital Cellulitis

Definition
  • Orbital cellulitis is an acute infection of the soft tissues of the orbit located behind the orbital septum.

Etiology
  • Exogenous Infection: Occurs due to penetrating injuries. Example: foreign body retention, surgical procedures like evisceration, enucleation, orbitotomy, dacryocystectomy.
  • Endogenous Infection: From metastatic infections. Example: breast abscess, puerperal sepsis, thrombophlebitis, septicemia
  • Extension from Neighboring Structures (most common): Paranasal sinuses (most common: ethmoid sinus), teeth, face, eyelids, intracranial cavity, and intraorbital structures.

Clinical Features

Symptoms:

  • Swelling and severe pain (worsened by eye movement or pressure).
  • Systemic symptoms: fever, nausea, vomiting, prostration.
  • Vision loss and/or diplopia in moderate to advanced cases.

Signs:

  • Swelling of lids with woody hardness and redness.
  • Chemosis (conjunctival swelling), which may lead to necrosis.
  • Axial proptosis.
  • Restricted eye movements.
  • RAPD (Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect) may occur due to optic neuropathy or central retinal artery occlusion.
  • Fundus examination may show retinal vein congestion, papillitis, or papilledema

Staging

Modified Chandler staging system:

  • Stage I: Preseptal cellulitis/ periorbital cellulitis (limited anterior to orbital septum)
  • Stage II: Inflammatory orbital oedema/ Orbital cellulitis (Posterior to orbital septum)
  • Stage III: Subperiosteal abscess
  • Stage IV: Orbital abscess
  • Stage V: Cavernous sinus thrombosis

[[figure-1]]

Investigations
  • Cultures: Nasal, conjunctival, and blood samples for bacterial culture.
  • Complete Blood Count: Leukocytosis.
  • X-ray PNS: To detect sinusitis.
    • Orbital Ultrasonography: To detect orbital abscesses.
  • CT Scan/MRI: Differentiates preseptal from postseptal cellulitis, detects abscesses, intracranial extension, and guides surgical drainage.

Incorrect Options:

Sinusitis (Option B): This option is incorrect as proptosis is visible on imaging.

Both A and B (Option C): This option is also incorrect.

Subperiosteal abscess (Option D): This option is incorrect as CT findings of periosteal abscess show abscess behind the orbit.



Reference:

Diseases of the Ear, Nose, and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page no: 153
question: A 30-year-old women present with upper respiratory tract infection and orbital pain. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: A) Rhinosporidiosis

  • The given histopathology and clinical scenario (bleeding, nasal obstruction, and red polyploidal mass) is suggestive of Rhinosporidiosis, as on histopathology there are sporangia with spores.

Rhinosporidiosis:

  • It is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by an aquatic protistan protozoa- Rhinosporidium seeberi.
  • It is a water-borne disease- contaminated water of ponds usually with cow dung.

Epidemiology:

  • Common in India, Sri Lanka, and Pakistan
  • More common in southern states than in northern India

Life cycle:

  • Trophic stage → Development of sporangium → Release of endospores

Clinical Features:

  • Blood-tinged nasal discharge
  • Nasal block
  • Epistaxis
  • Leafy, polypoidal, pink to purple colored mass attached to the nasal septum or lateral wall.
  • Very vascular mass and bleeds easily on touch.
  • White dots are studded on its surface representing the sporangia.

Incorrect Options:

Basal Cell Carcinoma (Option B):

  • This option is incorrect as basal cell carcinoma exhibits the findings given below.

Rhinoscleroma (Option C):

  • This is incorrect as Rhinoscleroma presents with nasal obstruction, erythematous granular or nodular swellings, crusts on the swellings, and swelling of the lips and gums.

Lupus Vulgaris (Option D):

  • This option is incorrect as Lupus vulgaris (also known as tuberculosis luposa) are painful cutaneous tuberculosis skin lesions with nodular appearance, most often on the face around the nose, eyelids, lips, cheeks, ears, and neck.


Reference:

Diseases of the Ear, Nose, and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page no: 153
question: A patient presents to the OPD with complaints of bleeding from nose, nasal obstruction, and difficulty in breathing. He gave the history of bathing in the local pool near his house. On examination, red polypoidal mass with whitish dots on the surface is observed. Based on the history, examination what will be the diagnosis of the patient?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: A) Frontal mucocele

  • CT image shows the left frontal sinus is completely filled with a homogeneous soft-tissue density.This is typical of a mucocele (mucus-filled, non-enhancing lesion)
  • A mucocele is a cyst-like structure that forms when the lining of a sinus cavity becomes inflamed or blocked.
  • This commonly occurs as a result of obstruction to the frontal ostium due to chronic disease of the frontal recess or due to postsurgical/ traumatic fibrosis causing blockage.
  • Frontal mucoceles can appear 10–20 years after trauma due to scarring and obstruction of frontal recess.
  • Trauma → scarring → frontal recess obstruction → delayed mucocele
  • Frontal mucocele pushes the globe inferolaterally → classic nonaxial proptosis.
  • Symptoms of a frontal mucocele include:
    • Proptosis (bulging) of the eye
    • Headache or facial pain
    • Vision changes or double vision
    • Nasal congestion or discharge
    • Sinus pressure or pain
    • Swelling or tenderness in the forehead

Incorrect Options:

Frontal meningioma (Option B):

  • A meningioma is a tumor that arises from the lining of the brain or spinal cord.
  • When a meningioma forms in the front of the head, it can cause eye proptosis.
  • However, meningiomas are relatively uncommon in young adults, and a history of trauma may not be associated with developing a meningioma.
  • CT shows sinus expansion rather than intracranial mass → favors mucocele.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (Option C):

  • Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a rare and benign tumor, typically in adolescent males.
  • It arises from the back of the nose or upper throat and can cause eye proptosis as it grows.
  • However, the history of trauma 15 years prior is not usually associated with developing a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Pseudotumor of the orbit (Option D):

  • Pseudotumor of orbit, also known as an idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome, is a condition in which the tissues around the eye become inflamed and swollen, causing eye proptosis.
  • The cause of the pseudotumor of the orbit is unknown, but it is thought to be related to an abnormal immune response.
  • While a history of trauma is not typically associated with developing pseudotumor of orbit, the condition can occur at any age.
  • pseudotumor causes painful, acute proptosis, not slowly progressive over years.


Reference:

Diseases of the Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page no: 279
question: What is the probable diagnosis for a 30-year-old male who has nonaxial proptosis in his left eye and a history of a road traffic accident 15 years ago, as suggested by the provided CT image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image, coupled with the clinical context of an elderly diabetic female, strongly suggests Mucormycosis as the most probable diagnosis.
  • The image shows black necrotic tissue near the orbit, which is characteristic of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis.

Mucormycosis
  • It is an invasive disease caused by zygomycetes (phycomycetes) - Rhizopus, Mucor and Absidia. Rhizopus Arrhizus is the most common pathogen

[[figure-1]]

Rhizopus

[[figure-2]]

Absidia

[[figure-3]]

Mucor (Lactophenol cotton blue stained)

Pathogenesis

Begins in the respiratory tract or nasal cavity, where spores germinate and form mycelia → invade adjacent tissues, leading to local destruction.

Fungi invade blood vessels, causing thrombosis and infarction in affected areas, which contributes to its high mortality rate (Angio-invasiveness)

Common Sites

  • Rhinocerebral Form: Involves the nose, nasal sinuses, and orbit; frequently seen in diabetic patients.
  • Pulmonary Infections: When the lungs are the primary site, the fungi can invade lung arteries, leading to serious complications.
  • Others: Cutaneous mucormycosis, GI mucormycosis, Disseminated mucormycosis

Clinical Features
  • Rhinocerebral Zygomycosis:
    • Facial swelling, nasal discharge (often black), fever, and mucosal necrosis.
    • Rapid progression can lead to severe complications, including visual loss and neurological symptoms.
  • Pulmonary Zygomycosis:
    • Symptoms may include cough, fever, and hemoptysis

Diagnosis

Histological Examination:

Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying broad, non-septate (or sparsely septate) hyphae.

[[figure-4]]

Culture:

  • After incubation for 3-4 days on Sabouraud agar at 30-37°C, the colonies are grey-white with a thick cottony, fluffy surface.
  • Under the microscope, nonseptate, broad hyphae with aerial sporangiophores which end in a sporangium (a sac containing spores are seen.)

a.

[[figure-5]]

b.

[[figure-6]]

a. Sabouraud's dextrose agar (SDA) medium showing Rhizopus growth

b.Microscopy of LPCB stained preparation demonstrating morphology of Rhizopus spp. (non-septate hyphae, sporangiophore, sporangium and spores)

Treatment:
  • Intravenous amphotericin B combined, where appropriate, with surgical drainage is the recommended treatment.
  • Medical control of diabetes is required.

Aspergillosis (Option A):

  • is a fungal infection affecting the nasal cavity, sinuses, and lungs.
  • In the nasal cavity, it may appear as a white, fluffy, or mold-like growth on the mucosal lining.
  • In the sinuses, it may cause thick mucus or pus-like discharge
  • in the lungs, it can cause fungal balls in pre-existing cavitary lesions.

Foreign body (Option C): A foreign body in the nose may present as unilateral nasal discharge, foul odor, and occasionally epistaxis (nosebleed). On physical examination, the foreign body may be visible in the nasal cavity and appear as small objects or debris.

Rhinosporidiosis (Option D): is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by a parasite, Rhinosporidium seeberi. It typically presents as a pedunculated or sessile polypoidal mass arising from the nasal mucosa. The mass is usually pink or red in color and may bleed on manipulation.



Reference:

Ananthanarayanan and Paniker's textbook of microbiology, 10th edition, Page 614, 615
question: An elderly diabetic female patient is presented, as shown in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hypertrophic rhinitis is a chronic condition characterized by inflammation and thickening of the nasal mucosa, often due to prolonged irritation (e.g., allergies, infection, or pollutants).
  • The mulberry appearance of the inferior turbinate is a hallmark of hypertrophic rhinitis, caused by nodular swellings on the turbinates.
  • Symptoms like headache and thick nasal discharge are common due to nasal obstruction and secondary infections.

Hypertrophic Rhinitis

  • Cause: Progression from untreated chronic simple rhinitis, leading to repeated infections and submucosal fibrosis, causing turbinate hypertrophy.
  • Commonly Affected Turbinate:
    • Inferior turbinate – develops a mulberry appearance.
  • Primary Symptom:
    • Nasal obstruction (due to fibrosis).
  • Management: Nasal obstruction due to fibrosis requires turbinate size reduction via partial or total turbinectomy.
    • Turbinectomy (partial or total): To reduce the size of hypertrophied turbinates.
    • Methods include:
      • Laser surgery.
      • Cryosurgery.
      • Diathermy.
      • Radiofrequency ablation.
      • Surgical submucous resection of turbinate.

Atrophic rhinitis (Option A): is a condition in which the nasal mucosa thins and dries out, leading to foul-smelling nasal discharge, crusting, and obstruction. The symptoms are not consistent with those seen in the patient.

Common cold (Option B): Is a viral infection that affects the upper respiratory tract. It typically presents with symptoms such as cough, runny nose, and sore throat.

Nasal polyp (Option D):

  • are benign growths that arise from the lining of the nose or sinuses.
  • They can lead to symptoms such as nasal obstruction, postnasal drip, and reduced sense of smell.
  • While they may cause nasal discharge, the mulberry appearance of the inferior turbinate is not a feature of nasal polyps.


Reference:

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2468548821000345

Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD):

question: An elderly diabetic female patient presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, a blackish necrotic mass has filled the nasal cavity and eroded the septum and hard palate. What is the most probable diagnosis?

question: A 60-year-old male presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and right ear pain. On examination, the right ear reveals conductive hearing loss with a dull tympanic membrane. Moreover, decreased mobility of the soft palate was also noted. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Aspergillosis is the most common fungal infection involving the maxillary sinus.
  • It is most commonly caused by Aspergillus fumigatus, although other Aspergillus species may also be involved.
  • The maxillary sinus is the sinus most frequently affected because fungal spores can become trapped within the sinus cavity.
  • Clinical presentations include:
    • Chronic unilateral nasal obstruction
    • Facial pain or pressure
    • Foul-smelling nasal discharge
    • Radiological evidence of sinus opacification, often with calcific densities
  • Forms of sinonasal aspergillosis include:
    • Fungal ball (mycetoma) – most common non-invasive form
    • Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis

Blastomycosis(Option A): It is caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. In immunocompetent, it primarily causes pulmonary infections and skin lesions, and in immunocompromised, it causes CNS infections.

Candidiasis(Option C): It mainly causes opportunistic infections, with diabetes mellitus being the most common predisposing factor. It is often implicated in cutaneous, mucosal, intestinal, bronchopulmonary, and systemic infections.

Histoplasmosis(Option D): Histoplasma capsulatum is a species of fungus that causes histoplasmosis. It is primarily a pulmonary infection but can also cause cutaneous and disseminated disease. It can cause infection in both immunocompetent and compromised patients. Histoplasma-causing sinusitis is uncommon.

Explanation:

  • A blow-out fracture is an isolated fracture of the orbital floor, usually resulting from blunt trauma to the orbit.

  • The classic CT findings include:

    • Fracture of the orbital floor

    • Herniation of orbital fat and/or inferior rectus muscle into the maxillary sinus (teardrop sign)

    • Opacification or hematoma within the maxillary sinus

  • Clinical features include:

    • Diplopia (double vision)

    • Restricted upward gaze due to entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle

    • Enophthalmos

    • Infraorbital nerve hypoesthesia

    • Epistaxis following facial trauma

  • The combination of trauma, diplopia, restricted eye movements, and the characteristic CT findings strongly suggests a blow-out fracture.

Blow out fracture

[[figure-1]]

Causes:

  • Direct impacts to the eye or surrounding area, such as from a punch, a baseball, or a car accident.
  • In some cases, the injury can be caused by a sudden increase in pressure, such as from a sneeze or cough.

Symptoms:

  • Pain around the eye, which may worsen with eye movement
  • Swelling and bruising around the eye and cheek
  • Double vision (diplopia)
  • Decreased or blurry vision
  • Inability to move the eye normally
  • Sunken or bulging eye

Treatment:

  • Rest and pain management
  • Surgery may be necessary in severe cases, such as when there is a large fracture or significant damage to the eye or surrounding structures.
  • Antibiotics may be prescribed to prevent infection.

Le Fort Fracture (Option A): Le Fort fractures involve the midface. Le Fort II and III may involve the orbit, but are associated with extensive midfacial fractures, nasal bone involvement, malocclusion, and facial mobility rather than an isolated orbital floor defect.

Fracture Maxilla (Option B): Maxillary fractures primarily involve the upper jaw and present with facial swelling, malocclusion, and maxillary tenderness. They do not characteristically show the teardrop sign.

Fracture Zygomatic (Option C): Zygomatic fractures typically involve the zygomatic arch and lateral orbital wall, producing malar flattening and infraorbital nerve symptoms. An isolated orbital floor defect with herniation is more suggestive of a blow-out fracture.

Saccharine test (Option A):

  • This test helps in assessing nasal mucociliary clearance. Saccharin is placed around 1 cm behind the anterior end of the inferior turbinate.

Charcoal powder method (Option C):

  • This helps in assessing nasal mucociliary clearance. In this test, 10 micrograms of charcoal are kept 1 cm behind the head of the inferior turbinate.
  • The patient is asked to inhale the charcoal particles. It is seen deposited over the respiratory epithelium. Every 30 seconds, the posterior pharyngeal wall is observed for a blackish discoloration.
  • After 30 minutes to 1 hour, the patient is asked to expectorate. The sputum is then examined for charcoal particles.

Scintigraphy (Option D):

  • It involves the administration of radioactive tracers like technetium-99c DTPA which is instilled into the respiratory tract.
  • A gamma camera is used to visualize the movement of the tracer through the respiratory pathway

Explanation:

The combination of upper respiratory tract involvement (saddle nose, septal perforation), lower respiratory tract involvement (cough, hemoptysis, cavitary lesions), and the biopsy findings (granulomas, multinucleated giant cells, and necrosis) strongly points towards Wegener's granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis).

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis:

  • Previously known as Wegener’s granulomatosis.
  • It is a systemic granulomatous inflammation and necrotizing vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels.
  • More common in Caucasians (90%).

Clinical features:

  • Upper respiratory tract symptoms:
    • Clear or purulent bloody nasal discharge
    • Sinusitis
    • On examination, crusting, granulations, septal perforation, and a saddle nose.
  • Lower respiratory tract symptoms: cough, pleuritic pain, and hemoptysis.
  • kidneys: Hematuria, later renal failure.
  • Oral: ‘strawberry’ gingival hyperplasia is said to be pathognomonic.
  • Skin: ulceration and nodules.

Diagnosis:

  • Chest X-ray: Nodules, fixed infiltrates or cavities
  • Urine analysis: Microscopic haematuria with or without red cell casts.
  • Biopsy: Necrosis and ulceration of mucosa, epithelioid granuloma, and necrotizing vasculitis involving small arteries or veins.
  • c-ANCA (cytoplasmic ANCA): Positive in 90% of the cases.
  • p-ANCA (perinuclear ANCA): Positive in 10% of the cases.
  • CT and MRI: Non-specific mucosal thickening in the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses, bone destruction, and new bone formation in the walls of the sinus cavities.

Treatment:

  • Systemic corticosteroids.
  • Cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, methotrexate and rituximab are used.

Tuberculosis (Option B): While TB can cause granulomas, the combination of nasal destruction (septal perforation, saddle nose) with lung cavities is more characteristic of GPA. TB can present with hemoptysis, but it's less commonly associated with the rapid destruction of nasal cartilage leading to saddle nose deformity as seen in GPA.

Syphilis (Option C): Congenital syphilis can cause a saddle nose deformity. However, the other symptoms described (cough, hemoptysis, cavitary lung lesions, and the specific biopsy findings) are not typical of syphilis. Also, lung involvement is not a common presentation of syphilis.

Sarcoidosis (Option D): Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease that can affect the lungs and upper respiratory tract. While it can cause granulomas on biopsy and lung involvement, it's less likely to cause destructive nasal changes like saddle nose deformity and septal perforation.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of a 6-year-old boy with swelling in the nose, breathing difficulties, smooth and rounded swellings on both sides of the septum, and soft, fluctuant masses suggests the presence of a septal hematoma. Septal hematomas occur due to trauma, such as a fall, and can result in blood collection between the cartilage and mucosa of the nasal septum. The treatment of choice for septal hematomas is incision and drainage. If left untreated, septal hematomas can lead to complications such as abscess formation, nasal deformities, or even septal perforation due to cartilage necrosis.

Septal Hematoma

[[figure-1]]

Aetiology
  • Collection of blood under the perichondrium or periosteum of the nasal septum.
  • Commonly caused by:
    • Nasal trauma.
    • Septal surgery.
    • Spontaneous occurrence in bleeding disorders.

Clinical features
  • Bilateral nasal obstruction (most common symptom).
  • Frontal headache and pressure over the nasal bridge.
  • Smooth, rounded, soft, and fluctuant swelling in both nasal fossae (or sometimes unilateral).

Treatment
  • Small hematomas: Aspirated with a wide-bore sterile needle.
  • Larger hematomas: Incision and drainage via a septal incision parallel to the nasal floor, excising a small piece of mucosa for better drainage.
  • Nasal packing on both sides to prevent reaccumulation.
  • Systemic antibiotics to prevent septal abscess.

Complications
  • Fibrous tissue formation leads to permanent septal thickening if untreated.
  • Secondary infection may lead to septal abscess, cartilage necrosis, and nasal dorsum depression.

Incorrect Options:

Systemic antibiotics (Option A): While systemic antibiotics might be used if there is evidence of infection, antibiotics alone would not address the hematoma or swelling in this case. Drainage is necessary to prevent further complications.

High-resolution computerized tomography (Option C): CT imaging is typically not required for the diagnosis or management of a septal hematoma. A clinical examination is sufficient to make the diagnosis. CT may be considered if there is suspicion of fractures or other complex injuries, but it's not necessary in this straightforward case.

Submucosal resection (Option D): Submucosal resection is a procedure used in the treatment of nasal obstructions or deformities, often due to structural issues like a deviated septum. It is not appropriate for managing a septal hematoma, which requires drainage rather than resection.



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page173,174
  2. Logan Turner’s Diseases of Nose, Throat and Ear, 11th Edition, Page.88

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The maxillary sinus is the largest of the paranasal sinuses, located within the maxilla (upper jaw bone). It is pyramid-shaped and lies lateral to the nasal cavity, with its base forming the lateral wall of the nose and its apex extending towards the zygomatic bone. On radiographic or anatomical images, it appears as a large, air-filled cavity inferior to the orbit and lateral to the nasal cavity.
  • Key features of the maxillary sinus:
    • Largest paranasal sinus.
    • Drains into the middle meatus of the nasal cavity through the semilunar hiatus.
    • Commonly involved in sinusitis due to the high location of its drainage opening.

The maxillary sinus or the Antrum of Highmore, is the largest of the paranasal sinuses, occupying the body of the maxilla.

  • Shape - Pyramidal
  • Size - 15mL
  • Base - toward the lateral wall of the nose
  • Apex - extends into the zygomatic process of the maxillary bone

Relations:

  • Anterior wall: Formed by the facial surface of the maxilla.
  • Posterior wall: Anterior surface of pterygopalatine fossa.
  • Medial wall: Thin and membranous in some areas, this wall borders the middle and inferior meatuses and separates the maxillary sinus from the nasal cavity.
  • Roof: Formed by the floor of the orbit
  • Floor: Located approximately 1 cm below the floor of the nasal cavity, it is formed by the alveolar and palatine processes of the maxilla. Closely related to the roots of the second premolar and first molar teeth. Cavities in these teeth are associated with oro antral fistula.

[[figure-1]]

Arterial supply: Branches of the maxillary artery, specifically the infraorbital artery, greater palatine artery, and the posterior superior alveolar artery.

[[figure-2]]

Venous drainage: Pterygoid venous plexus and the facial vein.

Lymphatic drainage: Submandibular lymph nodes.

Nerve supply: Infraorbital nerve, greater palatine nerve, and the posterior superior alveolar nerve, which are branches of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2).


Incorrect Options:

Frontal sinus (Option A): Located above the orbit in the frontal bone; appears superior to the nasal cavity and orbits in images.

Pyriform sinus (Option B): This is a structure in the hypopharynx, not a paranasal sinus. It is unrelated to the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses.

Ethmoid sinus (Option C): Consists of multiple small air cells located between the eyes, medial to the orbit, and posterior to the nasal cavity. These appear as smaller clusters on imaging.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis for an older diabetic woman with a malodorous black discharge from the nose, a necrotic black mass filling the nasal cavity, and erosion of the septum and hard palate is mucormycosis. This is a severe fungal infection caused by molds from the Mucoraceae family, often affecting immunocompromised individuals, such as those with diabetes, receiving steroids, and having viral infections like COVID-19. Mucormycosis commonly presents with:

  • Nasal or sinus involvement (as seen with black, necrotic tissue and discharge).
  • Erosion of surrounding structures, such as the septum and palate.
  • A rapidly progressive course, especially in diabetic and immunocompromised patients.
  • Malodorous discharge due to tissue necrosis.

Mucormycosis

Description

A severe fungal infection primarily affects the nose and sinuses but can quickly spread to the orbit, cribriform plate, meninges, and brain. The fungus invades arteries, causing endothelial damage, thrombosis, and rapid tissue destruction.

Characteristic Findings

Black necrotic material in the nasal cavity, eroding the nasal septum, hard palate, and turbinates. Black turbinate sign is seen on contrast enhanced MRI.

Risk Factors
  • Uncontrolled diabetes, especially with ketoacidosis
  • Prolonged steroid use (common in COVID-19 treatment)
  • Conditions causing immunosuppression: Neutropenia, HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, organ transplants, and kidney issues.

Diagnosis
  • Endoscopy: Shows pale mucosa early, progressing to black crusts and sloughing.
  • Biopsy: Multiple sites should be sampled for fungal identification; potassium hydroxide preparation is the gold standard for confirming invasive features.

Imaging
  • CT: Detects bony destruction and initial assessment of sinus involvement.
  • CECT: CECT provides better delineation of soft tissue structures, allowing for clearer identification of mucosal thickening, sinus opacification, and bony destruction.
  • MRI: Evaluates soft tissue invasion, assesses the extent of extra-sinus disease, and identifies complications, especially in the orbit and brain.

Treatment

Antifungal Therapy:

  • Amphotericin B: 0.6 to 1 mg/kg/day IV or liposomal Amphotericin B: 5 mg/kg/day.
  • Posaconazole: 300 mg twice daily orally on the first day, then 300 mg once daily.

Surgical Intervention:

  • Endoscopic debridement of necrotic tissues.
  • Severe cases: Total/Partial maxillectomy or orbital exenteration may be required.

Incorrect Options:

Aspergillosis (Option A): Aspergillosis is another fungal infection, but it typically does not present with black necrotic masses. It is more commonly associated with chronic sinusitis or allergic reactions, not with necrosis and tissue destruction seen here.

Foreign body (Option C): A foreign body might cause a localized obstruction and discharge but would not lead to the extensive necrosis and erosion of the nasal cavity, septum, and palate as described in this case.

Rhinosporidiosis (Option D): Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic infection caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi, typically involving the nasal mucosa. It causes polypoidal growths, not necrotic black masses. It is more common in endemic areas, such as India and Sri Lanka.



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 183, 184
  2. Scott Brown ENT, 8th Edition, Page 211

Trotter's triad is a classic presentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) involving:

  1. Conductive hearing loss: Due to obstruction of the Eustachian tube by the tumour, leading to middle ear effusion.
  2. Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia: Caused by tumour infiltration into the base of the skull, affecting branches of the trigeminal nerve.

Sensorineural hearing loss, contralateral temporoparietal neuralgia, palatal paralysis (Option B): Sensorineural hearing loss is not typically seen in NPC unless there is advanced cranial nerve involvement. Neuralgia and paralysis are ipsilateral to the tumour, not contralateral.

Conductive hearing loss, contralateral temporoparietal neuralgia, palatal paralysis (Option D): While conductive hearing loss and palatal paralysis are consistent with NPC, the neuralgia is ipsilateral to the tumour, not contralateral.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma: This benign but locally aggressive vascular tumour occurs predominantly in adolescent males. It commonly presents with repeated episodes of epistaxis (nosebleeds), nasal obstruction, and sometimes nasal discharge. Examination often reveals a solid, vascular, purplish mass in the nasopharynx. This is the most probable diagnosis in a 14-year-old male with these symptoms and findings.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA)

Site of Origin

Posterior nasal cavity, near the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen, where the sphenoid and palatine bones meet.

Gross Appearance

Reddish-purple, lobulated, sessile mass covered by mucosa; lacks a capsule despite being benign.

Microscopic Appearance
  • Vascular Tissue: Endothelium-lined spaces with incomplete/absent muscle coats, leading to bleeding; peripheral vessels are thin-walled, central vessels hyperplastic.
  • Stromal Cells: Stellate or spindle-shaped cells that produce collagen, affecting tumor firmness.

Immunohistochemistry
  • Fibroblasts, collagen, myofibroblasts, mast cells, and occasionally giant cells are present.
  • Reactivity to smooth muscle actin and beta-catenin, suggesting beta-catenin’s role in growth.

Growth Factors
  • JNA development likely results from a combination of hormonal influence, growth factors, and genetic factors.
  • Androgen Receptors: Present in 75% of JNA tumors, indicating male hormone involvement.
  • VEGF: Promotes endothelial and stromal cell growth.
  • IGF-II: Role is less clear.
  • Genetics: C-MYC proto-oncogene found in larger tumors; may interact with androgen receptor and beta-catenin genes.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Option A): This malignant tumour usually occurs in older adults and is rare in this age group. It often presents with neck lymphadenopathy, nasal obstruction, or ear symptoms but is unlikely to present with a solid, vascular growth in a young male.

Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option B): This is a malignant soft tissue tumour that can occur in the nasopharynx but is rare and less likely to cause repeated epistaxis without systemic signs like weight loss or fatigue.

Pyogenic granuloma (Option C): This is a vascular lesion but typically occurs on the nasal septum or oral mucosa, not in the nasopharynx. It is usually smaller, friable, and more superficial.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery 8th edition, Page 289-291

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Little's area, also known as Kiesselbach's plexus, is a highly vascular region located in the anterior part of the nasal septum. It is a site of frequent epistaxis (nosebleeds) due to the rich network of blood vessels that anastomose here.
  • Keisselbach's plexus is a network of arteries formed by anastomoses of branches from the internal carotid artery (like the sphenopalatine artery) and the external carotid artery (including the superior labial artery and anterior ethmoidal artery), which supply the nasal septum.
  • Kiesselbach’s plexus, also known as Little's area, is a highly vascularised region in the anteroinferior portion of the nasal septum, where multiple arteries converge.
  • It is the most common site of anterior epistaxis, especially in children and young adults.

[[figure-1]]

  • Vessels involved in forming the plexus

Artery

Branch of

Sphenopalatine artery

Maxillary artery

Anterior ethmoidal artery

Ophthalmic artery (from internal carotid artery)

Greater palatine artery

Maxillary artery

Superior labial artery

Facial artery (from external carotid artery)

Note: Posterior ethmoidal artery is not part of this plexus

Clinical Significance:

  • Anterior epistaxis occurs most often in children and young adults, usually due to trauma (nose-picking), dry air, infections, or irritants.
  • Epistaxis in this area is typically mild and self-limiting and can be controlled with local pressure or simple cauterization.

It is situated at the posteroinferior part of the nasal septum (Option B): is incorrect because Little's area is located at the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum, not the posterior.

Least common site for epistaxis (Option C): is incorrect because Little's area is the most common site for epistaxis, not the least.

Anastomoses of 7 major arteries occur here (Option D): is incorrect because the anastomoses of the major arteries involved in Little’s area are primarily derived from the internal and external carotid arteries, but not seven arteries. The arteries involved are generally 4-5, not seven.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page 205

Treatment

Antifungal Therapy:

  • Amphotericin B: 0.6 to 1 mg/kg/day IV or liposomal Amphotericin B: 5 mg/kg/day.
  • Posaconazole: 300 mg twice daily orally on the first day, then 300 mg once daily.

Surgical Intervention:

  • Endoscopic debridement of necrotic tissues.
  • Severe cases: Total/Partial maxillectomy or orbital exenteration may be required.

Incorrect Options:

Midline lethal granuloma (Option B): Midline lethal granuloma, also known as polymorphic reticulosis or nasal T-cell lymphoma, is a rare malignant lymphoma that primarily affects the midline facial structures, such as the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and nasopharynx. It typically presents with symptoms of nasal obstruction, facial swelling, and ulceration. The histological examination shows polymorphic lymphoid infiltrates.

Foreign body granuloma (Option C): A foreign body granuloma occurs when the body reacts to a foreign object that has been implanted or retained in the tissues. It typically presents as a localized inflammatory reaction with granulation tissue formation. However, the clinical presentation described in the question, with facial swelling, orbital edema, and subcutaneous nodules, is not consistent with a foreign body granuloma.


IgG4 granuloma (Option D): IgG4-related disease is a systemic fibro inflammatory condition characterized by the infiltration of affected tissues with IgG4-positive plasma cells. Often presents as tumefactive lesions or mass-like formations. However, the clinical presentation described in the question, along with the histological findings of PAS- positive and Grocott's methenamine silver-positive staining, is not indicative of IgG4 granuloma.

Explanation:

  • The image shows Inverted papilloma causing erosion or remodeling of adjacent bony structures, such as the nasal septum or the walls of the sinuses.
  • Inverted papilloma is a benign sinonasal tumor that arises from the lining of the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses.
  • It often presents with unilateral nasal obstruction, recurrent nosebleeds, and the potential for locally aggressive behavior.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Inverted Papilloma

Origin

Arises from the non-olfactory mucosa (Schneiderian membrane) of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses

Other Names

Transitional cell papilloma, Ringertz tumor, Schneiderian papilloma

Most Common Site

Lateral wall of the nose, particularly in the middle meatus.

Growth Pattern

Inward growth of hyperplastic tissue toward the stroma.

Association with HPV

Linked to Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection (particularly types 6 and 11)

Risk of Malignancy

Associated with squamous cell carcinoma in 10-15% of cases.

Symptoms

Unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis (nosebleeds), and possible recurrent sinus infections.

Diagnosis

Endoscopic examination and biopsy for histopathological confirmation.

Treatment

Primary treatment is complete endoscopic surgical excision to minimize the risk of recurrence and malignant transformation.

It can present with nasal obstruction, epistaxis (nosebleeds), anosmia (loss of smell), and facial pain or swelling.

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (Option D): Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a vascular tumor that primarily affects adolescent males. It arises from the back of the nasal cavity and can cause nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and sometimes facial swelling.

explanationHtml:
Epistaxis (nosebleed) that persists despite pinching the nostrils and nasal packing suggests posterior epistaxis, which is often due to bleeding from the sphenopalatine artery. The sphenopalatine artery is the main arterial supply to the nasal cavity, making it the primary target for surgical intervention in refractory cases.

Management Approach:

  1. Initial Management
    • Pinching nostrils (first-line conservative treatment)
    • Nasal packing (anterior and posterior)
  2. If Nasal Packing Fails
    • Endoscopic ligation or cauterization of the sphenopalatine artery is the preferred next step.
  3. If Epistaxis Persists
    • Ligation of the external carotid artery may be considered as a last resort.

Ligation of external carotid artery (Option A): Incorrect because sphenopalatine artery ligation is more effective and less invasive. External carotid artery ligation is reserved for extreme, uncontrolled cases.

Ligation of internal carotid artery (Option B): Incorrect because this is very high-risk, associated with stroke and severe complications, and is not required for managing epistaxis.

Ligation of maxillary artery (Option D): Incorrect because while the maxillary artery supplies the sphenopalatine artery, directly ligating the sphenopalatine artery is more targeted and less morbid.

  • The inferior turbinate is the largest of the three turbinates in the nasal cavity, located along the bottom part of the nasal passages.
  • During endoscopic examination of the right nasal cavity, the inferior turbinate is typically the most prominent structure visible.
  • It plays an important role in conditioning the air we breathe by warming, moistening, and filtering it before it enters the respiratory tract.

Inferior Turbinate:

  • The inferior turbinate is composed of bone and covered with mucosa.
  • Its main function is to regulate airflow and humidify the air that enters the nasal passages.
  • It is most commonly involved in conditions like nasal obstruction or rhinitis and may become enlarged due to various inflammatory conditions.

Incorrect Options:

Middle turbinate (Option B): is incorrect because the middle turbinate is positioned above the inferior turbinate and is typically smaller in size. It is located in the middle meatus and can be visible in endoscopic examinations, but it's not the structure being referred to here.

Superior turbinate (Option C): is incorrect because the superior turbinate is the smallest and located towards the top of the nasal cavity. It is not typically the most prominent structure in routine endoscopic views.

Uncinate process (Option D): is incorrect because the uncinate process is part of the ethmoid bone and located near the middle meatus. It is often visible in nasal endoscopy but is not as prominent as the inferior turbinate.

question: Please identify the structure indicated in the endoscopic image of the right nasal cavity.

explanationHtml:
Answer: C) Agger nasi

Explanation:

  • The Agger nasi is the first and most anterior air cell of the anterior ethmoidal sinus. It is located just beneath the frontal sinus and is often visible on CT scans of the paranasal sinuses.
  • It is situated near the middle turbinate and is a key landmark in the anatomy of the anterior ethmoid region.

Agger Nasi:

  • The Agger nasi is the anterior-most ethmoidal air cell and forms part of the anterior ethmoid complex.
  • It is typically seen in sinus imaging, and its location is important in surgical procedures such as functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS).
  • The Agger nasi often drains into the middle meatus and may contribute to sinus congestion when obstructed.

Incorrect Options:

Bulla ethmoidalis (Option A): is incorrect because the bulla ethmoidalis is a larger air cell in the middle part of the ethmoid sinus, not the first one.

Onodi cell (Option B): is incorrect because the Onodi cell is a posterior ethmoidal cell that lies near the sphenoid sinus, not the anterior ethmoidal cells.

Haller cell (Option D): is incorrect because the Haller cell is a variant air cell located in the floor of the orbit and not part of the anterior ethmoidal sinus system.

Answer: A) Anterior Ethmoidal Artery

Explanation:

  • The anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, which is derived from the internal carotid artery, not the external carotid artery.

Kiesselbach’s Plexus:

  • Kiesselbach's plexus is a vascular network located on the anterior part of the nasal septum, composed of arteries from the external carotid artery. The common arteries involved in Kiesselbach's plexus include:
    • Sphenopalatine artery (from the maxillary artery)
    • Greater palatine artery (from the maxillary artery)
    • Septal branch of the superior labial artery (from the facial artery)
    • Anterior ethmoidal artery – from ophthalmic artery (internal carotid)
    • Posterior ethmoidal artery – from ophthalmic artery (internal carotid)These vessels contribute to the blood supply to the nasal septum and are involved in conditions such as epistaxis (nosebleeds).

Incorrect Options:

Sphenopalatine artery (Option B): is incorrect because the sphenopalatine artery is a branch of the maxillary artery, a branch of the external carotid, and it contributes to Kiesselbach's plexus.

Greater palatine artery (Option C): is incorrect because the greater palatine artery is also a branch of the maxillary artery and contributes to Kiesselbach's plexus.

Septal branch of superior labial (Option D): is incorrect because the septal branch of the superior labial artery is a branch of the facial artery, also part of the external carotid, and contributes to Kiesselbach's plexus.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat - PL Dhingra - 8th Edition • Page no: 205

  • Surgical interventions, such as septal surgery or turbinate reduction, may be necessary to manage the symptoms and help prevent further damage to the nasal structures.

Atrophic Rhinitis:

  • Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic condition characterized by the thinning and atrophy of the nasal mucosa and turbinate bones.
  • It results in symptoms like dry nasal passages, crusting, foul-smelling nasal discharge, and in some cases, nasal obstruction.
  • In advanced cases, surgical procedures may be done to improve nasal patency or to occlude the nostril to reduce airflow and symptoms.

Vasomotor rhinitis (Option A): is incorrect because vasomotor rhinitis involves nasal congestion triggered by environmental factors, but it does not require surgery to occlude the nostril.

  • The preferred diagnostic procedure prior to performing Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) is a CT scan.
  • A CT scan provides detailed imaging of the sinus anatomy and helps to identify any sinus pathology such as sinusitis, nasal polyps, blockages, or anatomical variations that could affect the surgical approach.
  • It is crucial for planning the procedure and avoiding complications during surgery.

Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS):

  • FESS is a minimally invasive surgical procedure used to treat chronic sinusitis, nasal polyps, and other sinus conditions.
  • Before performing this surgery, it is essential to have a clear understanding of the patient's sinus anatomy and any underlying pathology.
  • CT imaging is the gold standard for evaluating the sinuses, as it provides high-resolution, cross-sectional images that allow for precise assessment of sinus structures, mucosal involvement, and any blockages.

Incorrect Options:

MRI scan (Option A): is incorrect because MRI is typically used for evaluating soft tissue or neurological issues, and it is not as effective as CT for assessing the sinus anatomy and bone structures, which are key for FESS planning.

X-ray (Option B): is incorrect because X-ray imaging is less detailed than CT and cannot provide the necessary clarity to evaluate the sinuses thoroughly, especially for complex sinus conditions.

Antral lavage (Option C): is incorrect because antral lavage is a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure used to irrigate the maxillary sinus in cases of chronic sinusitis. However, it is not used for detailed preoperative planning for FESS. A CT scan is the more accurate and comprehensive diagnostic tool for this purpose.

  • The most common location for an obstruction caused by a nasal polyp originating from the maxillary sinus is the middle meatus.
  • Nasal polyps are benign growths that arise from the mucosa of the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses.
  • When a polyp forms in the maxillary sinus, it typically expands into the middle meatus, which is the drainage pathway of the maxillary sinus.
  • This can lead to obstruction, sinusitis, or blockage of the sinus drainage.

Nasal Polyps:

  • Nasal polyps are non-cancerous growths that develop in the nasal passages or sinuses due to chronic inflammation.
  • They are frequently associated with conditions like chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma, and allergies.
  • The most common location for these polyps is the middle meatus, which is where the maxillary sinuses drain.
  • If the polyps obstruct the drainage system, it can lead to recurrent sinus infections, nasal congestion, and difficulty breathing through the nose.

Incorrect Options:

Inferior meatus (Option A): is incorrect because the inferior meatus primarily drains the nasolacrimal duct and not the maxillary sinus, so polyps from the maxillary sinus would not typically obstruct this area.

Superior meatus (Option B): is incorrect because the superior meatus drains the posterior ethmoidal sinuses, not the maxillary sinus, so it would not be the most common site of obstruction for a maxillary sinus polyp.

Sphenoethmoidal recess (Option D): is incorrect because the sphenoethmoidal recess is the drainage site for the sphenoid sinus, not the maxillary sinus, making it an unlikely location for obstruction due to a maxillary sinus polyp.

Explanation:

  • Seasonal influenza is the least likely cause of nasal septal perforation. While influenza can lead to symptoms like nasal congestion, sore throat, and fever, it typically does not result in nasal septal perforation.
  • This condition is more often associated with chronic inflammation, infection, or trauma to the nasal septum, such as in cases of rhinosporidiosis, syphilis, or tuberculosis.

Causes of Nasal Septal Perforation:

  • Nasal septal perforation is a hole or rupture in the nasal septum, the cartilage and bone that divides the two nostrils. Several conditions can lead to this, including:
    • Rhinosporidiosis: This is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by the fungus Rhinosporidium seeberi, often affecting the nasal mucosa and leading to the development of polyps or perforations in the nasal septum.
    • Syphilis: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Treponema pallidum, syphilis can cause granulomatous inflammation, particularly in the tertiary stage, leading to nasal septal perforation (a manifestation of gumma).
    • Tuberculosis: This chronic bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis can result in chronic granulomatous inflammation, leading to nasal septal perforation as part of the disease process, especially in advanced cases.
    • Seasonal influenza (Option B): is incorrect because while it causes acute viral upper respiratory tract infections, it does not typically result in chronic inflammation or tissue destruction that would lead to septal perforation.

Incorrect Options:

Rhinosporidiosis (Option A): is incorrect because this fungal infection is a well-known cause of nasal septal perforation due to chronic inflammation and polyp formation.

Syphilis (Option C): is incorrect because tertiary syphilis can cause granulomatous lesions, including perforation of the nasal septum.

Tuberculosis (Option D): is incorrect because tuberculosis, particularly in its chronic form, can cause nasal septal perforation due to granulomatous inflammation.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In the case of a nasal fracture with no involvement of the septum, the most appropriate approach is to wait for the swelling to subside before proceeding with closed reduction.
  • This period typically lasts around 10-14 days after the trauma, which allows for the edema (swelling) to decrease.
  • After the swelling is reduced, closed reduction can be performed to realign the nasal bones without the risk of additional trauma or incorrect positioning.
  • The reason for this approach is that if the closed reduction is performed too early, the swelling can obstruct proper visualization and alignment of the fractured nasal bones, potentially leading to complications or an incomplete reduction.

Nasal Fracture Management:

  • Closed reduction is the preferred management for nasal fractures that involve only the nasal bones, not the septum.
  • Waiting for swelling to decrease naturally allows for better visualization during the procedure, reducing the chances of complications or inadequate realignment.
  • Septo-rhinoplasty is typically only necessary for more complex fractures or when there is significant septal involvement that cannot be corrected with closed reduction.
  • Open reduction is used for more complicated fractures where closed reduction isn't feasible.

Incorrect Options:

Septo-rhinoplasty (Option A): is incorrect because it's a more invasive procedure used when there are issues with both the nasal bones and septum.

Open reduction (Option B): is incorrect because open reduction is generally only indicated in cases where closed reduction is not successful or in more complicated fractures.

Closed reduction after edema subsides in 20 days (Option C): is also incorrect because waiting for 20 days is unnecessary. The typical waiting period for swelling to subside is about 10-14 days, not 20 days.



Reference:
  • Scott Brown ENT, 8th Edition Pg - 1184,1185
  • Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Pg - 171

question: A boy fell down while playing and presented with deviated nose. The septum however was found to be normal. Following is the CT finding of the patient. What is the next step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In the case of a nasal fracture, the ideal time for closed reduction is typically within 5-7 days following the injury.
  • This time frame allows for the initial swelling to subside, providing better visibility and ensuring that the fractured bones can be accurately realigned.
  • Reducing the fracture within this window also minimizes the risk of complications and ensures better cosmetic and functional outcomes.

Timing of Nasal Fracture Reduction:

  • Early reduction (within the first 12 hours) may sometimes be appropriate for fractures with significant deformity or in cases where swelling is minimal.
  • However, it's generally not advisable to reduce the fracture within the first few hours because the swelling can obscure proper alignment and make it harder to achieve a precise reduction.
  • After 5-7 days, when swelling decreases, a closed reduction can be safely performed, and the nasal bones can be realigned without much obstruction from edema.
  • If the reduction is done too late (e.g., after 2 weeks or more), bony consolidation begins, making the bones harder to manipulate, and the chances of achieving an optimal result decrease.

Incorrect Options:

Within 12 hours following the injury (Option A): is incorrect because early reduction is often difficult due to swelling that can hinder the realignment of the nasal bones.

After 2 weeks of injury (Option C): is incorrect because waiting too long increases the risk of bony consolidation, making it harder to reduce the fracture and improving the chances of a less satisfactory result.

After 4 weeks of injury (Option D): is incorrect for the same reason. At this point, the bones may have healed or begun to heal, which would reduce the success rate of reduction.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The frontal sinuses are usually not visible on X-ray until around 4 years of age.

  • While their development begins earlier, they do not appear clearly on radiographs until this age, as the sinuses are still small and continue to grow throughout childhood.

Development of Paranasal Sinuses:

  1. Maxillary Sinus:

    • The maxillary sinus is the first to develop and is present at birth as a small cavity. It grows rapidly during the early years of life and reaches full size by 4 years of age.

  2. Ethmoid Sinus:

    • The ethmoid sinus is present as a small cluster of cells at birth and becomes more prominent in childhood. Development continues up to 6-8 years, with further changes through adolescence.

  3. Sphenoid Sinus:

    • The sphenoid sinus begins to develop around 2 years of age. It is typically visible on imaging after 3-5 years and reaches its adult size by 12 years.

  4. Frontal Sinus:

    • The frontal sinuses are not visible on imaging until about 4 years of age, with full development occurring much later, generally by the age of 16-18 years. Their growth continues until late adolescence.

Incorrect Options:

1 year (Option A): is incorrect because frontal sinuses are not present or visible on X-ray at this age.

2 years (Option B): is incorrect because while they start developing around this time, they aren't visible on X-ray yet.

3 years (Option C): is incorrect because although they begin developing around 2 years, frontal sinuses generally appear on X-ray by the age of 4 years, not 3 years.

  • Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) commonly presents with cervical lymphadenopathy, which can explain the neck nodes observed in this patient.

  • The patient also exhibits a dull tympanic membrane, which can be associated with eustachian tube dysfunction, a common manifestation in NPC due to obstruction or invasion of the nasopharynx. This dysfunction leads to middle ear effusion and the type B tympanogram seen in this case.

  • The presence of deafness and tinnitus further suggests that the nasopharyngeal carcinoma may be affecting the middle ear or the auditory pathway.

Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC):

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor arising from the epithelial cells of the nasopharynx. It is more common in certain geographic regions and in older individuals. The disease often presents with:

  • Cervical lymphadenopathy (neck nodes), as seen in this patient.

  • Deafness or tinnitus, due to eustachian tube obstruction, which leads to middle ear effusion, presenting with a dull tympanic membrane.

  • Type B tympanogram, which indicates middle ear effusion or obstruction.

Incorrect Options:

Chronic suppurative otitis media (Option A): is incorrect because this condition typically causes a purulent discharge and would not lead to the characteristic lymphadenopathy or dull tympanic membrane associated with NPC.

Glomus tumor (Option B): is incorrect because although it can cause tinnitus and middle ear effusion, it would not typically present with cervical lymphadenopathy or the eustachian tube dysfunction leading to type B tympanogram.

Sensorineural hearing loss (Option D): is incorrect because while it can cause hearing loss, the additional findings of cervical lymphadenopathy, a dull tympanic membrane, and type B tympanogram point toward a more localized pathology, such as NPC.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Rhinophyma is a severe form of acne rosacea and is characterized by the thickening and enlargement of the nasal skin, often with a bulbous appearance. It is more common in men and typically develops in individuals with a long history of rosacea.

  • The condition causes facial deformity due to the increased sebaceous gland activity and inflammation. The nose becomes enlarged and may appear red and nodular, which is consistent with the image shown.

Rhinophyma:

Rhinophyma is a subtype of acne rosacea, often associated with long-term rosacea that leads to the hypertrophy of the sebaceous glands on the nose. This condition manifests as:

  • Thickening of the skin, leading to a bulbous or enlarged nose.

  • Redness or telangiectasias (visible blood vessels) on the nose.

  • It typically affects middle-aged to older men and is often triggered or worsened by chronic inflammation from acne rosacea.

  • Treatment may involve laser therapy, surgical excision, or topical treatments to reduce the size and appearance of the nose.

Incorrect Options:

Rhinoscleroma (Option B): is incorrect because rhinoscleroma is a chronic bacterial infection (caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae) that leads to granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis, affecting the nasal and upper respiratory tract. It does not present with the same cosmetic deformity seen in rhinophyma.

Rhinosporidiosis (Option C): is incorrect because rhinosporidiosis is a chronic infection caused by the Rhinosporidium seeberi, which leads to the development of polyps, not the thickening and deformity of the nose characteristic of rhinophyma.

Scleroderma (Option D): is incorrect because scleroderma primarily causes skin tightening and fibrosis but does not lead to the characteristic redness and bulbous deformity of the nose seen in rhinophyma. Scleroderma can affect the face, but it does not cause the same localized changes in the nose as rhinophyma.



Reference:
  • Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg.166
  • Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology, 8th Edition, Volume 1, Pg.439

Explanation:

  • Holman Miller Sign is associated with juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), a highly vascular benign tumor commonly seen in young males.

  • It appears on imaging, typically on a contrast-enhanced CT scan, as a vascular mass in the nasopharynx or nasal cavity, and is indicative of JNA, which is associated with recurrent epistaxis, unilateral nasal obstruction, and denasal speech.

Holman Miller Sign:

  • Holman Miller Sign refers to the contrast-enhanced CT finding that highlights the vascular nature of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA). It is seen as a highly vascular mass in the nasopharyngeal region, often extending into the nasal cavity.

  • Seen as anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus.

  • JNA presents with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, denasal speech, and is often diagnosed in adolescent males.

  • JNA is a benign tumor but can cause significant morbidity due to its location and vascularity. Treatment typically involves surgical resection and sometimes preoperative embolization to reduce vascularity.

Incorrect Options:

Aquino Sign (Option A): is incorrect because it is not associated with juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma but rather describes a different vascular finding.

Teardrop Sign (Option C): is incorrect because it refers to a specific radiographic appearance in the case of subdural hematoma, not nasopharyngeal tumors.

Hanging Drop Sign (Option D): is incorrect because it is associated with posterior fossa lesions such as cerebellar or brainstem tumors, not nasal or paranasal sinus conditions.

Explanation:

  • Cottle’s Test is a diagnostic maneuver used to evaluate nasal obstruction, particularly to assess the patency of the nasal passages and nasal valve function.

  • During this test, the examiner applies external pressure to the lateral nasal walls (just below the cheekbone) to temporarily relieve nasal obstruction.

  • If this improves the patient’s airflow, it suggests nasal valve collapse or dysfunction, which is often seen in patients with deviated septum or nasal valve stenosis.

Cottle’s Test:

  • Cottle's test involves applying pressure to the lateral nasal wall while the patient is instructed to breathe in.

  • If improvement in nasal airflow is noted when external pressure is applied, it indicates that nasal valve collapse is the cause of the obstruction.

  • This test is frequently used before performing surgical interventions, such as septoplasty or rhinoplasty, to confirm the diagnosis of nasal valve insufficiency.

Epley’s maneuver (Option A): is incorrect because it is used for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), not for nasal or facial assessments.

[[figure-1]]

Heimlich maneuver (Option B): is incorrect because it is used for airway obstruction due to choking, not for assessing nasal function.

[[figure-2]]

Trotter’s method (Option D): is incorrect because it is a clinical sign of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, characterized by trismus and nasal obstruction but not a diagnostic maneuver like Cottle's test.
