question: Which clinical test is being shown in the image?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: B) Biopsy with histopathologic examination

  • The patient presents with one-sided facial pain with nasal and oral black mass, which can be a sign of Mucormycosis.
  • Biopsy with histopathologic examination is gold standard for diagnosis.

Mucormycosis

Description

A severe fungal infection primarily affects the nose and sinuses but can quickly spread to the orbit, cribriform plate, meninges, and brain. The fungus invades arteries, causing endothelial damage, thrombosis, and rapid tissue destruction.

Characteristic Findings

Black necrotic material in the nasal cavity, eroding the nasal septum, hard palate, and turbinates. Black turbinate sign is seen on contrast enhanced MRI.

Risk Factors
  • Uncontrolled diabetes, especially with ketoacidosis
  • Prolonged steroid use (common in COVID-19 treatment)
  • Conditions causing immunosuppression: Neutropenia, HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, organ transplants, and kidney issues.

Diagnosis
  • Endoscopy: Shows pale mucosa early, progressing to black crusts and sloughing.
  • Biopsy: Multiple sites should be sampled for fungal identification; potassium hydroxide preparation is the gold standard for confirming invasive features.

Incorrect Options:

X-ray (Option A):

  • X-rays are not the preferred imaging modality for visualizing fungal invasion of the sinuses. Imaging modalities like CT or MRI is preferred.

Serum ferritin (Option C):

  • Though patients with an iron overload are found to be more susceptible to post-COVID mucormycosis, serum ferritin is not an indicative test for Mucormycosis.

HbA1c (Option D):

  • HbA1c is a medical test used to measure long-term blood glucose control, and it is commonly used to screen for diabetes. Although poorly managed diabetes can increase the chances of developing Mucormycosis, HbA1c is not a specific test for Mucormycosis, and it is unlikely to be helpful in confirming the diagnosis.


Reference:
  • Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Pg - 183,184
  • Scott Brown ENT, 8th Edition, Pg - 211
question: A 60-year-old post-COVID male patient came with complaints of one-sided facial swelling, headache, and nasal sinus congestion. He is diabetic and it is uncontrolled. On examination black lesions on the nasal bridge and upper inside of the mouth were observed. Which investigation would you do to confirm the diagnosis of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: C) Aspirin

  • The patient is likely suffering from Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), which was formerly known as Samter's triad, which comprises asthma, nasal polyps, and NSAID Intolerance.
  • Ibuprofen and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) ought to be avoided in patients with Samter's triad due to the potential for serious allergic responses, such as bronchospasm and anaphylaxis.
  • Hence, the correct answer is C, aspirin.

Incorrect Options:

Cotrimoxazole (Option A): This medicine is a combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim and is commonly used to treat bacterial contaminations. It is not contraindicated in patients with Samter's triad.

Co-amoxiclav (Option B): This medication is a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid and is commonly utilized to treat bacterial diseases. It is not contraindicated in patients with Samter's triad.

Chloramphenicol (Option D): This medicine is an antimicrobial that's not commonly related to unfavorably susceptible responses. It is not contraindicated in patients with Samter's triad.



Reference:

Diseases of the Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page no: 243
question: A patient presents with acute exacerbation of asthma; he gives a history of sinusitis and headaches for which he had self-medicated. Examination reveals nasal polyposis; which of the following drugs is likely implicated in this episode of asthma in this patient?

correctAnswer: C. Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

Explanation:

  • The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane along with the superior laryngeal artery to supply sensory innervation to the mucosa of the larynx above the vocal cords, the pharynx, and the pyriform sinus.
  • In cases of foreign body removal from the pyriform sinus, this nerve lies in close proximity and is at high risk of injury.
  • Damage results in loss of sensation in the supraglottic larynx and pyriform sinus, predisposing to aspiration because the protective cough reflex is lost.
  • This nerve is a branch of the vagus nerve and has no motor component - purely sensory in this region.

Incorrect Options:

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option A): Supplies motor innervation to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid and sensory innervation below the vocal cords. It is not exposed during pyriform sinus procedures.
  • Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option B): Provides sensation to the oropharynx, posterior one-third of the tongue, and tonsillar region, not the pyriform sinus.
  • External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (Option D): Supplies motor innervation to the cricothyroid muscle and is located more superficially, away from the pyriform sinus mucosa, making injury unlikely during this procedure.

question: A patient presents with a fish bone stuck in the pyriform sinus. During the removal procedure, there is accidental nerve injury. Which nerve is most likely to be damaged?

correctAnswer: A. External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN)
explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN)

Explanation:

  • The EBSLN innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses the vocal cords to produce high-pitched sounds.
  • Injury during thyroid surgery can cause inability to raise pitch without causing hoarseness, since vocal cord mobility is preserved.
  • Professional voice users (singers, actors) often notice this subtle change more than regular speakers.

Unilateral SLN Palsy

  • Motor Loss: Cricothyroid muscle - decreased ability to tense the vocal cord.
  • Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cord on the affected side.
  • Vocal Cord Position: The affected vocal cord appears shortened and wavy; may exhibit flapping due to loss of tension.
  • Other Features:
    • Askew position of the glottis with the anterior commissure rotated towards the healthy side.
    • Voice changes such as weakness and inability to raise pitch, affecting singing ability.
  • Treatment: Primarily voice therapy to improve vocal function and manage symptoms.

Bilateral SLN Palsy

  • Motor Loss: Both cricothyroid muscles - bilateral loss of vocal cord tension.
  • Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cords bilaterally.
  • Vocal Cord Position: Both vocal cords may be shortened and lack tension, potentially leading to difficulties with voice production.
  • Other Features:
    • Inhalation of food and secretions resulting in coughing and choking.
    • The voice is weak and husky.
  • Treatment:
    • Tracheostomy with a cuffed tube and esophageal feeding tube, if aspiration is severe.
    • Epiglottopexy (reversible) - close laryngeal inlet - to protect the lungs from aspiration.
    • Voice pitch improvement through surgical approximation of the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

Joll’s Triangle (Sternothyroid-laryngeal triangle)

An anatomical landmark used for identifying and preserving the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN).

  • Superior border by the upper attachment of the strap muscles.
  • Medial border by the midline of the neck.
  • Lateral border by the upper pole of the thyroid gland and the superior thyroid vessels.
  • Floor of the Triangle: The EBSLN is located in the floor of the triangle, which is delineated by the cricothyroid muscle.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

  • Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN) (Option B): Provides sensory supply to the mucosa above the vocal cords; injury leads to loss of laryngeal sensation, not pitch alteration.
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) (Option C): Supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid); injury causes hoarseness due to vocal cord palsy, not isolated pitch change.
  • Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option D): Provides sensation to the oropharynx and taste to the posterior third of the tongue; unrelated to pitch control.


Reference:

question: A professional singer presents with difficulty in raising the pitch of her voice following thyroid surgery. There is no hoarseness, but high-pitched voice production is impaired. Which nerve is most likely injured?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B – Supraglottic:

Explanation:

Stridor is a high-pitched, harsh sound due to turbulent airflow through a partially obstructed upper airway.
Inspiratory stridor specifically occurs when obstruction is at or above the level of the vocal cords, because negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration tends to collapse the upper airway.

Supraglottic structures include:

  • Epiglottis

  • Aryepiglottic folds

  • False vocal cords

Obstruction here (e.g., epiglottitis, laryngomalacia, tumors) narrows the airway at a point where airflow is very sensitive to pressure changes during inspiration.
During inspiration → pressure above the glottis becomes subatmospheric → floppy tissue collapses inward → stridor.

Incorrect Options:

Glottic (Option A): Glottic obstruction (true vocal cords) can cause biphasic stridor (both inspiratory & expiratory), because the obstruction is fixed at the narrowest part of the larynx.

Subglottic (Option C): Subglottic narrowing (e.g., croup, subglottic stenosis) usually produces biphasic stridor as well, due to fixed airway narrowing just below the cords.

Trachea (Option D): Tracheal obstruction typically causes expiratory stridor or wheeze if intrathoracic, or biphasic if upper trachea is affected. Inspiratory-only stridor is less typical.

• The AP barium swallow image shows bilateral contrast-filled recesses lateral to the laryngeal inlet. These are characteristic of the pyriform fossae (also called piriform sinuses), which are pharyngeal recesses on each side of the laryngeal orifice.

Pyriform Sinus:

  • Part of the laryngopharynx (hypopharynx).
  • Lies on each side of the laryngeal inlet.
  • Shaped like an inverted tear-drop recess.
  • Bounded by:
    • Medially: Aryepiglottic fold + laryngeal inlet.
    • Laterally: Thyroid cartilage & thyrohyoid membrane.
    • Posteriorly: Pharyngeal wall.

Clinical Significance:

  • Foreign body impaction: Fish bones often lodge here → pain & risk of mucosal injury.
  • Cancer: Hypopharyngeal cancers often start in pyriform fossa → late presentation.
  • Surgical importance: Care to avoid injury to internal laryngeal nerve during endoscopic removal.

Epiglottis (Option B): Midline structure, not paired; appears as a thin flap, not recesses.

Vallecula (Option C): Between base of tongue & epiglottis, higher up than the structures seen here.

Thyroid cartilage (Option D): Skeletal framework, not contrast-filled space.

question: Which of the following signs can be appreciated in the given X-ray?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option : A) Cotton-Meyer classification

Explanation:

  • The patient has a history of prolonged intubation followed by respiratory distress, which is highly suggestive of subglottic/laryngotracheal stenosis.

  • The Cotton-Myer Classification is the most widely used staging system for subglottic stenosis.

  • It grades stenosis according to the percentage of airway obstruction.

  • Grade Airway Obstruction
    Grade I < 50%
    Grade II 51–70%
    Grade III 71–99%
    Grade IV No detectable lumen (100% obstruction)

  • This classification helps determine severity and guides management, ranging from observation and endoscopic dilation to reconstructive surgery.

Radkowski Classification (Option B): Used for staging Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) based on tumor extent.

TNM Classification (Option C): Used for staging malignant tumors according to Tumor size, Node involvement, and Metastasis.

question: A patient with prolonged intubation complained of respiratory distress. Which of the following staging systems is used to stage the condition shown in the image?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer : A) Cricothyroid

Explanation:

  • The cricothyroid muscle is the primary tensor of the vocal cords.
  • It acts by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward on the cricoid cartilage, thereby:
    • Lengthening the vocal cords
    • Increasing vocal cord tension
    • Raising the pitch of the voice
  • Dysfunction or paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle leads to:
    • Inability to produce high-pitched sounds
    • Vocal fatigue
    • Weak voice
    • Bowing and loss of tension of the vocal cords
  • This is particularly noticeable in singers and professional voice users, who rely on precise pitch control.
  • The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

Interarytenoid (Option B): An adductor of the vocal cords that helps close the posterior part of the glottis. It does not control pitch.

Posterior Cricoarytenoid (Option C): The only abductor of the vocal cords. Paralysis causes airway compromise but not isolated loss of high-pitched phonation.

Lateral Cricoarytenoid (Option D): An adductor of the vocal cords responsible for closing the glottis during phonation.

Logan turners, 11th Edition,Page no.291.

correctAnswer: C. Most common congenital abnormality in infants
explanationHtml:
Correct Option: C) Most common congenital abnormality in infants

Explanation:

  • Laryngomalacia is characterised by excessive flaccidity of epiglottis or supraglottis (Malacia: Weakness/ flaccidity of tissue).

Laryngomalacia or congenital laryngeal stridor

  • Most common congenital abnormality of the larynx.
  • During inspiration, an excessively flaccid supraglottic larynx gets sucked in and causes the symptoms.

Clinical features:
  • Presents at birth or immediately after
  • Stridor:
    • Increases on crying (increased negative intrathoracic pressure pulls the epiglottis inward, covering the laryngeal inlet)
    • Stridor present in supine position (as the epiglottis covers the laryngeal inlet)
    • Subsides in prone position (as the epiglottis falls away from the larynx)
  • Cyanosis seen sometimes
  • Normal cry
  • Usually disappears by 2 years of age

Investigations:

  • Direct laryngoscopy:
    • Elongated epiglottis, curled upon itself giving an “omega-shaped” appearance.
    • Floppy aryepiglottic folds
    • Prominent aretynoids
  • Flexible laryngoscopy is the most preferred

Management:

  • Conservative treatment in most cases
  • Tracheostomy: If severe respiratory obstruction
  • Supraglottoplasty: If severe laryngomalacia

Incorrect Options:

Expiratory stridor (Option A): This is a wrong statement as laryngomalacia is associated with Inspiratory stridor

Improve in supine position (Option B): This condition worsens in supine position.

Surgical management is required in most children (Option D): Laryngomalacia usually resolves by 1-2 years of age and can be managed conservatively.Surgical management plays a role if conservative management fails to resolve.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page no: 331

Vocal Nodule (Singer or screamer's nodule)

Cause

Chronic vocal abuse (teachers, actors, vendors or pop singers. )

Laterality

Bilateral or symmetrical

Location

Free edge of vocal cord at the junction of anterior 1/3rd and posterior 2/3rd. This

is the area of maximum vibration of the vocal cord.

Appearance

Sessile , Reddish in the early stage and white in the chronic stage

Symptoms

Treatment

  • A total laryngectomy is a surgical procedure in which the entire larynx is removed.
  • This procedure is typically performed in advanced laryngeal cancer cases that have not responded to other treatments, such as radiation therapy or chemotherapy.
  • During a total laryngectomy, the trachea is re-routed to the front of the neck to create an opening called a stoma, which serves as the new airway.
  • This procedure has significant implications for speech and swallowing, and patients typically require extensive rehabilitation to learn new communication and eating methods

It's commonly used for temporary or permanent airway support in conditions like obstructive sleep apnea or chronic respiratory failure, but it's not suitable for treating laryngeal cancer.

  • Indication: Cefotaxime is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections.

Antibiotics like cefotaxime are not effective against viruses and therefore are not used in the treatment of viral croup unless there is a secondary bacterial infection, which is not indicated in this case.

Other Options

Option A. Nebulized racemic epinephrine:

  • Indication: Used for moderate to severe croup to reduce airway swelling and relieve symptoms of stridor.
  • Mechanism: Acts as a vasoconstrictor to reduce edema in the subglottic space.
  • Recommendation: Appropriate for the treatment of croup.

Option C. Helium oxygen mixture (Heliox):

  • Indication: Used in severe cases of upper airway obstruction to improve airflow and reduce the work of breathing.
  • Mechanism: Heliox is a mixture of helium and oxygen that is less dense than air, allowing it to flow more easily through narrowed airways.
  • Recommendation: Appropriate as an adjunctive treatment in severe cases of croup to reduce respiratory distress.

OptionD. Intramuscular dexamethasone:

  • Indication: Used to reduce inflammation and edema in the airway.
  • Mechanism: Dexamethasone is a corticosteroid that decreases inflammation and swelling in the subglottic area.
  • Recommendation: Appropriate for the treatment of croup. It has been shown to reduce the severity and duration of symptoms.

explanationHtml:
Correct Option:

Option D: Tight suture around tracheostomy site (Correct Answer)

  • Tight suturing around the tracheostomy site can obstruct the normal passage of air, causing air to escape into the surrounding subcutaneous tissues. This can lead to the accumulation of air under the skin, resulting in surgical emphysema.
  • The tight suture creates a seal that prevents air from escaping through the tracheostomy tube, forcing it into the surrounding tissues instead.

Incorrect Options:

Option A. High tracheostomy:

  • A high tracheostomy refers to a tracheostomy performed above the second or third tracheal cartilage.
  • While a high tracheostomy can cause complications, such as injury to blood vessels or the thyroid gland, it is not directly associated with surgical emphysema.

Option B: Tear in posterior tracheal wall

  • A tear in the posterior tracheal wall can lead to air escaping into the mediastinum and potentially causing pneumomediastinum rather than subcutaneous emphysema.

Option C. Block in tracheostomy:

  • A block in the tracheostomy tube can lead to respiratory distress and the buildup of secretions. While it requires immediate attention, it is not directly related to surgical emphysema.

Explanation:

  • The internal laryngeal nerve is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which is, in turn, a branch of the vagus nerve.
  • It supplies the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords and prevents aspiration of any foreign substances by protective cough reflex.
  • Alcohol ingestion can cause alcohol-induced inhibition of the Central Nervous System, which can affect the internal laryngeal nerve, resulting in reduced laryngeal sensations and masked laryngeal reflexes.

The larynx receives both motor and sensory nerve supply from branches of the vagus nerve.

Motor innervation:

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve - All muscles that move the vocal cords, including abductors, adductors, and tensors. Except the cricothyroid muscle.
  • External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve - cricothyroid muscle. (Option C ruled out)

Sensory innervation:

  • The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve - above the vocal cords. (Option A)
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve - below the vocal cords.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve anatomy: (Option D ruled out)

  • The right recurrent laryngeal nerve branches from the vagus at the level of the subclavian artery, looping around it before ascending between the trachea and esophagus.
  • The left recurrent laryngeal nerve arises at the arch of the aorta, loops around it, and ascends along the tracheoesophageal groove, giving it a longer course compared to the right nerve, making it more prone to injury.

Superior laryngeal nerve:

  • Origin - from the inferior ganglion of the vagus nerve; courses behind the internal carotid artery; divides into external and internal branches at the level of the greater cornua of the hyoid bone.
  • The external branch innervates the cricothyroid muscle.
  • The internal branch provides sensory innervation to the larynx and hypopharynx after piercing through the thyrohyoid membrane.


Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX): This nerve provides sensory innervation to the posterior third of the tongue, pharynx, and tonsils. While it contributes to the gag reflex and has some role in swallowing, it's not the primary nerve responsible for sensation in the supraglottic larynx that triggers the cough reflex.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Correct Order: Uncinectomy → Visualisation of maxillary ostium → Bullectomy → Penetration of basal lamella → Removal of posterior ethmoidal cells.

  • 1. Uncinectomy
    • The uncinate process is removed to open the infundibulum
    • This is the gateway step in FESS because it allows:
      • Access to the middle meatus
      • Visualisation of the natural maxillary ostium
  • 2. Visualisation of the maxillary sinus ostium:
    • Once the uncinate is removed, the natural maxillary sinus ostium becomes visible.
    • Identification of the natural ostium is crucial to avoid creating false passages or iatrogenic openings.
  • 3. Bullectomy (removal of ethmoidal bulla):
    • The ethmoidal bulla is the largest anterior ethmoidal air cell.
      • It opens the anterior ethmoid region
      • Allows access to the basal lamella
  • 4. Penetration of the basal lamella:
    • The basal lamella divides the ethmoid sinus into:
      • Anterior ethmoids
      • Posterior ethmoids
    • Penetrating it correctly allows controlled entry into the posterior ethmoidal compartment.
  • 5. Removal of posterior ethmoidal cells:
    • Once the basal lamella is traversed, the surgeon can safely:
      • Remove posterior ethmoidal cells
      • Proceed toward the sphenoid sinus, if needed


Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 495.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Acute severe sensorineural hearing loss (sudden SNHL) is considered an otologic emergency. Systemic oral corticosteroids (such as high-dose Prednisolone) are considered the gold standard and first-line treatment for acute severe Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL).

They work by reducing inflammation, correcting microvascular perfusion deficits, and minimising immune-mediated damage within the inner ear. Therapy is most effective when initiated early, ideally within 48 to 72 hours of symptom onset.

  • Patients often present with:
    • Sudden unilateral hearing loss
    • Tinnitus
    • Aural fullness
    • Sometimes vertigo.
  • Early therapy improves the chance of hearing recovery.
  • Intratympanic steroids may be used as salvage therapy or when systemic steroids are contraindicated.

Topical Steroids (Option A): Topical steroids (like eardrops) do not penetrate the tympanic membrane or blood-labyrinth barrier in sufficient concentrations to reach the inner ear. While intratympanic steroid injections are an effective alternative or salvage therapy for SSNHL, "topical" steroids are completely ineffective.

Steroids + Aspirin (Option B): While aspirin has antiplatelet properties, routinely adding it to systemic steroid therapy is not standard first-line management for acute SSNHL and does not show superior outcomes compared to steroids alone.

Gentamicin + Steroid (Option C): Gentamicin is a vestibulotoxic aminoglycoside. Intratympanic gentamicin is utilised to ablate vestibular function in refractory Meniere's disease; administering it in acute SNHL would risk further irreversible cochlear damage.

Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome is a rare neurocutaneous disorder characterised by a classic clinical triad consisting of:

  • Recurrent orofacial oedema (usually involving the lips, known as cheilitis granulomatosa)
  • Recurrent facial nerve palsy (which can be unilateral or bilateral)
  • Fissured tongue (Lingua plicata)

[[figure-1]]

Proptosis is not associated with this syndrome; it is more commonly associated with:

  • Thyroid eye disease
  • Orbital tumors
  • Orbital cellulitis.

Facial palsy (Option A): This is a core component of the triad. It mimics Bell's palsy but is distinctly recurrent and can eventually lead to permanent axonal weakness.

Fissured tongue (Option B): Also known as pleated or scrotal tongue, this is a congenital feature present in approximately 30% to 40% of these patients and is a component of the triad.

Orofacial oedema (Option C): Typically, the presenting symptom, it features painless, non-pitting swelling of the lips and face that eventually becomes permanent due to non-caseating granulomatous inflammation

Explanation:

The clinical presentation of an immunocompromised individual (such as an advanced HIV/AIDS patient or uncontrolled diabetic) presenting with acute, invasive sinusitis, blood-stained nasal discharge, and a necrotic black eschar on the nasal mucosa or hard palate is classic for Mucormycosis.

The most common causative fungal genera are Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia, with Rhizopus oryzae accounting for the vast majority of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis cases.

  • The fungus is highly angioinvasive:
    • Invades blood vessels
    • Causes thrombosis and tissue necrosis.

[[figure-1]]

  • Tissue necrosis produces the characteristic black eschar over the nose/palate.
  • Common risk factors:
    • Diabetes mellitus (especially DKA)
    • HIV/AIDS
    • Steroid therapy
    • Neutropenia.
  • Histopathology shows:
    • Broad aseptate hyphae
    • Right-angle branching.

[[figure-2]]

  • Treatment:
    • Surgical debridement
    • IV amphotericin B.

Aspergillus (Option B): Aspergillus species can cause invasive fungal sinusitis with tissue necrosis, but Rhizopus is much more classically associated with rapid vascular invasion, extensive thrombosis, and the hallmark extensive black necrotic eschars on the palate and turbinates.

Cryptococcus (Option C): Cryptococcus neoformans typically presents as fungal meningitis or pulmonary infections in immunocompromised patients; it rarely causes destructive, necrotic sinonasal lesions.

Candida (Option D): Candida species cause superficial mucosal infections (like oral thrush) presenting as whitish, scrapable plaques, rather than deeply invasive, angioinvasive tissue destruction with black eschar formation.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario of chronic sinusitis with nasal crusting and saddle nose deformity is characteristic of Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), formerly called Wegener’s granulomatosis.

  • Autoimmune necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis
  • Clinical Features:
    • Chronic nasal obstruction and crusting
    • Recurrent sinusitis
    • Epistaxis and septal perforation
    • Saddle nose deformity due to septal cartilage destruction
    • Pulmonary nodules/hemoptysis
    • Glomerulonephritis (rapidly progressive)
  • Serology: c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) positive
  • Management:
    • Immunosuppression with corticosteroids + cyclophosphamide or rituximab
    • Long-term monitoring for relapse.

Allergic rhinitis (Option B) presents with sneezing, itching, watery rhinorrhea, and mucosal edema. Does not cause mucosal ulceration, crusting, or cartilage destruction, no saddle nose.

[[figure-1]]

Nasal polyposis (Option C) causes nasal obstruction, hyposmia, and may accompany chronic sinusitis. Polyps do not destroy cartilage and do not cause saddle nose deformity.

[[figure-2]]

Rhinoscleroma (Option D): Chronic granulomatous disease due to Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. Causes nasal crusting, obstruction, and granulomas, but saddle nose deformity is not typical.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 8th Edition, Page 187.
question: A patient presents with chronic sinusitis, nasal crusting, and saddle nose deformity. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The condition is Zenker’s diverticulum, a posterior hypopharyngeal pulsion diverticulum caused by mucosal herniation through Killian’s dehiscence, located between the oblique fibers of the thyropharyngeus and the transverse fibers of the cricopharyngeus.

Pathophysiology

Cricopharyngeal incoordination or failure to relax ↑ intrapharyngeal pressure, which causes mucosal herniation through a weak point and lead tpdiverticulum formation.

Location

Posterior midline above the upper esophageal sphincter.

Features
  • Dysphagia (progressive)
  • Regurgitation of undigested food
  • Halitosis
  • Aspiration episodes
  • Gurgling on swallowing

Treatment
  • Diverticulectomy open/endoscopic
  • Dohlman procedure.

[[figure-1]]

Inferior constrictor & middle constrictor (Option C) corresponds to Killian-Jamieson’s area, which produces a Killian-Jamieson diverticulum (lateral), not Zenker’s (posterior midline).

Stylopharyngeus & palatopharyngeus (Option D) elevate the pharynx during swallowing and are not involved in diverticulum formation.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat, 8th Edition, Page 323-324.
question: The following disease process shown in the image given below occurs as a result of weakness between which two muscles?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The posterior pharyngeal wall ulcer shown is superficial, erythematous, and centrally ulcerated, which is typical of mucosal injury rather than deep glandular or lymphoid pathology.

  • Lesion characteristics: Superficial, erythematous, centrally ulcerated → indicates mucosal involvement.
  • Origin: Pharyngeal mucosa (surface epithelium) rather than deeper structures.
  • Common causes of mucosal ulcers:
    • Viral infections (EBV, adenovirus)
    • Aphthous ulcers
    • Mechanical trauma (sharp foods)
    • Gastroesophageal reflux / Laryngopharyngeal reflux
    • Chronic infections (TB, syphilis).

Minor salivary glands (Option A) produce mucoceles or adenomas, not superficial ulceration.

Subepithelial region (Option C) would cause submucosal swelling, not an ulcer.

Lymphoid tissue (Option D): Relative to Waldeyer’s ring, produces hypertrophy or plaques, not isolated posterior wall ulcers.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat, 8th Edition, Page 355.
question: A patient presents with an ulcer on the posterior pharyngeal wall, as shown in the image. This lesion most likely originates from which structure?

correctAnswer: C. Between the 2nd and 3rd tracheal rings
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The best and safest site for performing a standard elective tracheostomy is between the 2nd and 3rd tracheal rings.

Tracheostomy:

  • Is making an opening in the anterior wall of the trachea and converting it into a stoma on the skin surface.
  • Types:

High Tracheostomy

Mid-Tracheostomy

Low Tracheostomy

  • Location: Done above the thyroid isthmus (isthmus lies against 1st, 2nd, and 4th tracheal rings) and involves the 1st tracheal ring.
  • Risks: Perichondritis of cricoid cartilage and subglottic stenosis.
  • Only Indication: Carcinoma of the larynx (since the entire larynx will be removed, and a new tracheostome will be made lower).
  • Location: Done through the 2nd or 3rd tracheal rings and involves the division of or retraction of the thyroid isthmus to expose the trachea.
  • Most Preferred technique
  • Location: Done below the level of thyroid isthmus (below the 3rd tracheal ring).
  • Challenges:
    • Trachea is deeper at this level.
    • Close proximity to large blood vessels.
    • Difficulty with tracheostomy tube impinging on the suprasternal notch.

Through the cricothyroid membrane (Option A): This site is used for emergency cricothyrotomy, not for elective or planned tracheostomy.

Between the 4th and 5th tracheal rings (Option B): This lower site increases the risk of bleeding, tracheal instability, and damage to mediastinal structures.

Just below the cricoid cartilage (Option D): Performing tracheostomy too close to the cricoid can cause subglottic stenosis due to cartilage injury



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 369, 370
question: What is the best and safest site for performing a tracheostomy?

correctAnswer: A. Long-term antibiotics with surgical debulking
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This clinical picture is classic for rhinoscleroma (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis infection), seen in young individuals from low socio-economic backgrounds with chronic nasal obstruction, foul-smelling discharge, crusting, epistaxis, and a pale granular/nodular mass.
  • Treatment of choice is prolonged antibiotic therapy to eradicate the organism
  • Surgical debulking is added when there is significant obstruction or fibrotic mass

Treatment of Rhinoscleroma:

  • Medical therapy:
    • Streptomycin + tetracycline for a minimum duration of 4-6 weeks.
    • After 1 month, it is repeated if necessary.
    • Treatment is stopped only if two consecutive cultures from the biopsy material are negative.
    • To reduce fibrosis, steroids can be combined
  • Surgery:
    • Surgical debridement, laser ablation, and correction of sclerotic defects.
    • These are considered only secondary to antibiotic therapy.

Corticosteroids with antihistamines (Option B): Useful for allergic rhinitis, not infective granulomatous disease

Radiotherapy (Option C): No role in rhinoscleroma

Short-course oral antibiotics with nasal decongestants (Option D): Inadequate; disease requires long-term therapy



Reference:

  1. Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 181-184
  2. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/rhinoscleroma

question: Young women from a low socio-economic background present with long-standing nasal obstruction, foul-smelling nasal discharge, crusting with hardening of the external nose, and episodic epistaxis. On examination, the nasal cavity shows a pale, granular, nodular mass causing obstruction. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The tragal pointer is a cartilaginous projection from the tragus of the external ear. The facial nerve trunk lies ~1 cm deep and inferior to the tragal pointer.
  • Hence, it is a reliable and commonly used landmark to identify the facial nerve during parotid surgery.
  • Parotidectomy involves the removal of part or the whole of the parotid gland, with preservation of the facial nerve whenever possible.

Indications

  • Benign tumours (e.g. pleomorphic adenoma, Warthin tumour)
  • Malignant parotid tumors
  • Chronic sialadenitis, abscess, or recurrent parotitis

Types of parotidectomy

  • Superficial parotidectomy: Most common
  • Total conservative parotidectomy: Facial nerve preserved
  • Radical parotidectomy: Facial nerve sacrificed (malignancy)

Facial nerve identification (key landmarks)

  • Tragal (Conley’s) pointer: The facial nerve lies 1 cm deep and inferior to the tip of the tragal cartilage
  • Posterior belly of the digastric muscle: The facial nerve can be identified above the upper border.
  • Tympanomastoid suture: The facial nerve lies inferior to this suture line as it overlies the stylomastoid foramen.

Sternocleidomastoid muscle (Option A): Used for exposure and orientation, but it is not a precise landmark for locating the facial nerve trunk.

Digastric muscle (Option B): The posterior belly is a helpful landmark, but it is less specific and less constant than the tragal pointer.

Tympanomastoid suture (Option D): A deep bony landmark that requires extensive dissection and is not the most practical intraoperative guide.



Reference:

Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 845, 846, 849.
question: During the parotid gland surgery, which structure is a landmark for identifying the facial nerve?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of vocal cord fixation alone elevates the stage to at least T3. The involvement of the inner thyroid cortex further confirms T3 (invasion of inner thyroid cartilage/cortex).

Staging of supraglottic tumor:

  • T1: Tumour limited to one subsite of supraglottis with normal vocal cord mobility.
  • T2: Tumour invades the mucosa of more than one adjacent subsite of the supraglottis, glottis, or region outside the supraglottis.
  • T3: Tumor limited to larynx with vocal-cord fixation or invades post-cricoid area, pre-epiglottis tissues, paraglottic space, thyroid cartilage erosion.
  • T4a: Tumour spreads through thyroid cartilage, trachea, soft tissues of the neck, deep/extrinsic muscle of the tongue, strap muscles, and thyroid oesophagus.
  • T4b: Tumor spreads prevertebral space, mediastinal structures, carotid artery.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 359.

Explanation:

  • Eagle syndrome involves the elongation or calcification of the stylohyoid ligament or styloid process, which can cause symptoms such as throat pain, referred ear pain (otalgia), and difficulty swallowing (dysphagia).
  • Surgical intervention may be needed, and care should be taken to avoid damaging nearby structures.
  • The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), derived from the second pharyngeal arch, is most likely to be affected during surgery due to its proximity to the stylohyoid ligament.

Derivatives of the Pharyngeal arches:

Pharyngeal arch

Muscles derived

Bones derived

Cranial nerve

Derivatives of clefts and pouches

Muscles of mastication,

tensor veli palatini,

mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric.

  • Incus

(Option A)
  • External auditory canal.
  • The pouch of the first and second arches merges to further develop into the eustachian tube and the middle ear cavity.

Hyoid Arch

(Arch II)

Muscles of facial expressions, stapedius, stylohyoid,

posterior belly of the digastric muscle.

The cleft of the 2nd pharyngeal arch merges with the clefts of the 3rd, 4th and 6th arches to form the cervical sinus, which typically disappears during development.

Glossopharyngeal arch

Stylopharyngeus
  • Greater cornua of hyoid

(Arch IV & V)


Pharyngeal and laryngeal musculature

(Option C)

Persistence of the cervical sinus may result in a collaural fistula, establishing an abnormal connection between the external auditory canal and the middle ear.

question: A 36-year-old patient presents with severe sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and neck pain. On examination, there is noticeable swelling on the lateral aspect of the neck and a muffled voice. Imaging studies reveal an abscess located in the space between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscles. Which structures pass through this space?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D) Eustachian tube

Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms align with Trotter's syndrome, commonly associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma. This condition involves:
    • Conductive hearing loss due to obstruction of the Eustachian tube, which is responsible for equalising ear pressure.
    • Trigeminal neuralgia affects the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, 5thleading to facial pain.
    • Palatal asymmetry resulting from tumour infiltration into the levator palatini muscles.

Mnemonic:N-5th nerve Neuralgia

P- Palatal palsy

C- CHL

  • This occurs when malignant tumours infiltrate the lateral wall of the nasopharynx or originate in the Sinus of Morgagni (the space between the base of the skull and the superior constrictor muscle).
  • Structures passing through the Sinus of Morgagni are
    • Levator veli palatini
    • Auditory tube/eustachian tube
    • Tensor veli palatini
    • Ascending palatine artery

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Structures passing through the Sinus of Morgagni

question: A 55-year-old male presents with progressive hearing loss in his right ear over the past few months, along with intermittent facial pain, difficulty swallowing, palate asymmetry, and speech difficulties. Nasopharyngoscopy reveals a nasopharyngeal mass. Which structure is likely responsible for hearing loss in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pharyngobasilar Fascia or Pharyngeal Aponeurosis is a thick fibrous layer located between the mucosa and the muscular layer and forms the inner layer.
  • It provides structural integrity to the pharyngeal wall, especially where muscles are deficient, such as the posterior wall.
  • It also anchors the pharynx to the skull base, ensuring firmness and support.


Layers of pharyngeal wall:

The pharyngeal wall consists of four layers, from innermost to outermost:

  • Mucosal Membrane: Mucosa in the nasopharynx consists of Ciliated columnar epithelium and stratified squamous epithelium in the oropharynx and laryngopharynx.
  • Pharyngobasilar Fascia (Pharyngeal Aponeurosis): A fibrous layer that provides structural integrity and support to the pharyngeal wall, especially in the posterior area.
  • Muscular Layer consists of the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles and they function in the peristaltic movement of the pharynx during swallowing.
  • Buccopharyngeal Fascia (Option B):
    • This is the outermost layer of the pharyngeal wall.
    • It covers the external surface of the pharyngeal muscles and is continuous with the pretracheal fascia.
    • It also separates the pharyngeal wall from surrounding structures like the prevertebral fascia.

[[figure-1]]

Fig: Layers of the pharyngeal wall


Investing fascia (Option A) is the outermost layer of the deep cervical fascia, which encases the entire neck.

[[figure-2]]

Fig: Layers of Deep Cervical Fascia


Prevertebral fascia (Option C) is the inner layer of deep cervical fascia surrounding the vertebral column and its associated muscles.



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 303
  2. www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541091/#:~:text=The%20prevertebral%2C%20or%20deep%20layer,of%20the%20sympathetic%20trunk%20ganglia.

question: A 50-year-old patient presents with dysphagia and a sensation of a lump in the throat. On examination, a mass is noted on the posterior pharyngeal wall. Which anatomical structure primarily forms the inner layer?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The scenario and barium swallow findings suggest Zenker’s diverticulum, an outpouching occurring at a site known as Killian’s Dehiscence (often referred to as the "gateway of tears").
  • This space is formed by the two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle: the thyropharyngeus (oblique fibres) and the cricopharyngeus (transverse fibres). This arrangement creates a triangular gap known as Killian’s dehiscence.

Zenker’s Diverticulum (Hypopharyngeal Pouch/Pharyngeal Pouch):

Description

An acquired, false, and pulsion diverticulum formed by the protrusion of mucosa and submucosa through Killian's dehiscence.

Clinical manifestations
  • Dysphagia
  • Regurgitation
  • Food getting stuck (leading to coughing while eating)
  • Aspiration
  • Halitosis (bad breath)

[[figure-1]]

Investigation

Barium swallow reveals an outpouching of the pharyngeal mucosa above the upper oesophagal sphincter, often with slow emptying of the diverticulum.

[[figure-2]]

Management

  • Diverticulectomy and cricopharyngeal myotomy: Surgical removal of the diverticulum and myotomy of the cricopharyngeal muscle.
  • Diverticular suspension: Dissection and inversion of the diverticulum with its apex pointing cranially.
  • Myotomy through stapler transection: Transoral insertion of a linear stapler to divide the septum between the diverticulum and the true oesophagal lumen.

Dohlman Procedure: Endoscopic technique involving division of the diverticulum wall and cricopharyngeal myotomy.

[[figure-3]]

Cricopharyngeus and esophageal muscle fibres (Option A): Incorrect because Zenker’s diverticulum arises above the esophagus, not between these structures.

Thyropharyngeus and esophageal muscle fibres (Option B): Incorrect, as the esophagus lies inferior to the area of dehiscence.

Inferior constrictor along with upper esophageal muscle fibres (Option D): Incorrect because this does not specify the true anatomical gap (Killian’s dehiscence is between the two parts of the inferior constrictor, not between it and the esophagus).



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 281, 323, 324.
  2. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1126, 1127.

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with six months of dysphagia, regurgitation, and a feeling of food getting stuck, often coughing while eating. A barium swallow study shows specific findings on the radiograph. Which muscle pairs define the anatomical boundaries of the observed dehiscence?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The structure marked ‘X’ in the above image is the fossa of rosenmuller.

[[figure-1]]

Anatomy of Nasopharynx

  • The nasopharynx, also known as the epipharynx, is the uppermost portion of the pharynx, located behind the nasal cavities and extends from the base of the skull to the soft palate or the horizontal plane that passes through the hard palate.

  • From anterior to posterior, the structures seen on the lateral wall are as follows:

    • Eustachian tube

    • Torus tubarius – a cushion-like elevation that lies above and behind the Eustachian tube.

    • Fossa of Rosenmüller – a recess located above and behind the torus tubarius, and the most common site of carcinoma origin.

    • Salpingopharyngeal fold – a ridge extending from the lower end of the torus tubarius to the lateral pharyngeal wall.

[[figure-2]]

Pyriform fossa (Option A) or pyriform sinus (smuggler’s pouch) are the two depressions on the lateral sides of the aryepiglottic folds.

  • It is a site where foreign bodies can lodge and form the lateral channel for food.

Post cricoid region (Option D) is the part of the anterior wall of the laryngopharynx between the upper and lower borders of the cricoid lamina.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

PL DhingraDiseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page 282

question: A 35-year-old female presenting with persistent right ear fullness, hearing loss, and pressure particularly during flights is suspected of having Eustachian tube blockage. During rhinoscopy, a structure labelled as X in the image below is noted. Identify this structure.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The condition mentioned in the above question indicates palatal palsy, which can lead to velopharyngeal insufficiency.
  • Passavant’s ridge is the structure responsible for separating the nasopharynx from the oropharynx.

Passavant’s ridge

  • It is a mucosal ridge formed by the superior constrictor and palatopharyngeus, encircling the posterior and lateral walls of the nasopharyngeal isthmus.
  • The soft palate firmly contracts against Passavant’s ridge on the posterior pharyngeal wall and completely cuts off the nasopharynx from the oropharynx, a crucial function during swallowing, vomiting, gagging, and speech.

[[figure-1]]

Sinus of Morgagni (Option B) is a space between the base of the skull and the upper free border of the superior constrictor muscle.


[[figure-2]]

Rathke’s pouch (Option C) is represented clinically by a dimple above the adenoids and is reminiscent of the buccal mucosal invagination, to form the anterior lobe of pituitary.


[[figure-3]]



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 283
  2. Scott-Brown Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck surgery, 8th Edition, Page 192

question: A 7-year-old girl presents with hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation of fluids while drinking. She is diagnosed with palatal palsy. Which structure is responsible for separating the nasopharynx from the oropharynx during swallowing, preventing regurgitation?

correctAnswer: D. The posterior wall lies opposite the atlas vertebra.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The posterior wall of the oropharynx lies opposite to the 2nd and upper border of the 3rd vertebra, not the Ist vertebrae which is also known as ATLAS vertebrae.

Anatomy of the Oropharynx:

  • Oropharynx is the part of the pharynx which lies behind the oral cavity.
  • Oropharyngeal isthmus:
    • A communication between oropharynx and oral cavity.
    • The uvula and anterior pillar together define the oropharyngeal isthmus (Option C).

[[figure-1]]

  • Boundaries of Oropharynx:

Roof

The plane of the hard palate.

Floor

The plane of the hyoid bone.

Posterior wall

Lies opposite the 2nd and upper part of the 3rd cervical vertebrae (Option D) and is related to retropharyngeal space.

Anterior wall

It is deficient above (oropharynx communicates with the oral cavity)

Inferiorly it presents:

  • Base of tongue (posterior 1/3rd)
  • Lingual tonsil
  • Valleculae: Cup-shaped depressions, between the tongue and epiglottis, are bordered by the median glossoepiglottic fold and pharyngoepiglottic fold. They often contain retention cysts.

[[figure-2]]

Lateral wall
(Option A, B)
  • Palatine (faucial) tonsil
  • Anterior pillar/palatoglossal arch (formed by the palatoglossus muscle)
  • Posterior pillar/palatopharyngeal arch (formed by the palatopharyngeus muscle).


[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 283, 284

question: A teenager presented with a sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and a fever for the past three days. During the oral examination, the ENT surgeon asked the intern about the anatomy of the pharyngeal region located behind the oral cavity. Which of the following is not true about the anatomy of that region ?

correctAnswer: C. Carcinoma Esophagus, Post cricoid region
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a condition characterized by a triad of iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia due to esophageal webs, and an increased risk of upper esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Patients with this syndrome are at an increased risk for developing squamous cell carcinoma of upper esophagus and the most common site of carcinoma is post-cricoid region

Subdivisions of Hypopharynx:

Pyriform fossa (sinus) or Smuggler’s pouch

(Option A)
  • It lies on either side of the larynx and extends from pharyngoepiglottic fold to the upper end of the oesophagus.
  • It is bounded as,
    • Laterally: the thyrohyoid membrane and the thyroid cartilage.
    • Medially: aryepiglottic fold and posterolateral surfaces of arytenoid and cricoid cartilages.
  • It creates the lateral channel for food and can trap foreign bodies.

Post cricoid region

(Option C)
  • Part of the anterior wall of laryngopharynx between the upper and lower borders of cricoid lamina.
  • It is a common site for carcinoma in females suffering from Plummer-Vinson syndrome.

Posterior pharyngeal wall (Option B)

It extends from the level of hyoid bone to the level of cricoarytenoid joint.

[[figure-1]]

Valleculae (Option D) are cup-shaped depressions, between the tongue and epiglottis, and are bordered by the median glossoepiglottic fold and pharyngoepiglottic fold. They often contain retention cysts.


[[figure-2]]



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 284, 285
  2. Scott-Brown Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck surgery, 8th Edition, Page 275.

question: A 56-year-old woman with a history of Plummer-Vinson syndrome presents with dysphagia, hoarseness, weight loss, and right-sided cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms, and which area is most commonly affected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The marked structure is part of Waldeyer’s Ring and is identified as the pharyngeal tonsil, also known as the adenoids or Luschka’s tonsil.

Waldeyer’s Ring:

  • Lymphoid tissue scattered in the subepithelial layer of the pharynx forms aggregated masses called Waldeyer's ring, which serve to protect the respiratory and digestive tracts.
  • The lymphoid masses are:
    • Nasopharyngeal tonsil also known as the pharyngeal tonsil, adenoids, or Luschka’s tonsil, is a midline structure located in the nasopharynx.
    • Palatine tonsils (Option A): Paired structures situated laterally within the oropharynx.
    • Lingual tonsil (Option C): Located in the oropharynx along the midline at the base of the tongue
    • Tubal tonsils (in fossa of Rosenmuller) are also known as Gerlach’s tonsil (Option B). They paired structures, located in the fossa of Rosenmüller, near the eustachian tube opening into the nasopharynx.
  • Nodules on the posterior pharyngeal wall.
  • Lateral pharyngeal bands

[[figure-1]]



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 281, 282
  2. Scott-Brown Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck surgery, 8th Edition, Page 741

question: Identify the structure indicated as ‘X’ in the image.

correctAnswer: C. Palatine tonsil and superior constrictor
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given scenario suggests a peritonsillar abscess, also referred to as quinsy, which forms in the peritonsillar space, located between the palatine tonsil and the superior constrictor muscle.

[[figure-1]]

Peritonsillar space:

  • It is a paired structure, situated lateral to the tonsil.
  • Lies between the capsule of tonsil (palatine) and the superior constrictor muscle
  • The superior constrictor muscle forms the tonsil bed.

[[figure-2]]

  • Peritonsillar abscess/Quinsy:
    • It is a collection of pus in the peritonsillar space.
    • Tonsillar capsule may be breached by bacterial infections of the tonsil, resulting in abscess formation.
    • If left untreated, peritonsillar infections may spread to the parapharyngeal space.




Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 311, 315
  2. Scott-Brown Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck surgery, 8th Edition, Page 550

question: A 28-year-old female arrives at the emergency department with a severe sore throat, difficulty swallowing, fever, a muffled voice, and drooling. Examination reveals tonsil being pushed medially and uvula deviated to opposite side . Which of the following options defines the boundaries of the infected space?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Symptoms of infection along with swelling observed in the posterior throat and the involvement of the nodes of Rouviere are indicative of a Retropharyngeal Abscess.

Retropharyngeal space

  • Lies behind the pharynx between the buccopharyngeal fascia and the prevertebral fascia.
  • Extends from the base of the skull to the bifurcation of trachea.
  • The alar fascia divides the space into two lateral compartments, known as the spaces of Gillette, which contain the nodes of Rouviere (usually disappear at 3-4 years of age).
  • Infection usually presents as a Unilateral Bulge in the Posterior Pharyngeal wall
  • Infections can develop as a complication of tonsillitis or adenoids and may extend posteriorly behind the pharynx and esophagus into the mediastinum.

[[figure-1]]

Parapharyngeal space (Option A) is a pyramidal shaped space with base at the base of skull and apex at the hyoid bone and is divided by the styloid process into pre-styloid and post-styloid

compartments.

  • The boundaries are:
    • Medial: Buccopharyngeal fascia
    • Posterior: Prevertebral fascia and transverse processes of cervical vertebrae.
    • Lateral: Medial pterygoid muscle, mandible and deep surface of parotid gland.
  • It contains carotid vessels, jugular vein, IX, X, XI and XII cranial nerves and cervical sympathetic chain.
  • The source of infection in this space is from the tonsil.

Prevertebral space (Option C) is situated between the vertebral bodies posteriorly and the prevertebral fascia anteriorly, extending from the base of the skull to the coccyx. Infection of this space usually comes from the caries of spine.

Sublingual space (Option D) is located above the mylohyoid muscle and beneath the oral mucosa. Infections of the premolars and the first molar are the most common causes of abscess formation in this area.



[[figure-2]]



Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 312, 313, 315
  2. Scott-Brown Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck surgery, 8th Edition, Page 551

question: A 7-year-old girl presents with severe throat pain, high fever, difficulty swallowing, excessive drooling, and trouble breathing. Examination reveals swelling in the posterior throat. The ENT specialist mentions that the infected space includes the nodes of Rouviere. Which space is affected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Adenoids can be examined and normally are visible during Posterior Rhinoscopy.

Posterior Rhinoscopy

Purpose

A diagnostic procedure used to examine the posterior part of the nasal cavity, including the nasopharynx.

Structures

Following structures are normally visible in posterior rhinoscopy:

[[figure-1]]

Indications

  • Choanal polyp
  • Choanal atresia
  • Hypertrophy of posterior ends of inferior turbinates
  • Discharge in the middle meatus and above it.

Tubal tonsils (Option B) and Pyriform fossa (Option C) are not visible in posterior rhinoscopy.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 448, 449

question: A 5-year-old child presents with persistent nasal congestion, unilateral nasal discharge, and occasional nosebleeds, along with frequent ear infections and a slightly nasal voice. Posterior rhinoscopy is planned. Which of the following structures are normally visible during this procedure?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Orbicularis oris:

  • Controlled by the facial nerves (CN VII).

  • Mainly involved in lip closure and facial expression.

  • Damage → difficulty closing lips (some labial articulation issues), but does not significantly affect swallowing or most types of dysarthria.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Tongue muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus):

  • Controlled by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

  • Lesion → tongue weakness → impaired articulation (dysarthria) and difficulty moving food (dysphagia).

Option B - Pharyngeal constrictor muscles:

  • Controlled by the vagus nerve (CN X).

  • Lesion → impaired swallowing → dysphagia, nasal regurgitation.

Option D - Stylopharyngeus:

  • Controlled by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

  • Elevates pharynx during swallowing → lesion → dysphagia

question: Damage to which of the following muscles is least likely to cause dysarthria or dysphagia?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The child’s chronic nasal obstruction, snoring, mouth breathing, and facial features (adenoid facies) strongly suggest adenoid hypertrophy.
  • Nasal endoscopy is the most appropriate and accurate test for diagnosing adenoid hypertrophy as it provides a direct visual assessment of the nasopharynx and adenoid tissue.
  • It provides direct visualisation of the adenoids and accurately assesses their size and the degree of choanal obstruction.

Adenoid Hypertrophy

Aetiology
  • Physiological Enlargement: Common in childhood.
  • Chronic Conditions: Recurrent rhinitis, sinusitis, chronic tonsillitis, & allergies.

Clinical Features
  • Nasal Symptoms:
    • Nasal obstruction leading to mouth breathing and feeding difficulties.
    • Nasal discharge due to choanal obstruction and chronic rhinitis.
    • Sinusitis, Epistaxis & voice changes due to nasal obstruction. (Rhinolalia clausa)
  • Aural Symptoms:
    • Tubal obstruction causing retracted tympanic membrane and CHL.
    • Recurrent acute otitis media and chronic suppurative otitis media.
    • Otitis media with effusion due to intermittent eustachian tube obstruction.
  • Adenoid Facies: Characteristic facial appearance with an elongated face, open mouth, crowded upper teeth, and high-arched palate.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • Pulmonary Hypertension: Potential due to long-standing nasal obstruction.
  • Aprosexia: Difficulty concentrating

Clinical Examination
  • External Nose: Check for skin changes indicating frequent nose rubbing.
  • Nasal Assessment: Halogen light otoscope is used for simple anterior rhinoscopy (Option C), which examines the nasal cavity but not the adenoids.
  • Adenoid Assessment:
    • Nasal endoscopy: For detailed evaluation, a flexible pediatric endoscope with topical anaesthesia is preferred. It provides an accurate assessment of adenoid size in an outpatient setting.
    • Lateral Soft-Tissue Radiograph (Option B): This is useful when endoscopy is not tolerated; it correlates well with endoscopic findings.



Reference:
  1. PL DhingraDiseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page 286, 287

  2. Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 287
question: A 7-year-old child presents with chronic nasal obstruction, snoring, and mouth breathing. Physical examination reveals characteristic facial appearance as shown in the image and hypertrophy of the nasal turbinates. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test to confirm the suspected condition?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Grade III

Explanation:

The endoscopic image showing adenoid tissue filling from 50-75% of the choanae corresponds to Grade III.

Grading of Adenoid Hypertrophy:

  • Grade I: Adenoid occupies 0-25% of the choanal space.
  • Grade II: Adenoid occupies 25-50% of the choanal space.
  • Grade III: Adenoid occupies 50-75% of the choanal space.
  • Grade IV: Adenoid occupies >75% of the choanal space.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 287
question: An 8-year-old child presents with chronic nasal obstruction and recurrent otitis media. The physician performs endoscopy to evaluate adenoid hypertrophy. The endoscopic finding is given in the image. What is the grade of adenoid hypertrophy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Given the scenario where a child with persistent nasal obstruction and recurrent ear infections has not responded to Medical management, the most appropriate next step for definitive management is Endoscopic debridement.

Management of Adenoid Hypertrophy:

Medical Management: (For Mild Cases initially)
  • Breathing exercises
  • Decongestant nasal drops
  • Antihistamines for any nasal allergies
  • Topical Nasal Steroids (Option C) may reduce adenoid size and improve related symptoms.

Surgical Intervention: (Adenoidectomy)
  • Traditional Methods: Blind curettage adenoidectomy (Option A) remains common, but it has disadvantages, including unpredictable bleeding and poor access to the choanal adenoid. Hence, Endoscopic management is currently preferred.
  • Direct Vision Techniques:
    • Suction Diathermy
    • Endoscopic Coblation/Microdebridement (Option B) involves using endoscopy to visualise and allows for precise removal of obstructive adenoid tissue, addressing the underlying issue directly.
    • KTP Laser: Associated with a higher risk of nasopharyngeal stenosis, while the gold laser has not shown this risk.


Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 287
  2. Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 288
question: A 6-year-old child with persistent nasal obstruction and recurrent ear infections has not improved with decongestants and antihistamines. What is the most appropriate next step for definitive management currently being used?

correctAnswer: B. Delay the surgery until the infection resolves
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Elective surgery, including adenoidectomy, should be postponed in children with an acute upper respiratory infection to minimise complications.

Indications & Contraindications of Adenoidectomy

Indications
  • Adenoid hypertrophy causing snoring, mouth breathing, sleep apnea, or speech abnormalities (rhinolalia clausa).
  • Recurrent rhinosinusitis.
  • Chronic otitis media with effusion linked to adenoid hyperplasia.
  • Recurrent ear discharge in benign CSOM associated with adenoiditis.
  • Preventing recurrence of dental malocclusion after orthodontic treatment.

Contraindications
  • Cleft palate or submucous palate (risk of velopharyngeal insufficiency).
  • Hemorrhagic diathesis.
  • Acute upper respiratory infection.

Proceed with adenoidectomy as planned (Option A): Incorrect because an acute URI poses increased anesthesia risk.


Start antibiotics and proceed with surgery (Option C): Incorrect; antibiotics do not eliminate anesthetic risk during URI.


Discharge the patient with medical management (Option D): Incorrect because surgery is elective, not emergent; focus is on timing, not discharge.



Reference:

PL Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page 507

question: A 9-year-old child was scheduled for elective adenoidectomy but developed an acute upper respiratory infection the day before the surgery. The child has no cleft palate or bleeding disorders. What is the most appropriate next step?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Chronic Otitis Media is a condition that might be associated with adenoid hypertrophy and can be improved by adenoidectomy, but it is not a complication of the surgery itself.

Complications of Adenoidectomy:

  • Hemorrhage: Immediate postoperative bleeding may require postnasal packing.
  • Risk of injury: Eustachian tubes (Option D), pharyngeal musculature, and vertebrae. Special care for Down’s syndrome patients due to potential atlantoaxial instability.
  • Grisel’s Syndrome (Option B): Neck pain and torticollis, possibly from atlantoaxial dislocation.
  • Velopharyngeal Insufficiency (Option A): Check for submucous cleft palate preoperatively.
  • Nasopharyngeal Stenosis: Due to scarring.
  • Recurrence: Regrowth of adenoid tissue left behind.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 507, 508
question: A 6-year-old child undergoes an adenoidectomy. Following the surgery, the child is monitored for potential complications. Which of the following is not a recognised complication of adenoidectomy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The persistence of notochordal remnants can lead to the formation of midline cystic structures in the nasopharynx, which is consistent with Thornwaldt's disease.


Thornwaldt's disease

  • Thornwaldt’s bursa is an epithelial-lined recess in the nasopharynx, representing a remnant of the attachment of the notochord to the endoderm of the pharynx during early development.
  • Thornwaldt’s disease is characterised by a midline nasopharyngeal cyst resulting from the persistence of a remnant of the notochord.
  • It presents with persistent postnasal discharge or crusting, nasal obstruction, dull occipital headache, low-grade fever, recurrent sore throat, obstruction to the eustachian tube and serous otitis media.

[[figure-1]]


Remnant of Rathke’s pouch (Option A): Rathke’s pouch is an embryonic structure that forms the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland. Remnants of Rathke’s pouch typically result in Rathke’s cleft cysts, which are located in the sellar region of the skull and are not related to the nasopharynx.


Remnants of pharyngeal clefts (Option B) usually lead to branchial cleft cysts or sinuses, which are typically located along the lateral neck or anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. They are not associated with midline cystic lesions in the nasopharynx.


Persistence of the Thyroglossal Duct (Option D): The thyroglossal duct is a temporary embryonic structure that connects the thyroid gland to the base of the tongue. It normally obliterates after development, but when it fails to do so, it can form a thyroglossal cyst, which typically appears as a midline neck mass.



Reference:

PL Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 288
question: A 45-year-old patient presents with chronic nasopharyngeal discomfort and intermittent nasal obstruction. Imaging studies reveal a midline cystic structure in the nasopharynx. The patient is diagnosed with Thornwaldt's disease. Which of the following anatomical remnants is most likely associated with this condition?

correctAnswer: D. Lymphatic drainage primarily involves the lower deep cervical nodes.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The lymphatic drainage of the palatine tonsils primarily flows into the upper deep cervical nodes, not the lower deep cervical nodes.

Anatomy of Palatine tonsils

Location

Lateral wall of the oropharynx between the anterior and posterior pillars.

Surface Extensions

Upwards into the soft palate, downwards into the base of the tongue, and anteriorly into the palatoglossal arch.

Medial Surface Epithelium
  • Stratified squamous epithelium with crypts. (Option A)
  • Crypta magna, or intratonsillar cleft, is located near the upper part of the tonsil.

[[figure-1]]

Lateral Surface

It is covered by a fibrous capsule separated from the tonsil bed by loose areolar tissue. (Option C)

Tonsil Bed Muscles

Formed by the superior constrictor and styloglossus muscles.

[[figure-2]]

Arterial Supply
  • Tonsillar branch of the facial artery (main supply) (Option B)
  • Ascending pharyngeal artery
  • Ascending palatine artery
  • Dorsal linguae branches of the lingual artery
  • Descending palatine branch of the maxillary artery.

[[figure-3]]

Venous Drainage

It drains into the paratonsillar vein, which joins the common facial vein and the pharyngeal venous plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage

Flows into the upper deep cervical nodes.

Sensory Nerve Supply

Lesser palatine branches of the sphenopalatine ganglion (CN V) and the glossopharyngeal nerve.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 303, 304
