They receive blood mainly from the tonsillar branch of the facial artery.
A fibrous capsule with loose areolar tissue covers the lateral surface.
Lymphatic drainage primarily involves the lower deep cervical nodes.

question: A 10-year-old child presents with a sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and a fever. On examination, the child has enlarged tonsils with visible crypts. Which of the following anatomical features of the palatine tonsils is not true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The hypoglossal nerve is not directly associated with the tonsillar bed, but improper or deep dissection could affect it, although it is anatomically more distant compared to the other structures listed.

[[figure-1]]

Structures forming Tonsillar bed

Muscles forming the tonsillar bed
  • Superior Constrictor Muscle
  • Styloglossus Muscle

Structures close to the tonsillar bed (outside the superior constrictor muscle)
  • Facial Artery (Tonsillar Branch): Major blood supply to the tonsils, at risk for haemorrhage during surgery.
  • Paratonsillar Vein: Venous drainage of the tonsil, risk of bleeding during tonsillectomy.
  • Submandibular Salivary Gland
  • Posterior Belly of Digastric Muscle
  • Medial Pterygoid Muscle
  • Mandible
  • Glossopharyngeal Nerve: Provides sensory innervation to the tonsils.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg 303, 304
question: During a tonsillectomy, injury to structures within the tonsillar bed may result in significant complications. Which of the following structures is not directly associated with the tonsillar bed but can be affected by deep dissection or improper technique?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of a thick, whitish membrane on the tonsils in the image is indicative of acute membranous tonsillitis.

Type of Acute Tonsillitis

Description

Clinical Features

Acute Catarrhal Tonsillitis (Option A)

Most common type and is a part of generalised pharyngitis, often viral.

Redness and mild swelling of the tonsils; sore throat; no pus or membrane.

[[figure-1]]

Acute Follicular Tonsillitis (Option B)

Infection involves the tonsillar crypts that are filled with purulent material.

Yellowish spots at the openings of the crypts; sore throat; fever.

[[figure-2]]

Acute Parenchymatous Tonsillitis (Option D)

It affects the substance of the tonsil and leads to uniform enlargement and redness.

Uniformly enlarged, red tonsils; significant swelling; no membrane.

[[figure-3]]

Acute Membranous Tonsillitis

Progression from acute follicular tonsillitis; exudate from crypts forms a membrane on the tonsil surface.

The whitish or greyish membrane covering the tonsils; severe sore throat; fever.

[[figure-4]]

Chronic tonsillitis with tonsilloliths (Option C) presents with persistent symptoms like halitosis and recurrent infections, not acute fever and enlarged tonsils. The patient has acute symptoms, more suggestive of acute membranous tonsillitis.



Reference:

PL DhingraDiseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page 304
question: A 12-year-old patient presents with a sore throat and fever. Upon examination, the physician observes that the tonsils are enlarged and other findings as in the image below. Which type of tonsillitis does this clinical presentation indicate?

correctAnswer: B. Initiate a 7-10 day course of oral amoxicillin.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

For a child with confirmed streptococcal tonsillitis, (the most common cause of acute tonsillitis being group A Streptococcus) the appropriate management is to prescribe a full course of oral antibiotics, typically amoxicillin, for 7-10 days to treat the infection and prevent complications.

Management of Acute tonsillitis

Management Aspect

Treatment/Action

General Supportive Care

Bed Rest and adequate fluids to aid in comfort and prevent complications.

Symptomatic Relief

Analgesics (e.g., Aspirin, Paracetamol) to provide relief from pain and fever. (Option A)

Antibiotic therapy
  • Antibiotics are prescribed to treat bacterial infections, primarily Streptococcus.
    • First-line Antibiotics: Penicillin, Ampicillin, Amoxicillin, Amoxicillin with Clavulanic acid.
    • Alternative: Erythromycin (for penicillin allergy).
  • Treatment duration is typically 7-10 days.

Administer intravenous antibiotics (Option C) are typically reserved for patients unable to tolerate oral medications due to severe vomiting or inability to swallow, or showing signs of severe infection or complications such as an abscess or sepsis.

Perform an immediate tonsillectomy (Option D) is indicated for recurrent or chronic tonsillitis, not for acute cases. Immediate tonsillectomy is usually reserved for severe obstructive tonsillar hypertrophy and peritonsillar abscess unresponsive to medical therapy.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 305

options.text: Prescribe paracetamol and monitor for 48 hours.
Initiate a 7-10 day course of oral amoxicillin.

question: A 10-year-old boy presents with fever, sore throat, and difficulty swallowing for 3 days. On examination, there is bilateral tonsillar enlargement with purulent exudate. A rapid strep test is positive. What is the next step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Irwin Moore Sign is characteristic of chronic tonsillitis, where pressing the anterior tonsillar pillar expresses pus from the crypts of the tonsils. This occurs due to the accumulation of debris and bacteria in the crypts, leading to chronic inflammation.


Griesinger’s Sign (Option A) is characterised by pain, swelling, and tenderness over the mastoid process and is caused by the spread of infection from the middle ear to the mastoid air cells, leading to thrombophlebitis. It is indicative of mastoiditis with thrombosis of the sigmoid sinus and may suggest intracranial complications like lateral sinus thrombosis.


Battle's Sign (Option B) refers to ecchymosis (bruising) over the mastoid process and is seen in basilar skull fractures, particularly involving the temporal bone.

[[figure-1]]


Cottle's Sign (Option C) is used to assess nasal obstruction. Lateral traction of the cheek (Cottle manoeuvre) improves airflow if the obstruction is due to nasal valve collapse or dysfunction, one of the common causes of functional nasal obstruction.

[[figure-2]]



Reference:
  1. PL Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 172, 307, 308
  2. www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537104/#
question: A 32-year-old male presents with a recurrent sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and foul-smelling breath for the past year. He reports episodes of fever and malaise. Examination reveals enlarged tonsils that on pressing the crypt , pus oozes out and tender anterior cervical lymph nodes. What is the most likely sign seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Acute tonsillitis involves active infection and inflammation of the tonsils, which increases the risk of bleeding, poor wound healing, and postoperative infection. Surgeons typically wait for the infection to resolve with antibiotics before performing a tonsillectomy.

Indications of Tonsillectomy

Absolute Indications

Relative Indications
  • Recurrent Tonsillitis
  • Tonsillitis causing febrile seizures
  • Tonsils interfering with speech, swallowing or breathing
  • Suspicion of malignancy (Option B)
  • Obstructive sleep apnea (Option A)
  • Chronic tonsillitis with bad taste or halitosis
  • Peritonsillar abscess (Option C)
  • Diphtheria carriers, not responding to antibiotics.


Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 503
question: A 17-year-old male presents with recurrent sore throat, recent high-grade fever, and breathing difficulties during sleep. He is scheduled for a tonsillectomy. Which among the following is a contraindication for this procedure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Parapharyngeal abscess is not an immediate complication but can develop later as a secondary issue, often due to an infection. It typically presents days to weeks after the surgery, rather than immediately.

Complications of Tonsillectomy

Immediate complications

Delayed Complication
  • Primary Hemorrhage, it happens at the time of surgery. (Option A)
  • Reactionary Hemorrhage which happens within 24 hours of the surgery (Option C)
  • Injury to tonsillar pillars, uvula, soft palate, teeth, tongue or superior constrictor muscle
  • Aspiration of blood
  • Facial oedema, particularly of eyelids (Option B)
  • Surgical emphysema (not very common)
  • Secondary Hemorrhage, it happens anywhere between 5 to 10 days post-Op
  • Infection of tonsillar fossa might lead to para-pharyngeal abscess or otitis media.
  • Aspiration of blood, mucus or tissue fragments.
  • Scarring in soft palate and pillars
  • Tonsillar remnants which may get repeatedly infected.
  • Hypertrophy of lingual tonsil.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 506.
question: A 16 year old girl, who had a tonsillectomy 6 days ago, presents with high fever, throat pain, and swelling in the neck. All the following are immediate complications of this surgery except?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely cause of bleeding in this scenario is the slipping of a ligature. During tonsillectomy, ligatures control bleeding from the tonsillar bed.
  • If a ligature slips or becomes dislodged, it can lead to sudden bleeding, often occurring within the first 24 hours post-operatively (Reactionary hemorrhage). This can result in hypotension and tachycardia due to blood loss.

Hemorrhage is the most common complication post-tonsillectomy and is of 3 types based on the duration:

Type of Hemorrhage

Primary Hemorrhage

Reactionary Hemorrhage

Secondary Hemorrhage

Duration of occurrence

Immediate complication, occur at the time of surgery.

Happens within first 24 hours post surgery (Immediate complication)

Seen between 5th to 10th postoperative day.

Causes

Inadequate hemostasis or injury to the vessels (Option C)

Slipping of ligature (Option D), hypertension or the dislodging of clot.

Infection (Option B) or premature separation of the membrane (Option A)

Management

Application of pressure, ligation or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels.

Initially, remove the clot and apply pressure or use a vasoconstrictor. If these measures are ineffective, proceed with ligation or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels.

Initially by Antibiotics, if bleeding persists re-exploration is done.


Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat, PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page 506
question: A 15 years old female who had a tonsillectomy 16 hours ago is currently under post-op monitoring, suddenly begins to bleed from the mouth and is noted to have hypotension with tachycardia. What is the most likely cause of this bleeding?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The diagnosis is Adenoid Hypertrophy based on the lateral soft tissue X-ray showing a soft tissue mass obstructing the nasopharyngeal airway. Chronic enlargement of the adenoids leads to significant respiratory and developmental issues in children.

The clinical manifestations of Adenoid Hypertrophy include:

  • Airway Obstruction: The child resorts to mouth breathing as the primary route for ventilation due to the blockage of the posterior choanae. (Statement 1)
  • Growth and Development: Chronic upper airway obstruction can lead to failure to thrive due to the high energy cost of breathing, chronic hypoxia, and poor feeding. (Statement 2)
  • Sleep-Disordered Breathing: Enlarged adenoids are a primary cause of snoring and pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnoea (OSA), characterized by restless sleep and apneic spells. (Statement 3)
  • Adenoid Facies: This involves an elongated face, open mouth, high-arched palate, and the obliteration of the nasolabial folds. Therefore, a prominent nasolabial fold is not a feature of this condition. (Statement 4)
  • Voice Changes: Obstruction leads to hyponasality, also known as Rhinolalia clausa.
  • Aural Complications: Pressure on the Eustachian tube orifice can lead to conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion.


Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 287.
question:
Which of the following clinical features are associated with the condition represented in the imaging?

  1. Mouth breathing
  2. Failure to thrive
  3. Sleep apnoea
  4. Prominent nasolabial fold

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The facial features are characteristic of Adenoid Facies secondary to chronic adenoid hypertrophy, characterised by a flat, expressionless, long face with an open mouth, crowded teeth, and a high arched palate.
  • The voice abnormality associated with nasal or nasopharyngeal obstruction is Rhinolalia clausa (hyponasality).
  • Because the nasopharyngeal space is occupied by the enlarged lymphoid mass, the nose cannot act as a resonating chamber for speech.
  • This primarily affects the production of nasal consonants, where 'm', 'n', and 'ng' sound like 'b', 'd', and 'g' respectively.

Hot potato voice (Option A) is a thick, muffled voice characteristic of peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy) or acute tonsillitis.

Rhinolalia aperta (Option C) refers to hypernasality (open nose voice), which is seen in conditions of velopharyngeal insufficiency such as cleft palate or palatal paralysis.

Staccato voice (Option D) is a jerky, interrupted speech pattern, typically associated with cerebellar lesions or neurological disorders like multiple sclerosis.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 287.
question: A 7-year-old is brought by his mother with complaints of mouth breathing and characteristic facial features, as shown below. On examination, a high arched palate is noted. What is the voice abnormality that can be noted in this child?

explanationHtml:
The anatomical profile of the palatine tonsil is defined by a specific muscular bed, a non-keratinizing epithelial lining, and a distinct lateral fibrous capsule. The tonsil is a prominent collection of lymphoid tissue situated in the tonsillar sinus of the oropharynx, serving as a key component of Waldeyer’s ring.

Key anatomical features of the palatine tonsil:

  • Tonsillar Bed:
    • The tonsil rests on a muscular bed formed by the superior constrictor muscle in its upper part and the styloglossus muscle in its lower part.
    • Outside the superior constrictor muscle, tonsil is related to the facial artery, submandibular salivary gland, posterior belly of digastric muscle, medial pterygoid muscle and the angle of mandible.
  • Medial Surface:
    • This surface faces the oropharynx and is lined by non-keratinising stratified squamous epithelium.
    • This lining invaginates to form 12 to 15 tonsillar crypts.
  • Crypta Magna:
    • The largest of the tonsillar crypts, located in the upper portion of the gland, is the embryological remnant of the second pharyngeal pouch.
  • Lateral Surface:
    • The lateral aspect is covered by a well-defined fibrous capsule.
    • This capsule is separated from the superior constrictor muscle by loose areolar tissue, which provides the surgical plane of dissection during tonsillectomy. (Statement 4)


Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 303.

Classification of Tonsillitis

1. Acute Tonsillitis

  • Catarrhal (Superficial): Involvement of the generalised surface.
  • Follicular: Purulent material in tonsillar crypts.
  • Parenchymatous: Inflammation of the entire tonsil substance.
  • Membranous: Formation of a surface membrane.

2. Chronic Tonsillitis

  • Follicular: Crypts filled with yellowish cheesy material.
  • Parenchymatous: Hyperplasia/massive enlargement; causes sleep apnea or cor pulmonale.
  • Fibroid: Tiny, shrunken, and infected tonsils.

3. Causative Organisms

  • Most Common (Children): Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus.
  • Others: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae.

Jugulo-omohyoid (Option B) nodes belong to the lower deep cervical group and are primarily associated with the lymphatic drainage of the tongue.

Submandibular (Option C) nodes drain the submental nodes, the cheeks, the upper lip, and the lateral parts of the lower lip and gingiva.


Retropharyngeal (Option D) nodes are located in the buccopharyngeal fascia and primarily drain the nasopharynx, the posterior nasal cavity, and the Eustachian tube.

The clinical scenario describes Acute Tonsillitis. Acute tonsillitis presents in several distinct pathological forms depending on the extent of the infection.

Fibroid tonsillitis is a histological variant of Chronic Tonsillitis, characterized by the replacement of lymphoid tissue with fibrous scarring, leading to small, shriveled tonsils.

Key variants of acute tonsillitis include:

  • Acute Catarrhal or Superficial tonsillitis: Infection is limited to the generalized surface of the tonsillar mucosa, often seen as part of a viral pharyngitis.
  • Acute Follicular tonsillitis: Infection spreads into the crypts, which fill with purulent material, presenting as yellow spots. (Option A ruled out)
  • Acute Parenchymatous tonsillitis: The entire tonsil substance is infected and uniformly congested, resulting in massive tonsillar enlargement. (Option D ruled out)
  • Acute Membranous tonsillitis: This occurs when follicular exudates coalesce to form a yellowish-white clinical membrane over the tonsillar surface. (Option B ruled out)

question: A 4-year-old child presents with a sudden onset of fever and refusal to eat. On examination, the following finding is seen. Which among the following is not a known complication of this acute condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The diagnosis is Chronic Parenchymatous Tonsillitis based on the presence of kissing tonsils and mechanical obstructive symptoms involving speech, swallowing, and breathing. This condition represents a specific pathological response to recurrent infection where the structural components of the tonsil are permanently altered.

The characteristic features of Chronic Parenchymatous Tonsillitis include:

  • There is significant hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue within the tonsillar parenchyma.
  • The tonsils are very much enlarged and may bulge out from the tonsillar pillars, often meeting in the midline and may interfere with speech, resulting in a thick or muffled voice quality.
  • The enlargement may interfere with deglutition, making it difficult for the child to swallow solid boluses of food.
  • The mechanical obstruction may interfere with respiration, leading to symptoms of loud snoring, labored breathing, and potentially obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA).

Acute follicular tonsillitis (Option A) is an acute inflammatory phase where the tonsillar crypts are filled with purulent material, appearing as yellow spots, and is associated with high-grade fever.

Chronic fibroid tonsillitis (Option B) is characterized by small, shrunken, and shriveled tonsils due to the replacement of lymphoid tissue with fibrous scarring following recurrent infections.

Acute membranous tonsillitis (Option C) involves the formation of a yellowish-white coalesced membrane of exudate over the tonsillar surface during the acute stage of infection.

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 307.

correctAnswer: D. Beta-catenin, Androgen receptor, and C-MYC proto-oncogene
explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D) Beta-catenin, Androgen receptor, and C-MYC proto-oncogene

Explanation

Beta-catenin is critical for stromal cell proliferation, and its interaction with androgen receptors and C-MYC drives tumor growth. These factors are known to work together in the pathogenesis of JNA.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA)

Site of Origin

Posterior nasal cavity, near the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen, where the sphenoid and palatine bones meet.

Gross Appearance

Reddish-purple, lobulated, sessile mass covered by mucosa; lacks a capsule despite being benign.

Microscopic Appearance
  • Vascular Tissue: Endothelium-lined spaces with incomplete/absent muscle coats, leading to bleeding; peripheral vessels are thin-walled, central vessels hyperplastic.
  • Stromal Cells: Stellate or spindle-shaped cells that produce collagen, affecting tumor firmness.

Immunohistochemistry
  • Fibroblasts, collagen, myofibroblasts, mast cells, and occasionally giant cells are present.
  • Reactivity to smooth muscle actin and beta-catenin, suggesting beta-catenin’s role in growth.

Growth Factors
  • JNA development likely results from a combination of hormonal influence, growth factors, and genetic factors.
  • Androgen Receptors: Present in 75% of JNA tumors, indicating male hormone involvement.
  • VEGF: Promotes endothelial and stromal cell growth.
  • IGF-II: Role is less clear.
  • Genetics: C-MYC proto-oncogene found in larger tumors; may interact with androgen receptor and beta-catenin genes.

  • Androgen receptor, VEGF, and p53 (Option A): While VEGF promotes endothelial and stromal cell growth, p53 is not typically involved in JNA, and this combination does not account for the genetic factors directly interacting to enhance tumor growth.
  • C-MYC proto-oncogene, IGF-II, and Beta-catenin (Option B): C-MYC and Beta-catenin are important, but IGF-II’s role is less clear in direct tumor growth and proliferation compared to VEGF or androgen receptor interactions.
  • VEGF, BCL-2, and APC gene (Option C): VEGF promotes cell growth, but BCL-2 is mainly involved in apoptosis, and the APC gene does not play a key role in JNA development.


Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 289-291

explanationHtml:
Profuse, recurrent nosebleeds (epistaxis) are the hallmark symptom of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA0 and are often the first presenting sign due to the fragile, thin-walled vessels in the tumor.

JNA - Clinical Features

Nasal and Nasopharyngeal Symptoms
  • Epistaxis: Recurrent, profuse nosebleeds due to fragile, thin-walled vessels. (Option B)
  • Nasal Obstruction: Progressive blockage causing nasal voice.
  • Nasal Discharge: Often from secondary sinusitis or obstruction.(Option D ruled out)

Otologic Symptoms
  • Conductive Hearing Loss: Eustachian tube obstruction leading to fluid in the middle ear. (Option C ruled out)
  • Otitis Media with Effusion: Fluid build-up, possible ear pain.

Ophthalmo-neurological Symptoms
  • Proptosis: Eyeball protrusion from orbital invasion.
  • Diplopia: Double vision due to cranial nerve compression (CN III, IV, VI). (Option A ruled out)
  • Cranial Nerve Palsies: Various deficits like vision changes (CN II), facial pain (CN V), or swallowing difficulty (CN IX, X).

Facial Deformity
  • Broadening of Nasal Bridge: Widening from tumor pressure.
  • Cheek Swelling: Asymmetry due to tumor extension.
  • Frog-Face Deformity: Bilateral proptosis with bulging eyes and flattened profile.

[[figure-1]]

Other Features
  • Age and Sex: Predominantly affects adolescent males (10-20 years). Rare in females or older individuals.
  • Endoscopic Appearance: Smooth or lobulated reddish-purple mass blocking nasal passages.
  • Consistency: Firm but should not be palpated due to bleeding risk.

Investigations of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)

Contrast-Enhanced CT Scan
  • Investigation of choice; shows tumor size, location, and bony involvement.
  • Pathognomonic sign: Holman-Miller sign (bowing of maxillary wall).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)

Evaluates soft tissue and intracranial extension, differentiates between extradural and intradural spread. (Option A ruled out)

Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA)

Visualizes tumor vascularity, identifies feeding vessels and aids in preoperative embolization to reduce surgical blood loss.

Nasopharyngoscopy

Provides a direct view of the tumor, but biopsy is generally avoided due to high bleeding risk. (Option C ruled out)

Audiometry

Assesses hearing loss caused by Eustachian tube obstruction; establishes baseline and monitors post-treatment hearing.

Biopsy

Biopsy is contraindicated due to risk of profuse bleeding.


Ultrasound Doppler (Option B): Although Doppler ultrasound can assess blood flow, it is not routinely used to evaluate the vascularity of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma due to its limitations in this region.

Staging and Treatment of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)

Staging Systems for JNA
  • Classification based on tumor size, location, involvement of structures, and surgical accessibility.

Surgical approaches

F. Residual or recurrent disease (extracranial)

Preoperative Embolization

Performed using Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) to block arteries feeding the tumor and reduce blood loss during surgery.

Risks: Stroke, cranial nerve palsies, blindness.

Radiotherapy

Used for:

  • Inoperable tumors due to location/extent.
  • Recurrent tumors after surgery.
  • Intracranial extension with internal carotid artery supply.
  • Risks: Atrophic rhinitis, facial deformities, radiation-induced angiosarcoma (rare).

Other Treatment Modalities
  • Chemotherapy: For aggressive, recurrent, or residual tumors, though not curative.
  • Hormonal Therapy: Antiandrogens have been explored but with limited success.

Recurrence

Recurrence occurs in up to 35% of cases. Management includes observation, revision surgery or radiation therapy.

question: A 15-year-old male presents with recurrent epistaxis and a nasal mass that has been progressively growing. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The findings are characteristic of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), a tumor that occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males.

  • Histologically, it is a benign tumor composed of numerous vascular channels within a fibrous stroma, without cellular atypia or anaplasia.
  • Despite its benign histology, JNA behaves in a locally aggressive manner.
  • It expands along paths of least resistance, causing pressure erosion of surrounding bone and extension into adjacent spaces such as the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pterygopalatine fossa, infratemporal fossa, orbit, and cranial cavity.

Benign with no local invasion (Option B): Although histologically benign, juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma shows locally aggressive growth with bone erosion and extension into adjacent spaces, so it cannot be described as non-invasive.

Premalignant (Option C): JNA is not a premalignant lesion and does not undergo malignant transformation.

Malignant (Option D): JNA lacks cellular atypia, anaplasia, and metastatic potential, which are features required to classify a tumor as malignant.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 289.

correctAnswer: A. It is significantly more common in females
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation is characteristic of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), a highly vascular, benign but locally aggressive tumor that occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males.

  • It typically arises from the posterolateral wall of the nasal cavity near the sphenopalatine foramen and grows into the nasopharynx, with possible extension into the pterygopalatine fossa, infratemporal fossa, paranasal sinuses, orbit, and cranial cavity.
  • JNA usually presents during puberty (10-20 years) (Option B) and is thought to be androgen-dependent (Option C), explaining its marked male predominance.
  • The most common presenting features are recurrent epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction.
  • Because the tumor is extremely vascular, incisional biopsy is contraindicated (Option D) due to the risk of severe hemorrhage.
  • Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical features and imaging such as contrast-enhanced CT and MRI, which demonstrate a vascular mass and characteristic extension patterns.
  • Angiography may be used to identify feeding vessels and is often performed prior to preoperative embolization, which reduces intraoperative bleeding during surgical excision.
  • Histologically, JNA consists of numerous irregular, thin-walled vascular channels embedded within a fibrous stroma, lacking a muscular layer, which explains the tumor’s tendency for profuse bleeding.


Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 289, 292.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is composed of a dense fibrous stroma containing numerous irregular, thin-walled vascular channels. A key histological feature is that these vessels lack a well-developed smooth muscle layer.

  • Because the vascular channels lack a contractile muscular coat, they cannot undergo vasoconstriction or physiological vasospasm when injured.
  • As a result, even minor trauma such as biopsy or surgical manipulation can lead to profuse and potentially life-threatening hemorrhage, explaining the characteristic severe bleeding tendency of this tumor.

Absence of a well-defined tumour capsule (Option B): JNA may be poorly encapsulated, but this feature does not account for the severe bleeding tendency.

Secretion of local tissue plasminogen activators (Option C): Bleeding in JNA is not due to fibrinolytic activity but rather due to the abnormal vascular structure of the tumor.

Direct invasion into the internal carotid artery (Option D): Although JNA may extend into adjacent spaces, direct invasion of major arteries is not the mechanism responsible for its bleeding tendency.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 291.

question: Which histological characteristic of the nasopharyngeal tumour is responsible for the severe bleeding tendency?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Holman-Miller sign (Antral sign) refers to anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, a classic radiological finding seen in juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA).

  • JNA arises near the sphenopalatine foramen in the posterolateral wall of the nasal cavity and commonly spreads into the pterygopalatine fossa.
  • As the tumor expands laterally, it exerts pressure on the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, causing it to bow anteriorly, producing the Holman-Miller sign on CT imaging.

[[figure-1]]

Lyre sign (Option B) is an angiographic sign seen in carotid body tumours, where the expanding mass at the carotid bifurcation causes splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries, resembling a lyre.

[[figure-2]]

Phelp's sign (Option C) is a finding seen in glomus jugulare tumours, characterised by the erosion and loss of the bony crest between the jugular bulb and the carotid canal.

[[figure-3]]

Steeple sign (Option D) is seen on AP neck X-ray finding showing subglottic narrowing, associated with acute laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup) in children.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 292-293.
question: A 16-year-old male with a history of recurrent epistaxis undergoes a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the paranasal sinuses. The radiologist observes a highly enhancing mass in the pterygopalatine fossa that is causing the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. This specific radiological finding is classically referred to as:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The imaging shows the Holman-Miller sign, characterized by anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, a classic radiological feature of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA).

  • JNA is the most common benign tumor of the nasopharynx and occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males. (Statement 1)
  • The tumor is unencapsulated and spreads locally along natural tissue planes, often extending into the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae. (Statement 2)
  • Because JNA is highly vascular and its vessels lack a muscular layer, biopsy and digital palpation are contraindicated due to the risk of severe hemorrhage. (Statement 3)
  • Despite surgical treatment, recurrence rates are significant (~35%), particularly in tumors with skull-base extension. (Statement 4)


Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 289, 291-292, 295.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Prevertebral abscess, which is formed as a complication of cervical spine caries due to TB, presents as a fluctuant swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall centrally.

Prevertebral Abscess:

Prevertebral space
  • Extent: Base of skull to coccyx
  • Location: Between vertebrae on one side and prevertebral muscles and the prevertebral fascia on the other

Aetiology
  • Tubercular in nature, caused by:
    • Caries of the cervical spine (central abscess behind prevertebral fascia)
    • Tuberculous infection of retropharyngeal lymph nodes (unilateral abscess behind buccopharyngeal fascia)

Clinical Features
  • Throat discomfort
  • Mild dysphagia
  • Fluctuant swelling in posterior pharyngeal wall, either centrally or on one side of midline

Treatment
  • Incision and drainage
  • Antitubercular therapy

Comparison between retropharyngeal and prevertebral abscesses:

Retropharyngeal (Option B)

Prevertebral (Option A)

Location of the space

Behind the pharynx, between the buccopharyngeal fascia and prevertebral fascia, extending from the base of the skull to the bifurcation of the trachea.

Between vertebrae on one side and prevertebral muscles and the prevertebral fascia on the other, extenting from the base of skull to coccyx

Etiology

  • Children under 3 years (common)-suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes
  • Adults-penetrating injuries to the posterior pharyngeal wall or cervical esophagus.

Tubercular in nature, caused by: Caries of the cervical spine or tuberculous infection of retropharyngeal lymph nodes

Clinical features

  • Dysphagia
  • Breathing difficulty
  • Stridor
  • Croupy cough
  • Torticollis
  • Unilateral bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall
  • Throat discomfort
  • Mild dysphagia
  • Fluctuant swelling in posterior pharyngeal wall, either centrally or on one side of midline

[[figure-1]]

Parapharyngeal abscess (Option C): Incorrect as it causes lateral wall bulge, trismus, and more severe systemic symptoms.

Peritonsillar abscess (Option D): Incorrect since it is peritonsillar, not posterior pharyngeal, and presents with uvular deviation.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 313-315

Explanation:

  • The parapharyngeal space is anatomically divided into anterior and posterior compartments by the styloid process and its attached muscles (stylohyoid, stylopharyngeus, and styloglossus).

Feature

Anterior Compartment (Pre-styloid)

Posterior Compartment (Post-styloid)

Prolapse of tonsil, trismus, swelling behind the angle of the jaw (Statement 1)

Bulge behind the posterior pillar, paralysis of CN IX-XII, parotid region swelling

Marked (due to spasm of medial pterygoid muscle)

Minimal or absent

Neurological

Usually spared

Paralysis of CN IX, X (vocal cord paralysis), XI, XII, and the sympathetic chain (Horner's) (Statements 2 & 3)

Oropharynx

Medial displacement/prolapse of tonsil and tonsillar fossa

Minimal tonsillar prolapse; bulge occurs behind the posterior pillar

Swelling

External swelling behind the angle of the jaw

Swelling localized to the parotid region (Statement 4)

Symptoms

Marked odynophagia

Symptoms related to cranial nerve palsies

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Parapharyngeal Abscess is a deep neck space infection requiring urgent intervention. It occurs in the space lateral to the pharynx and is bounded by the layers of the deep cervical fascia.

The clinical and epidemiological profile includes:

  • Gender: It has a preponderance for the male gender. (Statement 1)
  • Etiology: It most commonly originates from infections of the palatine tonsils, the pharynx, or dental infections. (Statement 3)
  • Clinical Nature: It is an aggressive, life-threatening infection and is never self-limiting; it can lead to airway obstruction or vascular catastrophe. (Statement 2)
  • Management: Treatment requires hospitalization and high-dose parenteral antibiotics. Surgical drainage is mandatory if an abscess has formed. (Statement 4)

question:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding a parapharyngeal space abscess:

  1. Preponderance for male gender
  2. A self-limiting condition
  3. Often follows tonsillar infection
  4. Managed with parenteral antibiotics

explanationHtml:
Explanation
Parapharyngeal abscess is synonymous with pharyngomaxillary abscess and lateral pharyngeal abscess.

Key anatomical and clinical features regarding these synonyms include:

  • Pharyngomaxillary space is the most common synonym, reflecting the space's position between the pharyngeal constrictors medially and the maxilla, mandible, and pterygoid muscles laterally. (Statement 1)
  • Lateral pharyngeal space is used to emphasize its location lateral to the pharyngeal wall, distinguishing it from the midline retropharyngeal space. (Statement 3)

Retropharyngeal space is a distinct anatomical compartment located posterior to the pharynx. (Statement 2)

Medial pharyngeal space is not a recognized anatomical or clinical term; the space situated medial to the pharyngeal wall is the retropharyngeal space. (Statement 4)



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 314.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation described is characteristic of a Peritonsillar Abscess, which is colloquially and clinically known as Quinsy.
  • This condition involves a collection of pus in the peritonsillar space charcterised by severe unilateral pain, odynophagia, and a characteristic muffled or hot potato voice.
  • On examination, medial displacement of the tonsil, edema of the soft palate, and deviation of the uvula to the healthy side are observed.

Dental abscess (Option A) involves a collection of pus at the root of a tooth and may spread to the submandibular space.

Prevertebral abscess (Option C) is a collection of pus in the space between the prevertebral fascia and the vertebrae, often associated with spinal tuberculosis, presenting with midline swelling rather than lateral tonsillar displacement.

Parapharyngeal abscess (Option D) is a deep neck space infection, presenting with swelling behind the posterior pillar and more severe trismus, often occurring as a complication of Quinsy.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 311.

question: A 22-year-old patient presents with a severe sore throat, odynophagia, and hot potato voice. Clinical examination reveals a congested tonsil displaced medially and an edematous uvula pushed to the opposite side. This condition is clinically synonymous with which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis is Retropharyngeal Abscess based on the lateral neck X-ray showing pathognomonic widening of the prevertebral soft tissue shadow.
  • In children, this shadow should not exceed 7 mm at the level of C2 or 14 mm at the level of C6.
  • The presence of gas shadows or an air-fluid level within this widened space is highly suggestive of an acute suppurative process.
  • Clinically, this presents as stridor, odynophagia, and a hot potato voice, often with the head held in a neutral or extended position to maintain the airway.

Features

Acute retropharyngeal abscess

Chronic Tubercular Retropharyngeal Abscess

Etiology

Suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes (Nodes of Rouviere) following URI.

Usually secondary to Tuberculosis of the cervical spine (Pott's disease) or TB of retropharyngeal nodes.

Clinical features

High fever, dysphagia, stridor, croupy cough, and neck stiffness

Slowly progressive dysphagia, dull neck ache, and "cold abscess" (no fever/redness).

Examination

Bulge on one side of the midline of the posterior pharyngeal wall.

A slow-growing, fluctuant swelling located centrally behind the prevertebral fascia.

Management

Incision and drainage (Transoral): Performed in the Rose position (head-low) without anesthesia or with guarded suction to prevent aspiration. A vertical incision is made at the most fluctuant area.

Incision and Drainage (External Approach): Performed through an incision behind the sternocleidomastoid to avoid secondary infection from the oral cavity.

Medical therapy

High-dose intravenous antibiotics and airway monitoring.

Full course of Anti-Tubercular Therapy (ATT) and cervical immobilization if the spine is involved.


Epiglottitis (Option A): A lateral X-ray in this condition would show the thumb sign, representing a thickened, edematous epiglottis.

[[figure-1]]

Ludwig's angina (Option C) is a cellulitis involving the submandibular and sublingual spaces; while it causes airway compromise, the pathology is in the floor of the mouth.

TB spine (Option D) causes a chronic prevertebral abscess; the X-ray would typically demonstrate associated vertebral body destruction, narrowing of the disc spaces, and a lack of acute symptoms like high-grade fever and sudden-onset stridor.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 313.

question: The child presented with stridor and neck stiffness. X-ray neck reveals the following findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Alar fascia and Prevertebral fascia
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Danger Space is a potential space of the neck characterized by its unrestricted vertical extent, allowing infections to descend rapidly into the thorax.

Key anatomical and clinical features include:

  • Anterior Boundary: It is lined in front by the alar fascia (a division of the deep cervical fascia).
  • Posterior Boundary: It is lined in back by the prevertebral fascia.
  • Extent: It extends from the base of the skull through the neck into the posterior mediastinum, reaching the level of the diaphragm.
  • Clinical Significance: Because it is open inferiorly, a retropharyngeal abscess that breaches the alar fascia enters this space and causes life-threatening necrotizing mediastinitis.

[[figure-1]]

Buccopharyngeal fascia and Alar fascia (Option A) bound the true retropharyngeal space (Space of Gillette), which is anatomically limited at the level of the superior mediastinum (T1-T2).

Buccopharyngeal fascia and Prevertebral fascia (Option B) represent a broader clinical definition of the retropharyngeal area but ignore the intervening alar fascia, which creates the specific Danger Space.

Prevertebral fascia and Vertebral bodies (Option D) bound the prevertebral space, which is the anatomical site for chronic cold abscesses associated with spinal tuberculosis.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 312-313, 315.

question: The Danger Space of the neck, which acts as a direct conduit for the spread of infection from the skull base to the posterior mediastinum, is anatomically bounded in front and back by:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The retropharyngeal lymph nodes are located in the potential space behind the pharynx and serve as the primary drainage site for the upper aerodigestive tract.
  • The Node of Rouviere is specifically identified as the most superior node of the lateral retropharyngeal group.
  • These nodes are clinically significant in the pediatric population because their suppuration following an upper respiratory tract infection is the most common cause of an acute retropharyngeal abscess.

Delphian node (Option A) is a midline prelaryngeal lymph node located on the cricothyroid membrane, primarily involved in the spread of laryngeal and thyroid carcinomas.

Virchow's node (Option C) refers to the left-sided supraclavicular lymph node; its enlargement is associated with the metastatic spread of abdominal malignancies.

Cloquet's node (Option D), also known as the node of Rosenmüller, is a deep inguinal lymph node in the femoral canal draining the lower limbs and external genitalia.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 457.

question: Which of the following lymph nodes is the most superior member of the lateral retropharyngeal group, situated at the level of the atlas near the base of the skull?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The retropharyngeal space, also referred to as the Space of Gillette, is a potential space located posterior to the pharynx. It is bounded anteriorly by the buccopharyngeal fascia and posteriorly by the alar fascia.

This space extends from the base of the skull down to the level of the superior mediastinum. In children, it contains the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, which typically atrophy by the age of 6 years, explaining why acute suppurative retropharyngeal abscesses are predominantly seen in the pediatric age group.

[[figure-1]]

1 (Option A) is Visceral space, a central compartment in the infrahyoid neck extending from the hyoid bone to the superior mediastinum containing the thyroid, parathyroid, larynx, and oesophagus.

3 (Option C) is Danger space, which is located between the alar fascia anteriorly and the prevertebral fascia posteriorly, providing a direct conduit for infection to spread into the posterior mediastinum.

4 (Option D) is Prevertebral space, which lies between the prevertebral fascia and the vertebral bodies, and is the site for chronic abscesses usually secondary to spinal tuberculosis.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 312.

question: Which of the marked structures is known as the Space of Gillette?

correctAnswer: C. Between the submandibular and submental spaces
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Clinical scenario is suggestive of Ludwig’s angina. The infection typically begins in the submandibular space due to dental infection. The close anatomical connection between the submandibular and submental spaces allows for rapid spread across the midline, leading to bilateral involvement.

[[figure-1]]

  • Ludwig’s angina is a rapidly spreading cellulitis primarily affecting the mandibular spaces.

Ludwig’ angina - Anatomy

Primary Spaces

It involves three spaces around the mandible: the sublingual, submandibular, and submental spaces.

  • Sublingual space: Infections here typically arise from the premolars and first molar.
  • Submandibular space: It contains the submandibular gland and lymph nodes, and connects to both the sublingual and submental spaces. (Option C)
  • Submental space: Infections in the submandibular space can easily spread to the submental and contralateral sublingual spaces.

Secondary Spaces
  • The secondary spaces, known collectively as the masticator space, surround the muscles involved in mastication (masseter, medial and lateral pterygoid, and temporalis).
  • These spaces can become involved due to the posterior spread of infection from the primary spaces or from a third molar infection.
  • The primary clinical feature of masticator space infection is significant trismus.


[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 309, 310

question: A 7-year-old child presents to the ER with rapidly progressing swelling under the jaw and difficulty breathing. On examination, there is bilateral submandibular swelling with elevation of the tongue, but no trismus or fluctuation. He reports recent dental pain in his lower molars. Which anatomical connection is primarily responsible for the rapid bilateral spread of this infection?

correctAnswer: A. Penetrating injury to posterior pharyngeal wall
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Given is a scenario of an adult with an acute retropharyngeal abscess. The most common etiology of an adult with an acute retropharyngeal abscess is a penetrating injury to the posterior pharyngeal wall or cervical esophagus.

Acute retropharyngeal abscess:

Retropharyngeal space
  • Location: Behind the pharynx, between the buccopharyngeal fascia and prevertebral fascia.
  • Extent: From the base of the skull to the bifurcation of the trachea.
  • Divisions: Two lateral compartments (spaces of Gillette) divided by a fibrous raphe.
  • Communication: with the parapharyngeal space

Aetiology
  • Children under 3 years (common): suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes from infections in adenoids, nasopharynx, posterior nasal sinuses, or nasal cavity.
  • Adults: penetrating injuries to the posterior pharyngeal wall or cervical esophagus.

Clinical Features
  • Dysphagia
  • Breathing difficulty
  • Stridor
  • Croupy cough
  • Torticollis
  • Unilateral bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall

Diagnosis
  • X-ray neck lateral view shows widened prevertebral shadow, sometimes even the presence of gas

[[figure-1]]

  • Contrast-enhanced CT scan reveals the extent of the abscess

Treatment
  • Incision and drainage
  • Systemic antibiotics
  • Tracheostomy if needed



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 312-314

question: A 35-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and neck pain. On examination, there is a unilateral bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall and neck stiffness with limited movement. A lateral neck X-ray reveals a widened prevertebral shadow. What is the etiology?

correctAnswer: B. Parapharyngeal abscess in the posterior compartment
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Bulge of pharynx behind posterior pillar, paralysis of CN IX, X, XI, XII, and parotid region swelling are seen in the abscess of the posterior compartment of parapharyngeal space.

Parapharyngeal abscess:

Parapharyngeal Space
  • Pyramidal in shape
  • Base: skull
  • Apex: hyoid bone
  • Medial: buccopharyngeal fascia
  • Posterior: prevertebral fascia
  • Lateral: medial pterygoid muscle, mandible, deep surface of parotid gland

[[figure-1]]

Aetiology of Infection
  • Pharynx: Acute/chronic infections (tonsil, adenoid), peritonsillar abscess
  • Dental infections: usually lower last molars
  • Ear: Bezold abscess, petrositis
  • Infections of other spaces: Parotid, retropharyngeal, and submaxillary spaces
  • External trauma

Symptoms
  • Fever
  • Odynophagia
  • Sore throat
  • Torticollis
  • Signs of toxaemia

Compartment-wise symptoms
  • Anterior compartment-anterior to styloid process. Abscess here causes:
    • Prolapse of tonsil and tonsillar fossa
    • Trismus
    • External swelling behind angle of jaw
  • Posterior compartment-posterior to styloid process. Abscess here causes:
    • Bulge of pharynx behind posterior pillar
    • Paralysis of CN IX, X, XI, XII, and sympathetic chain
    • Parotid region swelling
    • Minimal trismus or tonsillar prolapse

Treatment
  • Systemic antibiotic
  • Drainage of abscess



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 314-316

question: A 45-year-old male presents with difficulty swallowing, a bulge in the pharynx behind the posterior pillar, and swelling in the parotid region. He also exhibits paralysis of cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Given clinical scenario is suggestive of Peritonsillar abscess, also known as Quinsy.

[[figure-1]]

Peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy):

Definition
  • Collection of pus in the peritonsillar space (between tonsil capsule and superior constrictor muscle).

Aetiology
  • Follows acute tonsillitis or can arise de novo.
  • Infection begins in the tonsillar crypt

Cause
  • Streptococcus pyogenes, S. aureus, anaerobes or mixed infection.

Clinical Features
  • Fever with chills & rigors
  • Severe unilateral throat pain
  • Odynophagia (difficulty swallowing)
  • Muffled "hot potato voice", foul breath
  • Ipsilateral earache (referred via CN IX)

Examination Findings
  • Swollen, congested tonsils, soft palate
  • Uvula pushed to the opposite side with bulging soft palate
  • No visible neck swelling seen

Investigations
  • Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to show abscess and extent
  • Needle aspiration for bacterial culture and sensitivity testing

Treatment
  • Conservative: IV fluids, Analgesics, IV antibiotics, Oral hygiene (hydrogen peroxide or saline mouthwash)
  • Incision and drainage for abscess
  • Surgical: Interval tonsillectomy (after 4–6 weeks)/ Hot tonsillectomy (Tonsillectomy consecutively along with I&D)

Complications
  • Parapharyngeal abscess/ Laryngeal edema
  • Pneumonitis or lung abscess/ Septicaemia
  • Jugular vein thrombosis

Parapharyngeal abscess (Option A) and Retropharyngeal abscess (Option D): both would present with a neck swelling.

Ludwig’s angina (Option B): Presents with submandibular swelling.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 311, 312, 453

question: Adult male with complaints of fever, throat pain on left side, painful swallowing with change in voice since 2 days. Oral examination revealed the following. No visible neck swelling is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Parapharyngeal space:

  • Pyramidal, with its base at the skull's base and its apex at the hyoid bone. (Statement 1)
  • Communications: retropharyngeal space (Statement 2) , submandibular, parotid, carotid, and visceral spaces.
  • Relations of the Parapharyngeal Space:
    • Medial: Buccopharyngeal fascia covering the constrictor muscles
    • Posterior: Prevertebral fascia covering prevertebral muscles and transverse processes of cervical vertebrae
    • Lateral: Medial pterygoid muscle, mandible, and deep surface of the parotid gland
  • The styloid process and its attached muscles divide the parapharyngeal space into two compartments:
    • Anterior compartment: Related to the tonsillar fossa (medially) and medial pterygoid muscle (laterally). (Statement 3)
    • Posterior compartment: Related to the posterior part of the lateral pharyngeal wall (medially) and the parotid gland (laterally). Structures: Carotid artery, jugular vein, cranial nerves IX, X, XI, XII, and the sympathetic trunk, along with upper deep cervical nodes. (Statement 4)

Retropharyngeal and Prevertebral spaces:

Space

Location

Features

Retro- pharyngeal Space
  • Behind the pharynx
  • Extent: from the skull base to tracheal bifurcation.
  • Infection may spread to the mediastinum.
  • Divided into spaces of Gillette by median raphe.

Pre- vertebral Space
  • Between vertebral bodies (posterior) and prevertebral fascia (anterior)
  • Extent: from the skull base to coccyx
  • Infections often from vertebral caries.
  • Abscess causes a midline bulge.

question:
Which of the following statements about the parapharyngeal space is/are correct?

1) The parapharyngeal space extends from the base of the skull to the tracheal bifurcation.

2) The retropharyngeal space communicates with the parapharyngeal space.

3) The anterior compartment of the parapharyngeal space is related to the medial pterygoid muscle.

4) The posterior compartment of the parapharyngeal space contains the carotid artery, jugular vein, and cranial nerves IX, X, XI, XII.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Zenker's Diverticulum:

  • Outpouching of the pharyngeal mucosa through a weak area in the posterior pharyngeal wall (Killian's dehiscence).

Clinical features:

  • Dysphagia is the most prominent feature appears when the pouch gets filled with food and presses on the oesophagus.
  • A gurgling sound is produced on swallowing.
  • Regurgitation at night of the undigested food, causing cough and aspiration pneumonia.
  • Halitosis(Chronic bad breathe)
  • Malnourished due to dysphagia.
  • Associated hiatus hernia

Diagnosis:

  • Barium swallow provides information regarding its size, location and character of the mucosal lining.

[[figure-1]]

  • Endoscopy reveal fibrosis and pooling of food in the diverticulum.

Treatment:

  • Excision of the pouch and cricopharyngeal myotomy done through cervical approach.
  • Dohlman’s procedure: Partition wall between the oesophagus and the pouch is exposed and divided by diathermy through a weerda scope.
  • Endoscopic laser treatment: Partition wall between the oesophagus and the pouch is exposed and divided by CO2 laser using endoscope. This procedure is known to have fewer recurrences and faster improvement in symptoms.

[[figure-2]]

Achalasia (OptionA): Lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax properly, leading to dysphagia for both solids and liquids. However, it typically does not cause halitosis or gurgling sound in the neck.

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) (Option B): Characterized by the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus leading to heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia. However, GERD usually does not present with bad breath, or gurgling sound in the neck.

Plummer-Vinson Syndrome (Option D): Characterized by dysphagia, iron-deficiency anemia, and esophageal webs. While it involves dysphagia, it does not typically cause regurgitation of undigested food, bad breath or gurgling sound in the neck.



Reference:
  1. Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 323, 324
  2. Zenker

question: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, chronic bad breath, and a gurgling sound in his neck during swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Killian’s dehiscence is more prone to the formation of a pharyngeal pouch or Zenker's diverticulum due to increased pressure during swallowing, leading to the outpouching of mucosal tissue.

Laimer's dehiscence: It is also present below Killian's dehiscence, but its position is in the midline below the cricopharyngeus


Vallecula (Option B) is a depression between the base of the tongue and epiglottis and is not an area of muscular weakness; hence, it is not involved in the formation of a pharyngeal pouch.


Pyriform sinus (Option C) is a recess in the hypopharynx lateral to the laryngeal inlet and is not the site of mucosal herniation in Zenker’s diverticulum.


Uvula (Option D) is a midline structure of the soft palate and has no anatomical or functional relation to the weak area responsible for pharyngeal pouch formation.

question: In the development of a pharyngeal pouch, which anatomical area is primarily affected?

correctAnswer: C. Initiate systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the absence of a well-formed abscess, the primary and critical initial management for Ludwig’s angina is to start systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics. This helps to address the mixed bacterial infection and prevent further progression.


Ludwig’s angina

Clinical Features
  • General Symptoms: Severe difficulty swallowing (odynophagia) and varying degrees of trismus (difficulty opening the mouth).
  • Symptoms depend on infection location and extent:
    • Sublingual Space: Swelling in the floor of the mouth, pushing the tongue upward and backwards.
    • Submandibular Region: Swelling and tenderness in the submandibular area, often described as "woody-hard."
    • Progression: The tongue can displace upward and backward, potentially obstructing the airway, with possible laryngeal edema.

Diagnosis
  • Clinical Evaluation: Assess symptoms, including swelling, tenderness, trismus, and airway compromise.
  • Imaging Studies:
    • Ultrasound: Identifies abscess presence and location.
    • Contrast-enhanced CT Scan: Differentiates between abscess and cellulitis (Phlegmon), revealing infection extent.

Treatment
  • Systemic Antibiotics: Broad-spectrum antibiotics to target mixed aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.
  • Incision and Drainage: Necessary if an abscess is present. (Option B ruled out)
    • Intraoral Approach: For infections confined to the sublingual space.
    • External Approach: For infections in the submandibular and submental spaces, involving a transverse incision along the mandible.
  • Airway Management: Maintaining a patent airway is crucial; tracheostomy may be needed in severe cases.

Complications
  • Spread of Infection: May extend to the parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal spaces and potentially to the mediastinum, causing mediastinitis.
  • Airway Obstruction
  • Septicaemia
  • Aspiration Pneumonia

Administer intravenous corticosteroids to reduce inflammation (Option A): While corticosteroids may help with inflammation in some cases, they are not the primary treatment for Ludwig’s angina, especially when systemic antibiotics are urgently needed.


Conduct a repeat contrast-enhanced CT scan to monitor progression (Option D): While monitoring is important, the immediate priority in managing Ludwig’s angina with diffuse cellulitis is to start systemic antibiotics rather than repeating imaging.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery 8th Edition, Page 310, 311

question: Which of the following structures are associated with dysphagia and dysarthria, except?

explanationHtml:
Correctr Answer : A) JNA

Explanation:

  • The combination of adolescent male, unilateral nasal obstruction, and recurrent epistaxis is classic for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA).

  • JNA is a benign but highly vascular tumor occurring almost exclusively in adolescent males.

  • The most common site of origin is the sphenopalatine foramen.

  • Although histologically benign, it is locally aggressive and can extend into the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, orbit, and cranial cavity.

  • Clinical features:

    • Recurrent spontaneous profuse epistaxis

    • Progressive unilateral nasal obstruction

    • Hyponasal speech

    • Conductive hearing loss due to Eustachian tube obstruction

    • Anemia due to repeated bleeding

    • Facial swelling or "frog-face deformity" in advanced cases

  • Imaging:

    • Contrast-enhanced CT/MRI

    • Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus (Holman-Miller sign)

  • Biopsy is contraindicated because of the risk of severe hemorrhage.

Allergic Rhinitis (Option B):Allergic rhinitis presents with sneezing, nasal itching, watery rhinorrhea, and bilateral nasal obstruction. Recurrent profuse epistaxis is not a typical feature.

Coagulation Disorder (Option C):Coagulation disorders may cause recurrent epistaxis but do not typically produce progressive unilateral nasal obstruction.

Antrochoanal Polyp (Option D):Antrochoanal polyps commonly present with unilateral nasal obstruction but are not usually associated with recurrent profuse epistaxis.

question: A 13-year-old boy presents with right-sided nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis for the past 6 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: A) Adenoidectomy

Explanation:

  • Adenoidectomy is the treatment of choice for children with significant symptoms such as nasal obstruction and sleep apnea.
  • Enlarged adenoids can block nasal airflow and contribute to sleep-disordered breathing.
  • Removing the adenoids improves airway patency rapidly.
  • It also enhances sleep quality, growth, and overall health outcomes.
  • Medical management does not resolve chronic obstruction.
  • Surgery is safe and highly effective with low complication rates.
  • Therefore, adenoidectomy alone is the preferred first-line treatment.

Incorrect Options Explanation

  • Option B) Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion: Grommets are needed only when the child has associated otitis media with effusion; not indicated in isolated adenoid hypertrophy.
  • Option C) Antibiotic therapy: Antibiotics treat acute infection but do not shrink adenoids or relieve chronic obstruction or sleep apnea.
  • Option D) Watchful waiting: Observation is inappropriate in symptomatic sleep apnea, which requires active intervention to prevent complications.


Reference:
  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg - 287
  2. Scott Brown ENT, 8th Edition, Pg - 288
question: What is the preferred management for a pediatric patient with symptomatic adenoid hypertrophy causing chronic nasal obstruction and sleep apnea?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The described clinical presentation is most consistent with diphtheria, a bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Key findings that support this diagnosis include:

  1. Pseudo membrane on tonsils: A hallmark feature of diphtheria, this greyish membrane adheres firmly to the underlying tissue and bleeds upon removal.
  2. Bull-neck appearance: Swelling of the neck due to cervical lymphadenopathy and soft tissue oedema is a classic sign of diphtheria.
  3. Fever, cough, and difficulty breathing: These are common systemic and respiratory symptoms of diphtheria.
  4. No immunisation history: The lack of vaccination increases susceptibility to diphtheria, which is preventable through the DPT vaccine.

Causes of Membrane over the tonsils include:

  • Moniliasis (Candidiasis)
  • Diphtheria (pseudomembrane)
  • Vincent’s angina (pseudomembrane)
  • Infectious mononucleosis
  • Malignancy of tonsil
  • Trauma
  • Aphthous ulcers
  • Leukaemia
  • Agranulocytosis

Infectious mononucleosis (Option A): While it may cause tonsillar swelling and pharyngitis, it does not cause a pseudomembrane or bull-neck appearance. Bleeding upon removal of the membrane is also not characteristic.

Tonsillitis (Option B): Tonsillitis can cause fever and difficulty swallowing, but it does not produce a pseudomembrane or bull-neck swelling. It is usually due to bacterial (e.g., Streptococcus pyogenes) or viral infections.

Candidiasis (Option D): Oral candidiasis can cause white patches on the mucosa, but these are easily scraped off without bleeding, unlike the pseudomembrane in diphtheria. It is also less likely to cause systemic symptoms like bull-neck swelling.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page 304
question: What is the most probable condition for a 6-year-old child who has not received immunization, presented to the Emergency Room by a concerned mother, experiencing symptoms such as fever, cough, and difficulty breathing? Physical examination reveals the presence of a pseudo membrane on the tonsils that bleeds upon attempted removal, as well as a swollen neck giving a bull-neck appearance.

explanationHtml:
The next course of treatment for this youngster would be an adenoidectomy with grommet insertion based on the symptoms and examination results. Snoring, mouth breathing, and a minor loss of hearing in the children are indications that the upper airway may be blocked, possibly as a result of swollen adenoids. The child's breathing would be made better by an adenoidectomy by removing the adenoids. Grommets would facilitate greater middle ear fluid outflow, enhancing the child's hearing. Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion may help the child's symptoms, which may also be caused by the child's high-arched palate.

Incorrect choices:

Option a: Adenoidectomy: In some instances where swollen adenoids are the cause of upper airway obstruction, adenoidectomy alone may be adequate. However, the child in this instance also has a high arched palate and a slight hearing loss, which indicates that there may be additional factors causing his symptoms.

Option b: Myringoplasty: A surgical treatment called myringoplasty can be used to seal an eardrum hole. However, in this instance, the child's primary symptoms are obstruction of the upper airway. Myringoplasty is not a suitable course of treatment for this reason.

Option d: Conservative management: For some cases of upper airway blockage brought on by enlarged adenoids, conservative care, such as observation and symptomatic treatment, may be suitable. The child's symptoms are, however, impacting his academic performance in this instance, and consequences could arise if the obstruction is not removed. The child's symptoms may not be sufficiently addressed and his quality of life may not be improved by conservative management, for this reason.

question: What would be the next step in managing the symptoms of a 7-year-old child who underwent a tonsillectomy and now presents with snoring, palpitations, mouth breathing, a slight hearing loss, a high arched palate, and a decline in school performance, causing concern to the mother?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Ludwig's angina is a deep neck space infection involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces. It does not produce a grey-white membrane over the tonsils. Instead, it is characterised by swelling of the floor of the mouth, raised tongue, and difficulty in breathing, speaking, or swallowing.

[[figure-1]]

Ludwig’s angina- Anatomy

Primary Spaces

It involves three spaces around the mandible: the sublingual, submandibular, and submental spaces.

  • Sublingual space: Infections here typically arise from the premolars and first molar.
  • Submandibular space: It contains the submandibular gland and lymph nodes, and connects to both the sublingual and submental spaces.
  • Submental space: Infections in the submandibular space can easily spread to the submental and contralateral sublingual spaces.

Secondary Spaces
  • The secondary spaces, known collectively as the masticator space, surround the muscles involved in mastication (masseter, medial and lateral pterygoid, and temporalis).
  • These spaces can become involved due to the posterior spread of infection from the primary spaces or from a third molar infection.
  • The primary clinical feature of masticator space infection is significant trismus.

Streptococcal tonsillitis (Option A): Although rare, severe forms can lead to exudative tonsillitis, with grey-white deposits on the tonsils. However, this is not as adherent or classic as the membrane seen in diphtheria.

Diphtheria (Option B): Diphtheria is a hallmark condition associated with the formation of a grey-white pseudomembrane over the tonsils, which is firmly adherent and bleeds upon removal.

Infectious mononucleosis (Option D): Caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, it can produce white or greyish exudates on the tonsils, especially in severe cases, alongside fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery 8th Edition, Page 309, 310
question: Which among the following conditions does not result in the development of a grey-white membrane over the tonsils?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Leukoplakia is characterised by a white patch or plaque on the oral mucosa that cannot be wiped off and cannot be attributed to another identifiable cause. It is commonly associated with chronic smoking, alcohol use, or other irritants. This lesion is considered a precancerous condition and warrants further evaluation and biopsy if necessary.

[[figure-1]]

Definition

White patch on oral mucosa, defined clinically, excluding conditions like lichen planus, candidiasis, etc.

Causes
  • Smoking, tobacco chewing
  • Alcohol abuse (especially with smoking)
  • Chronic trauma (ill-fitting dentures, cheek bites)
  • Associated with submucous fibrosis, hyperplastic candidiasis, Plummer-Vinson syndrome

Common sites
  • Buccal mucosa (most common in India)
  • Oral commissures, floor of mouth, tongue, gingivobuccal sulcus, lip mucosa

Age & Gender
  • Men in their 40s are 2-3 times more affected than females.

Clinical types
  • Homogenous: Smooth or wrinkled white patch, lower malignancy risk
  • Nodular (speckled): White patches on an erythematous base, higher malignancy risk
  • Erosive (erythroleukoplakia): Interspersed with red patches, fissures, highest malignancy risk

Malignant potential
  • 1-17.5% risk, average 5% malignant transformation
  • Higher risk in dysplastic lesions and certain locations

Treatment
  • Remove causative factors: Spontaneous regression in some cases.
  • Biopsy: For lesions with high malignant potential.
  • Surgical excision or laser/cryotherapy: For suspicious or small lesions

Erythroplakia (Option A): Erythroplakia presents as a red patch on the oral mucosa, often velvety in appearance, and is also a precancerous lesion. However, the lesion in this case is white, not red.

Fordyce’s granules (Option C): These are small, yellow or whitish papules representing ectopic sebaceous glands. They are benign and not related to smoking. They do not appear as a white patch like leukoplakia.

Koplik’s spots (Option D): Koplik’s spots are small white lesions with a red halo, typically seen on the buccal mucosa during the early stages of measles (rubeola). They are not associated with chronic smoking.



Reference:
  • Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 263,264
  • Scott Brown ENT 8th edition, 3rd volume, Pg. 434
  • Lichen planus
question: The image given below is from a chronic smoker’s oral examination. Identify the lesion given.

correctAnswer: A. Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the primary arterial supply to the palatine tonsils. The facial artery provides a direct tonsillar branch that supplies the tonsillar bed and adjacent structures.

Anatomy of Palatine tonsils

Location

Lateral wall of the oropharynx between the anterior and posterior pillars.

Surface Extensions

Upwards into the soft palate, downwards into the base of the tongue, and anteriorly into the palatoglossal arch.

Medial Surface Epithelium
  • Stratified squamous epithelium with crypts.
  • Crypta magna, or intratonsillar cleft, is located near the upper part of the tonsil.

Lateral Surface

It is covered by a fibrous capsule separated from the tonsil bed by loose areolar tissue.

Tonsil Bed Muscles

Formed by the superior constrictor and styloglossus muscles.

Arterial Supply
  • Tonsillar branch of the facial artery (main supply)
  • Ascending pharyngeal artery
  • Ascending palatine artery
  • Dorsal linguae branches of the lingual artery
  • Descending palatine branch of the maxillary artery.

Venous Drainage

It drains into the paratonsillar vein, which joins the common facial vein and the pharyngeal venous plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage

Flows into the upper deep cervical nodes.

Sensory Nerve Supply

Lesser palatine branches of the sphenopalatine ganglion (CN V) and the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Descending palatine branch of maxillary artery (Option B): This artery supplies the palate, including the soft and hard palates, but it is not the main source of blood supply for the palatine tonsils.

Buccal branch of maxillary artery (Option C): This artery primarily supplies the buccinator muscle and cheek mucosa, not the palatine tonsils.

Ascending palatine branch of facial artery (Option D): Although it contributes to the vascularisation of the pharyngeal region, it is not the primary supplier of the tonsils.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page 303, 304

explanationHtml:
• Adenoid facies, also known as adenoid face or long-face syndrome, refers to a characteristic facial appearance associated with chronic enlargement of the adenoids. Adenoid facies is characterized by specific facial features, which may include:
    • Long and narrow face
    • Open-mouth posture
    • High-arched palate
    • Dental crowding


Adenoid Hypertrophy: (Enlargement of the adenoids)

Aetiology
  • Physiological Enlargement: Common in childhood.
  • Chronic Conditions: Recurrent rhinitis, sinusitis, chronic tonsillitis, & allergies.

Clinical Features
  • Nasal Symptoms:
  • Nasal obstruction leading to mouth breathing and feeding difficulties.
  • Nasal discharge due to choanal obstruction and chronic rhinitis.
  • Sinusitis, Epistaxis & voice changes due to nasal obstruction. (Rhinolalia clausa)
  • Aural Symptoms:
  • Tubal obstruction causing retracted tympanic membrane and CHL.
  • Recurrent acute otitis media and chronic suppurative otitis media.
  • Otitis media with effusion due to intermittent eustachian tube obstruction.
  • Adenoid Facies: Characteristic facial appearance with an elongated face, open mouth, crowded upper teeth, and high-arched palate.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • Pulmonary Hypertension: Potential due to long-standing nasal obstruction.
  • Aprosexia: Difficulty concentrating

Clinical Examination
  • External Nose: Check for skin changes indicating frequent nose rubbing.
  • Nasal Assessment: Halogen light otoscope is used for simple anterior rhinoscopy, which examines the nasal cavity but not the adenoids.
  • Adenoid Assessment:
    • Nasendoscopy: For detailed evaluation, a flexible pediatric endoscope with topical anaesthesia is preferred. It provides an accurate assessment of adenoid size in an outpatient setting.
    • Lateral Soft-Tissue Radiograph: This is useful when endoscopy is not tolerated; it correlates well with endoscopic findings.

Goldenhar syndrome (Option B): Goldenhar syndrome, also known as oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum (OAVS) or hemifacial microsomia, is a rare congenital condition that affects the development of structures on one side of the face. The most prominent feature of Goldenhar syndrome is craniofacial asymmetry. This can involve facial asymmetry, microtia (underdeveloped or absent external ear), and facial clefts such as cleft lip and palate.

Horse facies (Option C): Also known as Greek warrior helmet appearance, is seen in Treacher Collins syndrome. It is characterized by a short philtrum, a downturned mouth, Small chin (micrognathia), and Poorly formed ears with small holes (pits) or flaps of skin (tags).


Frog facies (Option D): The term is often used to describe the facial features observed in individuals with juvenile nasal angiofibroma. Broadening of the nasal bridge, swelling of cheek, frog face deformity (in cases of bilateral proptosis).



Reference:
