question: Identify the condition shown in the image.

correctAnswer: B. Loss of sensation from the posterior ⅓ of the tongue
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Damage to the jugular foramen can compress or injure the glossopharyngeal nerve, leading to loss of both taste and sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue.

  • The tongue is divided into two regions:
    • Anterior two-thirds, innervated by the chorda tympani nerve (Option C)
    • Posterior one-third, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, separated by the Sulcus terminalis.

[[figure-1]]

  • Dysfunction in either of these nerves can cause impaired taste perception and loss of taste, as each nerve is responsible for sensation in its respective area.

Development of tongue and nerve innervation

Aspects

Anterior ⅔ of tongue

Posterior ⅓ of tongue

Posterior most of the tongue

Epithelial Development

Two lingual swellings and a tuberculum impar, made from the mesoderm of 1st arch, fuse to form the anterior ⅔ of tongue.

The hypobranchial arch is formed by the mesoderm of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal arches and is further divided into cranial and caudal parts. The cranial part of this arch gives rise to the posterior ⅓.

The Caudal parts derived from the hypobranchial arch develop to the posterior part of the tongue

Taste Sensation

Chorda Tympani

Glossopharyngeal nerve (supplies circumvallate papillae)

(Option B)

Internal laryngeal nerve (Branch of Vagus)

Sensory supply

Lingual nerve

Motor Supply

Except for the palatoglossus muscle, which is innervated by the vagus nerve, all other intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.

Muscles

All the Tongue muscles develop from Occipital Somites.

  1. Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Pg no 275
  2. BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Volume 3 & 4, 8th edition, Pg no 305.

question: Involvement of Jugular foramen leads to which of the following:

correctAnswer: A. Shift to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the vessel
explanationHtml:
Post-tonsillectomy bleeding is a serious complication that can lead to airway obstruction and significant blood loss. The immediate priority is to Securing the airway and ensuring hemodynamic stability are the first priorities.. The best course of action is to:

  1. Shift the patient to the operating theater (OT) for better visualization.
  2. Remove clots to identify the bleeding source.
  3. Cauterize or ligate the bleeding vessel to achieve hemostasis.

This is especially crucial in primary post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage (within 24 hours of surgery), which is usually due to inadequate hemostasis during the initial procedure.

Shift to OT, start IV antibiotics, and pack the tonsillar fossa (Option B): Incorrect because while IV antibiotics may be necessary in cases of secondary hemorrhage (after 24 hours, often due to infection), primary hemorrhage requires immediate surgical intervention rather than just packing.

Give anticoagulants, repeated gargling, and wait for 24 hours (Option C): Incorrect because anticoagulants would worsen the bleeding, and gargling is ineffective in stopping active hemorrhage. Waiting 24 hours without intervention could lead to life-threatening blood loss and airway compromise.

Do blood transfusion and wait and watch (Option D): Incorrect because while a blood transfusion may be needed in severe cases, it does not stop the active bleeding. Immediate surgical control is essential.



Reference:
  • Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat - PL Dhingra - 8th Edition • Page no: 506
  • Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery 8th Edition: Volume 3: Head and Neck Surgery, Plastic Surgery • Page no: 208, 635, 742, 755

question: What would be your immediate course of action in managing a patient who is experiencing bleeding from the surgical site following a tonsillectomy while in the recovery room?

explanationHtml:
Answer: B) Arytenoids

Explanation:

  • Arytenoids: The arytenoid cartilage is located in the larynx and is not visible during a posterior rhinoscopy, which examines the nasal cavity and nasopharynx using a mirror or endoscope.
  • The arytenoids are situated lower down in the larynx and are not accessible through the posterior nasal passage.

Posterior Rhinoscopy:

  • Posterior rhinoscopy is a clinical examination technique used to visualize the posterior part of the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, and adjacent structures like the adenoids, torus tubarius, and the upper surface of the soft palate.
  • This procedure is typically performed with a mirror or flexible endoscope, allowing the examiner to assess the nasopharyngeal area for any abnormalities.
  • Structures located in the nasopharynx and upper airway, but not the larynx, will be visible.

Incorrect Options:

Adenoids (Option A): are visible during posterior rhinoscopy, as they are located in the nasopharynx, which is the area examined in this procedure.

Torus tubarius (Option C): is the elevation of the mucosa over the eustachian tube orifice and is also visible during posterior rhinoscopy, being located in the nasopharynx.

Upper surface of soft palate (Option D): is visible during posterior rhinoscopy as it is part of the posterior oropharyngeal area and can be observed during the examination.

question: A senior resident in the hospital is performing the following clinical examination, as shown in the image below. Which of the following structures will not be visible to him?

explanationHtml:
• Quinsy (Peritonsillar abscess): Quinsy is the most likely diagnosis based on the symptoms. It typically follows an episode of acute tonsillitis and presents with fever, sore throat, difficulty swallowing (odynophagia), pain referred to the ear, and trismus (difficulty opening the mouth).
  • The absence of abnormalities on oral examination and the external facial exam makes this a more probable diagnosis.

Pharyngitis (Option A): is incorrect because pharyngitis generally presents with sore throat and fever, but it typically does not cause significant difficulty in opening the mouth or severe ear pain as seen in this case. There is no mention of visible throat redness or swelling, which would be expected in pharyngitis.

Parotid abscess (Option B): is incorrect because a parotid abscess usually causes swelling in the parotid gland area, which is not described here. Though ear pain is a symptom, there is no external facial swelling or pus drainage from the duct, which are typical signs of a parotid abscess.

Bezold’s Abscess (Option C): is incorrect because Bezold's abscess is a deep neck abscess that occurs as a complication of mastoiditis, usually presenting with swelling in the neck or behind the ear. The absence of such features and mastoiditis symptoms makes this diagnosis unlikely in this case.

question: Which of the following is the likely cause for the complaints of a 9-year-old boy presenting with right ear pain, difficulty in opening the mouth, painful swallowing, and fever, when the oral cavity examination shows no abnormalities in the external facial examination?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The fossa of Rosenmüller is a common site of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and is located posterior to the torus tubarius in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx.
  • On endoscopic examination, it appears as a deep recess lateral to the Eustachian tube opening.

[[figure-1]]

Nasopharyngeal Anatomy

Structure

Description

Fossa of Rosenmüller

Deep recess behind the torus tubarius, common site of nasopharyngeal carcinoma

Sinus of Morgagni

Gap between the base of the skull and superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle

Passavant’s Ridge

Muscular ridge formed by the superior pharyngeal constrictor, involved in velopharyngeal closure

Embryological remnant from which the anterior pituitary gland develops

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The symptoms described- difficulty breathing through the nose, an elongated face, lack of expression, mouth-breathing, high-arched palate, and crowded upper teeth- are classic signs of adenoid hypertrophy.

  • Adenoid hypertrophy occurs when the adenoid tissue, located in the nasopharynx, becomes enlarged, obstructing airflow through the nasal passages.

  • This leads to mouth breathing, sleep disturbances, and characteristic facial features, including an elongated face and a high-arched palate due to the prolonged open-mouth breathing pattern.

Adenoid Hypertrophy:

  • Adenoid hypertrophy is common in young children and can cause nasal obstruction, leading to mouth breathing and sleep disturbances (e.g., snoring, sleep apnea).

  • It may also result in facial deformities like the elongated face, high-arched palate, and crowded teeth due to chronic open-mouth breathing.

  • X-ray imaging typically shows enlargement of the adenoid tissue in the nasopharyngeal region.

Incorrect Options:

Lingual tonsils (Option A): is incorrect because while the lingual tonsils can contribute to obstructive symptoms, they are located at the base of the tongue, not in the nasopharynx.

Quinsy (Option B): is incorrect because quinsy refers to a peritonsillar abscess, typically presenting with severe throat pain, fever, and trismus, not with chronic nasal obstruction and facial deformities.

Tonsillar hypertrophy (Option C): is incorrect because tonsillar hypertrophy refers to the enlargement of the palatine tonsils, which is more likely to cause throat-related symptoms like difficulty swallowing, rather than the nasal obstruction seen in this case.

question: A 5-year-old girl is brought by her mother, with the complaint that the child is experiencing difficulties breathing through her nose. An X-ray image is provided for reference. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: A) Heimlich's maneuver.

  • It is a first-aid procedure utilized to dislodge an object from a person's windpipe when they are choking.
  • It includes standing behind the choking individual and applying powerful upward pressure on the abdomen, below the ribcage and above the umbilicus, to make sufficient pressure to dislodge the object.

Incorrect Options:

Back slap (Option B):

  • Back slapping is a first-aid strategy utilized for infants who are choking.
  • It includes the rescuer placing the newborn child face down on their forearm and delivering firm slaps to the infant's back between the shoulder blades.
  • Typically done to unstick the object from the infant's airway. However, this procedure isn't recommended for adults because it can cause harm.

Chest thrust (Option C):

  • Chest thrusts are a strategy utilized in CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) to clear an obstructed airway when the casualty isn't breathing.
  • This strategy includes setting the casualty on their back and delivering forceful thrusts to the lower half of their breastbone, between the nipples. This will help dislodge the object from the airway and reestablish breathing, but it isn't fitting for a conscious choking casualty who is still able to breathe.

Blind insertion of finger (Option D):

  • Blind insertion of finger isn't suggested as a first-aid method for choking casualties because it can thrust the object forward into the windpipe, making the circumstance worse.
  • It can also cause harm to the victim's throat and airway. It is important to utilize appropriate first-aid methods such as the Heimlich maneuver or chest thrusts to dislodge the object from the airway.


Reference:

Diseases of the Ear, Nose, Throat, 8th Edition, Page no: 289

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of a professional trumpet blower with a swelling on the side of the neck, associated with a gurgling sound upon compression, strongly suggests a laryngocele. A laryngocele is an abnormal air-filled dilation of the laryngeal saccule that can communicate with the laryngeal lumen. It is often seen in individuals who engage in activities requiring frequent or high-pressure breathing, such as wind instrument players or glassblowers.
  • Key clinical features of a laryngocele:
    • Swelling in the neck that may increase in size with activities like blowing.
    • Gurgling sound or fluctuation on palpation if it contains mucus or air.
    • Can present as an internal, external, or mixed type (external is visible as a neck swelling).

Pharyngeal pouch (Option A): Typically presents with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, and a swelling that may gurgle but is located posterior to the pharynx. It is not associated with trumpet blowing or activities requiring forced expiration.

Trachea-oesophageal fistula (Option C): This is a congenital or acquired condition presenting with recurrent aspiration, coughing, and feeding difficulties. It does not cause a compressible neck swelling or gurgling sound.

Tonsillar cyst (Option D): This would present as a localized swelling near the tonsillar region without the gurgling sound or association with forced expiratory activities.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The gag reflex (pharyngeal reflex) is a protective reflex that prevents aspiration and helps clear foreign material from the pharynx.

  • It involves both sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) components.

Component

Cranial Nerve

Function

Afferent limb

CN IX (Glossopharyngeal nerve)

Sensory supply from the posterior pharyngeal wall and oropharynx

Efferent limb

CN X (Vagus nerve)

Motor supply to the pharyngeal muscles causing elevation of the palate and pharyngeal contraction

  • Stimulation of the posterior pharyngeal wall sends sensory impulses through the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) to the brainstem.

  • The response is mediated through the vagus nerve (CN X), resulting in contraction of the pharyngeal muscles and elevation of the soft palate.

  • Therefore, lesions affecting either CN IX or CN X can result in an absent or impaired gag reflex.

CN V and VI (Option A):CN V is involved in facial sensation and mastication, while CN VI supplies the lateral rectus muscle. Neither forms part of the gag reflex pathway.

CN X and XI (Option B):CN X participates in the gag reflex, but CN XI primarily supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles and is not involved in the gag reflex.

CN VII and VIII (Option D):CN VII is responsible for facial expression and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, while CN VIII is responsible for hearing and balance. Neither is involved in the gag reflex.

The Buccopharyngeal fascia is a thin connective tissue layer that covers the outer surface of the pharynx and esophagus. Investigations of Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA)

Contrast-Enhanced CT Scan
  • Investigation of choice; shows tumor size, location, and bony involvement.

Evaluates soft tissue and intracranial extension, differentiates between extradural and intradural spread.

Visualizes tumor vascularity, identifies feeding vessels and aids in preoperative embolization to reduce surgical blood loss.

Provides a direct view of the tumor, but biopsy is generally avoided due to high bleeding risk.

Assesses hearing loss caused by Eustachian tube obstruction; establishes baseline and monitors post-treatment hearing.

Biopsy

Biopsy is contraindicated due to risk of profuse bleeding.

correctAnswer: B. Protection of the lower airways
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The primary and most essential function of the larynx is protection of the lower respiratory tract.

  • The larynx acts as a sphincteric mechanism that prevents aspiration of food, liquids, and foreign bodies into the tracheobronchial tree during swallowing.
  • This protective mechanism involves elevation of the larynx, closure of the laryngeal inlet by the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds, and tight adduction of the false and true vocal cords.
  • The larynx also performs other functions including phonation, respiration, and fixation of the chest during straining (Valsalva maneuver).

Phonation (Option A): The larynx produces voice through vibration of the vocal cords, but phonation is not its most fundamental function.

Fixation of the chest (Option C): The larynx contributes to thoracic fixation during activities such as coughing, lifting, or straining, but this is a secondary function.

Humidification of inspired air (Option D): The nasal cavity and turbinates are primarily responsible for warming, filtering, and humidifying inspired air, not the larynx.

question: Which of the following is considered its primary, most fundamental function of the larynx?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The pediatric larynx possesses several unique anatomical features that cater to the physiological needs of an infant.

  • It is situated much higher in the neck, with the cricoid cartilage resting at the level of the C3-C4 vertebrae, whereas in adults, it descends to C6. (Statement 1)
  • This high position allows the epiglottis to project upwards and interlock with the soft palate (Statement 2).
  • This creates a continuous, dedicated airway from the nasopharynx directly into the larynx.
  • This separation of the respiratory and digestive tracts enables the infant to breathe continuously while suckling and swallowing milk, protecting against aspiration. (Statement 3)

question:
Consider the following statements regarding the unique anatomy of the pediatric larynx compared to that of an adult:

  1. It is positioned higher in the neck (at the level of C3-C4).
  2. The high position allows the epiglottis to interlock with the soft palate.
  3. This anatomical arrangement prevents infants from breathing and swallowing simultaneously.
  4. The narrowest part of the infant's airway is the subglottis.

Which of the above statements are correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The epiglottis develops from the caudal part of the hypobranchial eminence, also known as the epiglottic swelling, which appears as a midline elevation in the floor of the primitive pharynx.

  • The hypobranchial eminence is formed mainly from the third and fourth pharyngeal arches.
  • The cranial part of the hypobranchial eminence contributes to the posterior third of the tongue, while the epiglottis develops from its caudal portion.
  • Other major laryngeal cartilages, including the thyroid, cricoid, and arytenoid cartilages, arise from the mesenchyme of the fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches.

Third pharyngeal pouch (Option C) endoderm gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus gland.

Tracheoesophageal septum (Option D) separates the trachea from the esophagus and does not form laryngeal cartilages.

Pharyngeal arch derivatives:

Part

Derivatives

Upper part of the body of hyoid bone, lesser cornu of hyoid bone, stylohyoid ligament

3rd arch (Option C)

Lower part of the body of hyoid bone and greater cornua

4th arch

Upper part of thyroid cartilage

6th arch

Lower part of thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, corniculate cartilage, cuneiform cartilage, intrinsic muscles of larynx

Tracheoesophageal septum (Option D): This is the partition that divides the foregut into the oesophagus (posteriorly) and the trachea (anteriorly). Defects here lead to tracheoesophageal fistulas, not laryngeal anomalies.

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 335.
question: A pediatric patient is evaluated for a congenital laryngeal anomaly. Which of the following embryological structures gives rise to the epiglottis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The cricoid cartilage is anatomically unique as it is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the entire upper and lower respiratory tract.

  • It is classically described as having a signet ring shape.
  • This shape is defined by a narrow anterior arch and a broad, flat posterior lamina.
  • The complete, non-collapsible nature of this ring is critical for maintaining the constant patency of the airway and providing a robust base for the articulation of the arytenoid cartilages.

[[figure-1]]

Shield-shaped (Option A) describes the thyroid cartilage, which consists of two laminae that meet anteriorly but are open posteriorly, resembling a protective shield.

Leaf-shaped (Option C) is the characteristic shape of the epiglottis, a fibroelastic cartilage that acts as a lid over the laryngeal inlet during deglutition.

Pyramid-shaped (Option D) describes the paired arytenoid cartilages, which have a base articulating with the cricoid, an anterior vocal process, and a lateral muscular process.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539821/
question: During an emergency cricothyroidotomy, the surgeon palpates the anatomical landmarks of the anterior neck. A complete cartilaginous ring is identified just inferior to the cricothyroid membrane. Which of the following best describes the characteristic anatomical shape of this specific cartilage?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The cartilages of Santorini are anatomically known as the corniculate cartilages.

  • These are two small, conical nodules composed of elastic cartilage that articulate directly with the apices of the paired arytenoid cartilages.
  • They are situated within the posterior part of the aryepiglottic folds and serve to prolong the arytenoid cartilages posteriorly and medially, providing structural support and rigidity to the mucosal fold.

[[figure-1]]

Cuneiform cartilages (Option A) are eponymously known as the cartilages of Wrisberg; they are elongated, club-shaped elastic cartilages situated laterally and anteriorly to the corniculate cartilages within the aryepiglottic folds.

Triticeal cartilages (Option C) are small, variable cartilaginous nodules found within the lateral thyrohyoid ligaments, connecting the superior cornu of the thyroid cartilage to the greater cornu of the hyoid bone.

Epiglottic tubercle (Option D) is a mucosal prominence situated at the lower end of the posterior surface of the epiglottis, entirely distinct from the paired minor cartilages.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 331.

question: A 5 y/o boy presents with a history of progressive hoarseness and stridor. Laryngoscopy reveals multiple warty lesions in the larynx. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:


Tuberculosis of the Larynx is the most likely diagnosis due to the presence of ulcerative lesions in the posterior larynx and cavitary lung lesions, indicative of pulmonary tuberculosis.

Tuberculosis of the Larynx

Lupus of larynx

Features
  • Secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis.
  • Affects middle-aged males.
  • Spread occurs via bronchogenic or haematogenous routes.
  • Tubercle bacilli from sputum settle in laryngeal mucosa, leading to infection
  • Indolent tubercular infection associated with lupus of the nose and pharynx.
  • Lupus primarily affects the anterior part of the larynx.

Pathology:
  • Affects the posterior larynx more than the anterior.
  • Common sites:Interarytenoid fold, ventricular bands, vocal cords, and epiglottis.
  • Formation of submucosal tubercles, which may ulcerate and cause cellular infiltration (pseudoedema).
  • Starts in the epiglottis, which may be destroyed.
  • Lesion spreads to the aryepiglottic folds and ventricular bands.
  • No association with pulmonary tuberculosis

Clinical Features:
  • Weakness of voice (early symptom)
  • Hoarseness
  • Severe pain, radiating to ears, especially with ulceration
  • Dysphagia in later stages.

[[figure-1]]
  • Painless condition.
  • Often asymptomatic, found incidentally during lupus evaluation.

Signs:
  • Hyperaemia of vocal cords (impaired adduction)
  • Swelling in inter arytenoid region with a mamillated appearance
  • Ulceration of vocal cords ("mouse-nibbled" appearance)
  • Superficial ragged ulcerations on arytenoids and inter arytenoid region
  • Granulation tissue in inter arytenoid region
  • Pseudoedema of the epiglottis ("turban epiglottis")
  • Swelling of ventricular bands and aryepiglottic folds

[[figure-2]]
  • Destruction of the epiglottis.
  • Involvement of aryepiglottic folds and ventricular bands.

Diagnosis:
  • X-ray of chest
  • Sputum examination for tuberculosis
  • Biopsy of laryngeal lesion to exclude carcinoma
  • Routine laryngeal examination in patients with lupus of the nose.
  • No pulmonary TB involvement.

Treatment:
  • Treat the pulmonary tuberculosis (antitubercular drugs).
  • Voice rest
  • Antitubercular drugs.


Laryngeal Papillomatosis (Option A): Typically involves multiple papilated lesions, less ulcerative lesions and is not usually associated with cavitary lung lesions.


Reinke’s Edema (Option B): Characterized by vocal cord swelling, not typically associated with ulcerative lesions and cavitary lung findings.


Lupus of the Larynx (Option C): Affects the anterior larynx and is usually asymptomatic; not associated with cavitary lung lesions.

question: A 50 y/o man with a history of chronic cough and weight loss presents with hoarseness and severe throat pain. Laryngoscopy reveals ulcerative lesions predominantly in the posterior part of the larynx, with some areas of hyperemia and swelling. His chest X-ray shows cavitary lesions. Based on the patient's history and laryngeal findings, which condition is most likely responsible for the observed laryngeal lesions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Reinke’s Edema is the most likely diagnosis due to the presence of fusiform swelling of the vocal cords with a pale, translucent appearance as shown in the image.
  • It is also consistent with the h/o chronic smoking.
  • Causes:
    • Chronic vocal cord irritation (voice misuse, heavy smoking). Aka smokers larynx
    • Chronic sinusitis, laryngopharyngeal reflux.
    • Myxoedema
    • More common in middle-aged men and women.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Hoarseness or husky voice.
    • Use of false vocal cords for voice production, leading to a low-pitched, rough voice.
  • Examination:
    • Laryngoscopy: Fusiform swelling of vocal cords with a pale, translucent appearance.
    • Ventricular bands may be hyperaemic and hypertrophic, obscuring true cords.
  • Treatment:
    • Decortication of vocal cords: Removal of a strip of epithelium, first on one side, then the other after 3-4 weeks.
    • Voice rest
    • Speech therapy: To improve proper voice production.

Vocal Polyp (Option A): Typically unilateral, pedunculated, and caused by sudden vocal abuse, not associated with the fusiform swelling shown.

Laryngeal Papillomatosis (Option C): Characterized by multiple lesions and not the fusiform swelling and pale appearance as shown.

Vocal Nodule (Option D): Usually bilateral but more discrete and located at the junction of the anterior and posterior thirds of the vocal cords; does not present with fusiform swelling.

question: A 45 y/o woman with a history of heavy smoking presents with a low-pitched, rough voice and noticeable hoarseness. Laryngoscopy reveals the following findings. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The presence of a smooth white patch on the laryngeal mucosa without ulceration in patients with h/o tobacco chewing suggests a diagnosis of leukoplakia.

[[figure-1]]

Definition

White patch on oral mucosa, defined clinically, excluding conditions like lichen planus, candidiasis, etc.

Causes
  • Smoking, tobacco chewing
  • Alcohol abuse (especially with smoking)
  • Chronic trauma (ill-fitting dentures, cheek bites)
  • Associated with submucous fibrosis, hyperplastic candidiasis, Plummer-Vinson syndrome

Common sites
  • Buccal mucosa (most common in India)
  • Oral commissures, floor of mouth, tongue, gingivobuccal sulcus, lip mucosa

Age & Gender
  • Men in their 40s are 2-3 times more affected than females.

Clinical types
  • Homogenous: Smooth or wrinkled white patch, lower malignancy risk
  • Nodular (speckled): White patches on an erythematous base, higher malignancy risk
  • Erosive (erythroleukoplakia): Interspersed with red patches, fissures, highest malignancy risk

Malignant potential
  • 1-17.5% risk, average 5% malignant transformation
  • Higher risk in dysplastic lesions and certain locations

Treatment
  • Remove causative factors
  • Biopsy: For lesions with high malignant potential.
  • Surgical excision or laser/cryotherapy: For suspicious or small lesions

Oral Candidiasis (Option A): Typically presents with white, creamy patches that can be easily scraped off.

Lichen Planus (Option C): Often presents with white, lace-like striations (Wickham’s striae) rather than a smooth white patch.

Oral submucous Fibrosis (Option D): Typically presents with oral mucosal stiffness and restricted mouth opening, not a white patch.

correctAnswer: C. Non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium; Rima glottidis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The vocal cords are lined by non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium and the space between them is called the rima glottidis.


LARYNGEAL CAVITY

  • The laryngeal cavity extends from the laryngeal inlet aryepiglottic fold to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, where it continues with the trachea.
  • It is divided into three parts by two pairs of folds, the vestibular and vocal folds:
    • Vestibule
    • Ventricle (Sinus of Larynx)
    • Subglottic Space
  • The rima vestibularis is the space between the vestibular folds (Option A & D ruled out), while the rima glottidis is the narrowest part of the larynx, located between the vocal folds.
  • It is divided into an anterior phonatory portion and a posterior respiratory portion.
  • Mucous membranes of the larynx:
    • Pseudostratified Ciliated Columnar Epithelium (Respiratory-Type):
      • Most of the larynx.
    • Non-Keratinizing Stratified Squamous Epithelium:
      • Upper Half of the Posterior Surface of the Epiglottis
      • Upper Part of the Aryepiglottic Fold
      • Posterior Glottis
      • Vocal Folds (Vocal Cords) (Option B ruled out)

[[figure-1]]

  • Cricovocal/ Conus elasticus membrane- Connects the thyroid, cricoid, and arytenoid cartilages, forming the vocal ligament and conus elasticus. It provides a site where subglottic foreign bodies may become impacted.

correctAnswer: C. The cuneiform cartilages provide support to the vocal cords.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cuneiform cartilages are rod-shaped and located in the aryepiglottic fold, but they provide support to the aryepiglottic fold, not the vocal cords.
  • The vocal cords are attached to the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilages.


CARTILAGE

DESCRIPTION

ARYTENOID
  • Paired Hyaline Cartilage.
  • Each arytenoid cartilage is shaped like a pyramid.
  • Base: The base of each arytenoid cartilage articulates with the cricoid cartilage. (Option A ruled out)
  • Muscular Process: A lateral projection where intrinsic laryngeal muscles attach.
  • Vocal Process: Anterior projection that provides attachment for the vocal cords.
  • Apex: The top part of the arytenoid cartilage that supports the corniculate cartilage.

CORNICULATE
  • Cartilages of Santorini
  • There are two corniculate cartilages, one on each side.
  • Elastic cartilage
  • Each corniculate cartilage articulates with the apex of the arytenoid cartilage. (Option B ruled out)
  • They resemble horns (hence the name "corniculate") and function to support the aryepiglottic fold. (Option D ruled out)

CUNEIFORM
  • Cartilages of Wrisberg
  • Paired elastic Cartilage.
  • Each cuneiform cartilage has a rod-like shape.
  • Positioned in the aryepiglottic fold in front of the corniculate cartilage.
  • Provides passive support to the aryepiglottic fold, enhancing its stability.

  2. Logan Turner’s Diseases Of Nose, Throat And Ear Head and Neck Surgery, 11th edition. Pages 150, 151

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the arytenoid, corniculate, and cuneiform cartilages?

correctAnswer: C. It is connected to the hyoid bone by the hyoepiglottic ligament.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The epiglottis is connected to the hyoid bone by the hyoepiglottic ligament.

Epiglottis

  • Unpaired Elastic Cartilage (Option A ruled out)
  • Shape: Leaf-shaped yellow elastic cartilage.
  • Location: Forms the anterior wall of the laryngeal inlet.
  • Attachments:
    • Connected to the hyoid bone by the hyoepiglottic ligament, dividing it into suprahyoid and infrahyoid portions.
    • The petiole attaches it to the thyroid cartilage just above the vocal cords.

  • Anterior Surface:

    • Preepiglottic Space: Located in front of the epiglottis, between the anterior surface and the thyrohyoid membrane/upper thyroid cartilage. Filled with fat, it may be involved in supraglottic cancers or the base of tongue carcinomas. (Option B ruled out)
  • Posterior Surface:
    • Tubercle of Epiglottis: A bulge that may obstruct the view of the anterior commissure during indirect laryngoscopy.
    • Contains pits for mucous glands and occasional perforations, which may facilitate cancer spread to the preepiglottic space.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Cancer Spread: Supraglottic cancers can invade the pre-epiglottic space through epiglottic perforations.
    • Non-Essential for Swallowing: The epiglottis can be safely amputated in cases of cancer or trauma without significant risk of aspiration. (Option D ruled out)

[[figure-1]]

question: Which of the following is true about the epiglottis?

correctAnswer: D. Age-related ossification of cricoid cartilage
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The cricoid cartilage, made of hyaline cartilage, tends to calcify as part of the aging process, typically beginning around 25 and completing by 65, leading to changes seen on imaging.

Cricoid Cartilage

  • Complete ring: The only laryngeal cartilage forms a full ring, resembling a signet ring with a broader posterior lamina and a narrow anterior arch.
  • Clinical relevance:
    • In children, the cricoid cartilage is smaller in diameter than the glottis, making it the narrowest part of the airway, crucial for choosing the correct endotracheal tube size.
    • Calcification in older adults can appear as a foreign body on X-rays.
    • Subglottic foreign bodies may lodge near the cricoid cartilage, especially in children.

[[figure-1]]

Displacement of the thyroid cartilage from its normal position (Option A): Displacement of the thyroid cartilage, such as dislocation from the cricoid, is not suggested by the presence of calcified structures on imaging.

Formation of fibrous tissue in the cricoid cartilage (Option B): The cricoid cartilage is primarily hyaline cartilage, and fibrous tissue is not a typical finding.it can be associated with prolonged ET tube insertion

Inflammatory changes in the arytenoid cartilage (Option C): Inflammatory conditions of the arytenoid cartilage might cause vocal cord dysfunction or airway obstruction, but would not lead to calcified structures in the cricoid cartilage.



Reference:

  2. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery , 8th Edition, 3rd Volume, Page 886

question: A 60-year-old male presents with hoarseness of voice and breathing difficulties following minor neck trauma. During evaluation, imaging reveals calcified structures in the laryngeal region. What is the most likely cause for this finding?

correctAnswer: C. It is an unpaired hyaline cartilage.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The thyroid cartilage is an unpaired hyaline cartilage of the larynx.

Thyroid Cartilage

  • The thyroid cartilage is the largest cartilage in the larynx. (Option A ruled out)
  • It is an unpaired hyaline cartilage of the larynx. (Option C)
  • It has two alae (wings) that meet at an angle: 90° in males and 120° in females. (Option B ruled out)
  • The vocal cords are attached to the middle of this thyroid angle.
  • Most foreign bodies in the larynx get trapped above the vocal cords above the middle of the thyroid cartilage. (Option D ruled out)
  • An emergency airway can be created by piercing the cricothyroid membrane, a procedure known as cricothyrotomy.

[[figure-1]]

question: Which of the following statements about the thyroid cartilage is correct?

correctAnswer: D. The cry is normal in this condition
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of a laryngeal web that causes a weak cry from birth and does not present with a normal cry like laryngomalacia or other congenital laryngeal abnormalities.

Laryngeal webs
  • Laryngeal webs are formed due to the failure of complete canalization of the larynx during embryogenesis.
  • It leads to the formation of glottic (Option C) or, very rarely, a supraglottic web and causes variable degrees of respiratory obstruction and dysphonia as per the length of the vocal cord involved.

[[figure-1]]

Clinical features
  • Severe respiratory obstruction
  • Dysphonia
  • Biphasic stridor
  • Weak, high-pitched, squeaky voice (Option A)
  • Weak cry or aphonia from birth





Management (depends on thickness of web)
  • Thin web: endoscopic division along the margin of one vocal cord with a knife or CO2 laser (Option B)
  • Thick web: excision via laryngofissure and a silicon keel is placed endoscopically to prevent recurrence for 2 weeks

[[figure-2]]

question: A baby presents with biphasic stridor and severe respiratory obstruction necessitating intubation. Identify the false statement about this condition.

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D) One-way (check valve) obstruction

Explanation:

  • The chest X-ray showing hyperinflation of the left lung with a mediastinal shift indicates a one-way (check valve) obstruction.
  • This occurs when the foreign body allows air to enter but prevents it from exiting, leading to trapped air and overinflation (obstructive emphysema).

Bronchial Foreign Body:

Common Location

Right bronchus (due to its wider lumen and alignment with the trachea)

Clinical Triad

Cough, wheezing, and diminished air entry to the lung.

Late Features

Lung collapse, emphysema, pneumonitis, bronchiectasis, or lung abscess.

Types of Obstruction

[[figure-1]]
  • Partial Obstruction: (Option B)
    • Air can pass in and out
    • Cause only wheezing
  • One-way Obstruction: (Option D)
    • Air can enter (during inspiration) but not exit
    • Cause emphysema of the lungs
  • Total Obstruction: (Option A)
    • Air cannot enter or exit
    • Cause obstructive atelectasis
  • One-way Obstruction :
    • Air can exit (during expiration) but not enter
    • Cause atelectasis

Complication

  • Obstructive Emphysema: Air trapped in the lungs due to a check-valve mechanism.
  • Spontaneous Pneumothorax: Due to rupture of emphysematous bullae.
  • Lung Collapse: Due to complete bronchial obstruction.
  • Chronic Complications: Retained foreign bodies may lead to pneumonitis, bronchiectasis, or lung abscess.

Investigation

  • Plain X-ray Chest (PA and Lateral Views):
  • Fluoroscopy/Videofluoroscopy: Evaluation during inspiration and expiration can be made.
  • CT Chest

Management

  • Emergency removal of foreign bodies is not typically indicated unless:
    • Airway obstruction is present.
    • Foreign bodies are of vegetable origin (e.g., seeds) and are likely to swell.


Bilateral obstruction (Option C) of bronchus with foreign bodies are more critical as it can cause rapid deterioration and often requires high-pressure ventilation, which may exacerbate complications like pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum.




Reference:
  1. Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th edition, Pages 375-378
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6848494/#

question: A 3-year-old presents with sudden coughing and wheezing after eating peanuts. A chest X-ray is taken and shown below. What is the most likely type of bronchial obstruction?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In cases of complete airway obstruction caused by a laryngeal foreign body, where measures such as the Heimlich maneuver have failed, an emergency tracheostomy is necessary to secure the airway and facilitate ventilation.

Tracheal Foreign Body

Laryngeal Foreign Body
  • Sharp Foreign Body: Cough and hemoptysis.
  • Loose Foreign Body (e.g., seed): May move between carina and vocal cords, causing:
    • "Audible slap" and "palpatory thud"
    • Asthmatoid wheeze heard best at patient’s open mouth
  • Complete Obstruction: Can cause asphyxia and sudden death unless urgent resuscitative measures are taken urgently.
  • Partial Obstruction: Cause discomfort or pain in throat, hoarseness, stridor, cough, aphonia, dyspnea, wheezing, and hemoptysis.

Radiology: Soft Tissue X-ray: PA and lateral views of neck in its extended position for radio-opaque and sometimes radiolucent foreign body in larynx/trachea.
  • Emergency removal of foreign bodies is not typically indicated unless:
    • Airway obstruction is present.
    • Foreign bodies are of vegetable origin (e.g., seeds) and likely to swell.
  • Methods for Foreign Body Removal
  1. Rigid bronchoscopy.
  2. Bronchoscopy with C-arm fluoroscopy.
  3. Use of Dormia basket or Fogarty's balloon for rounded objects. (Option A)
  4. Tracheostomy first followed by bronchoscopy through the tracheostome.
  5. Thoracotomy and bronchotomy for peripheral foreign bodies.
  6. Flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy in selected adult patients.

Complete Obstruction:

  • A large bolus of food above the vocal cords may cause total aphonia (inability to cry for help).
  • Immediate First Aid Measures:
    • Back pounding.
    • Turn the patient upside down.
    • Back Blows (for infants <1 year): Place the infant face down over the rescuer’s arm, head lower than the trunk, and deliver five back blows between the scapulae.

[[figure-1]]

  • Heimlich Maneuver (for >1 year):
    • Should not be done if only partial obstruction, for fear of causing total obstruction
    • Procedure: Stand behind the patient and wrap arms around the lower chest.
    • Perform four abdominal thrusts to use residual air in the lungs to dislodge the foreign body.

[[figure-2]]

  • If Heimlich fails: Perform cricothyrotomy or emergency tracheostomy to secure the airway. (Option B)
  • Post-Emergency: Foreign body removal using direct laryngoscopy or laryngofissure if the object is impacted. (Option C)

Initiate advanced airway management with intubation (Option D): Intubation is unlikely to succeed due to the obstruction; emergency tracheostomy provides immediate access to the airway, which is critical in a hypoxic situation.



Reference:
  1. Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 375- 378
  2. OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 10th Edition, Page 776

question: A 5-year-old child presents with complete airway obstruction after swallowing a coin and is showing signs of hypoxia. The Heimlich maneuver has failed. X-rays of the neck are shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario here is of partial obstruction that does not need decannulation and reintubation which is preferred in cases of complete obstruction.

Management of Tracheostomy Tube Obstruction

Partial Obstruction Management

  • Constant Supervision: Monitor the patient for signs of obstruction; a nurse or relative should be present.
  • Communication: Provide the patient with a bell or paper pad and pencil for communication.
  • Suctioning: (Option B)
    • Perform suction every 30 minutes as needed.
    • Use sterile catheters; only apply suction while withdrawing to prevent mucosal injury.
  • Prevent Crusting and Tracheitis:
    • Humidification: Use a humidifier, steam tent, or ultrasonic nebulizer.
    • Saline Instillation: Instill normal or hypotonic saline or Ringer’s lactate every 2-3 hours to loosen crusts. (Option C)
    • Mucolytics: Consider acetylcysteine to liquefy thick secretions. (Option D)

Complete Obstruction Management

  • Immediate Response:
    • If obstruction is suspected, ensure the tracheostomy tube is not blocked or displaced.
    • Assess for any displacement or blockage of the tube.
  • Decannulation :
    • Preparation
    • Plugging
    • Monitoring
  • Reintubation: Be prepared for immediate reintubation if the patient cannot tolerate the obstruction.

Complications to Monitor

  • Immediate:
    • Hemorrhage
    • Apnea due to CO₂ washout
    • Pneumothorax from pleural injury
    • Injury to recurrent laryngeal nerves
    • Aspiration of blood
    • Injury to the esophagus, potentially causing tracheoesophageal fistula
  • Intermediate:
    • Reactionary or secondary bleeding
    • Displacement of the tube


[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th edition, Page 372.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Mid-tracheostomy is preferred for long-term airway access and minimizes complications.

Tracheostomy:

  • Is making an opening in the anterior wall of the trachea and converting it into a stoma on the skin surface.
  • Types:

High Tracheostomy (Option A)

Mid-Tracheostomy

(Option C)

Low Tracheostomy

(Option B)

  • Risks: Perichondritis of cricoid cartilage and subglottic stenosis.
  • Only Indication: Carcinoma of the larynx (since the entire larynx will be removed, and a new tracheostome will be made lower).
  • Location: Done through the 2nd or 3rd tracheal rings and involves the division of or retraction of the thyroid isthmus to expose the trachea.
  • Most Preferred technique
  • The procedure
  • Location: Done below the level of thyroid isthmus (below the 3rd tracheal ring).
  • Challenges:
    • Trachea is deeper at this level.
    • Close proximity to large blood vessels.
    • Difficulty with tracheostomy tube impinging on the suprasternal notch.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

Cricothyrotomy (Option D) is not suitable for prolonged ventilation; it is a temporary measure and should be followed by a tracheostomy once the patient is stabilized.

question: A 60-year-old patient with severe asthma and airway edema is admitted to the ICU after multiple failed intubation attempts. Which type of procedure is most suitable for ensuring long-term airway management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cricothyrotomy quickly establishes an airway when intubation fails, especially in cases of severe maxillofacial trauma, to prevent hypoxia.

Cricothyrotomy

Definition

Procedure for opening the airway through the cricothyroid membrane.

Indication

  • Emergency cricothyrotomy is indicated in any CICO (Cannot Intubate, Cannot Oxygenate) scenario.
  • Situations that may lead to CICO include:
    • Oral or maxillofacial trauma
    • Cervical spine trauma
    • Profuse oral hemorrhage
    • Copious emesis
    • Anatomic abnormalities preventing endotracheal intubation

Clinical Significance

Cricothyrotomy is the final step in the difficult airway algorithm for CICO scenarios.

Types

1. Needle or Small Bore Cannula Cricothyrotomy:

2. Large Cannula Cricothyrotomy:

3. Surgical Cricothyrotomy:

Complications

  • Bleeding
  • Lacerations of tracheal cartilage
  • Perforation of the trachea
  • Creation of a false tract
  • Infection
  • Long-term complications: Subglottic stenosis, Voice change

Contraindications

  • No absolute contraindications in CICO scenarios.
  • Relative contraindications:
    • Known tracheal surgery
    • Fractured larynx
    • Laryngotracheal disruption
    • Children

Image

[[figure-1]]

Bag-mask ventilation (Option A) is ineffective in patients with maxillofacial trauma due to disarranged anatomy and potential bleeding, which hinder proper mask fit and air transfer to the lungs.

Endotracheal intubation (Option B) is likely to be difficult in maxillofacial trauma patients due to obstructed views of the vocal cords from blood, secretions, and tissue debris.

Supraglottic airway devices (Option C) may not be suitable for maxillofacial trauma patients due to limited oral space and the risk of displacement, making them unsuitable for definitive airway management.

question: A 14-day-old neonate presents with stridor. Which condition is not typically associated with stridor in this age group?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Inspiratory stridor is typically due to extrathoracic obstruction, such as a retropharyngeal abscess, which causes airway collapse during inspiration as intratracheal pressure falls below atmospheric pressure.

Stridor:

  • Noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through the narrowed air passages.
  • Types:

[[figure-1]]

Stridor

1. Inspiratory Stridor

2. Expiratory Stridor

3. Biphasic Stridor

Site of Lesion

Produced in obstructive lesions of supraglottis or pharynx (extrathoracic obstruction).

Produced in lesions of the thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi (intrathoracic obstruction).

Produced in lesions of glottis, subglottis and cervical trachea.

Mechanism

In extrathoracic obstruction:

During inspiration → intratracheal pressure falls below atmospheric pressure → airway collapse

In intrathoracic obstruction:

During expiration → elevated pleural pressure compresses the airway → reduction in airway size at the site of obstruction

In glottic or subglottic obstruction:

Airway segment → remains unchanged during respiration

Example

  • Laryngomalacia
  • Retropharyngeal abscess (Option C)
  • Bronchial foreign body (Option A)
  • Tracheal stenosis
  • Laryngeal papillomas (Option B)
  • Vocal cord paralysis
  • Subglottic stenosis (Option D)

question: A 3-year-old child has stridor only during inspiration. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario here points to the diagnosis of subglottic hemangioma, and the first line of treatment for this condition is propranolol.
  • Subglottic hemangioma is a benign endothelial cell tumor that occurs at the subglottis.
  • It has a proliferative phase of 6-12 months and a complete involution over 1-5 years.

Clinical features

  • Presents in the first few weeks or within the first 6 months
  • Biphasic stridor that worsens progressively; crying will increase the stridor
  • Normal cry
  • 50% of patients have a coexisting cutaneous lesion

Investigations

  • Endoscopy:
    • Typical compressible, pear-shaped red swelling in the subglottis on one side (left>right).
    • Larger hemangiomas are seen as circumferential and may extend into the trachea, surrounding soft tissues, and mediastinum.
  • MRI is done if spread beyond the airway is suspected.

Treatment:

  • Old modalities that are not followed now include:
    • Radiotherapy
    • CO2 laser ablation (Option A)
    • Systemic steroids
    • Intralesional steroid injection followed by intubation (Option B)
    • Interferon alpha-2a
  • Propranolol is the first-line treatment, given for at least 12 months and then weaned off. It reduces stridor.
  • Steroids can be used for acute management or with propranolol for unresponsive lesions.
  • Submucosal resection (Option D) is an alternative for non-circumferential hemangiomas and those not involving vocal cords.



[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery , 8th Edition, Page 338.

question: A 4-month-old baby is having an inspiratory stridor that has worsened from the day of onset. An endoscopy is done and shows a compressible, pear-shaped red swelling in the subglottis on the left side. The baby also has a reddish lesion over her trunk. What is the first line of treatment for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient presents with a low-pitched voice and a sensation of throat tightness, which are hallmark symptoms of Dysphonia Plica Ventricularis.
  • This condition occurs when the false vocal cords (ventricular folds), which normally do not participate in sound production, are abnormally engaged during phonation.
  • The laryngoscopic image showing abnormal vibratory patterns of the false vocal cords further supports this diagnosis.

Dysphonia Plica Ventricularis (Ventricular dysphonia):

Definition

Dysphonia Plica Ventricularis is a voice disorder where the false vocal cords (ventricular folds) vibrate instead of the true vocal cords, leading to their hypertrophy and affecting voice quality.

Characteristics
  • Low-pitched voice
  • Diminished voice quality

Causes
  • Organic Pathology: Structural abnormalities affecting the false vocal cords
  • Functional Dysphonia: Improper voice use or strain

Diagnosis
  • Laryngeal Examination: Laryngoscopy to visualize and assess false cord hypertrophy
  • Voice Assessment: Evaluates vocal quality, pitch, and range

Management
  • Speech Therapy: Corrects vocal habits and techniques
  • Counseling: Educates on voice care to prevent further damage
  • Surgical Intervention: Considered if symptoms persist despite therapy, to reduce hypertrophy and improve voice quality

Spasmodic Dysphonia:

  • Spasmodic dysphonia is a neurological voice disorder characterized by involuntary spasms of the laryngeal muscles, which disrupt normal voice production.
  • This condition is associated with various neurological disorders, including Parkinsonism and Alzheimer's disease, and can also be linked to other dystonias like oromandibular dystonia and blepharospasm.

Types of spasmodic dysphonia:

[[figure-1]]

Type

Cause

Voice Quality

Treatment

A. Adductor (Option C)

Spasm of thyroarytenoid muscles

Strained, croaky

Botox into thyroarytenoid muscle

B. Abductor (Option D)

Spasm of posterior cricoarytenoid muscles

Breathy, weak

Botox into posterior cricoarytenoid muscle

C. Mixed (Option A)

Combination of adductor and abductor spasms

Variable (strained and breathy)

Botox into both muscle groups

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with complaints of a low-pitched voice and a sensation of throat tightness for several months. A laryngoscopic image (shown below) reveals abnormal vibratory patterns of the false vocal cords (ventricular folds). Based on the image and clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. A subglottic diameter of less than 4mm in a full-term neonate makes the diagnosis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis of subglottic stenosis is made according to the subglottic diameter in neonates.
  • Congenital subglottic stenosis is caused due to the gross thickening of the anterior lamina of the abnormal cricoid or a small, elliptical, thickened cricoid with excessive submucosal soft tissue.
  • There may also be anterior fusion of the vocal cords, leading to a web formation with subglottic extension.

Diagnosis is made according to the subglottic diameter:

  • Full-term neonate: <4mm (normal 4.5-5.5mm) (Option C)
  • Preterm neonate: <3mm (normal 3.5mm)

Clinical features

  • Biphasic stridor
  • Normal cry
  • Recurrent croup if superimposed edema from upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) is present.

Investigations (Option D):

  • The gold standard for pediatric airway evaluation is rigid endoscopy.
  • Microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy (MLB) determine the exact location of the stenosis.
  • MRI helps measure the degree of strictures.

The Myer-Cotton grading of laryngotracheal stenosis

Management

Grade I: 0-50% obstruction

Grade I subglottic stenosis usually requires no surgical intervention. (Option B)

Grade II: 51-70% obstruction (Option A)

Grade II stenosis can be reconstructed by means of a laryngotracheal reconstruction (LTR).

Grade III: 71-99% obstruction
  • Mild grade III stenosis repaired by anterior graft with posterior cricoid split +/- posterior cartilage grafting.
  • Severe grade III stenosis repaired by anterior and posterior grafts.

Grade IV: 100% obstruction
  • Grade IV stenosis needs anterior and posterior grafts with prolonged stenting.
  • Partial cricotracheal resection (PCTR) can be done for severe grade III and grade IV stenosis.

[[figure-1]]


Other treatment modalities:

  • Mitomycin C
  • Montgomery T-Tube

[[figure-2]]

question: Which of the following statements about subglottic stenosis is true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario here points to the diagnosis of laryngomalacia, which presents with a stridor that increases on crying and an omega-shaped glottis on laryngoscopy.

Laryngomalacia or Congenital Laryngeal Stridor

  • Most common congenital abnormality of the larynx.
  • During inspiration, an excessively flaccid supraglottic larynx gets sucked in and causes the symptoms.

Clinical Features
  • Presents at birth or immediately after
  • Stridor:
    • Increases on crying (increased negative intrathoracic pressure pulls the epiglottis inward, covering the laryngeal inlet)
    • Stridor present in supine position (as the epiglottis covers the laryngeal inlet)
    • Subsides in prone position (as the epiglottis falls away from the larynx)
  • Cyanosis seen sometimes
  • Normal cry
  • Usually disappears by 2 years of age

Investigations
  • Direct laryngoscopy:
    • Elongated epiglottis, curled upon itself giving an “omega-shaped” appearance.
    • Floppy aryepiglottic folds
    • Prominent aretynoids
  • Flexible laryngoscopy is the most preferred

Management
  • Conservative treatment in most cases
  • Tracheostomy: If severe respiratory obstruction
  • Supraglottoplasty: If severe laryngomalacia


[[figure-1]]

Congenital subglottic stenosis (Option A) is a congenital condition where there is an abnormal thickening of the cricoid cartilage or fibrous tissue below the vocal cords. It may be asymptomatic until upper respiratory tract infections lead to dyspnoea and stridor. The cry is normal.

Subglottic hemangioma (Option B) is also a congenital condition but presents only by 3-6 months of age as hemangioma grows in size and causes stridor. Agitation and crying may increase the obstruction.

Laryngeal web (Option C) is caused due to incomplete recanalization of the larynx and presents with airway obstruction, weak cry, or aphonia from birth.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 344

question: A newborn baby presents with an inspirational stridor immediately after birth, which increases on crying. The stridor is alleviated when the baby is placed in the prone position, and the cry is normal. The flexible laryngoscopy is shown as follows.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The superior laryngeal nerve (external branch) supplies the cricothyroid muscle, which primarily acts as a tensor of the vocal cords and also contributes to fine adduction.

In SLN paralysis, the cricothyroid muscle is non-functional:

  • Vocal cord loses tension (↓ pitch control)
  • Also develops relative abduction/lateralisation due to unopposed abductors
  • This leads to poor glottic closure and a weak voice

In real clinical practice, the major problem affecting voice is incomplete adduction (glottic gap) rather than just loss of pitch.

Thyroplasty Types (Isshiki Classification)

Type

Procedure

What it does

Indications (When used)

Key Clinical Use

Type I

Medialization thyroplasty

Pushes the vocal cord medially

Unilateral vocal cord paralysis (esp. weak/abducted cord)

Improves glottic closure → voice strength (Option D)

Type II (Option A ruled out)

Lateralization thyroplasty

Pulls the vocal cord laterally

Adductor spasmodic dysphonia

Reduces excessive adduction

Type III (Option C ruled out)

Relaxation thyroplasty

Shortens & relaxes the vocal cords

Puberphonia (high-pitched voice in males)

Decreases pitch

Type IV (Option B ruled out)

Cricothyroid approximation

Lengthens & tenses the vocal cord

Androphonia, pitch insufficiency

Increases pitch

[[figure-1]]

question: During an indirect laryngoscopy, which of the following laryngeal structures is typically not visible?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Barking dog position:

  • Supine with the head tilted back and neck extended.
  • Optimal for laryngoscopy as it aligns the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes, enhancing visibility and access to the larynx.

Direct Laryngoscopy

[[figure-1]]

The "barking-dog" (Boyce's) position involves neck flexion on the thorax and head extension at the atlanto-occipital joint. (Option C)

[[figure-2]]

Complications

  • Injury to Lips/Tongue
  • Dental Injury
  • Bleeding: From the operative site.
  • Laryngeal Edema: Potentially leading to respiratory distress.

Rose position (Option A): The patient is placed in a supine position with the head extended and supported by a pillow or ring placed under the shoulders.

  • This facilitates neck extension,
  • Commonly used for procedures involving the mouth, throat, and larynx, such as tonsillectomy, adenoidectomy, and endotracheal intubation.
  • The position allows for optimal visualization of the airway and easier access for surgical procedures in the head and neck region.

[[figure-3]]

Fowler's position (Option B): Seated with the back of the bed elevated.

  • This position can hinder airway alignment, making visualization of the larynx challenging.

[[figure-4]]

Fowler's position is a seated position (45-60 degrees) used for:

  • Respiratory Support: Enhances lung expansion for easier breathing.
  • Cardiovascular Stability: Improves venous return and reduces heart workload.
  • Gastrointestinal Motility: Aids digestion and reduces aspiration risk.

Supine Neutral position (Option D): Flat with the head in a natural alignment.

  • Not ideal for laryngoscopy; may require adjustments for proper laryngeal visualization.

[[figure-5]]

question: A 35-year-old teacher complains of hoarseness, vocal fatigue, and a weak voice, especially after prolonged speaking. Laryngoscopic examination reveals keyhole appearance of the glottis during phonation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Immature growth of vocal cords leading to relative shortening of vocal cords
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The case describes puberphonia (mutational falsetto) → persistently high-pitched voice after puberty.

  • Cause: Vocal cords fail to mature properly → they remain relatively short and thin.

  • Short cords vibrate faster → high-pitched, feminine voice despite normal physical development.

  • Normally in males, puberty causes cords to lengthen + thicken, deepening the voice.

  • When this maturation is incomplete → pitch does not drop.

  • Treatment: Voice therapy (mainstay); resistant cases → Type III thyroplasty

Immature growth of vocal cords leading to lengthening of vocal cords (Option A): Lengthening typically results in a deeper voice, not a higher-pitched one.

Immature growth of vocal cords leading to incomplete closure of the anterior part of vocal cords (Option C): Incomplete closure usually causes hoarseness, not a high-pitched voice.

Immature growth of vocal cords leading to excessive thickening of vocal cords (Option D): Excessive thickening results in a deeper voice, not a higher-pitched one.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 367.

question: A 16-year-old boy presents with a voice that sounds similar to that of a female, characterized by a high-pitched voice despite the completion of puberty. What could be a potential underlying cause related to the vocal cords for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

EBV is associated with Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and is less commonly linked to laryngeal cancer compared to other risk factors.

Risk Factors and Etiology of Laryngeal Cancer:

  • Tobacco Use:(most common cause)
    • Smoking is a well-established risk factor due to carcinogens like benzopyrene and other hydrocarbons.
  • Alcohol Consumption:
    • Alcohol use is a significant risk factor, with a synergistic effect when combined with smoking.
  • Synergistic Effect:
    • The combined effect of tobacco and alcohol is greater than the sum of their individual effects and has a 15-fold increased risk of laryngeal cancer compared to using either factor alone. (Option A ruled out)
  • Radiation Exposure:
    • Previous radiation treatment to the neck for benign conditions or laryngeal papilloma can increase the risk of developing laryngeal cancer.
  • Genetic Factors:
    • Reports from Japanese and Russian studies suggest that genetic predisposition may play a role in familial cases of laryngeal cancer.
    • Genetic syndromes like Fanconi anemia and congenital dyskeratosis are also associated with a higher risk. (Option B ruled out)
  • Occupational Exposure:
    • Exposure to occupational hazards such as asbestos, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, wood dust, coal dust, cement dust, mustard gas, and petroleum products has been linked to laryngeal cancer. (Option C ruled out)
  • Demographic Data:
    • Laryngeal cancer is significantly more common in males compared to females, with a reported male-to-female ratio of 4–5 : 1
    • Lower socioeconomic status and manual ‘blue-collar’ occupations also experience a higher risk.
  • HPV
    • HPV 6 and 11 cause juvenile respiratory papillomatosis, which rarely undergoes malignant change
    • Sexual behaviors and HPV infection are strongly associated with oropharyngeal cancers, but there is limited epidemiological evidence connecting these factors with laryngeal cancers.
    • Unlike oropharyngeal cancer, current studies do not show an improved prognosis for HPV-positive laryngeal tumors.


Reference:
  1. Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 358, 357
  2. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery , 8th Edition, 3rd Volume, Pages 237, 238

options.text: Genetic predisposition due to Fanconi anemia

question: A 60-year-old male with a history of persistent hoarseness, throat pain, and difficulty swallowing was recently diagnosed with Laryngeal Carcinoma. Which of the following is not a known risk factor for developing laryngeal cancer in this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Post-surgical trauma to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given scenario involves delayed unilateral vocal cord paralysis (ULVCP) following coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), with an absence of extrinsic compressive factors like a mediastinal mass or aortic aneurysm.

  • The left RLN is anatomically vulnerable during thoracic surgeries like CABG due to its course under the aortic arch.
  • Surgical trauma, especially stretching or manipulation during cardiac or thoracic procedures, can result in delayed RLN injury, manifesting as vocal cord paralysis.
  • Electromyography (EMG) showing denervation of laryngeal muscles supports a nerve injury rather than compression.

Causes of Vocal Cord paralysis:

  • Malignancy
  • Iatrogenic surgical trauma
  • Idiopathic
  • Non-surgical trauma
  • Intubation
  • Neurological disorders
  • Infections - Lyme disease, Herpes zoster, EBV, HSV, CMV, in immunocompromised patients.

Causes of RLN Injury:

  • Trauma to the neck
  • Thyroid disease and surgery
  • CA cervical esophagus, CA apex of right lung
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Subclavian artery aneurysm
  • Tuberculosis of cervical pleura
  • Idiopathic

Additionally, the Left RLN (which has a longer course than the right) can be injured in the mediastinum due to:

  • Bronchogenic cancer
  • Carcinoma thoracic esophagus
  • Aortic aneurysm
  • Mediastinal lymphadenopathy
  • Idiopathic
  • Enlarged left auricle
  • Intrathoracic surgery

Left atrial enlargement due to mitral valve disease (Option A):

  • While left atrial enlargement from mitral valve disease can compress the left RLN as it loops around the aortic arch (causing Ortner’s syndrome), this patient has no echocardiographic or clinical evidence of mitral valve disease or left atrial enlargement.

Compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve by aortic aneurysm (Option C):

  • Aortic aneurysms can cause RLN compression, leading to left-sided vocal cord paralysis.
  • However, in this case, the chest CT scan ruled out aortic aneurysm or other compressive lesions, making this diagnosis less likely.

Idiopathic unilateral vocal cord paralysis (Option D):

  • Idiopathic causes account for a significant portion (20%) of unilateral vocal cord paralysis.
  • However, given this patient’s history of recent cardiac surgery, an idiopathic cause is less likely than iatrogenic trauma.



Reference:
  1. Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 347-351.
  2. Logan Turner’s Diseases Of Nose, Throat And Ear Head and Neck Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 302, 303.
