question: A 58-year-old male presents with progressive hoarseness of voice and mild dyspnea on exertion. He underwent coronary artery bypass grafting 6 months ago. A fiberoptic laryngoscopy reveals left-sided vocal cord paralysis in the paramedian position. A chest CT scan shows no mediastinal mass or aortic enlargement. Electromyography of the laryngeal muscles reveals denervation. What is the most likely cause of his vocal cord paralysis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The electrolarynx allows for immediate speech production after surgery, making it a practical solution for patients who need to communicate right away.
  • It is a transistorized, battery-operated portable device.

[[figure-1]]

Vocal rehabilitation-methods:

  • After laryngectomy, the patient loses his speech completely.
  • The various methods by which communication can be established are given below:

Oesophageal Speech

  • In this, the patient is taught to swallow air and hold it in the upper esophagus and then slowly eject it from the esophagus into the pharynx.
  • The patient can speak 6-10 words before re-swallowing air.
  • The voice is rough but loud and understandable.

Artificial Larynx It is used in those who fail to learn oesophageal speech.

  • Electrolarynx:
    • Its vibrating disc is held against the soft tissues of the neck and a low-pitched sound is produced in the hypopharynx which is further modulated into speech by the tongue, lips, teeth, and palate.

  • Transoral pneumatic device (Option B)
    • It is a transoral device.
    • Here vibrations produced in a rubber diaphragm are carried by a plastic tube into the back of the oral cavity where sound is converted into speech by modulators.
    • This is a pneumatic type of device and uses expired air from the tracheostome to vibrate the diaphragm.

Tracheo-Oesophageal Speech

  • Here an attempt is made to carry air from the trachea to the esophagus or hypopharynx by the creation of a skin-lined fistula or by placement of an artificial prosthesis.
  • The vibrating column of air entering the pharynx is then modulated into speech.
  • This technique has the disadvantage of food entering the trachea.
  • These days prostheses (Blom-Singer or Panje) are being used to shunt air from the trachea to the esophagus (Option C)
  • They have inbuilt valves which work only in one direction thus preventing problems of aspiration.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 365
question: In a patient who has undergone a total laryngectomy, a portable vocal rehabilitation device needs to be prescribed immediately post-surgery. Choose the device from the given options:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the given case scenario of stage 3 laryngeal carcinoma with no involvement of thyroid cartilage since the patient is not willing to do chemoradiotherapy, total laryngectomy would be the treatment of choice.

Treatment of Stage 3 and Stage 4A of Laryngeal Carcinoma:

  • Concurrent Chemo-RT: for stage 3 and early stage 4 (Cisplatin/ Carboplatin/Cetuximab).
    • This treatment is suitable for all the stage 3 & stage 4a cases which do not involve any cartilage(thyroid/cricoid).
  • Near Total Laryngectomy: Stage 3 and Stage 4a cases with one arytenoid spared.
    • It is the treatment of choice in stage 3 & stage 4a cases involving thyroid/cricoid cartilage.

Total laryngectomy

Indications:

  1. T4a with thyroid cartilage invasion.
  2. Stage 3 and 4a who cannot tolerate chemotherapy.
  3. Stage 3 and 4 recurrent tumours
  4. Bilateral arytenoid involvement.

Conservative Surgery (Option B) is done in cases of recurrence when the radiation therapy fails to treat.

Micro laryngeal surgery (Option C) is done for stages 1 and 2 when the carcinoma is in the middle 1⁄ 3 of the vocal cord.

Vertical hemilaryngectomy (Option D) is done in cases of recurrence where one-half of the larynx (vertical) is involved along with subglottic extension not more than 1cm.

  • This is a type of conservative surgery done in stages 1 and 2 of laryngeal carcinoma.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 363
question: In a patient diagnosed with stage 3 laryngeal carcinoma with no involvement of thyroid cartilage, the patient is unwilling to undergo chemoradiotherapy. What will be the treatment of choice in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • According to stage grouping, T2N0M0 glottic carcinoma is grouped under Stage II.
  • For Stage II carcinoma along with impaired cord mobility, radiotherapy is not preferred because of the possibility of developing perichondritis which would require total laryngectomy afterwards.
  • For these patients, the best option is to do conservative surgery such as vertical hemilaryngectomy.
Treatment of Stage I and Stage II Laryngeal Carcinoma

TNM Staging

Stage Grouping

Treatment

T1N0M0

Stage I

Glottic- Radiotherapy or Endoscopic CO2 laser resection

Supraglottic- Radiotherapy or Endoscopic CO2 laser resection

Subglottic- Radiotherapy

T2N0M0

Stage II

Glottic-

  • Radiotherapy- when the cord is mobile
  • Vertical hemilaryngectomy- when cord mobility is impaired or Involvement of anterior commissure/arytenoid

Supraglottic-

  • Supraglottic laryngectomy with/without neck dissection- when lung function is good
  • Supraglottic laryngectomy with/without neck dissection + Radiotherapy- when lung function is poor

Subglottic- Radiotherapy

Total laryngectomy (Option A) is not the primary choice of treatment in T2 laryngeal carcinoma. It is mostly preferred for T3 and T4.

Radiotherapy (Option B) alone will not be sufficient, as the patient has impaired vocal cord mobility and is showing vocal cord involvement.

Endoscopic CO2 laser excision (Option C) is done only in cases where vocal cord mobility is not impaired.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 363, 364
question: A 55-year-old patient is diagnosed with glottic carcinoma involving the right side of the vocal cord. The tumor extends to the supraglottis with impaired vocal cord mobility. What is the most appropriate primary treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the site of lesion, the patient has a diagnosis of glottic laryngeal carcinoma.
  • Tumor limited to both vocal cords represents T1b stage of glottic laryngeal carcinoma.
Supraglottis

T1

Tumor is limited to one subsite of supraglottis with normal vocal cord mobility.

T2

Tumor invades mucosa of more than one adjacent subsites of supraglottis or glottis or region outside the supraglottis (e.g. mucosa of base of tongue, vallecula, medial wall of pyriform sinus) without fixation of the larynx.

T3

Tumor is limited to the larynx with vocal cord fixation and/or invades any of the following: postcricoid area, pre-epiglottic tissues, paraglottic space and/or minor thyroid cartilage invasion.

T4a

Tumor invades through the thyroid cartilage and/or invades tissues beyond the larynx (e.g. trachea, soft tissues of neck including deep extrinsic muscle of tongue, strap muscles, thyroid or esophagus).

T4b

Tumor invades prevertebral space, encases carotid artery or invades mediastinal structures

Glottis

T1

Tumor limited to vocal cord(s) (may involve anterior or posterior commissures) with normal mobility.

T1a

Tumor is limited to one vocal cord. (Option A)

T1b

Tumor involves both vocal cords.

T2

Tumor extends to supraglottis and/or subglottis, and/or with impaired vocal cord mobility. (Option C)

T3

Tumor is limited to the larynx with vocal cord fixation and/or invades paraglottic space and/or minor thyroid cartilage erosion. (Option D)

T4a

Tumor invades through thyroid cartilage and/or invades tissues beyond the larynx (e.g. trachea, soft tissues of neck including deep extrinsic muscles of the tongue, strap muscles, thyroid, or esophagus).

T4b

Tumor invades prevertebral space, encases the carotid artery or invades mediastinal structures.

Subglottis

T1

Tumor is limited to the subglottis.

T2

Tumor extends to the vocal cord(s) with normal or impaired mobility.

T3

Tumor limited to larynx with vocal cord fixation.

T4a

Tumor invades cricoid or thyroid cartilage and/or invades tissues beyond the larynx (e.g. trachea, soft tissues of neck including deep extrinsic muscle of tongue, strap muscles, thyroid or esophagus).

T4b

Tumor invades prevertebral space, encases the carotid artery or invades mediastinal structures.

Regional lymph nodes (N)

Nx

Regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed.

N0

No regional lymph node metastasis.

N1

Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, 3 cm or less in greatest dimension.

N2

Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, more than 3 cm but not more than 6 cm in greatest dimension, or multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes, none more than 6 cm in greatest dimension, or bilateral or contralateral lymph nodes, none more than 6 cm in the greatest dimension.

N2a

Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node more than 3 cm but not more than 6 cm in greatest dimension.

N2b

Metastasis in multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes, none more than 6 cm in greatest dimension.

N2c

Metastasis in bilateral or contralateral lymph nodes, none more than 6 cm in greatest dimension

Na

Metastasis in a lymph node more than 6 cm in the greatest dimension

Distant metastasis

Mx

Distant metastasis cannot be assessed

M0

No Distant metastasis

M1

Distant metastasis



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 359, 360
question: A 55-year-old man presents with hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. Laryngoscopy reveals a tumor involving both vocal cords with normal mobility. There is no evidence of spread beyond the larynx or lymph node involvement. Based on the TNM classification of laryngeal carcinoma, what is the most appropriate staging for this patient's condition?

correctAnswer: D. Prognosis is generally better than glottic carcinoma
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Prognosis for subglottic carcinoma is generally worse than glottic carcinoma because of:

  • Late symptomatology
  • Early lymphatic spread
  • Poor differentiation on histopathological examination
Subglottic laryngeal carcinoma

Incidence

Least common site of laryngeal cancer (1-5% of cases)

Site

Extends from undersurface of vocal cords to lower border of cricoid cartilage

Vocal cord involvement

Usually late; vocal cords often appear normal in early stages

Local Spread

Can spread circumferentially, invade cricothyroid membrane, thyroid gland, and trachea

Lymphatic spread

Common to prelaryngeal, pretracheal, paratracheal, and lower jugular nodes (Option B)

Symptoms

Early: Stridor, laryngeal obstruction (Option C)

Late: Hoarseness, cough, hemoptysis (Option A)

Histopathology

Poorly differentiated

Predominantly squamous cell carcinoma

Prognosis

Generally worse than glottic carcinoma due to late diagnosis and higher rate of lymph node metastasis



Reference:
  1. Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 358, 361
  2. Pubmed

options.text: Hoarseness is typically a late symptom
Lymphatic spread is common to prelaryngeal and paratracheal nodes
It often presents with airway obstruction as an early symptom
Prognosis is generally better than glottic carcinoma

question: A 58-year-old woman presents with progressive stridor and difficulty breathing for the past 2 months. Laryngoscopy reveals a mass in the subglottic region with normal appearing and mobile vocal cords. Which of the following statements about subglottic carcinoma is incorrect?

correctAnswer: C. Lymph node metastases are common in early stages
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Nodal metastases are typically never seen in glottic laryngeal carcinoma.
  • There are few lymphatics in vocal cords, and nodal metastases are practically never seen, unless the disease spreads beyond the region of the membranous cord.
Glottic laryngeal carcinoma

Incidence
  • Most common site of laryngeal cancer origin (Option A)

Site
  • Free edge and upper surface of vocal cord, mainly in anterior and middle third

Vocal cord involvement
  • Involvement of vocal cord occurs early so the patient presents early with hoarseness of voice (Option B)
  • Vocal cord fixation indicates spread to thyroarytenoid muscle and is a bad prognostic sign

Lymphatic spread
  • Rare due to few lymphatics in vocal cords

Local Spread
  • Can spread locally to anterior commissure, opposite cord, arytenoid region, ventricle, false cord, and subglottic region

Symptoms
  • Hoarseness is an early sign; stridor and laryngeal obstruction in advanced cases

Histopathology
  • Well differentiated and less malignant (Option D)



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 358-361

options.text: It is the most common site of origin for glottic carcinoma
Hoarseness is typically an early symptom
Lymph node metastases are common in early stages
Histopathologically well differentiated and less malignant

question: A 60-year-old man presents with persistent hoarseness for the past 2 months. Laryngoscopy reveals a small lesion on the anterior third of the right vocal cord with normal cord mobility. Further investigations lead to the diagnosis of Glottic laryngeal carcinoma. Which of the following statements about the condition is incorrect ?

correctAnswer: A. Bilateral lymph node metastases are common but occurs late
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The involvement of epiglottis in laryngeal carcinoma is indicative of supraglottic laryngeal carcinoma, in which nodal metastases occur early and are commonly bilateral.

Supraglottic Laryngeal Carcinoma

Incidence

Less frequent than glottic cancer; about 30-35% of all laryngeal cancers

Site

Majority on epiglottis, false cords, followed by aryepiglottic folds

Vocal cord involvement

Usually late; vocal cords often spared in early stages

Lymphatic spread
  • Early and often bilateral
  • Upper and middle jugular nodes commonly involved
  • Cancer of infrahyoid epiglottis & anterior ventricular band may extend into pre-epiglottic space (Option D)

Symptoms
  • Early: Often silent, dysphagia, throat pain
  • Late: Hoarseness, weight loss, respiratory obstruction, halitosis (Option B)

Histopathology
  • 90-95% squamous cell carcinoma (Option C)
  • Others include verrucous carcinoma, spindle cell carcinoma
  • Highly anaplastic

Prognosis

Generally worse than glottic cancer due to:

  • Late diagnosis
  • High rate & early lymph node metastasis
  • Anaplastic nature


Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 358

options.text: Bilateral lymph node metastases are common but occurs late
Hoarseness is usually a late symptom
The most common histological type is squamous cell carcinoma
It may spread to the pre-epiglottic space

question: A 58-year-old man presents with dysphagia, throat pain, and a palpable neck mass. Laryngoscopy reveals a lesion on the epiglottis. Further investigations lead to the diagnosis of Laryngeal carcinoma.Which of the following is not a typical characteristic of this condition?

correctAnswer: B. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the larynx below the vocal cords.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The larynx receives both motor and sensory nerve supply from branches of the vagus nerve.

Motor innervation:

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve - All muscles that move the vocal cords, including abductors, adductors, and tensors. Except the cricothyroid muscle.
  • External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve - cricothyroid muscle. (Option C)

Sensory innervation:

  • The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve - above the vocal cords. (Option B)
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve - below the vocal cords.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve anatomy:

  • The right recurrent laryngeal nerve branches from the vagus at the level of the subclavian artery, looping around it before ascending between the trachea and esophagus. (Option A)
  • The left recurrent laryngeal nerve arises at the arch of the aorta, loops around it, and ascends along the tracheoesophageal groove, giving it a longer course compared to the right nerve, making it more prone to injury. (Option A and D)

Superior laryngeal nerve:

  • Origin - from the inferior ganglion of the vagus nerve; courses behind the internal carotid artery; divides into external and internal branches at the level of the greater cornua of the hyoid bone.
  • The external branch innervates the cricothyroid muscle.
  • The internal branch provides sensory innervation to the larynx and hypopharynx after piercing through the thyrohyoid membrane.


[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 347

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the larynx below the vocal cords.
The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve has a longer course than the right, making it more prone to paralysis.

question: Which of the following statements about the laryngeal nerve supply is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Reeve’s Space is the avascular space between the upper pole of the thyroid gland and the cricothyroid muscle.
  • Identifying and opening this space is crucial for locating and preserving the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN).

Cricothyroid space of Reeves:

  • An avascular space crucial for the identification and preservation of the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN).
  • Location: Found between the upper pole of the thyroid gland and the cricothyroid muscle.
  • Identification: Achieved by performing medial dissection at the superior pole of the thyroid gland.
  • Opening the Space: The ipsilateral thyroid lobe is pulled downward and outward.
  • Relation to Joll’s Triangle: Opening Reeve’s Space helps in accessing and exposing Joll’s Triangle (sternothyroid-laryngeal triangle), which is used to identify the EBSLN.

[[figure-1]]

Reinke’s Space (Option A) is located under the epithelium of the vocal cords and is involved in conditions like Reinke’s edema.

  • It does not relate to the identification of the EBSLN.

Space of Boyer (Option C) or the Preepiglottic Space is bounded by the thyroid cartilage, thyrohyoid membrane, hyoepiglottic ligament, and the quadrangular membrane.

  • It is not related to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN).

Paraglottic Space (Option D) is located between the thyroid cartilage and the ventricle, and it is continuous with the preepiglottic space.

  • This space is not specifically used for identifying the EBSLN but is more relevant in cases of laryngeal tumors.



Reference:
  1. Important Triangles in Thyroid Surgery
  2. The rationale of triangles in relation to thyroid surgery
  3. Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 334
question: During a thyroidectomy, the surgeon encounters difficulty identifying the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN). To improve nerve visualization, the surgeon decides to explore a specific avascular space between the upper pole of the thyroid gland and the cricothyroid muscle. Which of the following spaces is the surgeon aiming to open to aid in the preservation of the EBSLN?

correctAnswer: B. External Branch of the Superior Laryngeal Nerve
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Joll’s Triangle is designed to help identify and preserve the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN) during surgery.


Joll’s Triangle (Sternothyroid-laryngeal triangle)

An anatomical landmark used for identifying and preserving the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN).

  • Superior border by the upper attachment of the strap muscles.
  • Medial border by the midline of the neck.
  • Lateral border by the upper pole of the thyroid gland and the superior thyroid vessels.
  • Floor of the Triangle: The EBSLN is located in the floor of the triangle, which is delineated by the cricothyroid muscle.

[[figure-1]]


Joll’s Triangle is not used for locating the Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option A) or Internal Branch of the Superior Laryngeal Nerve (Option C) or Vagus Nerve (Option D).



Reference:
  1. drsanu.com/articles/important-triangles-in-thyroid-surgery/
  2. www.ijashnb.org/article-download/full-text/7215#

options.text: External Branch of the Superior Laryngeal Nerve
Internal Branch of the Superior Laryngeal Nerve

question: Joll’s Triangle is used to identify which of the following nerves?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Joll’s Triangle is specifically used for identifying and preserving the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN), not the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN).

RLN identification triangles

Description

Beahrs Triangle (Riddle’s Triangle) (Option C)

[[figure-1]]
  • Boundaries:
    • Common carotid artery (base)
    • Inferior thyroid artery (superior)
    • Recurrent laryngeal nerve (third side)
  • Location: Posterior to thyroid gland in the tracheoesophageal groove.
  • Importance: Used to safeguard the recurrent laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery

Simon’s Triangle (Option A)

[[figure-2]]
  • Boundaries:
    • Common carotid artery (lateral)
    • Esophagus (medial)
    • Inferior thyroid artery (superior)
  • Importance: RLN crosses the triangle and is identified intraoperatively.

Lore’s Triangle (Option D)

[[figure-3]]
  • Boundaries:
    • Trachea/esophagus (medial)
    • Common carotid artery (lateral)
    • Surface of the inferior pole of thyroid (superior)
  • Importance: Used for identification of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve (RLN) Triangle
  • Boundaries:
    • Apex: Thoracic inlet (inferior)
    • Medial: Trachea
    • Lateral: Medial edge of retracted strap muscles
    • Superior: Lower edge of inferior thyroid pole
  • Importance: RLN exits as a single trunk at the thoracic inlet.


Reference:
  1. drsanu.com/articles/important-triangles-in-thyroid-surgery/
  2. www.ijashnb.org/article-download/full-text/7215#
question: Which of the following triangles is not used to identify the recurrent laryngeal nerve?

correctAnswer: D. Bilateral recurrent and superior laryngeal nerve paralysis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Bilateral recurrent and superior laryngeal nerve paralysis explains the complete loss of voice (aphonia), total paralysis of both vocal cords in the cadaveric position, laryngeal anesthesia, aspiration, and recurrent bronchopneumonia described in the scenario.
  • It is a known complication of thyroid surgery.

Feature

Unilateral Combined Paralysis

Bilateral Combined Paralysis

Affected Nerves
  • One side (Recurrent and Superior Laryngeal Nerves)
  • Thyroid surgery is the most common cause.
  • Both sides (Recurrent and Superior Laryngeal Nerves)

Vocal Cord Position
  • Paralyzed cord in cadaveric position (3.5 mm from midline)
  • Healthy cord unable to fully approximate paralyzed cord
  • Both cords in the cadaveric (Intermediate) position (neutral, apart from midline)
  • Complete lack of movement in both cords

Clinical Features
  • All the muscles of the larynx on one side are paralyzed except the interarytenoid.
  • Hoarseness: Due to glottic incompetence
  • Aspiration: Liquids pass through the glottis
  • Ineffective cough: Due to air waste from incomplete vocal fold closure
  • Mild aspiration risk
  • Breathing: Usually unaffected as airway remains adequate
  • Speech: Weak or breathy, but functional
  • All the laryngeal muscles are paralyzed.
  • Total anesthesia of the larynx.
  • Aphonia: Complete loss of voice as cords do not meet
  • Severe aspiration: Total glottic incompetence, laryngeal anesthesia
  • Inability to cough: Cords cannot meet to generate pressure for coughing
  • Bronchopneumonia: Due to frequent aspiration of secretions into the lungs
  • Respiratory distress: Due to compromised airway and retention of secretions
  • Speech: Completely absent

Treatment
  • Voice therapy - for compensation by the healthy cord
  • Injection laryngoplasty (temporary or permanent fillers)
  • Thyroplasty Type I with or without arytenoid adduction
  • Tracheostomy to clear pulmonary secretions
  • Gastrostomy to prevent aspiration and maintain nutrition
  • Epiglottopexy to prevent aspiration
  • Vocal cord plication to prevent aspiration
  • Total laryngectomy or diversion procedures in severe cases


Bilateral superior laryngeal nerve paralysis (Option A) primarily affects the cricothyroid muscles, leading to a weak and husky voice, but not complete aphonia or significant airway obstruction.

  • There is typically upper laryngeal anesthesia causing aspiration and coughing fits, but both vocal cords remain mobile. This does not fully explain the severe symptoms described in the scenario (total voice loss and significant aspiration).

Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis (Option B) leads to airway obstruction with both cords in a median or paramedian position, causing dyspnea and stridor, but the voice would typically remain intact.

  • The airway compromise described here is much more severe, and aphonia and laryngeal anesthesia suggest additional nerve involvement.

Unilateral recurrent and superior laryngeal nerve paralysis (Option C) would cause hoarseness and aspiration on one side, but not complete aphonia or severe respiratory issues.

  • The healthy side usually compensates, which is inconsistent with the symptoms described in the scenario (bilateral involvement, total loss of voice).



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 350, 351

options.text: Unilateral recurrent and superior laryngeal nerve paralysis
Bilateral recurrent and superior laryngeal nerve paralysis

question: A 55-year-old male underwent total thyroidectomy for a large multinodular goiter. Postoperatively, he presents with complete loss of voice, frequent aspiration of liquids, and an inability to cough effectively. On laryngoscopy, both vocal cords are found in a cadaveric position, and there is no sensation in the larynx. He is also experiencing difficulty breathing and frequent episodes of bronchopneumonia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In this scenario, the patient is a professional singer who reports difficulty with high-pitched sounds, which is a hallmark of unilateral SLN palsy.
  • The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses the vocal cords, crucial for producing high-pitched sounds.
  • In unilateral SLN palsy, the patient does not experience breathing or swallowing difficulties, and laryngoscopic examination may appear normal.

Unilateral SLN Palsy

  • Motor Loss: Cricothyroid muscle - decreased ability to tense the vocal cord.
  • Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cord on the affected side.
  • Vocal Cord Position: The affected vocal cord appears shortened and wavy; may exhibit flapping due to loss of tension.
  • Other Features:
    • Askew position of the glottis with the anterior commissure rotated towards the healthy side.
    • Voice changes such as weakness and inability to raise pitch, affecting singing ability.
  • Treatment: Primarily voice therapy to improve vocal function and manage symptoms.

Bilateral SLN palsy (Option A):

  • The patient would have more pronounced symptoms, including a monotonous voice, significant difficulty with high-pitched sounds, and aspiration due to poor sensation in the upper larynx.

Unilateral RLN palsy (Option C)

  • Causes hoarseness and, on laryngoscopy, shows one vocal cord in a paramedian position.
  • In contrast, this patient's difficulty is specifically related to high-pitched sounds, pointing to SLN involvement rather than RLN.

Bilateral RLN palsy (Option D):

  • It is a severe condition that typically results in stridor or significant respiratory difficulty due to both vocal cords being fixed in the paramedian position.
  • The absence of breathing or swallowing problems in this patient rules out bilateral RLN palsy.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 350.
question: A 45-year-old professional singer presents with complaints of vocal fatigue and difficulty producing high-pitched sounds for the last 3 months. She denies any difficulty in swallowing or breathing. On laryngoscopic examination, no significant abnormalities are seen, and one vocal cord appears to be in normal resting position while other vocal cord is in abducted position . What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient presents with symptoms and laryngoscopic findings consistent with bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) palsy, likely due to iatrogenic injury during thyroid surgery.
  • In bilateral RLN palsy, both vocal cords are typically fixed in a paramedian or intermediate position, leading to a narrow airway.
  • This can cause severe dyspnea and stridor, potentially life-threatening complications.
  • The immediate priority in managing such cases is to secure the airway, which is best achieved through a tracheostomy.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) palsy can occur either unilaterally or bilaterally, leading to varying clinical manifestations and airway complications.

[[figure-1]]

Vocal cord lateralization (Option B): While this is a treatment option for bilateral RLN palsy, it is not the immediate management of choice.

  • This procedure is typically considered after the airway is secured and the patient is stabilized.

Arytenoidectomy (Option C): This is another surgical option for treating bilateral RLN palsy, but like vocal cord lateralization, it's not the immediate management of choice.

  • This is usually considered at a later stage if other options fail.

Observation and voice therapy (Option D): This approach is inadequate for bilateral RLN palsy with significant airway compromise.

  • While voice therapy can be beneficial in the long-term management of RLN palsy, it does not address the immediate airway emergency presented in this scenario.



Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 348, 349.
question: A 45-year-old female presents with hoarseness , shortness of breath and stridor following thyroid surgery. Laryngoscopy reveals bilateral vocal cord paralysis with both cords fixed in paramedian position. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

correctAnswer: B. Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) paralysis
explanationHtml:
In unilateral RLN paralysis, the affected vocal cord typically rests in the paramedian position.

  • The vocal cord is approximately 1.5 mm from the midline, and this position allows for a strong whisper but impaired phonation.

Vocal cord positions in healthy and diseased states:

Location from Midline

Diseased State

3 mm

—

Full abduction

[[figure-1]]

Bilateral RLN paralysis (Option A) would result in both cords being at the median or paramedian position, leading to significant airway obstruction.

SLN paralysis (Option C) would cause difficulty with pitch control but not affect the cord position this way.

Paralysis of both RLN and SLN (Option D) would result in an intermediate (cadaveric) position, not paramedian.

question: A 45-year-old male patient presents with hoarseness of voice following a thyroidectomy. On laryngoscopic examination, his vocal cord is found to be in the paramedian position. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle is primarily responsible for adducting the vocal folds and closing the rima glottidis during phonation.
  • It rotates the arytenoid cartilage internally, bringing the vocal processes and vocal folds together.

Phonation:

  • The process of sound production in the larynx as air passes through the vocal cords.
  • During this process, the vocal cords or vocal folds adduct and vibrate as air from the lungs passes through the narrow space between them, the glottis.

Various intrinsic laryngeal muscles regulate the tension, length, and position of the vocal cords:

  • Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle: vocal cord abduction, facilitating the opening of the rima glottidis. (Option A)

[[figure-1]]

  • Lateral cricoarytenoid, interarytenoid, and thyroarytenoid muscles: adduct the vocal cords, resulting in the closure of the rima glottidis. (Option B)
  • Cricothyroid and vocalis muscles: Increase tension in the vocal cords.

[[figure-2]]

  • Thyroepiglottic muscle: Opens the laryngeal inlet. (Option C)
  • Aryepiglottic and oblique arytenoid muscles: Close the laryngeal inlet.

Phonation depends on neural control through the following nerves:

  • The recurrent laryngeal nerve - most of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles
  • The superior laryngeal nerve - the cricothyroid muscle- is essential for modulating pitch.

Thyrohyoid muscle (Option D): This is an extrinsic laryngeal muscle. It elevates the larynx and depresses the hyoid bone.

  • While it plays a role in laryngeal positioning, it does not directly adduct the vocal folds.



Reference:
  1. Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 332, 333, 335.

question: Which of the following muscles is primarily responsible for adducting the vocal folds and closing the rima glottidis during phonation?

correctAnswer: A. Unilateral superior laryngeal nerve palsy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation is consistent with a thyroglossal duct cyst.

Surgical treatment (Sistrunk procedure) occurs in close proximity to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which supplies the cricothyroid muscle. The cricothyroid muscle functions as a tenser and elongates the vocal cords, allowing production of high-pitched sounds.

Injury to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve results in:

  • Inability to raise the pitch of the voice
  • Weak voice, especially during high-frequency phonation

Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (Option B) would cause airway obstruction, biphasic stridor, and hoarseness, not isolated loss of pitch control. Voice may be weak, but high pitched loss is more characteristic of superior laryngeal nerve injury.

Hypoglossal nerve injury (Option C) causes tongue deviation to the injured side and dysarthria, not changes in vocal pitch.

Vagus nerve injury (Option D) causes widespread palatal, pharyngeal, and laryngeal dysfunction, including nasal regurgitation and hoarseness, not specifically difficulty raising pitch.



Reference:

  1. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology Head & Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 894, 897-903.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario of a low-pitched, husky voice in a chronic smoker with bilateral, diffuse, pale fusiform swelling of vocal cords points towards the diagnosis of Reinke’s edema.

Risk factors

Chronic smoking (primary), voice misuse, LPR, hypothyroidism

Pathophysiology

Accumulation of gelatinous fluid in Reinke’s space of true vocal cords due to chronic irritation → increased mass, decreased stiffness

Clinical features

  • Low-pitched, husky, rough voice
  • Bilateral, diffuse, pale, fusiform, boggy vocal cord swelling

Management

  • Conservative: Smoking cessation, voice rest, speech therapy
  • Definitive: Microlaryngeal surgery (one cord at a time) to remove fluid and preserve voice.

Vocal cord polyp (Option B) is usually unilateral and sessile/pedunculated from phonotrauma, does not produce diffuse edema or low-pitched voice.

Bilateral vocal cord cyst (Option C) are tense subepithelial spheres, not floppy edema; they restrict the mucosal wave.

Laryngeal papillomatosis (Option D) are multiple wart-like, HPV-related lesions causing stridor rather than a classic low-pitched voice.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose & Throat, 8th Edition, Page 342.

The clinical presentation of stridor since birth, worsening with feeding/supine position, improving at the prone position, is the classic presentation of Laryngomalacia, which is the most common cause of congenital stridor.

The laryngoscopic finding of a curled epiglottis with inward collapse of supraglottic structures is known as the Omega sign, confirming the diagnosis.

Thumb sign (Option B) is a finding on a lateral neck X-ray suggestive of a swollen epiglottis in Acute Epiglottitis (a severe, acute infection).

question: A 2-month-old infant is brought with noisy breathing since birth, which worsens on crying, feeding, and when lying supine, and improves in the prone position. Flexible laryngoscopy reveals inward collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration, with a curled epiglottis. What is the characteristic sign seen and the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the image, label 3 corresponds to the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle. The Posterior Cricoarytenoid (PCA) muscle is universally recognised as the sole abductor of the vocal cords.

  • It originates from the posterior surface of the cricoid lamina and inserts into the muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage.
  • Contraction of the PCA rotates the arytenoid cartilages laterally, widening the rima glottidis for respiration.
  • Nerve supply: Recurrent laryngeal nerve.
  • Bilateral paralysis can cause:
    • Severe airway obstruction
    • Stridor.
  • Hence, it is called the “Safety muscle of the larynx.”

Intrinsic Muscles of Larynx

[[figure-1]]


1 (Option A): The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle originates from the arch of the cricoid cartilage and inserts into the muscular process of the arytenoid. It acts as a primary adductor of the vocal cords by medially rotating the arytenoid cartilages.

2 (Option B): The transverse and oblique arytenoid muscles bridge the gap between the two arytenoid cartilages. They act to adduct the vocal cords by approximating the arytenoid cartilages, closing the posterior glottis.

4 (Option D): The thyroarytenoid muscle/Vocalis runs from the thyroid angle to the vocal process of the arytenoid. It acts to shorten and relax the vocal ligaments, altering the pitch of the voice, and assists in adduction.



Reference:

PL Dhingra’s Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 332,333.

Explanation:

  • Young's operation is a surgical procedure used to treat atrophic rhinitis (also known as "ozena"), which is characterized by dryness of the nasal mucosa, crusting, and sometimes foul-smelling discharge.

  • This condition can cause nasal congestion and a reduced sense of smell, which aligns with the symptoms described in this patient.

  • Young’s operation involves removing the affected mucosa and sometimes involves creating a more functional nasal environment.

Young’s Operation:

  • Indication: Young’s operation is commonly used in cases of atrophic rhinitis where there is dry, crusty discharge from the nasal passages along with a reduced sense of smell and nasal obstruction.

  • Procedure: The surgery typically involves removing the affected, atrophic mucosa and possibly re-establishing the function of the nasal passages to improve breathing and reduce symptoms like dryness and crusting.

Incorrect Options:

Submucous resection (Option A): is incorrect because it is performed to treat nasal septal deviation, not for conditions with excessive dryness or crusting, such as atrophic rhinitis.

Vidian neurectomy (Option D): is incorrect because Vidian neurectomy is used to reduce excessive nasal secretion in chronic rhinitis or other conditions with excessive nasal discharge, but not for atrophic rhinitis.

Septoplasty (Option C): is incorrect as it is performed for nasal septal deviation to correct airflow, but the patient in question is dealing with dryness and crusting, rather than a structural issue like septal deviation.

question: A female homemaker arrives with symptoms of nasal congestion, reduced sense of smell, and a dry discharge from the nose that is greenish and crusty. Upon examination, the nasal passages appear spacious, and the turbinates are found to be shriveled. Which surgical procedure would be suitable for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A tracheostomy is a surgical procedure where an opening is created in the neck, directly into the trachea (windpipe), to provide an airway and to allow for breathing when the upper airway is blocked or compromised.
  • This is usually performed in cases of long-term mechanical ventilation needs, upper airway obstruction, or trauma to the neck.

Tracheostomy:

Aspect

Details

Indications

Upper airway obstruction (tumors, foreign body)

Prolonged mechanical ventilation

Neurological conditions (e.g., spinal cord injury)

Procedure

Incision made below vocal cords, tube inserted into trachea.

Tube Types

Cuffed: for ventilation support.

Uncuffed: for stable airway or weaning.

Complications

Infection, bleeding, tracheal stenosis, accidental dislodgement, swallowing difficulty.

Care

Regular cleaning, monitoring for infection, and tube changes.

Advantages

Comfortable for long-term ventilation, lower risk of airway damage compared to intubation.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Endotracheal intubation (Option A): is incorrect because it involves the insertion of a tube into the trachea via the mouth or nose, not through a neck incision.

Needle cricothyroidotomy (Option B): is incorrect because this emergency procedure involves inserting a needle through the cricothyroid membrane in the neck to secure an airway in life-threatening situations, but does not involve creating a permanent opening as in a tracheostomy.

Oropharyngeal airway (Option D): is incorrect because this is a device inserted into the mouth to maintain an open airway, typically in unconscious patients, and does not involve a surgical incision or permanent airway opening.



Reference:
  • Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th edition, Pages 369, 370
question: The image below shows a procedure that was done on the patient. What is the procedure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dohlman’s procedure is a minimally invasive endoscopic technique used to treat Zenker’s diverticulum, a pharyngoesophageal pouch that forms due to cricopharyngeal muscle dysfunction.
  • The procedure involves endoscopic diverticulotomy, which divides the cricopharyngeal bar, allowing food to pass freely into the esophagus.

Zenker’s Diverticulum & Dohlman’s Procedure

Feature

Description

Definition

Outpouching of mucosa through Killian’s dehiscence (weak area in the posterior pharynx)

Cause

Cricopharyngeal dysfunction leading to high pressure and diverticulum formation

Symptoms

1. Dysphagia

2. Regurgitation of undigested food

3. Halitosis (bad breath)

4. Aspiration pneumonia

Diagnosis

Barium swallow X-ray (shows a posterior pharyngeal pouch)

Treatment

Dohlman’s procedure (endoscopic diverticulotomy)

Open surgery if large

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Meckel’s diverticulum (Option A): is incorrect because Meckel’s diverticulum is a congenital remnant of the vitelline duct in the small intestine and is managed surgically by Meckel’s diverticulectomy, not Dohlman’s procedure.

Bochdalek hernia (Option C): is incorrect because Bochdalek hernia is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia due to failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close and is repaired via surgical closure of the diaphragm defect.

Menetrier’s disease (Option D): is incorrect because Menetrier’s disease is a rare gastric hypertrophic condition with protein loss and increased mucus secretion, treated with medical therapy or gastrectomy in severe cases, not Dohlman’s procedure.



Reference:
  1. Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery 8th edition, page 323&324.
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1742115/#:~:text=Pharyngeal%20pouches%20occur%20most%20commonly,physiological%20abnormality%20of%20the%20cricopharyngeus.
question: Dohlman’s procedure is for:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Glossopharyngeal nerve: The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx and tonsillar region. It also has referred sensory pathways to the ear through its tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve). This referral pathway explains the ear pain commonly experienced after a tonsillectomy.

Facial nerve (Option B): The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) is primarily involved in motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression and does not provide sensory innervation to the tonsillar or pharyngeal region.

Trigeminal nerve (Option C): The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) provides sensory innervation to the face, including the external ear via its auriculotemporal branch, but it is not directly involved in tonsillar pain.

Vagus nerve (Option D): The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) provides sensory innervation to parts of the larynx and pharynx, but it is less commonly associated with referred ear pain in tonsillectomy cases.



Reference:

Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Page 303, 304

  • Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion is the preferred approach for a child presenting with recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, nasal breathing difficulty, hearing problems, and a high-arched palate. These symptoms suggest adenoid hypertrophy causing upper airway obstruction and Eustachian tube dysfunction, leading to otitis media with effusion (OME).
    • Adenoidectomy relieves nasal obstruction and reduces recurrent infections.

Tonsillectomy (Option A): Tonsillectomy alone is not indicated as the child primarily has symptoms related to adenoid hypertrophy and Eustachian tube dysfunction, not recurrent tonsillitis.

question: What is the appropriate approach to treat a child who is attending school and has a repeated occurrence of infections in the upper respiratory tract, difficulty in breathing through the nose, and hearing problems, along with the observation of a palate that is significantly raised in shape?

correctAnswer: B. Myringoplasty using a temporalis fascia graft
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Myringoplasty is indicated in cases of dry tympanic membrane perforation to restore hearing. A graft such as temporalis fascia is commonly used.

Myringoplasty (Type I tympanoplasty) (Option B)

  • Purpose: Repair of tympanic membrane perforation using a graft (e.g., temporalis fascia, perichondrium, dura, vein, fascia, cadaver membrane).
  • Techniques:
    • Underlay Technique: Graft is placed medial to the perforation and supported by gelfoam.
    • Overlay Technique: Graft is placed lateral to the fibrous layer after removing squamous epithelium.
  • Indications
    • Used to treat conductive hearing loss due to tympanic membrane perforation.
    • Not indicated for treating otitis media with effusion (fluid accumulation without perforation).
  • Hearing Improvement
    • Hearing loss from tympanic membrane perforation: 10–40 dB.
    • Hearing loss from ossicular interruption with an intact tympanic membrane: 54 dB.
  • In chronic otitis media, the procedure is delayed until the ear is dry and free from cholesteatoma (a destructive epithelial growth in the middle ear).

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Myringotomy, Tympanostomy tube placement (Options A & C): used for ventilating the middle ear and has no role in repairing the tympanic membrane

Antibiotic therapy with corticosteroids (Option D): This treatment is useful in active infections but not in repairing perforations or addressing hearing loss.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Pages 36, 75, 77.

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a history of chronic otitis media. Examination shows a dry tympanic membrane perforation without active infection. She has a 30 dB hearing loss. Which of the following procedures is most appropriate to improve her hearing?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Total maxillectomy

Explanation:

  • The Weber–Ferguson incision is a classical surgical approach for accessing the maxilla and paranasal sinuses, providing wide exposure.
  • The image shows an exposed maxillary cavity with removal of anterior and medial walls, which is characteristic of a total maxillectomy.
  • Total maxillectomy involves removal of the entire maxilla, including anterior, medial, posterior, and inferior walls, usually performed for malignant tumors of the maxilla or advanced sinonasal malignancies.
  • In the given scenario, the surgical field and the incision markings confirm the diagnosis of total maxillectomy.

Incorrect Options:

Total ethmoidectomy (Option A): Complete removal of the ethmoid air cells, done for extensive ethmoid sinus disease, not for lesions requiring maxillary bone removal.

Partial ethmoidectomy (Option B): Involves selective removal of diseased ethmoid cells while preserving healthy mucosa, unrelated to the maxillary walls.

Partial maxillectomy (Option D): Involves removal of only part of the maxilla (e.g., medial wall in medial maxillectomy) while sparing other bony walls; in the image, multiple walls are removed indicating a total, not partial, procedure.

question: What surgery is being performed in the image shown?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Facial artery:

Explanation:

The structure marked ‘X’ is identified as the facial artery.

In this image:

  • The submandibular gland is clearly exposed.
  • The vessel marked is coursing through or very close to the gland, which is a characteristic feature of the facial artery.
  • It needs to be ligated and divided during submandibular gland removal.

The facial artery is a key anatomical landmark during submandibular gland excision. It typically runs deep to or within the submandibular gland and is often seen as a prominent vessel in this surgical field. It originates from the external carotid artery, passes deep to the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, and then enters the submandibular gland before looping over the mandible to supply the face.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

The facial nerve (Option A) does not run through the submandibular region. It enters the parotid gland and branches within it.

The marginal mandibular nerve (Option B) is closely related to the submandibular gland and is at risk during surgery, it is a thin, delicate nerve running superficial to the gland, not a thick, pulsatile structure like in the image.

The trigeminal nerve (Option D) and its major branches are not present in this surgical plane. It does not pass through or near the submandibular gland.
question: A structure passing deep to the submandibular gland and curving around the inferior border of the mandible during submandibular gland excision surgery. Identify the structure labeled ‘X’ in the following image.

correctAnswer: C. Midway between the suprasternal notch and the lower border of the cricoid cartilage
explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Midway between the suprasternal notch and the lower border of the cricoid cartilage

Explanation:

  • Proper incision placement is key to a safe tracheostomy. A transverse incision placed approximately midway between the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage and the suprasternal notch allows for optimal access to the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings. This position avoids being too high, which risks injury to the cricoid cartilage (leading to subglottic stenosis), and too low, which risks injury to the great vessels of the superior mediastinum (e.g., the innominate artery).

Incorrect Options:

  • Option A: This location corresponds to the cricothyroid membrane, the site for a cricothyrotomy, not a tracheostomy.
  • Option B: An incision directly on the cricoid is contraindicated.
  • Option D is incorrect.


Reference:

Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th edition, Pages 342, 343

Types of Tympanoplasty (Wullstein's Classification)

  • Tympanoplasty: Surgical procedure for eradicating disease and reconstructing the hearing mechanism.

correctAnswer: A. Extracranial internal carotid artery aneurysm
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The unilateral tonsillar swelling with pulsation suggests a vascular etiology, and the presence of Marfan’s syndrome in the family history increases the likelihood of an aneurysm due to connective tissue disorder.
  • The extracranial internal carotid artery (ICA) aneurysm is a rare but recognized cause of tonsillar swelling and can mimic a mass lesion.
  • It is located medially to the tonsil and can be identified by pulsation on examination.

Extracranial Internal Carotid Artery Aneurysm

Feature

Description

Cause

Weakening of ICA wall (due to atherosclerosis, Marfan’s syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, infections, or trauma)

Symptoms

1. Unilateral tonsillar swelling

2. Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing)

3. Pulsation on oral exam

4. Absence of infection or inflammatory signs

Risk Factors

Connective tissue disorders (Marfan's, Ehlers-Danlos), atherosclerosis, hypertension

Complications

Rupture, thrombosis, stroke, or cranial nerve compression

Diagnosis

CT/MR angiography, Doppler ultrasound

Treatment

Surgical repair or endovascular stenting

Incorrect Options:

Intracranial External Carotid Artery Aneurysm (Option B): is incorrect because the external carotid artery does not run close to the tonsils, and intracranial aneurysms do not present as tonsillar swelling.

Extracranial External Carotid Artery Aneurysm (Option C): is incorrect because the external carotid artery runs laterally in the neck, not medially near the tonsils.

Intracranial Internal Carotid Artery Aneurysm (Option D): is incorrect because an intracranial ICA aneurysm presents with stroke-like symptoms (headache, visual disturbances, or cranial nerve palsies) rather than tonsillar swelling.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Wigand technique, which proceeds from posterior to anterior, is ideal for cases of extensive polyposis or revision surgeries where anatomical landmarks have been distorted.

In this scenario, the patient has undergone multiple surgeries, making this approach more suitable to ensure complete disease clearance along the skull base and medial orbital wall.

Surgical approaches used in functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS):

Stammberger’s technique (Option A) (Anterior to Posterior):

  • The surgery starts at the uncinate process and extends posteriorly to the sphenoid sinus, offering a conservative, adjustable approach suited for early or localized disease.

Wigand’s technique (Option B) (Posterior to Anterior):

  • The surgery starts at the sphenoid sinus and advances anteriorly, using a more aggressive approach suited for extensive polyposis, revisions, or advanced disease with distorted anatomy.

The Messerklinger approach (Option C) (similar to the Stammberger’s technique) is widely used for managing early disease affecting the anterior sinuses.

The Caldwell-Luc procedure (Option D) is a surgical technique used to access the maxillary sinus by creating an opening in the anterior wall of the sinus, typically through the canine fossa. It is commonly performed to remove chronic infections, polyps, or tumors from the maxillary sinus.



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of the Ear, Nose and Throat. Ed.8, page 494, 495.
question: A 45-year-old male presents with severe nasal obstruction, headaches, and a history of multiple nasal surgeries for chronic sinusitis and nasal polyps. On endoscopic examination, there is extensive polyposis with distortion of normal anatomical landmarks. The surgeon decides to use a posterior-to-anterior surgical approach for better access and disease clearance. Which surgical technique is most appropriate in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has a caudal septal dislocation, which refers to a deviation or dislocation of the septal cartilage near the base of the nose (caudal end), for which either transfixion or hemitransfixion incision can be used.
  • In this situation, the surgeon wants to access and correct the dislocated part without making an incision through the entire thickness of the septum.
  • Hence, Hemitransfixion incision is appropriate in this scenario.

Types of septal incisions for septoplasty

Killian’s (Option A)
  • In the nasal mucosa, cephalic to the caudal end of the septum
  • Slightly curvilinear incision, 2-3 mm above the caudal end of septal cartilage on the concave side.

Transfixion (Option C)
  • Through and through incision, close to but caudal to caudal end of the septum.
  • Used in caudal septal dislocation

Hemitransfixion

(Freer’s incision)

(Option B)
  • Same as the transfixion incision but on one side, not through and through.
  • Used in caudal septal dislocation
  • Septocolumellar incision between caudal end of septal cartilage and columella.

Horizontal on the Spur (Option D)
  • For endoscopic spurectomy.

Mnemonic:

  • Killian incision kills the septum, more complications, not done frequently
  • Freer's incision -frees the septum, lesser complications, more commonly done

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of the Ear, Nose and Throat, 8th Edition, Pages 489 - 491.
question: A 40-year-old male has a deviated septum with a significant dislocation at the caudal end. The surgeon prefers a unilateral approach, avoiding a full-thickness incision. Which incision is most appropriate in this case?

correctAnswer: B. Non-traumatic atlantoaxial subluxation secondary to infection or surgery
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The child developed painful torticollis following a recent adenoidectomy, which is characteristic of Grisel's syndrome.
  • This condition typically occurs due to nontraumatic causes such as an infection or surgery in the head and neck region.

[[figure-1]]

Grisel's Syndrome

Etiology

Nontraumatic atlantoaxial subluxation (Option B), often secondary to upper respiratory infections or post-surgery in the head and neck region (e.g., adenoidectomy).

Pathophysiology

Loosening of the transverse and alar ligaments due to inflammation in the atlantoaxial joint.

Presentation
  • Painful torticollis
  • neck stiffness
  • "Cock-robin" head position.

Imaging

X-ray or CT shows rotational subluxation of C1-C2.

Management
  • Early intervention with bed rest
  • Cervical immobilization
  • Antibiotics
  • Anti-inflammatory agents to prevent neurological sequelae.

question: A 7-year-old male presents to the clinic with painful neck stiffness and torticollis four days after undergoing adenoidectomy for chronic adenoiditis. Physical examination reveals restricted neck movement in all directions and a “cock-robin” position of the head. Neurological examination is normal. Which of the following best describes the underlying condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This clinical scenario is suggestive of a carotid body tumor (CBT), and the angiogram shows the characteristic Lyre sign.
  • The Lyre sign refers to the splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries due to the tumor at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery.

[[figure-1]]

Phelp Sign (Option A) refers to erosion of the carotico jugular spine between the carotid canal and jugular fossa in glomus jugulare on CT.

[[figure-2]]

Dodd Sign (Option B) refers to the column of air present between the mass and the posterior pharyngeal wall in antro choanal polyp, on lateral x-ray of the skull.

Steeple Sign (Option C) is seen on neck X-rays and is associated with croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), showing narrowing of the subglottic airway, resembling the steeple of a church.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Scott Brown’s otorhinolaryngology, 8th Edition, Page 160.
question:
A 45-year-old male presents with a slowly enlarging, painless neck mass near the angle of the mandible. An angiogram of the neck shows the image below:

What is this sign known as?

correctAnswer: D. Narrowing at the subglottic region.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario and the imaging is suggestive of a retropharyngeal abscess, which is a collection of pus in the retropharyngeal space.
  • Narrowing at the subglottic region (steeple sign) is a feature of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) and is not associated with retropharyngeal abscess.

Retropharyngeal abscess: It is caused by a collection of pus in the retropharyngeal space, typically presenting with symptoms such as severe sore throat, dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), stridor, and a stiff neck.

Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess

Chronic Retropharyngeal Abscess (Prevertebral Abscess)

Causes
  • Children: Lymphadenitis of lymph nodes of Rouvier
  • Adults: Penetrating injury
  • TB spine (Caries spine)

Clinical features
  • Dysphagia and difficulty in breathing
  • Stridor and croupy cough
  • Torticollis
  • Bulge in posterior pharyngeal wall
  • Discomfort in throat
  • Dysphagia is not marked
  • Posterior pharyngeal wall shows a fluctuant swelling centrally or on one side of midline
  • Neck may show tuberculous lymph nodes

O/E:

Bulge on posterior pharyngeal wall

Unilateral deviation

Diffuse midline

X-ray findings
  • Widening of Prevertebral Soft Tissue Shadow: (Option A)
    • Soft tissue shadow is twice the size of the vertebral body.
  • Straightening of Cervical Spine: (Option C)
    • Loss of normal curvature.
  • Presence of Air Bubbles: (Option B)
    • Indicates possible infection or abscess formation.

X-rays are diagnostic in case of caries of cervical spine

Treatment

IV antibiotics → incision & drainage

Antitubercular treatment



Reference:

Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 313.

question: A 6-year-old child presents with severe dysphagia, stridor, and a stiff neck. The physician orders a lateral soft tissue X-ray of the neck as shown. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition on the lateral soft tissue X-ray of the neck?

correctAnswer: D. Dye is injected into the salivary gland’s blood vessels.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In sialography, the contrast dye is injected directly into the salivary duct, not the blood vessels.

  • This allows visualization of the ductal system and any blockages or abnormalities within it.
  • A diagnostic method to evaluate salivary gland duct blockage. (Option A ruled out)

Procedure for Parotid Gland Assessment:

  • Cannulation: The parotid gland duct, located near the upper second molar, is cannulated.
  • Dye Injection: A contrast dye is injected into the duct. (Option B ruled out)
  • X-ray Imaging: An X-ray is taken after dye injection.

Interpreting Results:

  • Unrestricted Dye Flow: Indicates no obstruction in the duct.
  • Restricted Dye Flow: May suggest issues such as:(Option C ruled out)
    • Calculi (salivary stones)
    • Duct ectasia (dilation of the duct)

[[figure-1]]



Reference:
  1. Dhingra Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Page 273
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9406592/

question: A 45-year-old patient is experiencing persistent headaches and frontal sinus pain. A radiograph is taken with the patient in a chin-down position to assess the involvement of the frontal sinus. What is this imaging view called?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Halo sign is a classic characteristic used to identify CSF rhinorrhea. It is observed when nasal discharge on a handkerchief or tissue shows a central clear fluid surrounded by a ring of blood, creating a halo pattern.

  • This indicates the presence of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaking from the subarachnoid space into the nasal cavity, usually due to a fracture in the skull base, often in the area around the ethmoid sinuses.

CSF Rhinorrhea:

  • CSF rhinorrhea occurs when cerebrospinal fluid leaks from the brain's subarachnoid space into the nasal cavity. This may be due to a skull base fracture, usually from trauma or surgery.

  • The Halo sign is diagnostic when the fluid leaks from the nose and has a clear center with a blood ring around it, indicative of CSF.

  • Symptoms often include clear nasal discharge, headaches, and a history of trauma.

Incorrect Options:

Handkerchief sign (Option B): is incorrect because it is not a widely recognized term in clinical practice and does not specifically refer to the pattern seen in CSF rhinorrhea.

Schwartz sign (Option C): is incorrect because it refers to a sign used in Biermer's disease (megaloblastic anemia) and is unrelated to CSF rhinorrhea.

Phelps sign (Option D): is incorrect because it does not refer to any known clinical sign associated with CSF rhinorrhea.



Reference:
  • Dhingra's Diseases Of Ear, Nose And Throat, & Head and Neck Surgery, Ed 8, Pg.191,192
  • Logan Turner’s Diseases of Nose, Throat and Ear, 11th Edition, Pg.88
  • Cribriform plate
question: A 23-year-old male patient visits you reporting a nasal discharge that appears like the image shown on a handkerchief. Which of the following characteristics aids in identifying the presence of CSF rhinorrhoea in this patient?

correctAnswer: A. Retention cyst of major salivary glands
explanationHtml:
Answer: A) Retention cyst of major salivary glands

Explanation:

  • The lesion in the image is mucocele, which arises from minor salivary glands, most commonly located on the lower lip.

  • It occurs due to extravasation or retention of mucus following ductal injury or obstruction.

  • Therefore, the statement “Retention cyst of major salivary glands” is false, because:

    • Retention cysts of major salivary glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) occur in those gland regions, not on the lower lip.

    • Mucoceles originate from minor salivary glands, not major ones.

Most common site is lower lip (Option B): This is true. The lower lip is the most frequent site for mucoceles

Is a benign condition: (Option C): This is true. Mucoceles are benign lesions.

Treatment is surgical excision (Option D): This is true. The standard treatment for mucoceles is surgical excision.



Reference:
  1. P L Dhingra Diseases of Ear Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery - 7th Edition Page no: 252
  2. P L Dhingra Diseases of Ear Nose and Throat and Head and Neck Surgery - 8th Edition Page no: 263
